ποταμοὶ πυρὸς δάπτοντες ἀγρίαις γνάθοις.
rivers of fire devouring with wild jaws.
ἀγρίαις γνάθοις λειχήνες ἐξέσθοντας.
with wild jaws, lichens eating away.
ἐν ματαίοις κἀγρίοις· ποιφύγμασιν.
in vain and wild pursuits.
ἀγρίας ἁλὸς ἀντήσαντες.
having met with the wild sea.
ἀκήρατόν τε μητρὸς ἀγρίας απο ποτὸν, παλαιᾶς ἀμπέλου γάνος τόδε.
and the pure drink of the wild mother, this joy of the ancient vine.
δεσμοῖς ἀλύτοις ἀγρίως (sic ex apogr. pro ἀγρίοις) πελάσας.
having brought near with unbreakable bonds wildly.
πρὸς τάσδ' ἀγρίως ἀπανηναμένας.
toward these women who refused wildly.
πάντων τ᾿ ἀγρονόμων φιλομάστοις θηρῶν ὀβρικάλοισι.
and of all field-dwelling beasts, to the young that love the breast.

sense.note: [vitiose pro ἀγρέτηςleader , quod v.]
[corrupt for ἀγρέτης, which see]

cit.quote: Ζηνός ἄγρυπνον βέλος.
the sleepless bolt of Zeus.

sense.def: epitheton Apollinis cuius ara ante fores stat, qui saepissime αγυιεύςgod of streets dicitur.
epithet of Apollo whose altar stands before the door, who is very often called αγυιεύς [god of streets]

cit.quote: Ἀπολλον Απολλον ἀγυιᾶτ᾽, ἀπόλλων ἐμός,
Apollo, Apollo, god of streets, my destroyer,

cit.note: Syllaba media longa in anapaestis.
The middle syllable is long in anapaests.

cit.quote: ἄγχι πελαγίας ἁλός.
near the sea's salt water.
ἄγχι πλευμόνων.
near the lungs.
τὰς ἀγχιάλους ἐκράτυνε μεσάκτους Λήμνον Ικάρου θ᾽ ἕδος.
He fortified the sea-girt Lemnos and the seat of Icarus.
cit.note: sic alii quoque poetae insulas ἀγχιάλουςnear the sea dixerunt: v. Lobeck. ad Soph. Αi. 134.
Thus other poets too have called islands ἀγχιάλους [near the sea]: see Lobeck on Sophocles' Ajax 134.

cit.quote: Τήνῳ τε συνάπτουσ᾽ Ανδρος ἀγχιγείτων.
Andros, neighboring Tenos, joins it.
Ογκα Παλλάς, ἥτ᾽ ἀγχίπτολις.
Onca Pallas, who is near the city.
οἱ θεῶν ἀγχίσποροι.
those closely related to the gods.
δύναται γὰρ Διὸς ἀγχιστα σὺν Ηρα.
For he is able, very near to Zeus, with Hera.
πέλοιτο δ᾽ οὖν τἀπὶ τούτοισιν εὔπραξις, ώς | θέλει τόδ᾽ ἄγχιστον Απίας | γαίας μονόφρουρον ἕρκος.
May there be success in these matters, as this nearest single-guardian bulwark of the Apian land wills.
cit.note: Vana sunt interpretum de vocabulo άγχιστονnearest commenta, merito reprehensa ab Meinekio in Philologo vol. 20 p. 71, qui ἀρχηγὸνleader coniecit, comparatis quae statim sequuntur coryphaei verbis, ἥκω σεβίζων σόν, Κλυταιμνήστρα, κράτος· δίκη γάρ ἐστι φωτὸς ἀρχηγοῦ τίειν | γυναῖκ᾽ ἐρημωθέντος ἄρσενος θρόνουI come honoring your power, Clytemnestra; for it is right to honor the wife of a leader when the male throne is empty , quae tanquam paraphrasis sunt verborum superiorum. Ae reste, ut opinor, de sensu vocabuli ab Aeschylo scripti iudicavit Meinekius. Verum quum parum probabile sit vocabulum satis notum ἀρχηγόνleader in ἄγχιστονnearest esse corruptum, ἄρχιστονsupreme potius scribendum videtur, quod nemo mirabitur in ἄγχιστονnearest esse mutatum. To restituto aptissima prodit sententia, qua supremum imperium nunc penes Clytaemnestram esse dicitur. ἄρχιστοςsupreme autem ab ἀρχόςleader formatum ut βασιλεύτατοςmost kingly ab βασιλεύςking et alia huiusmodi, de quibus dictum in Thesauro vol. 2 p. 168. Mirabilius est ἀρχέστατοςmost ancient (pro αρχαιότατοςmost ancient , ut videtur, ab grammaticis acceptum) quod ex Aeschyli Penelopa memorat Philoxenus in Etym. M. p. 31, 5.

The interpreters' comments on the word άγχιστον [nearest] are vain, rightly criticized by Meineke in Philologus vol. 20 p. 71, who conjectured ἀρχηγὸν [leader], comparing the words of the chorus leader that immediately follow, ἥκω σεβίζων σόν, Κλυταιμνήστρα, κράτος· δίκη γάρ ἐστι φωτὸς ἀρχηγοῦ τίειν | γυναῖκ᾽ ἐρημωθέντος ἄρσενος θρόνου [I come honoring your power, Clytemnestra; for it is right to honor the wife of a leader when the male throne is empty], which are as a paraphrase of the previous words. And rightly, I think, Meineke judged the sense of the word written by Aeschylus. But since it is hardly probable that the well-known word ἀρχηγόν [leader] was corrupted into ἄγχιστον [nearest], it seems better to write ἄρχιστον [supreme], which no one will wonder was changed into ἄγχιστον [nearest]. With this restored, a most apt meaning emerges, by which the supreme power is said to be now in Clytemnestra's hands. ἄρχιστος [supreme] is formed from ἀρχός [leader] as βασιλεύτατος [most kingly] from βασιλεύς [king] and others of this kind, about which see the Thesaurus vol. 2 p. 168. More remarkable is ἀρχέστατος [most ancient] (for αρχαιότατος [most ancient], as it seems, accepted by grammarians), which Philoxenus cites from Aeschylus' Penelope in Etym. M. p. 31, 5.

cit.quote: νῦν ἀγχόνης μοι τέρματ᾽ ἢ φάος βλέπειν.
Now for me the end is a noose or to see the light.

sense.def: [cum imperfecto ἦγονI was leading (Dorice ἆγονI was leading (Doric) ), futuro ἄξωI will lead , aoristo ἤγαγονI led ). Futuri forma media άξειhe will lead duceris pro ἄξηyou will lead restituta Ag. 1632] duco, adduco, abduco.
[with imperfect ἦγον (Doric ἆγον), future ἄξω, aorist ἤγαγον). The middle future form άξει you will be led for ἄξη restored at Ag. 1632] I lead, bring, carry away.

cit.quote: ὑφ᾽ ἅρματ᾽ ἤγαγον φιληνίους ἵππους.
I led the horses, delighting in the reins, under the chariot.
ποῖ μὲ ἄγουσι τηλέπλανοι πλάναι;
Where are the far-wandering wanderings leading me?
χρυσήλατον γὰρ ἄνδρα - ἄγει γυνή τις.
For a woman is leading a man made of beaten gold.
cit.note: in descriptione scuti
in the description of the shield

cit.quote: οἵπερ πρόσω πέμψαντες ἤγαγον πάλιν.
Those who sent me forward led me back again.
ποῖ ποτ᾽ ἤγαγές με;
Where have you led me?
ποὶ δή με δεῦρο τὴν τάλαιναν ήγαγες;
Where have you led me, wretched as I am, here?
ὁ μὲν γὰρ (Orpheus) ήγε πάντ' ἀπὸ φθογγής χαρᾷ.
For he (Orpheus) led all things with joy by his voice.
ἄγ᾽ αὐτὸν εἰς ἀνδρῶνας εὐξένους δόμων.
Lead him into the hospitable men's quarters of the house.
ναύτην άγοντας τόνδ᾽ ἐφέστιον θεών.
Leading this sailor as a suppliant at the hearth of the gods.

sense.note: De ducibus militum
About military leaders

cit.quote: ώς πάλῳ λαχών ἕκαστος αὐτῶν (ducum) πρὸς πύλας ἄγοι λόχον.
So that each of them (the leaders), having obtained his post by lot, might lead his company to the gates.
χιλιὰς μὲν ἦν ὧν ἤγε πλῆθος.
The multitude he led was a thousand.
Ξέρξης μὲν ἄγαγεν (sic Blomfieldus pro ήγαγεν) — Ξέρξης δ' ἀπώλεσεν.
Xerxes led them (thus Blomfield for ήγαγεν [led]) — but Xerxes destroyed them.

sense.note: De navibus copias vehentibus
About ships carrying troops

cit.quote: νῦν δὲ κυανώπιδες θοαὶ νὰες μὲν ἄγαγον, τοτοῖ, νάες δ᾽ ἀπώλεσαν, τοτοί.
But now dark-prowed swift ships led them, alas! and ships destroyed them, alas!

sense.note: De reducibus ex bello
About those returning from war

cit.quote: νόστοι δ᾽ ἐκ πολέμων ἀπόνους ἀπαθεῖς — εὖ πράσσοντας ἄγον οἴκους
And returns from wars led them home without toil and without suffering, prospering.
cit.note: (i. e. εἰς οἴκουςto the house ).
(i.e. to their homes).

sense.note: De navibus merces vehentibus
About ships carrying merchandise

cit.quote: ἄγοντα πολλά παντόφυρτο ἄνευ δίκας βιαίως ξὺν χρόνῳ καθήσειν.
That he will bring down in time, by force, the one who carries many things all mixed together without justice.
cit.note: Sic Weilius pro τὰ πολλάthe many things , praeeunte Pauwio qui τὰ πολλά παντόφυρτ᾽ ἄγοντ᾽ ἄνευ δίκαςcarrying many things all mixed together without justice coniecerat. παντόφυρταall mixed together schol. exp. παντόθεν συνηγμέναgathered from all sides .

Thus Weilius for τὰ πολλά [the many things], following Pauw, who conjectured τὰ πολλά παντόφυρτ᾽ ἄγοντ᾽ ἄνευ δίκας [carrying many things all mixed together without justice]. The scholiast explains παντόφυρτα [all mixed together] as παντόθεν συνηγμένα [gathered from all sides].

cit.quote: ἄγουσά τ᾿ ἀντίφερνον Ἰλίῳ φθοράν.
And bringing as a dowry destruction to Ilium.
ἄξειν νιν ὑπτίασμα κειμένου πατρός.
That he will lead him as a means of overturning his fallen father.
κακῶν δ᾽ ὥσπερ θάλασσα κύμα ἄγει.
And like the sea, a wave of evils leads.
ἄγειν κελεύει δορυφόρους οπάονας.
He orders the spear-bearing attendants to lead.
σὺ δ᾽ ἐξορίνας νηπίοις ὑλάγμασιν ἄξει, κρατηθεὶς δ᾽ ἡμερώτερος φανεῖ
But you, having roused him with childish barkings, will lead him; and when he is overpowered, he will appear gentler.
cit.note: (sic Porsonus pro ἄξη – φανῇyou will lead – it will appear ).
(thus Porson for ἄξη – φανῇ [you will lead – it will appear]).

cit.quote: ταύτας δ' ἑκούσας - άγοις ἄν.
And you might lead these willing women.
ἄλλος δ᾽ ἄλλον ἄγει.
And one leads another.
καὶ μήτ' ἐνοίκων μήτ᾽ ἐπηλύδων τινὰ ἄγειν.
And not to lead any of the inhabitants or of the newcomers.
ἄγειν θέλοντες ῥυσίων ἐφάπτορας.
Wishing to lead those who lay hold of the pledges.
τὰς δὲ κεχειρωμένας ἄγεσθαι.
And the captured women to be led away.
ἀπὸ βρετέων βίᾳ δίκας ἀγομέναν.
Being led away by force from the images, in violation of justice.
ἄγει γὰρ αἷμα μητρῷον.
For the mother's blood leads.

sense.def: i. q. ἀνάγωI lead up sursum duco, sustollo
the same as ἀνάγω [to lead up], I lead up, lift up

cit.quote: παῖδες γὰρ ἀνδρὶ κληδόνες σωτήριοι θανόντι· φελλοὶ δ᾽ ὡς ἄγουσι δίκτυον, τὸν ἐκ βυθοῦ κλωστῆρα σώζοντες λίνου,
For children are saving voices for a man when he is dead; and like corks they buoy up the net, preserving the spun thread of flax from the deep.
cit.note: ubi schol. φελλοὶ τὰ κοῦφα ξύλα τὰ ἀναβαστάζοντα ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ τὰ δίκτυαcorks are the light pieces of wood that buoy up the nets in the sea .
where the scholiast says: φελλοὶ τὰ κοῦφα ξύλα τὰ ἀναβαστάζοντα ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ τὰ δίκτυα [corks are the light pieces of wood that buoy up the nets in the sea].

cit.quote: κρεουργὸν ἡμάρ εὐθύμως ἄγειν.
To lead the day of slaughter cheerfully.
ἄγοιμ' ἂν (θεοὺς), εἴ τις τάσδε μὴ 'ξαιρήσεται.
I would lead (the gods), if someone does not take these women away.
ὅτε τὰν ὁμοπάτριον ἄγαγες Ησιόναν.
When you led Hesione, who shared the same father.
άλοχον ἤγαγεν φίλην.
He led his dear wife.

sense.def: Imperativus ἄγεcome vel ἄγετεcome (plural) , age vel agite, in formulis adhortandi, singulari ǎye etiam cum numero plurali coniuncto.
Imperative ἄγε or ἄγετε, come! or come on!, in exhortations, with singular ǎye even joined to a plural number.

cit.quote: ἀλλ᾽ ἄγε, Πέρσαι θώμεθα.
But come, Persians, let us take counsel.
ἄγε δή, βασιλεῦ, — πῶς σε προσείπω;
Come now, king, how shall I address you?
ἄγε δὴ καὶ χορὸν ἅψωμεν.
Come now, let us also begin the dance.
ἄγε δή, λέξωμεν — εὐχὰς ἀγαθάς, ἄγετε.
Come now, let us speak good prayers; come.
ἄγετε, τῶν πάλαι πεπραγμένων λύσασθε αἷμα.
Come, release the blood of deeds done long ago.
ἐμῆς ἀγωγῆς ἀντιτίσασθαι φόνον.
To exact punishment for the murder of my abduction.

form.gloss: assembly (of deliberating and contending people) / contest

cit.quote: τὰ δ᾽ ἄλλα πρὸς πόλιν τε καὶ θεοὺς κοινοὺς ἀγῶνας θέντες ἐν πανηγύρει βουλευσόμεσθα.
But the other matters, having appointed common contests for the city and the gods in a general assembly, we will deliberate.
νῦν ὑπὲρ πάντων ἀγών.
Now the contest is for everything.
ἀγὼν — νείκης παλαιᾶς.
A contest of ancient strife.
ξιφηφόρους ἀγῶνας ὀρθώσαντί μοι.
Having set up sword-bearing contests for me.
ἐφοδεῦσαι ξιφοδηλήτοισιν ἀγῶσιν.
To go around in contests destructive by the sword.
πῶς ἀγὼν κριθήσεται.
How will the contest be decided?
τῶν ἀρειφάτων δ᾽ ἐγὼ πρεπτῶν ἀγώνων οὐκ ἀνέξομαι.
But I will not endure the contests of those slain in war, which are fitting.
ἀγὼν γὰρ ἄνδρας οὐ μένει λελειμμένους.
For the contest does not await men who are left behind.

sense.note: ἀγώνιοι θεοίgods of contests dii certaminum praesides (de quibus v. quae in Thes. collecta sunt vol. 1 p. 602.)
ἀγώνιοι θεοί [gods of contests] are the gods who preside over contests (about which see what has been collected in the Thesaurus vol. 1 p. 602).

cit.quote: θυσίαν ετέραν ἄνομόν τιν', ἄδαιτον.
Another sacrifice, lawless, not to be feasted on.
ἀδαμαντίνων δεσμῶν ἐν ἀρρήκτοις πέδαις.
in unbreakable fetters of adamantine bonds.
ἀδαμαντίνου σφηνὸς αὐθάδη γνάθον.
the stubborn jaw of the adamantine wedge.
ἀδαμαντοδέτοισι λύμαις
with adamant-bound outrages
cit.note: adamantinorum vinculorum dedecore.
with the disgrace of adamantine bonds.

cit.quote: ἐν πόνοις δαμέντ᾽ ἀδαμαντοδέτοις Τιτᾶνα λύμαις.
the Titan subdued in adamant-bound toils and outrages.
διὰ θεῶν πόλιν νεμόμεθ᾽ ἀδάματον.
we dwell in the city of the gods, unconquered.
εὐνὰς ἀνδρῶν ἄγαμον ἀδάματον ἐκφυγείν.
to escape the beds of men, unwedded and unconquered.
σέβας δ᾽ ἄμαχον, ἀδάματον, ἀπόλεμον τὸ πρίν.
awe invincible, unconquered, unwarlike before.
cit.note: Quibus in locis omnibus in M est ἀδάμαντονunconquered , quod correxerunt editores. In aliis tragicorum locis librarii constanter ἀδάμαστοςunconquered scripserunt, quo usus est Homerus. Tragicos una constanter usos esse forma ἀδάματοςunconquered observavit Elmsl. ad Soph. OR. 196.

In all these places M has ἀδάμαντον [unconquered], which the editors corrected. In other passages of the tragedians the scribes consistently wrote ἀδάμαστος [unconquered], which Homer used. Elmsley observed (on Soph. OR. 196) that the tragedians consistently used the form ἀδάματος [unconquered].

Hesychius. ἄδασμον: οὐδένα δασμὸν ἐκτελοῦσα, οἷον οὐ (οὐnot paying tribute: paying no tribute, that is, not (not addidit H. Stephanus) τελοῦσα ἐνοίκιονpaying rent . Photius p. 8, 4 ἄδασμος: οὐδένα δασμὸν ἐκτίνουσα, οὐδὲ μερίζουσα δασμὸν τῆς οἰκήσεως. οὕτως Αἰσχύλοςnot paying tribute: paying no tribute, nor apportioning tribute for the dwelling. Thus Aeschylus .

Hesychius: ἄδασμον [not paying tribute]: paying no tribute, that is, not (οὐ [not] added by H. Stephanus) paying rent. Photius p. 8, 4: ἄδασμος [not paying tribute]: paying no tribute, nor apportioning tribute for the dwelling. Thus Aeschylus.

sense.note: [vitiose pro ἄδηνto one's fill , quod v.]
[corrupt for ἄδην [to one's fill], which see]

cit.quote: οὐδαμῶς ἐμαυτῆς οὐσ᾽ ἀδείμαντος.
in no way being fearless of myself.
ὡς ἀδειμάντως κλύη.
so that he may hear fearlessly.

sense.note: [V. ἀδελφόςbrother .]
[See ἀδελφός [brother].]

cit.quote: πέλας δ᾽ ἀδελφαὶ τῶνδε τρεῖς κατάπτεροι.
and near are three winged sisters of these.
πέλας δ' αΐδ᾽ ἀδελφαί ἀδελφῶν.
and near are these sisters of brothers.
cit.note: Versus ex iambico dimetro corruptus, ut s. v. ἀδελφόςbrother dicetur.
The verse is corrupt from an iambic dimeter, as will be said under ἀδελφός [brother].

cit.quote: θρῆνον ἀδελφῆς.
the lament of a sister.
ἀδελφὴν τὴν ἐμήν.
my sister.
ἀδελφὸς τοῦ πάρος λελεγμένου.
brother of the one mentioned before.
θρήνον ἀδελφοῖν.
the lament of two brothers.
τούτου δ᾽ ἀδελφόν.
and this man's brother.
ἀδελφὸν τὸν ἐμόν.
my brother.
εὐνὰς ἀδελφοῦ.
the bed of a brother.
αὑτοῦ τ᾽ ἀδελφόν.
and his own brother.
σαυτῆς ἀδελφοῦ.
of your own brother.
πιστὸς δ᾽ ἀδελφὸς ἦσθα.
You were a faithful brother.
ἀδελφὸς δ᾽ ἐστὶ πεντηκοντάπαις.
He is a brother with fifty children.

sense.note: Forma ἀδελφεόςbrother ab interpolatore illata Sept. 576 καὶ τὸν σὸν αὖθις προσμόραν ἀδελφεόνand again your brother, destined to die , ubi veram scripturam προσμολών ὁμόσπορονhaving come, of the same seed restituerunt Blomfieldus et G. Burgesius. Incertum est alterum exemplum ib. 974 πέλας δ᾽ αἵδ᾽ ἀδελφαὶ ἀδελφεῶνand near are these sisters of brothers , quum verba πέλας δ᾽ αἵδ᾽ ἀδελφαίand near are these sisters , pro quibus dipodia iambica requiritur, ut versus docet antistrophicus 985, nondum sint emendata. Non improbabile tamen est scribendum esse πέλας δ᾽ ἀδέλφ᾽ ἀδελφῶνand near are brotherly things of brothers , a quo proxime abfuit Hermannus, quum aliam de metro opinionem secutus πέλας ἀδελφέ᾽ ἀδελφεῶνnear, brotherly things of brothers scriberet. Quod in antistropha 985 altera dipodia ab syllaba longa incipit δίυγρα τριπάλτων πημάτωνmoist with triple-brandished woes , idem factum est v. 1983 δορός γε τῷδ' ἀντηρέταςof the spear, rowers against this man , licet praecedens Antigonae versus ex puris compositus sit iambis ἐπεὶ κατῆλθες ἐς πόλιν. δέsince you came down to the city. But autem particula hic non minus apta quam in aliis huius stichomythiae versibus.

The form ἀδελφεός [brother] was introduced by an interpolator at Sept. 576 καὶ τὸν σὸν αὖθις προσμόραν ἀδελφεόν [and again your brother, bringing doom], where Blomfield and G. Burges restored the true reading προσμολών ὁμόσπορον [having come, of the same seed]. The other example is uncertain, at line 974 πέλας δ᾽ αἵδ᾽ ἀδελφαὶ ἀδελφεῶν [and near are these sisters of brothers], since the words πέλας δ᾽ αἵδ᾽ ἀδελφαί [and near are these sisters], for which an iambic dipody is required, as the antistrophic verse 985 shows, have not yet been emended. However, it is not improbable that it should be written πέλας δ᾽ ἀδέλφ᾽ ἀδελφῶν [and near are the brothers' sisters], from which Hermann was very close when, following a different opinion about the meter, he wrote πέλας ἀδελφέ᾽ ἀδελφεῶν [near the brothers' sisters]. That in the antistrophe 985 the second dipody begins with a long syllable δίυγρα τριπάλτων πημάτων [wet with thrice-hurled woes], the same occurs at v. 1983 δορός γε τῷδ' ἀντηρέτας [rowers against this spear], although the preceding verse of Antigone is composed of pure iambs ἐπεὶ κατῆλθες ἐς πόλιν [since you came to the city]. But the particle δέ [but] is no less suitable here than in other verses of this stichomythia.

cit.quote: ἀδελφαῖς χερσὶν ἠναίροντο.
They were slain by kindred hands.
ἀδελφά
brotherly things
cit.note: et fortasse, de quo modo dixi, paria fratrum mala significans, ut Soph. Αnt. 192 dixit καὶ νῦν ἀδελφὰ τῶνδε κηρύξας ἔχωand now I have proclaimed things akin to these .
and perhaps, as I just said, signifying equal evils of brothers, as Soph. Ant. 192 said καὶ νῦν ἀδελφὰ τῶνδε κηρύξας ἔχω [and now I have proclaimed things equal to these].

cit.quote: ἄδην ἔλειξεν αἵματος τυραννικού.
He licked to satiety the blood of the tyrant.
ἄδην με πολύπλανοι πλάναι γεγυμνάκασι,
My many-wandering wanderings have exercised me to satiety.
cit.note: ubi in apogr. multis ἄδδηνto satiety consueto librariis errore. De spiritu sive leni sive aspero dissenserunt grammatici etymologicis rationibus ducti: v. Thes. vol. 1 p. 647.

where in many copies it is written ἄδδην [to satiety] by the usual error of scribes. About the breathing, whether smooth or rough, grammarians have disagreed, led by etymological reasoning: see Thes. vol. 1 p. 647.

cit.quote: τὸ τῆς ἀνάγκης ἔστ᾽ ἀδήριτον σθένος.
The strength of necessity is unconquerable.

sense.note: (Nomen in codicibus tragicorum prope constanter cum punctis diaereseos ἀΐδηςHades pariterque in reliquis casibus scriptum, modo Orcum deum significat, modo locum inferorum ubi regnat deus, modo ita dictum est ut utraque significatio locum habeat. Usitata in diverbiis declinatio est Ἅιδης Ἅιδου Ἅιδης ἍιδηνHades, of Hades, Hades, Hades , in melicis Ἅιδας Ἅιδα ἍιδανHades, of Hades, Hades , vel tribus syllabis Ἀΐδας Ἁίδα Ἀΐδα ἈΐδανHades, of Hades, Hades, Hades .)

(The name in the manuscripts of the tragedians is almost constantly written with diaeresis dots ἀΐδης [Hades] and likewise in the other cases, sometimes it signifies the god Orcus, sometimes the place of the underworld where the god reigns, sometimes it is so used that both meanings are possible. The usual declension in dialogue is Ἅιδης Ἅιδου Ἅιδης Ἅιδην [Hades, of Hades, Hades, Hades], in lyric parts Ἅιδας Ἅιδα Ἅιδαν [Hades, of Hades, Hades], or with three syllables Ἀΐδας Ἁίδα Ἀΐδα Ἀΐδαν [Hades, of Hades, Hades, Hades].)

cit.quote: ἐν Ἅιδου.
in Hades.
εἰς Ἅιδου μολεϊν.
to go to Hades.
εἰς ἀναύγητον μολεῖν Ἅιδην.
to go to sunless Hades.
οἶμος εἰς Ἅιδου φέρουσα.
a path leading to Hades.
Ἅιδου σάκτορι.
to the keeper of Hades.
δίκτυόν τί γ᾽ Αιδου.
a net of Hades, indeed.
Ἅιδου μητέρα.
the mother of Hades.
Ἅιδου πύλας.
the gates of Hades.
τοῦ κατὰ χθονός Ἅιδου νεκρῶν σωτῆρος ευκταίαν χάριν.
the prayed-for grace of Hades beneath the earth, savior of the dead.
μέγας γάρ Ἅιδης ἐστὶν εὔθυνος βροτών.
For great Hades is the judge of mortals.
Ἀίδην πόντιον πεφευγότες.
having escaped the sea Hades.

sense.note: Formae trisyllabae duo sunt exempla,
There are two examples of the trisyllabic forms,

cit.quote: πρόπαρ θανούσας δ᾽ Ἀϊδας ἀνάσσοι.
and may Hades rule over those who died before.
οἰκτρὸν γὰρ πόλιν — Ἄϊδᾳ προϊάψαι, δορὸς ἄγραν.
For it is pitiful to hurl the city to Hades, the prey of the spear.
cit.note: In anapaestis vero Pr. 152 νέρθεν τ' Αϊδουand below of Hades recte in νέρθεν θ' Ἅιδουand below of Hades mutavit Turnebus, nec dubitandum quin Sept. 868 ἀχεῖν Ἀΐδα τ᾽ | ἐχθρὸν παιᾶν ἐπιμέλπεινto sing a hostile paean to Hades scribendum sit Ἅιδου τof Hades ': de quo comparanda quae in Lexico Sophocleo dixi p. 6 a.

But in the anapaests Pr. 152 νέρθεν τ' Αϊδου [and below of Hades] Turnebus rightly changed to νέρθεν θ' Ἅιδου [and below of Hades], and there is no doubt that in Sept. 868 ἀχεῖν Ἀΐδα τ᾽ | ἐχθρὸν παιᾶν ἐπιμέλπειν [to sing a hostile paean to Hades] should be written Ἅιδου τ' [of Hades]: about which compare what I said in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 6 a.

sense.note: Tertia forma est Αis in casibus obliquis, cuius unum est exemplum Aeschyli
The third form is Αis in the oblique cases, of which there is one example in Aeschylus

cit.quote: κελαινὸς Αϊδος δ' ὑποβρέμει μυχός γᾶς,
and the dark recess of Hades rumbles beneath the earth,
Ἀΐδος ὅτε μοῖρ᾽ ἀνυμέναιος — αναπέφηνε.
when the fate of Hades, without marriage, has appeared.
cit.note: unumque Sophoclis
and one in Sophocles

cit.quote: οἶσθα μέν τὸ μἀδικεῖν.
You know what it is not to do wrong.
φόβος τε συγγενὴς τὸ μἀδικεῖν σχήσει.
And kindred fear will hold back from doing wrong.
τὸ μἀδικεῖν σέβοντες ἐν διαιρέσει.
revering not doing wrong in the division.

entry.note: Quibus in locis tribus μἀδικεῖνnot to do wrong scripsi pro μὴ ἀδικεῖνnot to do wrong , de quo s. v. μήnot dicetur.
In which three places I wrote μἀδικεῖν [not to do wrong] for μὴ ἀδικεῖν [not to do wrong], about which will be said under the word μή [not].

cit.quote: φωτ᾽ ἄδικον.
an unjust man.
δίκαν δ᾽ ἐξ ἀδίκων ἀπαιτῶ.
I demand justice from the unjust.
τόλμης ἕκατι κἀδίκου φρονήματος.
because of daring and unjust pride.
cit.note: (κἀδίκουand unjust Turnebus pro κάν δίκουand in justice , quod etiam κἀκδίκουand avenging esse potest, quod Ahrensius coniecit.)
(κἀδίκου [and unjust] Turnebus for κάν δίκου [and in justice], which could also be κἀκδίκου [and avenging], which Ahrens conjectured.)

cit.quote: νέμων εἰκότως ἄδικα μὲν κακοῖς, ὅσια δ᾽ ἐννόμοις.
rightly allotting unjust things to the bad, holy things to the lawful.
άχαριν χάριν ἀντ᾽ ἔργων μεγάλων ἀδίκως ἐπικρᾶναι.
to embitter unjustly a graceless favor in return for great deeds.

cit.note: Hesychius ἀδίοπον: ἄναρχον καὶ ἀφύλακτον. Αἰσχύλος Φρυξί· δίοποι γὰρ οἱ τῆς νεώς φύλακεςἀδίοπον [without a steersman]: without a ruler and unguarded. Aeschylus in Phrygians: for δίοποι [steersmen] are the guards of the ship . Est fr. 261, ubi v. quae ex aliis grammaticis attuli.

Hesychius: ἀδίοπον [without a steersman] — without a ruler and unguarded. Aeschylus in Phrygians: for δίοποι [steersmen] are the guards of the ship. It is fr. 261, where see what I have cited from other grammarians.

form.gloss: unwedded, a frequent epithet of maidens

sense.def: unwedded, a frequent epithet of maidens
sense.note: v. Thes. vol. 1 p. 688.
See Thes. vol. 1 p. 688.

cit.quote: ἄδμητος (Αρτεμις) ἀδμήτας δύσιος γενέσθω.
Let the unwedded (Artemis) be the unwedded one's escape.
cit.note: Sic correxi quod est in M cum metri vitio ἀδμήτας ἀδμήταἀδμήτας ἀδμήτα [unwedded, unwedded] . Formae Doricae ἄδματος ἀδμάταςἄδματος ἀδμάτας [unwedded, unwedded] an sint restituendae incertum est, de quo dixi in Lex. Soph. p. 6a.

Thus I corrected what is in M with a metrical fault ἀδμήτας ἀδμήτα [unwedded, unwedded]. Whether the Doric forms ἄδματος ἀδμάτας [unwedded, unwedded] should be restored is uncertain, about which I have spoken in Lex. Soph. p. 6a.

form.gloss: one who goes down to Hades

sense.def: one who goes down to Hades

cit.quote: ᾀδοβάται γὰρ πολλοὶ φῶτες.
For many men are goers-down to Hades.
cit.note: Sic Passovius emendavit pro ἀγδαβάταιἀγδαβάται [those who go down to Hades] . Similiter ἄνδρες άδοφονταιἄνδρες άδοφονται [men who go down to Hades] dicti sunt ab Aristophane fr. 198, 6.
Thus Passow emended for ἀγδαβάται [those who go down to Hades]. Similarly ἄνδρες άδοφονται [men who go down to Hades] are said by Aristophanes fr. 198, 6.

form.gloss: without guile, sincere; improperly of unadulterated ointment

sense.def: dolo carens, sincerus. Improprie de unguento non adulterato
without guile, sincere; improperly of unadulterated ointment

cit.quote: χρίματος ἁγνοῦ μαλακαῖς ἀδόλοισι παρηγορίαις.
with pure anointing and gentle, guileless consolations.
αδόλως δολίας,
guilelessly of a guileful woman,
cit.note: scriptura propter verborum adiunctorum corruptelam incerta.
the reading is uncertain because of the corruption of the adjacent words.

form.gloss: Adrasteia, the goddess also called Nemesis

sense.def: Adrastea, dea eadem quae et Nemesis
Adrasteia, the goddess also called Nemesis
sense.note: (ΑδρήστειαΑδρήστεια [Adrasteia] in dialecto Ionica) de qua multa collecta sunt in Thes, vol. 1 p. 701 et a Blomfieldo in Glossario ad
(Αδρήστεια [Adrasteia] in the Ionic dialect) about which many things have been collected in Thes. vol. 1 p. 701 and by Blomfield in his Glossary to

cit.quote: οἱ προσκυνοῦντες τὴν Ἀδράστειαν σοφοί.
those who worship Adrasteia are wise.
Βερέκυντα χώρον, ἔνθ᾽ Αδραστείας έδος.
the Berecyntian land, where is the seat of Adrasteia.
cit.note: V. s, v. ΙδηΙδη [Ida] .
See under the word Ιδη [Ida].

cit.quote: πρὸς ἅρμ᾽ Αδράστου.
to the chariot of Adrastus.
κακῶν τ' Αδράστῳ τῶνδε βουλευτήριον.
and the council-chamber of these evils for Adrastus.
ἥβας δ' ἄνθος ἄδρεπτον ἔστω.
let the unplucked flower of youth be.
Ἀδριαναί τε γυναῖκες τρόπον ἕξουσι γόων.
And Adrian women will have a manner of wailing.
cit.note: Bekk. Anecd. p. 346, 9 'Αδριαναὶ γυναῖκεςΑδριαναὶ γυναῖκες [Adrian women] . Qui versus est Ionicus tetrameter, in quo Aeschylum formam Ionicam 'Adpinναίναί [yes] ut magis poeticam praetulisse coniecit Hermannus, ut τᾶς Ἀδριηνᾶςτᾶς Ἀδριηνᾶς [of the Adriatic woman] dixit Euripides Hipp. 735. De lugendi modo, quem servaturae sint feminae ad Padum, v. Polybius 2, 16, Seymnus v. 399, Diodorus 5, 23.

Bekk. Anecd. p. 346, 9 'Αδριαναὶ γυναῖκες [Adrian women]. The verse is an Ionic tetrameter, in which Hermann conjectured that Aeschylus preferred the Ionic form 'Adpinναί [Adrian women] as more poetic, just as Euripides said τᾶς Ἀδριηνᾶς [of the Adriatic woman] Hipp. 735. On the manner of mourning which the women by the Po are to observe, see Polybius 2, 16, Scymnus v. 399, Diodorus 5, 23.

cit.quote: πρὸς δὲ καρδίᾳ φόβος ᾄδειν ἕτοιμος.
and in my heart fear is ready to sing.
το Κισσίων πόλισμ᾽ ἀντίδουπον ᾄσεται.
the city of the Cissians will sing in response.
cit.note: Sic Burneius pro ἔσεταιἔσεται [will be] (i. e. αἴσεταιαἴσεται [will sing] ), quod est in M, in apogr. pluribus in ἔσσεταιἔσσεται [will be] corruptum.
Thus Burney for ἔσεται [will be] (i.e. αἴσεται [will sing]), which is in M, corrupted in several copies to ἔσσεται [will be].

sense.note: [Formam Atticam dei Aristophanis codices frequentius servarunt quam tragicorum, in quibus saepissime αἰείalways pariterque in compositis scriptum est, interdum adeo contra metri legem: ex quo sequitur nullam in hac re librorum auctoritatem esse. Librarii enim Homeri lectioni assueti αἰείalways non solum poetis scenicis intulerunt, sed etiam prosae orationis scriptoribus et veteribus et recentioribus, quibus nunc dei plerumque ex codicibus antiquioribus est restitutum, ne Thucydide quidem excepto, quem Marcellinus, vitae eius scriptor, codicis sui auctoritatem secutus, αἰείalways praetulisse credidit, ὡς ἐπὶ πλεῖστον δὲ χρῆται τῇ ἀρχαίᾳ Ἀτθίδι, ὅταν τὴν δίφθογγον τὴν αἱ ἀντὶ τοῦ α γράφη, αἰεί λέγωνhe uses the ancient Attic form as much as possible, when he writes the diphthong αι instead of α, saying αἰεί , cuius sententiae ne codices superstites quidem favent, quorum optimi et antiquissimi satis constanter ἀείalways praebent, quod non est verisimile ab librariis esse illatum. Ad mensuram quod attinet, non dubitandum quin Apollonius in libro de adverbiis (in Bekk. Anecd. p. 600), ubi de at in à longum mutato agit, recte iudicaverit ἀναλογώτερονmore regular esse ἀεί ἐν μακρῷ τῷ ἄalways with long α . In sermone tamen quotidiano Atticorum dei nunquam aliter quam a brevi pronuntiatum esse videtur, eaque mensura iam epici poetae interdum usi sunt ubi metrum propriam dialecto epicae formam αἰείalways non ferret, ut ap. Hom. Il. 12, 211 Εκτορ, ἀεὶ μέν πωςHector, always somehow —. Attici vero poetae, qui epico et Ionico αἰείalways non utebantur, dei modo correpto modo producto a dixerunt, prout metro commodum erat: unde utriusque mensurae exempla plurima apud poetas scenicos reperiuntur.] quod vel de tempore non interrupto dicitur vel adverbii ἑκάστοτεeach time , quod per ἀείalways explicare solent grammatici, significationem habet.

[The Attic form dei is preserved more frequently in the manuscripts of Aristophanes than in those of the tragedians, in which αἰεί [always] is very often written, and likewise in compounds, sometimes even against the meter: from which it follows that there is no authority of the books in this matter. For scribes accustomed to the Homeric reading introduced αἰεί [always] not only into the scenic poets, but also into prose writers both old and recent, for whom dei has now generally been restored from older manuscripts, not even excepting Thucydides, whom Marcellinus, the writer of his life, following the authority of his manuscript, believed to have preferred αἰεί [always], ὡς ἐπὶ πλεῖστον δὲ χρῆται τῇ ἀρχαίᾳ Ἀτθίδι, ὅταν τὴν δίφθογγον τὴν αἱ ἀντὶ τοῦ α γράφη, αἰεί λέγων [and he uses the ancient Attic for the most part, whenever he writes the diphthong ai instead of a, saying aiei], to which opinion not even the surviving manuscripts are favorable, of which the best and oldest fairly consistently offer ἀεί [always], which is not likely to have been introduced by scribes. As to the measure, there is no doubt that Apollonius in his book on adverbs (in Bekker's Anecdota p. 600), where he discusses the change of a into long ā, rightly judged ἀναλογώτερον [more analogical] to be ἀεί [always] with long ā. In the everyday speech of the Athenians, however, dei seems never to have been pronounced otherwise than with short a, and this measure was already sometimes used by the epic poets where the meter would not admit the form αἰεί [always] proper to the epic dialect, as in Homer Il. 12, 211 Εκτορ, ἀεὶ μέν πως — [Hector, always somehow —]. But the Attic poets, who did not use the epic and Ionic αἰεί [always], said dei sometimes with short a, sometimes with long, as was convenient for the meter: whence very many examples of both measures are found in the scenic poets.] which is said either of uninterrupted time or has the meaning of the adverb ἑκάστοτε [each time], which grammarians are accustomed to explain by ἀεί [always].

cit.quote: ἀεὶ δὲ τοῦ παρόντος ἀχθηδών κακοῦ τρύσει σε.
Always the pain of the present evil will wear you down.
ἀεί γε δὴ νηλής σὺ καὶ θράσους πλέως.
Always indeed you are pitiless and full of boldness.
ὁ δ᾽ ἐπικότως ἀεὶ θέμενος ἄγνάμπτον νόον.
But he, ever wrathful, set an unbending mind.
τί γὰρ πέπρωται Ζηνὶ πλὴν ἀεὶ κρατεῖν;
For what is fated for Zeus except to rule always?
ἀεὶ γὰρ ὄψεις ἔννυχοι – παρηγόρουν.
For always nightly visions – they were comforting.
ἄνακτι πίστιν ἐν πρώτοις ἀεί.
To the lord, faith first of all always.
ἀεὶ γὰρ ἡβᾷ τοῖς γέρουσιν εὖ μαθεῖν.
For always it is youth for the old to learn well.
μέτοικον ἐς τὸ πᾶν ἀεὶ ξένον,
A resident alien for all time, always a stranger,
cit.note: quod Schneiderus in Lexico ἀείξενονalways welcoming strangers scribi maluit.
which Schneider in his Lexicon preferred to write ἀείξενον [always hostile to strangers].

cit.quote: χαμαιπετεῖς ἔκεισθ᾽ ἀεί.
You lie always on the ground.
ἔσται δὲ καὶ τὸ λοιπὸν — ἀεὶ δικαστῶν τοῦτο βουλευτήριον.
And for the future there will be – always this council of judges.
ἀεὶ γυναικῶν ἐστι δεῖμ᾽ ἐξαίσιον.
Always is the fear of women excessive.
καί με συμφορᾶς ἀεὶ βαθεῖα κηλὶς — ἀναστρέφει.
And a deep stain of misfortune always turns me back.
ἀεὶ φυλάσσων τὴν ὑπὲρ πυρὸς στάσιν.
Always guarding the station over the fire.
Ἀρης φιλεῖ ἀεὶ τὰ λῷστα πάντα τανθρώπων (sensus postulat παντὸς ἀγρεύειν vel simile quid) στρατοῦ.
Ares always loves all the best things of men (the sense requires "to hunt" or something similar) of the army.
ἢν μὲν γὰρ αὐτῷ σκοπὸς ἀεὶ τούμὸν κάρα,
For if his target is always my head,
cit.note: si recte ab Dobraeo correctum est quod apud Athenaeum 15 p. 667e legitur κότταβος ἀείalways the kottabos .
if it was correctly corrected by Dobree from what is read in Athenaeus 15 p. 667e κότταβος ἀεί [kottabos always].

cit.quote: ἀεὶ δὲ μίσει ἀποικιεῖ.
And always he will dwell apart in hatred.
θώπτε τὸν κρατοῦντ᾽ ἀεί,
Flatter the one in power always,
cit.note: i. e, τὸν ἑκάστοτε κρατοῦνταthe one in power at any given time , singulos singulis temporibus regnantes, etsi ἀείalways hoc sensu dictum plerumque inter articulum et nomen ponitur.
i.e., τὸν ἑκάστοτε κρατοῦντα [the one ruling at each time], each one ruling at each time, although ἀεί [always] in this sense is generally placed between the article and the noun.

cit.quote: πολλοῖς μὲν ἀεὶ νυκτέροις ὀνείρασι ξύνειμι.
I am always with many nightly dreams.
τὸν αὐτὸν ἀεὶ δαίμον᾽ οὐριεῖν τύχης.
To guide the same fortune always.
μόλοι τὸν ἀεὶ φέρουσ᾽ ἐν ἡμῖν μοῖρ᾽ ἀτέλευτον ὕπνον.
May the fate that always brings endless sleep come upon us.
βεβῶτ᾽ ἂν ἀν' Herm.) ἀεὶ τὴν πλανοστιβή χθόνα.
Having gone always over the earth trodden by wanderers.
πόλιν τὴν Παλλάδος τιμῶσιν ἀεὶ τήνδε.
They always honor this city of Pallas.
εύφρονας ἀεὶ μέγα τιμώντες.
Always greatly honoring the kindly ones.
τίκτεσθαι δὲ φόρους γᾶς ἄλλους εὐχόμεθ᾽ ἀεὶ.
And we pray that other tributes of the earth may always be born.
θεοὺς δ᾽ οἳ γᾶν ἔχουσιν ἀεὶ τίοιεν.
And may they always honor the gods who hold the land.
ὃς ἀεὶ (αἰέν Μ) δι᾿ Αχέροντ᾽ ἀμείβεται.
Who always (αἰέν M) crosses through Acheron.
ἵν᾽ ὁ παντόπτης Ἥλιος ἀεὶ — ἀναπαύει.
Where the all-seeing Sun always rests.
καὶ δεῦρό γ' ἀεὶ (i. e. semper adhuc) τὴν τύτην οὐ μέμφομαι.
And even here always (i.e. always up to now) I do not blame this small thing.
θύη — ἔχουσ᾽ ἐς ἀεὶ τόνδ᾽ ἐπαινέσεις λόγον.
Having sacrifices, you will praise this word forever.
cit.note: ἐς ἀεὶforever in perpetuum.
ἐς ἀεὶ [forever] in perpetuity.

cit.quote: αἰἐν ὑπέροχον σθένος κραταιὸν ὀχῶν στενάζει.
Always groaning, bearing the mighty strength that is supreme.
cit.note: Forma epica aiév tragici non utuntur nisi postulante metro: de quo dixi in Lex. Soph. p. 7a.
The epic form aiév the tragedians do not use except when the meter demands it: on which I have spoken in Lex. Soph. p. 7a.

cit.quote: τῆς τ' αἰὲν ἐν φύλλοισι θαλλούσης ἴσον – ἐλάας.
And of the olive that always flourishes in its leaves, equal to...
κλάουσα λαμπτηρουχίας ατημελήτους αἰέν͵ ἐν δ᾽ ὀνείρασι
Weeping, always neglecting the torch-bearing, and in dreams

entry.note: Male vero Sept.857 πίτυλον, ὃς αἰὲν δι᾿ Αχέροντ' ἀμείβεταιthe oar-stroke, which always crosses through Acheron , ubi dei scribendum.
But wrongly at Sept. 857 πίτυλον, ὃς αἰὲν δι᾿ Αχέροντ' ἀμείβεται [the oar-stroke, which ever passes through Acheron], where dei should be written.

cit.quote: ὅταν δ' ἀείδειν ἢ μινύρεισθαι δοκῶ.
But when I think to sing or to warble.
ὃς τότ᾽ ἐπέρρεπεν γαμβροῖσιν ἀείδειν (ὑμέναιος).
Who then prevailed upon the bridegrooms to sing (the wedding song).
ὁ τὴν ἀείζων ἄφθιτον πόαν φαγών
He who eats the ever-living, imperishable grass
καὶ γεύομαι πως τῆς ἀειζώου πόας.
And I somehow taste of the ever-living grass.
cit.note: De qua herba v. Athenaeus 14 p. 679a et 7 p. 296 f. Cum forma minus Attica άειζώουever-living , qua metri causa usus est Aeschylus, comparandum φιλόζωοςfond of life , quod Sophocles (fr. 807) hand dubie eadem de causa dixit pro φιλόζωςfond of life . Formam Atticam ἀείζωνever-living annotavit Phrynichus in Bekk. Anecd. p. 22.

Concerning which plant see Athenaeus 14 p. 679a and 7 p. 296 f. With the less Attic form άειζώου, which Aeschylus used for metrical reasons, compare φιλόζωος [fond of life], which Sophocles (fr. 807) undoubtedly said for the same reason instead of φιλόζως [fond of life]. The Attic form ἀείζων [ever-living] was noted by Phrynichus in Bekker's Anecdota p. 22.

cit.quote: χώρα δ᾽ ἄχθος ἀείζων πέλοι.
And may the land be an ever-living burden.
δεσμὸν ἀεική.
an unseemly bond.
δεσμούς ἀεικεῖς.
unseemly bonds.
οὐδὲν ἀεικές.
nothing unseemly.

sense.def: Forma disyllaba αἰκηςunseemly , qua Sophocles quoque usus est,
The disyllabic form αἰκης, which Sophocles also used,

cit.quote: αἰκὲς πῆμα,
an unseemly calamity,
cit.note: quod Porsonus restituit pro ἀεικέςunseemly .
which Porson restored for ἀεικές.

Bekk. Anecd. p. 347,33 ἄειλα: τα πολύσκια χωρία, κατά στέρησιν τῆς ἕλης (εἵληςἄειλα: the very shady places, from the privation of ἕλη (εἵλη) ap. Hesych. et in Etym. Μ.) οὕτως ΑἰσχύλοςM.) thus Aeschylus .
Bekker's Anecdota p. 347,33: ἄειλα [shady places]: the very shady places, from the privation of ἕλη [sunlight] (εἵλη in Hesychius and in the Etymologicum M.) thus Aeschylus.

cit.quote: ἔργον – μέγιστον, ἀείμνηστον,
a deed – greatest, ever to be remembered,
cit.note: ubi αἰείμνηστονever to be remembered apogr. nonnulla.
where some copies have αἰείμνηστον.

sense.note: [hospes perpetuus. Incerta Schneideri coniectura Ch. 684 pro ἀεὶ ξένονalways a stranger .]
[perpetual host. Uncertain conjecture of Schneider at Ch. 684 for ἀεὶ ξένον.]

cit.quote: ἄλλο δ᾽ ἀείρει τρίχαλον κύμα.
And another wave lifts a triple-crested one.
κροκόβαπτον ποδὸς εὔμαριν ἀείρων.
Lifting the saffron-dyed sandal of his foot.

sense.note: Hesychius άελπτοι: δεινοί, καὶ ἄαπτοι. Αἰσχύλος Πρωτεῖunhoped-for: terrible, and untouchable. Aeschylus in Proteus (fr. 211). Aeschylus aut ἄεπτοιunhoped-for aut, quod probabilius, ἄαπτοιuntouchable dixisse videtur, quae ex Homerico (Ι. 1, 567) χεῖρας ἀάπτουςhands that cannot be touched nota est scripturae diversitas, quae fortasse similiter in Aeschyli Proteo exstitit, sed verum haud dubie est ἄαπτοιuntouchable , ut in loco Homeri ἀάπτουςuntouchable (cum interaspiratione, quae significat χεῖρας ὧν οὐκ ἂν ἅψαιτό τιςhands that no one could touch ) probavit Aristarchus. || Librarii errorem qui Suppl. 911 ἄεπταuntouchable pro ελπταunhoped for scripsit, notavi s. v. ἄελπτοςunhoped for . || Alio modo erratum est in versibus Αg. 140 141 sic scriptis in Μ τόσσων περ εὔφρων καλά | δρόσοισιν ἀέλπτοις μαλερῶν ὄντωνM: though being so many, kindly fair things with unhoped-for dews of raging beasts , quae in Praef. editionis Lips. quintae p. LXXXIV - LXXXVI sic emendanda esse ostendi ὄσσων παρ᾽ εὐφρόνων καλὰ Διὸς κόρα | δρόσοισιν μαλερῶν τε λεόντων -. Ριο αέλπτοιςfrom kindly eyes fair things of Zeus's daughter with dews of raging lions - unhoped-for scholiasta aut legit aut legi voluit ἀέπτοιςuntouchable . Nam ad δρόσοισινwith dews in M annotatum est τοῖς νεογνοῖς "χωρίς δ᾽ αὖτ᾽ ἔρσαιto the newborn "and separately again dews" ” (Hom. Od. 9, 222) ἀέλπτοιςunhoped for (sic codex contra mentem scholiastae) δὲ τοῖς ἕπεσθαι τοῖς γονεῦσι μὴ δυναμένοιςbut to those unable to follow their parents . Prior huius annotationis pars ab vetere grammatico scripta est, ut ex Etym. Μ. p. 377, 37 intelligitur, ubi δρόσωνof dews nomen pariter cum Homerico ἔρσαιdews comparatur, ἔρση γάρ ἐστιν ἡ δρόσος. καὶ Αἰσχύλος ἐν Ἀγαμέμνονι τοὺς σκύμνους τῶν λεόντων δρόσους κέκληκε μεταφράζων τοῦτοFor 'erse' is dew. And Aeschylus in Agamemnon called the cubs of lions 'drosoi', translating this . Altera vero scholii pars, qua ἀέπτοιςunhoped for explicatur, recentioris grammatici inventum est, qui non animadverterat vocabulum hoc temere huic versui esse illatum, quae sententia etiam eo confirmatur quod in codice δρόσοισινwith dews scriptum est, non δρόσοιςwith dews , quod Triclinius posuit, ut versus initium iambicum esset. Nec catulorum leonis tanta est teneritas quanta avicularum vix ovo exclusarum, ut Aeschylo operae pretium videri potuerit δρόσωνof dews nomini, cui ipsi iam teneritatis notio inest, istiusmodi aliquod epitheton adiungere. Prorsus ridiculus vero est Byzantinus scholiasta, qui ἀέπτοιςunhoped for interpretatus est τοῖς μὴ δυναμένοις πτῆναιto those unable to fly , quasi leones, qui hodie quattuor pedibus incedere solent, Aeschyli aetate volaverint: nisi forte homo ingeniosus figurate illud dictum esse voluit, quemadmodum Sophocles OR. 17 infantes οὐδέπω πτέσθαι σθένονταςnot yet able to fly dixit, comparatione ab νεοσσοῖςto chicks ducta, quo nomine infantes saepe a poetis sunt appellati. Manifestum est ἀέπτοιςunhoped for istud ex vetere corruptum esse glossemate ἀετοῖςto eagles , quod adscriptum olim fuit verbis v. 136 πτανοῖσιν κυσί πατρόςwinged dogs of the father : de quo pluribus dixi in Fleckeiseni Annalibus a. 1863 vol. 87 p. 75 - 79.

Hesychius: άελπτοι [unhoped-for, unexpected]: δεινοί [terrible], and ἄαπτοι [untouchable]. Aeschylus in Proteus (fr. 211). Aeschylus seems to have said either ἄεπτοι [unhoped-for] or, more probably, ἄαπτοι [untouchable], which is known from the Homeric (Il. 1, 567) χεῖρας ἀάπτους [untouchable hands] as a variant reading, which perhaps similarly existed in Aeschylus' Proteus, but the truth is undoubtedly ἄαπτοι [untouchable], as in the Homeric passage Aristarchus approved ἀάπτους [untouchable] (with the rough breathing, which means χεῖρας ὧν οὐκ ἂν ἅψαιτό τις [hands that no one would touch]). || The copyist's error who wrote ἄεπτα [unhoped-for] for ελπτα in Suppl. 911 I noted under the word ἄελπτος [unhoped-for]. || In another way there is an error in the verses Ag. 140-141 written thus in M: τόσσων περ εὔφρων καλά | δρόσοισιν ἀέλπτοις μαλερῶν ὄντων [of so many, kindly, beautiful things, with unhoped-for dews of fierce ones], which I have shown in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. LXXXIV-LXXXVI should be emended thus: ὄσσων παρ᾽ εὐφρόνων καλὰ Διὸς κόρα | δρόσοισιν μαλερῶν τε λεόντων [from kindly eyes, beautiful daughter of Zeus, with dews of fierce lions]. The scholiast either read or wanted to read ἀέπτοις [unhoped-for] for αέλπτοις. For on δρόσοισιν [dews] in M is annotated: τοῖς νεογνοῖς [to the newborn] "χωρίς δ᾽ αὖτ᾽ ἔρσαι" [and apart from them the dew] (Hom. Od. 9, 222) ἀέλπτοις [unhoped-for] (so the codex, against the scholiast's intention) but τοῖς ἕπεσθαι τοῖς γονεῦσι μὴ δυναμένοις [to those unable to follow their parents]. The first part of this annotation was written by an old grammarian, as is understood from Etym. M. p. 377, 37, where the noun δρόσων [dews] is similarly compared with the Homeric ἔρσαι [dews], for ἔρση γάρ ἐστιν ἡ δρόσος [for dew is the dew]. And Aeschylus in Agamemnon called the cubs of lions δρόσους [dews], translating this. But the other part of the scholium, in which ἀέπτοις [unhoped-for] is explained, is the invention of a more recent grammarian, who had not noticed that this word had been rashly introduced into this verse, which opinion is also confirmed by the fact that in the codex δρόσοισιν [dews] is written, not δρόσοις [dews], which Triclinius put, so that the beginning of the verse would be iambic. Nor is the tenderness of lion cubs so great as that of birds scarcely hatched from the egg, that it could have seemed worthwhile to Aeschylus to add to the noun δρόσων [dews], which itself already contains the notion of tenderness, some epithet of that sort. Truly ridiculous is the Byzantine scholiast, who interpreted ἀέπτοις [unhoped-for] as τοῖς μὴ δυναμένοις πτῆναι [to those unable to fly], as if lions, which today are accustomed to walk on four feet, flew in the age of Aeschylus: unless perhaps the clever fellow wanted it to be said figuratively, just as Sophocles OR. 17 called infants οὐδέπω πτέσθαι σθένοντας [not yet able to fly], with a comparison drawn from νεοσσοῖς [chicks], by which name infants are often called by poets. It is manifest that this ἀέπτοις [unhoped-for] was corrupted from an old gloss ἀετοῖς [eagles], which was once written next to the words in v. 136 πτανοῖσιν κυσί πατρός [winged dogs of the father]: about which I have said more in Fleckeisen's Annals, year 1863, vol. 87, p. 75-79.

sense.note: Ea tragici vel simplici utuntur aiaî modo intra modo extra metrum posita, vel duplicata αἰαὶ αἰαῖalas! alas! , plerumque extra versum posita. De scriptura alaî (non aiai ut apud Apollon. in Bekk. Anecd. p. 556, 26 et in M a m. pr. apud Sophoclem OR. 754) constat Herodiani auctoritate περὶ μόν. λέξOn Peculiar Words . p. 27, librarii vero in tragicorum codicibus prope constanter diremerunt in ai ai (rarius aî ai) et αἱ αἱ αἱ αἶalas! alas! alas! alas! , interdum ter scripto ai, quo nemo usus est, vel aiaî in è e mutato. Exempla Aeschylea sunt

The tragedians use either the simple αἰαῖ [alas!] sometimes within, sometimes outside the meter, or the doubled αἰαὶ αἰαῖ [alas! alas!], mostly placed outside the verse. About the spelling αἰαῖ (not αἰαί as in Apollonius in Bekker's Anecdota p. 556, 26 and in M by the first hand in Sophocles Oedipus Rex 754) it is established by the authority of Herodian in περὶ μόν. λέξ. [On Peculiar Words] p. 27, but the copyists in the manuscripts of the tragedians almost constantly divided it into αἶ αἶ (more rarely αἶ αἶ) and αἱ αἱ αἱ αἶ, sometimes writing αἶ three times, which no one used, or changing αἰαῖ into ἒ ἔ. The Aeschylean examples are

cit.note: Hesychius αἰγίζειν: διασπᾶν, ἐκ μεταφορᾶς, παρὸ καὶ τὸ αἰγίζεσθαι ἀπὸ τῶν καταιγίδων. Αἰσχύλος. ὁ δ᾽ αὐτὸς ἐν Ἠδωνοῖςαἰγίζειν [to tear apart]: διασπᾶν [to tear apart], by metaphor, from which also αἰγίζεσθαι [to be storm-tossed] from καταιγίδων [squalls]. Aeschylus. The same author in the Edonians (fr. 60) καὶ τὰς νεβρίδας οὕτω λέγειalso calls the fawn-skins thus . Quae partim etiam apud Suidam leguntur, de quo v. annot. Poetae verba fuisse coniecit Hermannus. Verba οὕτω λέγει (καλεῖcalls them thus (calls apud Suidam) signifcare videntur νεβρίδαςfawn-skins ab Aeschylo αἰγίδαςgoat-skins esse appellatas.

Hesychius αἰγίζειν [to tear apart]: διασπᾶν [to tear apart], by metaphor, from which also αἰγίζεσθαι [to be storm-tossed] from καταιγίδων [squalls]. Aeschylus. The same author in the Edonians (fr. 60) also calls the fawn-skins thus. These words are partly read also in Suidas, on which see the annotation. Hermann conjectured that these were the poet's words. The words οὕτω λέγει [calls them thus] (καλεῖ [calls] in Suidas) seem to mean that the fawn-skins were called αἰγίδας [goat-skins] by Aeschylus.

entry.note: Apparet ex his tempora huius verbi partim ab αἰδοῦμαιI feel shame partim ab αἴδομαιI feel shame esse formata. Praesentis tamen participio αἰδόμενοςfeeling shame pro αἰδούμενοςfeeling shame tragici non sunt usi nisi postulante metro, ut Eum. 549 ἐπιστροφὰς δωμάτων αιδόμενός τις ἔστωlet someone be in awe of the turns of the house . Suppl. 362 ποτιτρόπαιον αἰδόμενος. ἠδέσωrevering the suppliant. you felt shame pro ἠρκέσωyou kept away restitui volebat Wellauerus Eum. 213, de quo loco v. s. v. ἥκωI have come .

It appears from these that the tenses of this verb are formed partly from αἰδοῦμαι [I feel shame] and partly from αἴδομαι [I feel shame]. However, the tragedians did not use the present participle αἰδόμενος [feeling shame] for αἰδούμενος [feeling shame] except when the meter required it, as Eum. 549 ἐπιστροφὰς δωμάτων αιδόμενός τις ἔστω [let someone be in awe of the turns of the house]. Suppl. 362 ποτιτρόπαιον αἰδόμενος [revering the suppliant]. Wellauer wanted to restore ἠδέσω [you felt shame] for ἠρκέσω [you kept away] at Eum. 213, on which passage see under ἥκω [I have come].

Anecd. p. 310, 3 αἱμούς: τοὺς δρυμούς. ἴσως ἀπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἀφ᾽ οὗ καὶ ἡ αἱμασιά λέγεται. αἵμουςαἱμούς: τοὺς δρυμούς. ἴσως ἀπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἀφ᾽ οὗ καὶ ἡ αἱμασιά λέγεται. αἵμους [thickets: the woods. Perhaps from the same root from which αἱμασιά is also said. thickets] falso, ut videtur, accentu et δρυμούςδρυμούς [woods] in δρόμουςδρόμους [courses] corrupto Eustath. p. 1851, 27. Hesychius αἱμοί: δρυμοί (αἱμοίδρυμοιαἱμοί: δρυμοί (αἱμοίδρυμοι [thickets: woods (thicket-woods] codex). Αἰσχύλος ΑἰτναίαιςΑἰσχύλος Αἰτναίαις [Aeschylus in the Aetnaeae] .

Bekker's Anecdota p. 310, 3 αἱμούς: τοὺς δρυμούς [thickets: the woods]. Perhaps from the same root from which αἱμασιά [a wall of dry stones] is also said. αἵμους [thickets] falsely, as it seems, in accent, and δρυμούς [woods] corrupted into δρόμους [courses] in Eustathius p. 1851, 27. Hesychius αἱμοί: δρυμοί [thickets: woods] (αἱμοίδρυμοι [thicket-woods] in the codex). Aeschylus in the Aetnaeae.

cit.note: Incertum propter verborum adiunctorum corruptelam Aeschyli exemplum est. Certum est ἐπάμιδαupon the sheaves ex ἐπ᾽ ἄμαλαupon the sheaves corruptum esse, quod restituit Hermannus. Pro αἵμονες ὡςbloody ones, as Turnebus scripsit αἵμονίζω σI make you bloody ', ex annotatione scholiastae ἡμαγμένονhaving been bloodied (recte ήμαγμένηνhaving been bloodied (feminine) Weilius) σε καθίζωI seat you .

The example from Aeschylus is uncertain because of the corruption of the adjoining words. It is certain that ἐπάμιδα [a word of uncertain meaning] is corrupted from ἐπ᾽ ἄμαλα [upon the sheaves], which Hermann restored. For αἵμονες ὡς [bloody ones, as] Turnebus wrote αἵμονίζω σ' [I make you bloody], from the scholiast's note ἡμαγμένον [having been bloodied] (correctly ήμαγμένην [having been bloodied, feminine] according to Weil) σε καθίζω [I seat you].

cit.note: Adiectivum αἶνάdreadful , adverbialiter dictum, pro δεινάterrible , restituendum esse conieci ib. 576 propter rationes in Philologo vol. 13 p. 489 expositas. αἰνῶνof dread things addidi Ag. 153 post νεικέωνof quarrels .

The adjective αἶνά [dreadful], used adverbially, for δεινά [terrible], I conjectured should be restored at line 576 for reasons set out in Philologus vol. 13 p. 489. I added αἰνῶν [of dread things] at Ag. 153 after νεικέων [of quarrels].

cit.quote: φόβος μ' έχει φρένας δρᾶσαί τε μὴ δρᾶσαί τε καὶ τύχην ἑλεῖν.
fear holds my mind to do and not to do, and to take the fortune.
cit.note: Schol. καὶ τοῦ συμφέροντος ἐπιτυχεῖνand to attain what is advantageous . Similiter Pseudo-Euripides Iph. Α. 56 δοῦναί τε μὴ δοῦναί τε τῆς τύχης θ' (θA. 56: to give and not to give, and of fortune (θ ' addidit Marklandus) όπως ἅψαιτ' ἄρισταso that he might grasp best .

Schol. καὶ τοῦ συμφέροντος ἐπιτυχεῖν [and to attain what is advantageous]. Similarly Pseudo-Euripides Iph. A. 56 δοῦναί τε μὴ δοῦναί τε τῆς τύχης θ' (θ' added by Markland) όπως ἅψαιτ' ἄριστα [both to give and not to give, and to grasp the best of fortune].

sense.def: Forma media αἱροῦμαιI choose capio mihi, sumo
middle form αἱροῦμαι I take for myself, I take

cit.quote: ἄριστα, δείπνα, δόρπα θ' αἱρεῖσθαι τρίτα.
to choose the best, dinners, and third suppers.
ἑλέσθαι δ᾽ οὔτιν᾽ ἐκ γαίας λίθον ἕξεις, ἐπεὶ πᾶς χῶρός ἐστι μαλθακός.
you will have no stone to take from the earth, since every place is soft.
ἐκ χερῶν εἴλεσθέ μου.
you took from my hands.
τοιαῦθ᾽ ἑλέσθαι σοι πάρεστιν ἐξ ἐμοῦ.
such things are yours to choose from me.
τὰς δ᾽ ἑβδόμας (πύλας) Απόλλων εἵλετο,
and the seventh gates Apollo chose,
cit.note: quod schol. exp. per ἔσωσενhe saved , i. e. in se recipiebat, ne ab exercitu hostili expugnarentur.
which the schol. explains by ἔσωσεν [he saved], i.e. he received them into himself, so that they might not be captured by the enemy army.

cit.quote: θάνατον εἵλετ᾽ ἐν πόλει.
he chose death in the city.
δωμάτων γὰρ εἱλόμαν ἀνατροπάς.
for I chose the overthrow of the house.
cit.note: de munere suscipiendo
of undertaking a task

cit.quote: ἑλοῦ γὰρ, ἢ πόνων τὰ λοιπά σοι φράσω σαφηνῶς ἢ τὸν ἐκλύσοντ᾽ ἐμέ.
choose, then, whether I shall tell you clearly the rest of your toils or the one who will release you, me.
οὓς Ξέρξης είλετο χώρας εφορεύειν.
whom Xerxes chose to oversee the land.
πολλών γὰρ ἐσθλῶν τήνδ' ὄνησιν εἰλόμην.
for I chose the enjoyment of many good things.
τεροσκόπον δὲ τῶνδέ σ' αἱροῦμαι πέρι.
and I choose you as an interpreter of these things.
τοῦθ᾽ ὅμως αἱρούμεθα.
nevertheless we choose this.
ἄμομφον ὄντα σ' αἱροῦμαι πόλει.
I choose you, being blameless, for the city.
ξύμμαχον δ᾽ ἑλόμενος Δίκαν.
having chosen Justice as an ally.
μή μ' αἱροῦ κριτήν.
do not choose me as judge.
τοῦτ᾽ ἀντ᾽ ἐκείνων τούπος αἱροῦμαι σέθεν,
I choose this word from you in return for those,
cit.note: i. e. lubens accipio.
i.e. I gladly accept.

cit.quote: φόνων δικαστὰς ὁρκίους αἱρουμένη.
choosing sworn judges of murders.
cit.note: Sic Casaubonus pro ὁρκίων αἰρουμένουςchoosing oaths .
Thus Casaubon for ὁρκίων αἰρουμένους [choosing oaths].
ἑλοίμανmay I choose vitiose pro ολοίμαν πᾶνmay I destroy everything .
ἑλοίμαν [may I choose] corruptly for ολοίμαν πᾶν [may I destroy all].

cit.quote: ἀνὴρ κατ᾽ ἄνδρα τοῦτον ᾑρέθη.
man against man was chosen.

sense.def: (cum imperf. ρονρον , aoristo ἦρα ἄρειας ἄραςI raised, you raised, having raised , futuro ἀρῶI will raise praesente et aoristo passivo αίρεσθαι, ἤρθην ἀρθείςto be raised, I was raised, having been raised , medio αἴρομαι, ἄροισθε ἀρόμενοςI raise for myself, may you raise, having raised for oneself ) - tollo, erigo
(with imperfect ρον, aorist ἦρα ἄρειας ἄρας, future ἀρῶ, present and aorist passive αίρεσθαι, ἤρθην ἀρθείς, middle αἴρομαι, ἄροισθε ἀρόμενος) - to lift, raise

cit.quote: ἆρ᾽ ὀρθὸν αἴρεις — τὸ σὸν κάρα;
Do you lift your head straight?
άρεϊ (sic Bambergerus pro ἐρεῖ) καὶ κατ᾽ ὀφθαλμοὺς βαλεῖ.
άρεϊ (thus Bamberger for ἐρεῖ) and will cast it upon the eyes.
όλβον, ὃν Δαρεῖος ἦρεν.
the wealth which Darius raised.
ἀπὸ σμικροῦ δ᾽ ἂν ἄρειας μέγαν δόμον.
From small beginnings you might raise a great house.
ἐπεὶ νιν μέγαν ἄρας.
when he had raised him greatly.
δὴ τότ᾽ ἤρθην φόβῳ πρὸς μακάρων λιτάς.
then I was lifted by fear to prayers to the blessed ones.
ή κάρτα προς γυναικός αἴρεσθαι κέαρ.
or greatly is the heart lifted by a woman.

sense.def: Of raising a paean with loud voice

cit.quote: κἀγὼ δὲ μόρον τῶν οἰχομένων φρενός ἐκ φιλίας θρηνῶν παιᾶν' αἴρω δοκίμως πολυπενθῆ,
And I, lamenting the fate of the departed from a loving mind, raise a paean, duly, full of sorrow,
cit.note: ubi verba φρενός παιᾶνa paean of the mind lacunae explendae causa addidi, de quo dixi in Leutschii Philologo vol. 13 p. 469.
where I added the words φρενός παιᾶν [a paean of the mind] to fill a lacuna, about which I spoke in Leutsch's Philologus vol. 13 p. 469.

sense.def: Of setting a military expedition in motion

cit.quote: ἀλλ᾽ εὐσταλῆ τοι λεκτὸν ἀροῦμεν στόλον.
But we shall raise a well-equipped, chosen expedition.
στόλον — τῆσδ᾽ ἀπὸ χώρας ῆραν.
the expedition — they raised from this land.
στόλον ἡμέτερον νάϊον ἀρθέντ᾽ ἀπὸ προστομίων.
our naval expedition raised from the mouth of the harbor.
ἀπὸ γάρ με τιμᾶν δαναιᾶν θεῶν δυσπάλαμοι παρ' οὐδὲν ῆραν δόλοι.
For the hard-to-wrestle wiles of the gods raised me from honors of the Danaans to nothing.

sense.def: Forma media αἴρομαιI raise for myself comparo mihi, nanciscor
Middle form αἴρομαι: I procure for myself, I obtain

cit.quote: ἄροισθε κῦδος τοῖσδε πολίταις
may you win glory for these citizens
cit.note: (apud huius urbis cives).
(among the citizens of this city).

cit.quote: βλοσυρὸν ἀρόμενον (sic Abreschius pro αιρόμενον) ἄγος.
taking up grim pollution (thus Abresch for αιρόμενον).
πόλεμον αἴρεσθαι νέον.
to undertake a new war.
πόλεμον αἴρεσθαι μέγαν.
to undertake a great war.
cit.note: Eadem verba 950, ubi ἐρεισθενέον Μἐρεισθενέον Μ , quod correxit Porsonus.
The same words at 950, where M has ἐρεισθενέον [strong in strife], which Porson corrected.

cit.quote: οὐκ εὔκοσμον αίρονται φυγήν.
they take a disorderly flight.
cit.note: Sic pro αίροῦνταιthey choose Elmsleius.
Thus Elmsley for αίροῦνται [they choose].

cit.quote: ψῆφον αἴρειν,
to cast a vote,
cit.note: ut ψῆφον φέρεινto cast a vote 674.]
as ψῆφον φέρειν [to cast a vote] 674.]

sense.note: V. ἍιδηςHades .
See Ἅιδης [Hades].

cit.quote: Ἀἶσα φασγανουργός
Fate, worker with the sword
τὴν πεπρωμένην αίσαν.
the destined fate.
εἰδὼς ἂν αἶσαν τήνδε συγγνοίη βροτοῖς.
knowing this fate, he would pardon mortals.
ἐν αἴσα,
in fate,
cit.note: pro sortis necessitate, quod schol. exp. ἐν εἱμαρμένηin destiny .
for the necessity of fate, which the scholiast explains as ἐν εἱμαρμένη [in destiny].

cit.quote: ὃς πολιῷ νόμῳ αἶσαν όρθοῖ.
who by ancient law directs fate rightly.
δούλιον ἐσᾶγον αἶσαν.
they brought a slavish fate.
θανατηφόρον αἶσαν.
death-bringing fate.
πατρὸς αἶσα.
father's fate.
παρ' αἶσαν.
contrary to fate.
δισσούς τυράννους ἐκπεσόντας ἠσθόμην.
I perceived that two tyrants had been driven out.
χαίρετε χαίρετ' ἐν αἰσιμίαισι πλούτου.
Rejoice, rejoice in prosperity of wealth.
cit.note: Quum αἴσιμαthings that are right dicantur quae bona et utilia sunt, αἰσιμίας πλούτουprosperity of wealth afluentes divitias dixisse videtur Aeschylus. Est igitur idem quod εὐτυχίαιgood fortunes .

Since αἴσιμα [things that are right] are said to be things that are good and useful, Aeschylus seems to have said αἰσιμίας πλούτου [prosperity of wealth] meaning abundant riches. Therefore it is the same as εὐτυχίαι [good fortunes].

cit.quote: όδιον κράτος αἴσιον ἀνδρῶν
auspicious might of men

sense.note: V. ἄσσωto dart, rush .
See ἄσσω [to dart, rush].

cit.quote: ὤλετ᾽ ἄκλαυτος, ᾆστος,
he perished unlamented, unseen,
cit.note: ubi ἄιστοςunseen metri causa in ᾆστοςunseen contractum est, ut ἀϊστοῦνmaking unseen et ᾀστοῦνmaking unseen dictum est.
where ἄιστος [unseen] is contracted to ᾆστος for metrical reasons, just as ἀϊστοῦν [making unseen] and ᾀστοῦν are said.

cit.quote: πάρεστι σιγὰς ἀτίμως ἀλοιδόρως | ἄστους ἀφημένων ἰδεῖν,
it is possible to see the silence dishonored, unreviled, unseen of those who sit upon,
cit.note: Idem restituendum esse conieci, de quo dixi in Praef. ed. Lips. quintae p. LXIII. In apographis (nam in M haec pars fabulae excidit) legitur πάρεστι σιγᾶς ἄτιμος. ἀλοίδορος ἥδιστος ἀφεμένων ἰδεῖνit is possible to see the silence dishonored, unreviled, sweetest of those released . Karstenus coniecerat πάρεστι σιγὰς ἀτίμους ἀλοιδόρους αἴστους ἐφημένων ἰδεῖνit is possible to see the silences dishonored, unreviled, unseen of those who sit upon .

I conjectured that the same reading should be restored, about which I spoke in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. LXIII. In the copies (for in M this part of the play is lost) is read πάρεστι σιγᾶς ἄτιμος. ἀλοίδορος ἥδιστος ἀφεμένων ἰδεῖν [it is possible to see the silence dishonored, unreviled, sweetest of those released]. Karsten had conjectured πάρεστι σιγὰς ἀτίμους ἀλοιδόρους αἴστους ἐφημένων ἰδεῖν [it is possible to see the silences dishonored, unreviled, unseen of those who sit upon].

cit.quote: ὃς αὐτὸν ἐκ τυραννίδος θρόνων τ' ἄἴστον ἐκβαλεῖ.
who will cast him out unseen from tyranny and thrones.
βωμοὶ δ᾽ ἄΐστοι,
and the altars are unseen,
βωμοὶ δ᾽ ἄΐστοι,
and the altars are unseen,
cit.note: nisi Agamemnoni hic versus ex Persis est illatus, quod coniecit Salzmannus.
unless this verse was inserted into the Agamemnon from the Persians, which Salzmann conjectured.

cit.quote: ἐν δ᾽ ἀΐστοις τελέθοντος οὔ τις αλκά.
and when one is among the unseen, there is no defense.
αποτρέψειεν ἄϊστον ὕβριν,
may turn away unseen violence,
cit.note: ubi άϊστονunseen efectum verbi αποτρέψειενmay turn away indicat.
where άϊστον [unseen] indicates the effect of the verb αποτρέψειεν [may turn away].

cit.quote: τὰ πρὶν δὲ πελώρια νῦν ἀϊστοῖ.
the former monstrous things he now destroys.
αϊστώσας γένος τὸ πᾶν.
having destroyed the whole race.

sense.note: V. αἰσχρῶςshamefully .
See αἰσχρῶς.

cit.quote: μηδ' αἶσχος ἡμῖν, ἡδονὴν δ᾽ ἐχθροῖς ἐμοῖς πράξωμεν.
let us not bring shame upon ourselves, but pleasure to my enemies.
αἴσχη τε Πέρσαις καὶ λιγέα κωκύματα.
shame for the Persians and shrill lamentations.
αἰσχρόμητις τάλαινα παρακοπά πρωτοπήμων.
shameful-planning, wretched, maddening, first cause of woe.
cit.note: Schol. αἰσχρὰ ποιεῖν ἀναγκάζουσαcompelling to do shameful things .
Schol. αἰσχρὰ ποιεῖν ἀναγκάζουσα [compelling to do shameful things].

cit.quote: σοφῷ γὰρ αἰσχρὸν ἐξαμαρτάνειν.
for it is shameful for a wise man to err.
αἰσχρῶν γὰρ ἀργὸς, μὴ κακὸς δ᾽ εἶναι φιλεῖ.
for he is idle in shameful things, but loves not to be base.
κακῶν δὲ κᾆσχρῶν οὔτ τιν' εὐκλείαν ἐρεῖς.
and of evils and shameful things you will not speak of any glory.
ὁ κόμπος – οὐκ αἰσχρός.
the boast – not shameful.
νόσημα αίσχιστον.
a most shameful disease.
αἰσχρῶς δ᾽ ἀλῶμαι.
and I wander shamefully.
αἰσχρῶς τε βουλευτοῖσιν ἐν καλύμμασιν.
and shamefully in the veils of the councilors.
τεθνάσιν αἰσχρῶς δυσκλεεστάτῳ μόρῳ,
they died shamefully by a most inglorious fate,
cit.note: probabilius est οἰκτρῶςpitifully , quod ex apogr. restitui.
more probable is οἰκτρῶς [pitifully], which I restored from the copies.

cit.quote: τέθνηκεν αἰσχρῶς χρημάτων ἀπαιόλη.
he died shamefully, a cheat of money.
αἴσχιστα καὶ τάχιστα.
most shamefully and most swiftly.
ᾔσχυνε ξενίαν τράπεζαν κλοπαῖσι γυναικός.
he shamed the hospitable table with the thefts of a woman.
εὐνὴν ἀνδρὸς αἰσχύνουσα.
shaming the bed of her husband.

sense.def: αἰσχύνομαιI am ashamed pudet me. Cum infinitivo
αἰσχύνομαι I am ashamed. With infinitive

cit.quote: οὐκ αἰσχυνοῦμαι τοὺς φιλάνορας τρόπους λέξαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς.
I will not be ashamed to speak to you of my husband-loving ways.
αἰσχύναμαί σοι τοῦτ᾽ ὀνειδίσαι σαφῶς.
I am ashamed to reproach you clearly with this.
οὐδ᾽ αἰσχύνομαι ἔχουσ᾽ ἄπιστον τήνδ' ἀναρχίαν πόλει.
nor am I ashamed to hold this faithless anarchy in the city.
καίτοι καὶ λέγουσ᾿ αἰσχύνομαι.
and yet even as I speak I am ashamed.
cit.note: In M ὀδύρομαιI lament , sed adscripto γρ. αἰσχύνομαιγρ. I am ashamed , quod in textu habent apogr. nonnulla.
In M ὀδύρομαι [I lament], but with γρ. αἰσχύνομαι [I am ashamed] written in the margin, which some copies have in the text.

cit.quote: είπερ κακόν φέρει τις αἰσχύνης άτερ.
if someone bears evil without shame.
πέμπτος δὲ Μάρδος ῆρξεν, αἰσχύνη πάτρα.
and fifth Mardus ruled, a shame to his fatherland.
τὸν Αἰσχύνης θρόνον τιμῶντα.
honoring the throne of Shame.
cit.note: Alterum huius προσωποποιίαςpersonification exemplum est in epigr. Dioscoridis Anth. Pal. 7, 450 Αἰσχύνην οὐ νομίσασα θεόνnot considering Shame a goddess .
Another example of this personification is in the epigram of Dioscorides Anth. Pal. 7, 450 Αἰσχύνην οὐ νομίσασα θεόν [not considering Shame a goddess].

cit.quote: έχει γὰρ αἰσχυντῆρος, ὡς νόμος, δίκην.
for he has the justice of a shamer, as is customary.
cit.note: de Aegistho adultero in versibus spuriis
about Aegisthus the adulterer in spurious verses

cit.quote: δόμων καταισχυντήρσι.
to the shamers of the house.
cit.note: De eodem et Clytaemnestra. Neutrum vocabulum alibi legitur.
About the same and Clytaemnestra. The neuter word is read elsewhere.

cit.quote: θεοὺς μὲν αἰτῶ τῶνδ᾽ ἀπαλλαγὴν πόνων.
I ask the gods for release from these toils.
τερπνὰ τούτων αἰτεῖ Σύμβολα κρᾶναι,
He asks to accomplish pleasing tokens of these things,
cit.note: ubi τερπνά ξύμβολα κράναιto accomplish pleasing tokens (modo optativo), eiecto τούτων αἰτεῖhe asks for these things , scribendum esse ostendi in Praef. ed. Lips. quintae p. LXXXV.

where τερπνά ξύμβολα κράναι [to accomplish pleasing tokens] (in the optative mood), with τούτων αἰτεῖ [he asks for these things] removed, I have shown that it should be written in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. LXXXV.

cit.quote: αὐτοῦσι μὴ ἐκδῷς παισὶν Αἰγύπτου πάλιν.
Do not give me up to the sons of Aegyptus again.
δωρεάν αἰτεῖ.
He asks for a gift.
χάριν δὸς ἥντιν᾽ αὐτούμεσθα.
Grant whatever favor we ask.
αὐτοῦ τῶνδ᾽ ἀποτροπὴν λαβεῖν.
To ask for a turning away of these things.
πρευμενῶς δ᾽ αὐτοῦ τάδε.
And kindly ask him for these things.
ἡμεῖς δ᾽ ὕμνοις αἰτησόμεθα φθιμένων πομπούς εὔφρονας εἶναι κατὰ γαίας.
But we with hymns will ask that the escorts of the dead be kindly beneath the earth.
αιτουμένῳ μοι κούφον εἰ δοίης τέλος.
If you grant me, who asks, a light fulfillment.
σωτήρ γενοῦ μοι ξύμμαχός τ' αιτουμένῳ.
Be my savior and ally, as I ask.
αἰτουμένῳ μοι δὸς κράτος τῶν σῶν δόμων.
Grant me, who asks, power over your house.
αἰτίαν καθ' ἥντινα αἰκίζεται με.
The reason for which he mistreats me.
ἐκτὸς αἰτίας κυρεῖς
You are free from blame.
ἐκτὸς αἰτίας κακῆς εἶναι.
To be free from evil blame.
αἰτίαν δ᾽ ἔχω τῆς τοῦδε μητρός του φόνου.
I am accused of the murder of this man's mother.
θεός μὲν αἰτίαν φύει βροτοῖς.
A god produces blame for mortals.
εἰ μὲν γὰρ εὖ πράξαιμεν, αἰτία Θεοῦ.
For if we fare well, the cause is God's.
ἔχω μεγίστην αἰτίαν κείνων ὕπο.
I have the greatest blame from them.
ἢ κἀπ᾿ ἐμοὶ τρέποιτ᾽ ἂν αἰτίας τέλος;
Or would the end of blame be turned against me too?
οὐδὲ μὴ ν Ἅιδου θανών φύγῃ ματαίων αἰτίας.
Not even in death may he escape the charges of vain deeds in Hades.
ποίῳ λαβών σε Ζεὺς ἐπ᾽ αἰτιάματι;
On what charge did Zeus seize you?
τοιοῖσδε δή σε Ζεὺς ἐπ᾽ αἰτιάμασιν αἰκίζεται.
On such charges, then, Zeus mistreats you.

sense.def: one who is at fault, author

cit.quote: πόνων – τῶν νῦν παρόντων οὐδὲν αἰτία τέχνη.
Of the present toils, no art is the cause.
τᾶς νῦν ματρόπολις τῶνδ᾽ αἰτία στεναγμῶν.
The mother-city of these groans is the cause.
τὸν αἴτιον δ᾽ ἐξαπολλὺς μόρου.
Destroying the one responsible for the death.
διαλγής ἄτα διαφέρει τὸν αἴτιον.
Grievous ruin carries off the guilty one.
τοῖς αἰτίοις — τοῦ φόνου.
To those responsible for the murder.
εἰ μὴ μέτειμι τοῦ πατρὸς τοὺς αἰτίους,
Unless I pursue those responsible for my father's death,
cit.note: ubi πατρόςof the father pro φόνουof the murder illatum videtur ab interpolatore vetere qui versus 274-296 composuit: de quo dixi in Praef. ed. Lips. quintae p. XCIII.

where πατρός [of the father] seems to have been introduced in place of φόνου [of the murder] by an old interpolator who composed verses 274-296: about which I have spoken in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. XCIII.

cit.quote: ἰπούμενος ῥίζάισιν Αἰτναίαις ὕπο.
Pressed down beneath Aetnaean roots.

sense.note: ἈἰτναῖαιAetnaean Women inscripta fuit Aeschyli fabula (fr. 5—10), de qua dixi ad Fragm. p. 100. Duplex eius exstitit editio, altera genuina, altera νόθοςspurious , ut annotavit auctor Catalogi fabularum Aeschyli.

Ἀἰτναῖαι [Aetnaean Women] was the title of a play by Aeschylus (fr. 5—10), about which I have spoken at Fragm. p. 100. There were two editions of it, one genuine, the other νόθος [spurious], as the author of the Catalogue of Aeschylus's plays noted.

entry.note: [vitiose pro ἀφνίδιοςsudden , quod v.]
[erroneously for ἀφνίδιος [sudden], which see]

form.gloss: to wield a spear, fight with a spear

sense.def: I brandish a spear, I fight with a spear.

cit.quote: τὸν δ᾽ ἀνανδρίας ὑπο ἔνδον αἰχμάζειν,
But him, under cowardice, to wield a spear at home,
cit.note: de Xerxe dictum qui ignavus domi desidet. Per οἰκουρεῖνto stay at home explicat scholiasta.
said of Xerxes, who idly sits at home like a coward. The scholiast explains it by οἰκουρεῖν [to stay at home].

cit.quote: ἐν αἰχμαλώτοις Τρωϊκοῖς οἰκήμασιν.
In Trojan captive dwellings.
τῶν αἰχμαλώτων χρημάτων λάχος μέγα.
A great share of the captive spoils.
ἥ τ' αἰχμάλωτος ἥδε καὶ τερασκόπος.
This captive woman and seer.
εὐνὰν αἰχμάλωτον ἀνδρὸς εὐτυχοῦντος,
The captive bed of a fortunate man,
cit.note:
de mulieribus
captivis in servitutem abductis. Sic Soph. Ai. 12 de Tecmessa ἐπεί σε λέχος δουριάλωτον στέρξας ἀνέχει θούριος Αἴας.Since fierce Ajax, having loved you as his spear-won bride, keeps you.

of captive women led away into slavery. Thus Sophocles Ai. 12 of Tecmessa: ἐπεί σε λέχος δουριάλωτον στέρξας ἀνέχει θούριος Αἴας [since fierce Ajax, having loved you as his spear-won bride, keeps you].

sense.note:
Usitata tragicis verbi ἀΐωI hear mensura est u u _, ut Pers. 633. Ag. 55, vel _ u _ ut Suppl. 58 et Pers. 873 άϊονI heard , quod est imperfectum sine augmento. In versu vero choriambico Eum. 844 (repetito 876) θυμὸν ἄϊεhear my cry amphibrachi mensuram habet, ut ap. Hesiod. Op. 213 ὦ Πέρση, σὺ δ᾽ ἄϊε δίκηςO Perses, do you hear justice . Nam sic ex Etym. M. p. 43, 5 corrigendum quod in codicibus nunc legitur ἄκουεlisten . Eadem interpolatione codicibus Hom. Od. 1, 352 illatum ἀκουόντεσσιto those listening pro ἀϊόν
τεσσιto those hearing , quod ex Platonis Rep. p. 424b restituendum, ubi in ἀείδοντεσσιto those singing corruptum est, ortum ex scriptura antiqua ἀειόντεσσιto those hearing (ut apud Hesychium ἀείοις: ἀκούοιςyou might hear ): de quo dixi in Praef. ad Hom. Il. ed. Oxon, a. 1856 p. V.

The usual metrical pattern of the verb ἀΐω [I hear] in the tragedians is u u _, as at Pers. 633, Ag. 55, or _ u _ as at Suppl. 58 and Pers. 873 άϊον [I heard], which is the imperfect without augment. But in the choriambic verse Eum. 844 (repeated at 876) θυμὸν ἄϊε [hear my cry] has the measure of an amphibrach, as in Hesiod Op. 213 ὦ Πέρση, σὺ δ᾽ ἄϊε δίκης [O Perses, do you hear justice]. For thus, from Etym. M. p. 43, 5, the reading now found in the manuscripts, ἄκουε [listen], must be corrected. By the same interpolation in the manuscripts of Homer Od. 1, 352 ἀκουόντεσσι [to those listening] was introduced for ἀϊόντεσσι [to those hearing], which is to be restored from Plato's Republic p. 424b, where it is corrupted to ἀείδοντεσσι [to those singing], arising from the old spelling ἀειόντεσσι [to those hearing] (as in Hesychius ἀείοις: ἀκούοις [you might hear]): on which I have spoken in the Preface to the Oxford edition of Homer's Iliad, 1856, p. V.

ἀπ'from mutavit. Metrum postulat dipodiam trochaicam, qualem praebet Ahrensii coniectura ψαμμὶς ἀκτάsandy shore .

entry.note: Restitui ἀκλαγγείςnot barking , quod quum in libris antiquioribus ἀκλαγεῖςnot barking scriptum esset, ut verbi κλαγγάνωto bark formae plures vocabulaque ab eo derivata saepe simplici γgamma scripta sunt, in ἀκραγείςnot barking , quod nune legitur in M, est mutatum ab librariis non cogitantibus canes non clamare, sed latrare dici. Eodem errore κύνες κεκραγυῖαιdogs barking , ex κεκλαγυίαιhaving barked ortum, in codicibus plerisque Xenophontis Cyneg. 3, 9 et 6,27 scriptum est pro κεκλαγγυταιthey have barked , quod est servatum in aliis. In Ch. 535, ubi codex κέκλαγενhe has barked , H. L. Ahrens κέκλαγγενhe has barked scripsit, Robortellus κέκραγενhe has cried out . ἀκλαγγείςnot barking autem κύναςdogs Aeschylus dixit ut canes metaphorice dictos ab canibus qui proprie dicuntur distingueret: quae satis usitata tragicis loquendi forma est. Cum a privativo ante mutam cum liquida producto comparandum ἄτρυτον πόδαunwearied foot in trimetro Aeschyli Eum. 403. et άτρωτοςunwounded in trimetro Eubuli apud Athen. 9 p. 4491. ἓν ὄνομα πολλοῖς· τρωτός ἄτρωτος, δασύςone name for many: vulnerable, invulnerable, hairy . Cum canibus autem Grypes comparantur quia auri sunt custodes: quemadmodum mulierem, quae domum absente marito custodit, γυναῖκα πιστὴν — δωμάτων κύναa faithful woman — a dog of the house dixit Aeschylus Αgam. v. 607. Adiectivum ἀκραγήςnot barking ex ἄκροςhighest et ἄγοςcurse compositum nusquam legitur nisi in grammaticorum glossis quibusdam.

I have restored ἀκλαγγείς [not barking], which, since in older manuscripts it was written ἀκλαγεῖς [not barking], as many forms of the verb κλαγγάνω [to bark] and words derived from it are often written with a single γ [gamma], was changed by scribes, who did not consider that dogs are said not to cry out but to bark, into ἀκραγείς [not barking], which is now read in M. By the same error κύνες κεκραγυῖαι [dogs barking], arising from κεκλαγυίαι [having barked], is written in most manuscripts of Xenophon's Cynegeticus 3, 9 and 6, 27 instead of κεκλαγγυται [they have barked], which is preserved in others. In Choephori 535, where the manuscript has κέκλαγεν [he has barked], H. L. Ahrens wrote κέκλαγγεν [he has barked], Robortellus κέκραγεν [he has cried out]. Aeschylus called the dogs ἀκλαγγείς [not barking] to distinguish dogs used metaphorically from dogs in the proper sense: a form of speech quite common among the tragedians. With the alpha privative before a mute with a liquid lengthened, compare ἄτρυτον πόδα [unwearied foot] in a trimeter of Aeschylus Eum. 403, and άτρωτος [unwounded] in a trimeter of Eubulus in Athenaeus 9 p. 4491: ἓν ὄνομα πολλοῖς· τρωτός ἄτρωτος, δασύς [one name for many: vulnerable, invulnerable, hairy]. The Grypes are compared with dogs because they are guardians of gold: just as Aeschylus called a woman who guards the house in her husband's absence γυναῖκα πιστὴν — δωμάτων κύνα [a faithful woman — a dog of the house] in Agam. v. 607. The adjective ἀκραγής [not barking], compounded from ἄκρος [highest] and ἄγος [curse], is nowhere read except in certain glosses of grammarians.

for the opener (for the toucher Scaliger) there is no remedy of bridal chambers.

and remedies are not secure.
ἔστι τοῦδ᾽ ἄκος.
there is a remedy for this.
πολλῶν γὰρ τόδ᾽ ἐν βροτοῖς ἄκος.
for this is a remedy among mortals for many things.

πημονῆς ἄκη.

cit.note: [Sed ib. 266 μηνεῖται ἄκηthe remedies are revealed? corruptum ex μηνιαῖ᾽ ἄχηmonthly griefs .]

cit.note: Sine casu
Without a case

ἄκουε δή.
listen then.

a deed — fine to hear and to tell to those who are drunk.

listen, such are the laments on your behalf.

so be it. I hear.

we have heard.

as he will hear (ἀκούση [he may hear] M).

sense.note: cum accusativo rei.

cit.quote: ἄκουε τὰς ἐμὰς ἐπιστολάς: ἀντὶ τοῦ τῶν ἐμῶν ἐπιστολῶν. οὕτως Αἰσχύλος (fr. 423).
Hear my commands: instead of "of my commands". Thus Aeschylus (fr. 423).
τὰς προσερπούσας τύχας ἀκούσατε.
Hear the fortunes that are creeping upon you.
τοὺς σοὺς δὲ πόνους χρήζω διὰ παντὸς ἀκοῦσαι.
I desire to hear your toils throughout.
ταν βροτοῖς, δέ πήματα ἀκούσατε.
Hear the sufferings of mortals.
τὰ λοιπὰ νῦν ἀκούσατε.
Now hear the rest.
οὓς γὰρ νῦν ἀκήκοας λόγους.
For the words you have now heard.
ἄλλην δ᾽ ἄκουσον δυσχερή θεωρίαν.
Hear another grievous sight.

ἀκούετ' ἢ οὐκ ἀκούετ᾽ ἀσπίδων κτύπον;

Having heard the chariot-made din.
ἀκούειν τόδε πήμ᾽ ἄελπτον.
To hear this unexpected calamity.
πάντα γάρ, Δαρεῖ᾽, ἀκούσει (ἀκούσῃ Μ) μῦθον.

ἢ πολλά — ἤλγησ᾽ ἀκούσας – πήματα.

To hear these words.

Having heard the rest.

Hearing these things.

Hearing such things, write them in your heart.
θύρας ἄκουσον ἑρκείας κτύπον.

τοσαῦτ᾽ ἀκούσας εἶπον.
Having heard so much, I spoke.

πολλῶν ἄκουσον τέρματ᾽ αἰδοίων λόγων.

sense.note: Schol. Theocr. 4, 62 τοὺς Σατύρουςthe Satyrs (ἀκρατείςunrestrained ex scholio inferiore addidit Casaubonus) οἱ πλείονές φασιν, ὡς καὶ τοὺς Σειληνούς Σοφοκλῆς δὲ Ἀνδρομέδα.most say, as also the Sileni; but Sophocles in Andromeda. Non sequitur ex his καὶ Πᾶνας, ὡς Αἰσχύλος μὲν ἐν Γλαύκῳand the Pans, as Aeschylus in Glaucus (fr. 29), Aeschylum et Sophoclem ipso usos esse adiectivo κρατήςstrong .

Schol. Theocr. 4, 62: τοὺς Σατύρους [the Satyrs] (Casaubon added ἀκρατείς [unrestrained] from the lower scholium) most say, as also τοὺς Σειληνούς [the Sileni]; but Sophocles in Andromeda. It does not follow from these that καὶ Πᾶνας [the Pans too], as Aeschylus in Glaucus (fr. 29), and Sophocles themselves used the adjective κρατής [strong].

cit.note: a propugnaculis desuper iacientibus lapidum imber descendit. Alii passive intellexerunt de propugnaculis quae lapidibus petuntur. Utramque interpretationem proposuit Thom. Mag.

cit.quote: ἀκρωνία λευσμός τε.
akronia and stoning.

entry.note: Incertae significationis vocabulum, quod pro ἀκρωτηριασμόςmutilation (mutilatio) dictum acceperunt H. Stephanus aliique, significatione aliunde non magis cognita quam quae ab scholiasta memoratur κακῶν ἄθροισις ἢ λιθοβολίαa gathering of evils or stoning (λιθοβολίαςof stoning codex). Ἡρωδιανὸς δὲ τὸ σύστημα καὶ ἄθροισμαHerodian says the organized body and gathering . Similiter Bekk. Αnecd. p. 372, 2 ἀκρωνία τὰ ἀθροίσματα. καὶ ἡ ἀκρότης καὶ ἡ ἀκμή. καὶ τὸ ἐπίλεκτον σύστημαakronia: the gatherings; and the highest point and the prime; and the select body . et Etym. Μ. p. 53, 41. et Hesychius.

A word of uncertain meaning, which H. Stephanus and others took as said for ἀκρωτηριασμός [mutilation], a meaning not otherwise known except that mentioned by the scholiast: κακῶν ἄθροισις ἢ λιθοβολία [a gathering of evils or stoning] (the codex has λιθοβολίας [of stoning]). Herodian says τὸ σύστημα καὶ ἄθροισμα [the organized body and gathering]. Similarly Bekker, Anecd. p. 372, 2: ἀκρωνία τὰ ἀθροίσματα. καὶ ἡ ἀκρότης καὶ ἡ ἀκμή. καὶ τὸ ἐπίλεκτον σύστημα [akronia: the gatherings; and the highest point and the prime; and the select body]. And Etym. M. p. 53, 41. And Hesychius.

cit.quote: ώς μήτε σωκεῖν μήτε μ' ἀκταίνειν βάσιν,

cit.note: ubi στάσινstanding Μ, sed superscr. ab διορθωτῇto the corrector γρ. βάσινwritten βάσιν [step] .
where M has στάσιν [standing], but the corrector wrote above γρ. βάσιν [variant: step].

sense.note: Schol. κουφίζειν. σημαίνει δὲ καὶ τὸ γαυριᾶν καὶ ἀτάκτως πηδᾶνto lift up. It also means to prance and to leap disorderly . Phrynichus in Bekk. Anecd. p. 23, 12 ἀκταινῶσαι - Αἰσχύλος “οὐκέτ᾽ ἀκταίνω” φησὶ βαρυτόνως, οἷον οὐκέτι δύναμαι ὀρθοῦν ἐμαυτήνἀκταινῶσαι [to raise oneself] - Aeschylus says "οὐκέτ᾽ ἀκταίνω" [I no longer raise myself] with barytone accent, as if to say "I can no longer hold myself upright" .

Schol. κουφίζειν [to lift up]. It also means γαυριᾶν [to prance] and ἀτάκτως πηδᾶν [to leap disorderly]. Phrynichus in Bekk. Anecd. p. 23, 12 ἀκταινῶσαι [to raise oneself] - Aeschylus says "οὐκέτ᾽ ἀκταίνω" [I no longer raise myself] with barytone accent, as if to say "I can no longer hold myself upright."

cit.note: (in Bekk. Anecd. p. 351, 4)
(in Bekk. Anecd. p. 351, 4)

στύφλους παρ' ἀκτάς.

ἀλαοῖσι καὶ δεδορκόσιν ποινάν,

πάντα δὲ πύργων κτήνη – Μοῖρ᾽ ἀλαπάξει,
and all the flocks of the towers - Fate will destroy,
cit.note: ubi Triclinius Μοίρα λαπάξειFate will destroy , qua forma Aeschylus alibi utitur metro postulante.
where Triclinius Μοίρα λαπάξει [Fate will destroy], which form Aeschylus uses elsewhere when the meter demands.

cit.quote: ἄλαστα στυγνὰ πρόκακα.
unforgettable, hateful, and harmful things.
φανεὶς ἀλάστωρ ἢ κακὸς δαίμων ποθέν.

cit.quote: δέχου δὲ πρευμενώς αλάστορα.
