entry.note:
[ ἀλάστορος.of the avenger
De hac forma Epimerismi Homer. in Crameri Anecd. Oxon. vol. 1 p. 62, 12 παρὰ τὸ ἀλαστῶ ῥῆμα ἀλάστωρ ὁ Ζεὺς ἐπὶ τῶν χαλεπόν τι πρασσόντων, παρῆκται δὲ ἡ εὐθεῖα παρὰ τὴν ἀλάστορος γενικήν.from the verb alastō, alastōr is Zeus in the case of those doing something grievous, and the nominative is derived from the genitive alastoros. Αἰσχύλος ΙξίονιAeschylus in Ixion (fr. 90) πρευμενὴς ἀλάστορος.gracious avenger. Aliud ex Aeschylo exemplum attulit grammaticus in Bekk. Anecd. p. 382, 30 αλάστορον ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀλάστορα, ἀπὸ τῆς εὐθείας ὁ ἀλάστορος.alastoron for alastora, from the nominative ho alastoros. ΑἰσχύλοςAeschylus “μέγαν ἀλάστορον”“great avenger” εἶπενsaid . His inter se comparatis Nauckius grammatici prioris verba sic redintegranda esse coniecit, Αἰσχύλος ΙξίονιAeschylus in Ixion “μέγαν ἀλάστορον”“great avenger” καὶ ἀλλαχοῦand elsewhere “πρευμενῶς ἀλάστορον”“graciously an avenger” , ex Eumen. 236 “δέχου δὲ πρευμενῶς ἀλάστορον”.“receive graciously the avenger”. ubi nunc ἀλάστοραavenger (accusative) legitur, versu proximo ab οὐnot incipiente. ]

[ἀλάστορος [of the avenger]. On this form the Homeric Epimerisms in Cramer's Anecdota Oxoniensia vol. 1 p. 62, 12: παρὰ τὸ ἀλαστῶ ῥῆμα ἀλάστωρ ὁ Ζεὺς ἐπὶ τῶν χαλεπόν τι πρασσόντων, παρῆκται δὲ ἡ εὐθεῖα παρὰ τὴν ἀλάστορος γενικήν [from the verb alastō, alastōr is Zeus in the case of those doing something grievous, and the nominative is derived from the genitive alastoros]. Aeschylus in Ixion (fr. 90) πρευμενὴς ἀλάστορος [gracious avenger]. Another example from Aeschylus was adduced by the grammarian in Bekker's Anecdota p. 382, 30: αλάστορον ἀντὶ τοῦ ἀλάστορα, ἀπὸ τῆς εὐθείας ὁ ἀλάστορος [alastoron for alastora, from the nominative ho alastoros]. Aeschylus said “μέγαν ἀλάστορον” [great avenger]. Comparing these, Nauck conjectured that the words of the former grammarian should be restored as follows: Aeschylus in Ixion “μέγαν ἀλάστορον” [great avenger] and elsewhere “πρευμενῶς ἀλάστορον” [graciously an avenger], from Eumenides 236 “δέχου δὲ πρευμενῶς ἀλάστορον” [receive graciously the avenger], where now ἀλάστορα [avenger] is read, the next verse beginning with οὐ [not].

entry.note: Hesychius ἀλαιός· ὁ παλαιός, ἄφρων.alaios: the old, foolish ΑἰσχύλοςAeschylus (fr. 409). Immo ἀλεόςaleos : v. Herodian. περὶ μον. λέξon anomalous words . p. 4, 19. schol. Αrist. Lys. 988. Etym. Μ. p. 59, 45.
Hesychius ἀλαιός· ὁ παλαιός, ἄφρων [alaios: the old, foolish]. Aeschylus (fr. 409). But rather ἀλεός [aleos]: see Herodian on anomalous words p. 4, 19. schol. Arist. Lys. 988. Etym. M. p. 59, 45.

cit.quote: ἄλευ δᾶ.
Avoid, O earth.
cit.note:
Legitur in M ἄλευ ᾶ δαavoid, O earth , litteris αλευαaleua in litura scriptis
et accentibus omnibus ab manu διορθωτοῦcorrector additis. Pro ââ prima manu scriptum fuit ὦO , quod servatum in apographis plerisque, in quibus ἄλευ'avoid cum apostropho et ὦ δᾶO earth scriptum. His διορθωτήςcorrector scholion adscripsit cuius pars prior ipso quam vetere grammatico Alexandrino dignior est, γρ.gr. (hoc est γράφεταιit is written vel γραπτέονit should be written ) ἀλευάδα πατρωνυμικῶς ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀλεύας. ἢ ὂν δεῖ φυλάξασθαι. τινὲς οὕτως, ἄλευ ὦ δᾶ· ἄλευ, ἀναχώρει, ἔκκλινε· τὸ δὲ ὦ δᾶ, ὦ γῆ. οἱ γὰρ Δωριεῖς τὴν γῆν δῆν καὶ δᾶν φασιν καὶ τὸν γνόφον δνόφον.Aleuada, patronymically from Aleuas; or one who must be guarded against. Some read it thus: aleu o da [avoid, O earth]; aleu [avoid], anachorei [withdraw], ekkline [turn aside]; and o da [O earth] means o ge [O earth]. For the Dorians call ge [earth] de and dan, and gnophon [darkness] dnophon. Horum postrema similia sunt iis quae leguntur in Etym. M. p. 60,8 ἀλευάδα εἴρηται ὡς τὸ φεύδαAleuada is said like pheuda (id est φεῦ δᾶAlas, earth ). οἱ γὰρ Δωριεῖς τὴν γῆν δᾶν λέγουσιν, ὡς καὶ τὸν γνόφον δνόφον. φεύδα οὖν φεῦ γῆ. οὕτως οὖν καὶ τὸFor the Dorians call the earth dan, as also darkness dnophon. Pheuda therefore is pheu ge. Thus therefore also the (τὸthe om. cod. Voss. λευάδαleuada ) ἀλέου δᾶAvoid, earth (δῆde , superscripto γῆearth , codex Voss. δηλdel cod. Dorvill.) τοῦ δὲ ἀντὶ τοῦ γῆ κειμένουBut the [word] standing for earth , ubi in lemmate ἀλευάδαAleuada solo librarii errore scriptum est pro ἄλευ δᾶaleu da [avoid, O earth] , vel ἀλεύδαaleuda , ut φεύδαpheuda pro φεῦ δᾶpheu da [flee, O earth] scriptum, postrema vero, sublata dittographia, sic corrigenda, οὕτως οὖν καὶ ἄλευ δᾶThus therefore also avoid, earth (vel ἀλεύδαaleuda ), τοῦ δὲ ἀντὶ τοῦ γῆ κειμένουBut the [word] standing for earth . Nam commentum de Aleuada proprium est διορθωτοῦof the corrector Aeschylei alienumque ab glossa Etymologi, cuius in verbis nihil est quod ad Aleuadae nomen spectet. Apparet ex his veterem apud Aeschylum scripturam ἈΛΕΥΔΑALEUDA fuisse, cui ὦO ante da ab interprete additum fuit, quod servavit prima codicis Medicei manus, metro violato. Quamobrem eiecto ὦO revocavi ἄλευ δᾶaleu da [avoid, O earth] , etsi haec singularis est apocope. Nam quod Aristophanes Equit. 821 παῦ παύεpau paue [stop, stop] dixit et Aeschylus δίαιν δίαινεdiain diaine [moisten, moisten] , quod restitui Pers. 1038, ubi codex δίαινε δίαινεdiaine diaine [moisten, moisten] , diversum est, ut monui in Annot. Oxon. anni 1841 ad versum Persarum p. 318 his verbis "Sponte intelligitur apocopen hanc ibi tantum locum habere ubi idem verbum repetatur. Itaque Aeschylus et Aristophanes recte dicere potuerunt δίαιν διαίνεdiain diaine [moisten, moisten] et ποῦ παῦεpou paue [where? stop] , non potuissent simpliciter δίαινdiain [moisten] et παῦpau [stop] .” Nec si ἄλευ δᾶaleu da [avoid, O earth] , sive primus sive alio praeeunte, dixit Aeschylus, sequitur eum ἄλευaleu [avoid] etiam extra formulam illam unquam dicturum fuisse.

In M is read ἄλευ ᾶ δα [avoid, O earth], with the letters αλευα written over an erasure and all the accents added by the hand of the διορθωτοῦ [corrector]. For the first hand had written ὦ [O] instead of â, which is preserved in most copies, in which is written ἄλευ' [avoid] with an apostrophe and ὦ δᾶ [O earth]. To this the διορθωτής [corrector] added a scholion whose first part is more worthy of the ancient Alexandrian grammarian himself: γρ. [that is, γράφεται or γραπτέον] ἀλευάδα [Aleuada] patronymically from ἀλεύας [Aleuas]. Or 'which one must guard against.' Some read thus: ἄλευ ὦ δᾶ [avoid, O earth]; ἄλευ [avoid], ἀναχώρει [withdraw], ἔκκλινε [turn aside]; and ὦ δᾶ [O earth], ὦ γῆ [O earth]. For the Dorians call the earth δῆν [earth] and δᾶν [earth], and darkness δνόφον [darkness]. The last of these are similar to what is read in Etym. M. p. 60,8: ἀλευάδα [Aleuada] is said like φεύδα [alas, earth] (that is φεῦ δᾶ [alas, earth]). For the Dorians call the earth δᾶν [earth], as also darkness δνόφον [darkness]. φεύδα [alas, earth] therefore is φεῦ γῆ [alas, earth]. Thus therefore also the (τὸ [the] omitted by cod. Voss. λευάδα [Aleuada]) ἀλέου δᾶ [avoid, earth] (δῆ [earth], with γῆ [earth] written above, codex Voss. δηλ cod. Dorvill.) with τοῦ δὲ [but the] standing for γῆ [earth], where in the lemma ἀλευάδα [Aleuada] alone by a scribal error is written for ἄλευ δᾶ [avoid, earth], or ἀλεύδα [avoid, earth], as φεύδα [alas, earth] is written for φεῦ δᾶ [alas, earth], but the last part, with the dittography removed, should be corrected thus: οὕτως οὖν καὶ ἄλευ δᾶ [thus therefore also avoid, earth] (or ἀλεύδα [avoid, earth]), with τοῦ δὲ [but the] standing for γῆ [earth]. For the comment about Aleuada is peculiar to the Aeschylean διορθωτοῦ [corrector] and foreign to the gloss of the Etymologicum, in whose words there is nothing that refers to the name Aleuada. From these things it appears that the ancient reading in Aeschylus was ἈΛΕΥΔΑ [ALEUDA], to which ὦ [O] before da was added by an interpreter, which the first hand of the Medicean codex preserved, with the meter violated. Therefore, having ejected ὦ [O], I have restored ἄλευ δᾶ [avoid, earth], although this is a singular apocope. For what Aristophanes Equit. 821 said παῦ παύε [stop, stop] and Aeschylus δίαιν δίαινε [moisten, moisten], which I restored Pers. 1038, where the codex has δίαινε δίαινε [moisten, moisten], is different, as I noted in Annot. Oxon. of the year 1841 on the verse of the Persians p. 318 with these words: "It is readily understood that this apocope has a place only where the same word is repeated. Therefore Aeschylus and Aristophanes could rightly say δίαιν διαίνε [moisten, moisten] and ποῦ παῦε [stop, stop], but they could not simply say δίαιν [moisten] and παῦ [stop]." Nor if Aeschylus said ἄλευ δᾶ [avoid, earth], whether first or following another, does it follow that he would ever have said ἄλευ [avoid] outside that formula.
Aoristi imperativus est
It is the imperative of the aorist

Cuiusmodi infinitivi in codicibus παροξυτόνωςwith an acute accent on the penult scribi solent.

Bekker's Anecdota p. 383,31: ἀλκάθω καὶ ἀλκάθειν [I help and to help]. Sophocles and Aeschylus (fr. 425), and it means βοηθεῖν [to help]. There is no present ἀλκάθω ἀλκάθειν [I help, to help], but the aorist άλκαθεῖν [to have helped]. Infinitives of this kind are usually written with an acute accent on the penult in manuscripts.

entry.note:
Aoristus secundus Eum. 368 ἁλομένα,having leapt
Nam sic in apogr. correctum quod in M est αλλωμέναleaping , altero λl eraso. Similiter inter ἁλόμενοιhaving leapt , ἁλώμενοιwandering (sic) et αλλόμενοιleaping variant libri Xen. Anab. 4, 2, 17 et alibi. Tragici aoristum priorem ἡλάμηνI leapt alteri praetulerunt ἡλόμηνI leapt (de quo dixit Veitch. Irreg. verbs p. 47), cuius modis quibusdam ab a brevi incipientibus usi sunt metri causa: unde Aeschylus ἁλομέναhaving leapt dixit, non ἁλαμέναhaving leapt , cuius a longum esse videtur, ut ἁλάμενοςhaving leapt ap. Arist. ΑνAv. . 1395. Similiter ἀράμενοςhaving lifted a longo dicitur, ἀρόμενοςhaving lifted vero brevi. Aoristi secundi exempla ἐνήλουhe leapt in
Pers. 515 (ubi ενήλλουyou were leaping in apogr. multa) et ἐξήλλουyou were leaping out apud Soph. O R.1311 librariorum debentur erroribus. Recte ἐνήλωhe leapt in et ἐξήλωhe leapt out Elmsleius, et ἐξήλωhe leapt out apud Sophoclem apogr. duo, ut v. 263 et 1261 ενήλατοhe leapt in legitur, non ενήλετοhe leapt in vel ενήλλετοhe was leaping in , et ἀφήλατοhe leapt away apud Aeschylum Pers. 305 .

Second aorist Eum. 368 ἁλομένα [having leapt]. For thus it is corrected in the apograph, whereas in M it is αλλωμένα [leaping], with the second λ erased. Similarly between ἁλόμενοι [having leapt], ἁλώμενοι [wandering] (sic) and αλλόμενοι [leaping] the manuscripts vary in Xen. Anab. 4, 2, 17 and elsewhere. The tragedians preferred the first aorist ἡλάμην [I leapt] to the second ἡλόμην [I leapt] (on which Veitch, Irregular Verbs p. 47 has spoken), certain forms of which beginning with short a they used for metrical reasons: hence Aeschylus said ἁλομένα [having leapt], not ἁλαμένα [having leapt], whose a seems to be long, as ἁλάμενος [having leapt] in Arist. Av. 1395. Similarly ἀράμενος [having lifted] is said with long a, but ἀρόμενος [having lifted] with short. Examples of the second aorist ἐνήλου [he leapt in] Pers. 515 (where ενήλλου [you were leaping in] in many apographs) and ἐξήλλου [you were leaping out] in Soph. O R. 1311 are due to scribal errors. Elmsley rightly wrote ἐνήλω [he leapt in] and ἐξήλω [he leapt out], and ἐξήλω [he leapt out] in Sophocles in two apographs, as at v. 263 and 1261 ενήλατο [he leapt in] is read, not ενήλετο or ενήλλετο, and ἀφήλατο [he leapt away] in Aeschylus Pers. 305.

entry.note:
Apocopen restitui Suppl. 782, ubi in M legitur τὸ πᾶν δ᾽ ἄφαντος ἀμπετήσαις δόσως | κόνις ἄτερθεν πτερύγων ὀλοίμαν.and I, wholly invisible, having flown up with gifts, may I perish as dust without wings Monstra vocabulorum ἀμπετήσαισδόσωςhaving flown up with gifts , ut alia non pauca in extrema huius fabulae parte originem suam debent antiquiori codici, in quo litterae aliae vix legi poterant, aliae prorsus evanuerant. Restitui igitur quod sensus postulat ἃμ πνοαῖς διψάς ὡς.as thirsty dust with the breezes
ἅμwith pro ἅμαat the same time dictum (fere ut ἄμup pro ἀνάup dicitur) est in glossa Hesychii, etsi huic non multum tribuendum. ἅμα πνοαῖςwith the breezes dictum ut ap. Homerum Il. 15, 149 ἅμα πνοιῇσι πετέσθην,they flew with the breezes et addito ἀνέμοιοof the wind Od. 2, 148 ἐπέτοντο μετὰ πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο.they flew amid the breezes of the wind
διψάς κόνιςthirsty dust comparandum cum διψία κόνιςthirsty dust , quod dixerunt Aeschylus Agam. 495 et Sophocles Antig. 246 429.

I restored the apocope at Suppl. 782, where in M is read: τὸ πᾶν δ᾽ ἄφαντος ἀμπετήσαις δόσως | κόνις ἄτερθεν πτερύγων ὀλοίμαν [and I, wholly invisible, having flown up with gifts, may I perish as dust without wings]. The monstrosities of words ἀμπετήσαισδόσως [having flown up with gifts], like not a few others in the last part of this play, owe their origin to an older manuscript, in which some letters could scarcely be read, others had completely vanished. I therefore restored what the sense requires: ἃμ πνοαῖς διψάς ὡς [as thirsty dust with the breezes]. ἅμ [with] is used for ἅμα [at the same time] (much as ἄμ [up] is used for ἀνά [up]) in a gloss of Hesychius, although not much weight should be given to him. ἅμα πνοαῖς [with the breezes] is said as in Homer Il. 15, 149 ἅμα πνοιῇσι πετέσθην [they flew with the breezes], and with the addition of ἀνέμοιο [of the wind] Od. 2, 148 ἐπέτοντο μετὰ πνοιῇς ἀνέμοιο [they flew amid the breezes of the wind]. διψάς κόνις [thirsty dust] is to be compared with διψία κόνις [thirsty dust], which Aeschylus Agam. 495 and Sophocles Antig. 246, 429 used.

Accusativus tanquam ab nominativo ἄμαλςa ship , quo nemo usus est. Hesychius ἄμαλα: τὴν ναῦν, ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀμᾶν τὴν ἅλα.ἄμαλα [the ship]: the ship, from ἀμᾶν [to reap] τὴν ἅλα [the sea]. Αἰσχύλος Πρωτεῖ σατυρικῷAeschylus in the satyric Proteus (fr. 212). Corrupte Etym. Μ. p. 75.22 ἀμάδα τὴν ναῦν Αἰσχύλος.ἀμάδα [the ship] in Aeschylus.
ἐπ᾽ ἅμαλαupon the ships in ἐπαμίδαa kind of cake corruptum Suppl. 842 847 restituit Hermannus.

Accusative as if from a nominative ἄμαλς [a ship], which no one has used. Hesychius: ἄμαλα [the ship]: the ship, from ἀμᾶν [to reap] τὴν ἅλα [the sea]. Aeschylus in the satyric Proteus (fr. 212). Corruptly in Etym. M. p. 75.22: ἀμάδα [the ship] in Aeschylus. Hermann restored ἐπ᾽ ἅμαλα [upon the ships] for the corrupt ἐπαμίδα [a kind of cake] in Suppl. 842, 847.

cit.note:
eximia est Henrici Weilii emendatio pro γάμῳ δαπτομέναν,being torn in marriage quod M habet litteris τοthe letters το a manu paullo recentiore in litura trium litterarum scriptis, quas non dubium est ανωthe letters ανω fuisse, i. e, δαπανωμένην,being consumed quod in pluribus servatum est apographis, partim sic partim δαπανομένηνbeing consumed scriptum. Vocabulum autem γάμῳin marriage non ex μέγαgreat corruptum est, quod Schuetzius multis persuasit, sed longe aliam habet originem. Nam postquam in libro multo quam cod. Mediceus antiquiore ἈΜΑΛΑΠΤΟΜΕΝANbeing utterly destroyed in ἈΜΑΔΑΠΤΟΜΕΝΑΝbeing torn corruptum fuerat, ad AMA,AMA quod ἅμαtogether with esse videbatur, dativus γάμῳin marriage adscriptus est, ἅμαtogether with in margine annotato, δαπτομένανbeing torn vero per δαπανωμένηνbeing consumed explicatum. Hinc confectum est quod nunc in M legitur, addito in margine scholio, quod fortasse ab διορθωτῇcorrector , ut alia multa, est compositum, γάμψ: ἅμα τῷ γάμῳ· λείπει γὰρ τὸ ἅμα.marriage: together with the marriage; for 'together with' is missing.
ἐνin supplevit Thomas Mag. cuius in scholio inter alia haec leguntur, εἰσορῶσα αὐτὴν δαπτομένην καὶ δαμαζομένην ἐν τῷ γάμῳ τοῦ Διός,seeing her being torn and subdued in the marriage of Zeus et in gl. interlineari τὴν παρθενίαν δηλοῖ ἀφανιζομένην.it indicates her virginity being destroyed Antiquior scholiasta Byzantinus, τῷ γάμῳ τῷ τοῦ Διὸς δαπτομένην καὶ δακνομένην.being torn and bitten by the marriage of Zeus In apogr. Vitebergensi gl κινδυνεύουσανbeing in danger .

Excellent is the emendation of Henri Weil for γάμῳ δαπτομέναν [being torn in marriage], which M has with the letters το written by a somewhat later hand in an erasure of three letters, which were undoubtedly ανω, i.e. δαπανωμένην [being consumed], which is preserved in several copies, written partly thus, partly δαπανομένην [being consumed]. The word γάμῳ [in marriage] is not corrupted from μέγα [great], as Schütz persuaded many, but has a far different origin. For after in a book much older than the Medicean codex ἈΜΑΛΑΠΤΟΜΕΝAN [being utterly destroyed] had been corrupted into ἈΜΑΔΑΠΤΟΜΕΝΑΝ [being torn], to AMA, which seemed to be ἅμα [together with], the dative γάμῳ [in marriage] was added, with ἅμα [together with] noted in the margin, and δαπτομέναν [being torn] explained by δαπανωμένην [being consumed]. Hence was produced what is now read in M, with a scholium added in the margin, which was perhaps composed by a corrector, like many others: γάμψ: ἅμα τῷ γάμῳ· λείπει γὰρ τὸ ἅμα [marriage: together with the marriage; for 'together with' is missing]. Thomas Magister supplied ἐν [in], in whose scholium among other things these are read: εἰσορῶσα αὐτὴν δαπτομένην καὶ δαμαζομένην ἐν τῷ γάμῳ τοῦ Διός [seeing her being torn and subdued in the marriage of Zeus], and in the interlinear gloss: τὴν παρθενίαν δηλοῖ ἀφανιζομένην [it indicates her virginity being destroyed]. An older Byzantine scholiast: τῷ γάμῳ τῷ τοῦ Διὸς δαπτομένην καὶ δακνομένην [being torn and bitten by the marriage of Zeus]. In the Wittenberg copy the gloss is κινδυνεύουσαν [being in danger].

cit.quote: πολλαὶ δ᾽ ἀμαλαῖς (sic Prienus pro ἀπαλαῖς, quod in apographis ἁπαλαῖς vel ἀταλαῖς scriptum) χερσὶ καλύπτρας κατερεικόμενοι (addidi μητέρες οἰκτραί).
many with weak hands (thus Prien for ἀπαλαῖς [soft], which in copies is written ἁπαλαῖς [soft] or ἀταλαῖς [tender]) tearing their veils (I added μητέρες οἰκτραί [wretched mothers]).
τόνδ᾽ ἁμαξήρη θρόνον.
this chariot-mounted throne

form.gloss: to miss, to fail to hit; to err, to sin

sense.def: aberro ab aliqua re, non attingo aliquid.
to miss, to fail to hit

cit.quote: πῶς λιπόναυς γένωμαι Συμμαχίας ἁμαρτών;
How could I become a deserter of the fleet, having failed the alliance?
τοῦ ῥυσίου θ᾽ ἥμαρτε.
and he missed the prey.
σώφρονος γνώμης δ᾽ ἁμαρτείν.
to miss a prudent mind.
ἔρριψεν, οὐδ᾽ ἥμαρτε.
he threw, and did not miss.
ἥμαρτον, ἢ θηρῶ τι τοξότης τις ώς;
Did I miss, or do I hit something like some archer?
οὐχ ὁρᾷς ὅτι ἥμαρτες, ὡς δ᾽ ἥμαρτες οὔτ᾽ ἐμοὶ λέγειν καθ᾽ ἡδονὴν σοί τ᾽ ἄλγος.
Do you not see that you have erred, and how you have erred is not pleasant for me to say nor for you to hear?
ἑκὼν ἑκὼν ἥμαρτον.
willingly, willingly I erred.
τί ποτε ταῖσδ᾽ ἐνέζευξας εὑρὼν ἁμαρτοῦσαν ἐν πημοσύναις;
Why did you yoke her to these, finding her erring in misfortunes?
καὶ πολλ᾽ ἁμαρτῶν οὐδὲν ὤρθωσας φρενί.
And having erred in many things, you set nothing right in your mind.

cit.note: (apud Stob. Flor. 3, 10)
(in Stobaeus, Florilegium 3, 10)
cit.quote: ἁμαρτάνει τι (sic cod. Scor.: τοι Paris. A) καὶ σοφοῦ σοφώτερος.
He errs in something (thus the Scorialensis codex: τοι [in something] Parisinus A) and is wiser than a wise man.
τοιᾶσδέ τοι ἁμαρτίας σφε δεῖ θεοῖς δοῦναι δίκην.
For such a sin they must pay the penalty to the gods.
αὐτὸς φρενῶν καρποῖτο τὴν ἁμαρτίαν.
He himself may reap the fruit of his own mind's error.
παλαιάς τῶνδ᾽ ἁμαρτίας δόμων.
The ancient sins of this house.
τὰ δῶρα μείω δ' ἐστὶ τῆς ἁμαρτίας.
The gifts are less than the sin.
ἔνθεν Ἰὼ φεύγει ἁμαρτίνοος.
From there Io flees, erring in mind.
δίδυμα γοᾶν ἁμάρτια.
Twin sins of lamentation.
διπλά δ᾽ ἔτισαν Πριαμίδαι θάμάρτια.
The sons of Priam paid double for their sins.
ἐξ ἀμαυρᾶς κληδόνος λέγει μαθών.
He speaks having learned from an obscure report.
Ἐρινύες χρόνῳ τυχηρὸν ὄντ᾽ ἄνευ δίκας · τιθεῖσ ἀμαυρόν.
The Erinyes, in time, make him who is fortunate without justice dim.
ἀμαυρᾶς ἐκ φρενός.
From a dim mind.
ἐξ ἀμαυρᾶς φρενός.
From a dim mind.
τἄμπαλιν δὲ τῶνδε γαίας κάτοχ᾽ ἀμαυροῦσθαι σκότῳ,
But the opposite of these things, the things that hold down the earth, to be dimmed in darkness,
cit.note: ubi κάτοχα μαυροῦσθαιto be dimmed, held down Blomfieldus, quae forma metro postulante legitur Ag. 296. Eum. 359.
where Blomfield reads κάτοχα μαυροῦσθαι [to be dimmed, held down], which form is read as the meter demands at Ag. 296, Eum. 359.

cit.quote: ἀμαχέτου δίκαν ὕδατος ὀροτύπου.
Like an unconquerable mountain-torrent of water.
ἄμαχον κύμα θαλάσσας.
The unconquerable wave of the sea.
ἀκάκας, ἄμαχος βασιλεύς ἰσόθεος Δαρείος.
Blameless, unconquerable king, godlike Darius.
ἄμαχον ἄλγος.
Unconquerable grief.
δαίμονά τε τὰν ἄμαχον, ἀπόλεμον, ἀνίερον.
And the daimon that is unconquerable, unwarlike, unholy.
οἳ δ᾽ οὔποτ᾽ ἐλπίσαντες ἤμησαν καλῶς.
And they who never expected it reaped well.

cit.note: in Μ πρὸς ἀμβάσειςto the steps male ριο προσαμβάσειςto the approaches .
in M πρὸς ἀμβάσεις [to the steps] wrongly ριο προσαμβάσεις [to the approaches].
Improprie
Improperly
cit.quote: καὶ θέσφατ᾽ οὐκ ἀμβλύνεται,
And the oracles are not blunted,
cit.note: ubi per ἀπρακτεῖis ineffective exp. schol.
where the scholiast explains it by ἀπρακτεῖ [is ineffective].

cit.quote: οὐ προστρόπαιον, οὐδ᾽ ἀφοίβαντον χέρα, ἀλλ᾽ ἀμβλὺν ἤδη.
Not a suppliant's hand, nor one unwashed of blood, but already blunt.
δακρύων βίον ἀμβλωπόν
a life dim with tears
cit.note: vitam lacrimis ita plenam ut hominum oculi hebescant, ut interpretatur Wellauerus.
a life so full of tears that men's eyes grow dim, as Wellauer interprets it.

cit.quote: ἀωρόνυκτον ἀμβόαμα μυχόθεν ἔλακε.
A cry at untimely night sounded from within.

sense.def: (for ἀναβοάω [to cry aloud]) to cry aloud

cit.quote: βαρὺ δ᾽ ἀμβόασον.
Cry aloud heavily.
διαμβοάσω
I will shout across
cit.note: restitui pro διαβοάσωI will shout across .
I restored it for διαβοάσω [I will shout across].

cit.quote: θεᾶς ἀμβρότου.
Of the immortal goddess.
ἄμβωνες: αἱ προσαναβάσεις (ἀναβάσεις Erotianus p. 86) τῶν ὁρῶν.
ἄμβωνες [ridges]: the ascents (ἀναβάσεις [ascents] Erotianus p. 86) of the mountains.
ἀμέγαρτα γὰρ τάδε Ζεὺς ἰδίοις νόμοις κρατύνων.
For these things are wretched, which Zeus strengthens with his own laws.
ποίμναν τάνδ᾽ ἀμέγαρτον.
This wretched flock.
cit.note: Schol. ἀφθόνητον, διὰ τὸ ἀτελές.not to be envied, because of its incompleteness
Schol. ἀφθόνητον, διὰ τὸ ἀτελές [not to be envied, because of its incompleteness].

form.gloss: to exchange, to pass, to answer, to repay

cit.quote: χροιᾶς ἀμείψεις ἄνθος.
You will exchange the flower of your complexion.
ἀμείβων χρῶτα πορφυρᾷ βαφή.
Changing his skin with purple dye.
πορθμὸν ἀμείψας Ἀθαμαντίδος Ελλας.
Having crossed the strait of Athamantian Helle.
εἰ δ᾽ οὖν ἀμείψω βαλὸν ἑρκείων πυλῶν.
But if I pass through the gates of the courtyard,
χάριν τροφᾶς γὰρ ἀμείβων.
Repaying the favor of nurture.
παλίμποινα θέλων ἀμείψει.
Wishing to repay with requital.
ἔπος δ᾽ ἀμείβου πρὸς ἔπος.
Answer word with word.
τούτοις ἀμείβου πᾶσιν εὐμαθές τί μοι.
Answer all these things with something easy for me to learn.
αἰδοῖα ἔπη ξένους ἀμείβεσθε.
Answer the strangers with respectful words.
πρὸς ταῦτ᾽ ἀμείβου καὶ λέγ᾽ εὐθαρσῶς ἐμοί.
Answer these things and speak boldly to me.

sense.def: to occupy a place in exchange, to enter

cit.quote: ποῖον δ᾽ ἀμείψεσθε γαίας πέδον τᾶσδ᾽ ἄρειον;
What better land than this will you exchange for?
πίτυλον, ὃς ἀεὶ δι᾽ Αχέροντ᾽ ἀμείβεται τὰν ἄστονον — θεωρίδα.
The oarage, which ever crosses the Acheron, the un-groaning — sacred ship.
τάχα δὲ παντελὴς χρόνος ἀμείψεται πρόθυρα δωμάτων.
Soon all-fulfilling time will pass the threshold of the house.
σκοπεῖτε κἀμείβεσθε τόνδε τὸν τόπον.
Consider and exchange this place.
οὔτις μερόπων ἀσινῆ βίοτον – ἀμείψεται,
No one of mortals will pass through life unharmed,
cit.note: ubi metro postulante ἀμείψειwill exchange restituit Erfurdtius.
where Erfurdt restored ἀμείψει [will exchange] as the meter demands.

cit.quote: ἐπεὶ δ᾽ ἐπεμνησάμαν ἀμειλίχων πόνων.
But when I recalled the unrelenting toils.
πολλῷ γ᾽ ἀμείνων τοὺς πέλας φρενοῦν ἔφυς ἢ σαυτόν.
You are far better at advising others than yourself.
οἱ κατὰ χθονὸς θεοὶ λαβεῖν ἀμείνους εἰσὶν ἢ μεθιέναι.
The gods below are better at taking than at letting go.
μηδ' αὐθαδίαν εὐβουλίας ἀμείνον᾽ ἡγήσῃ ποτέ.
Never consider stubbornness better than good counsel.
ἀπὸ στρατείας γάρ νιν ἠμποληκότα τὰ πλεῖστ᾽ ἀμείνον᾽ εὐφροσιν δεδεγμένη,
For having received him returning from the expedition, having gained most things better for her joy,
cit.note: post quae verba versus unus excidit.
after which words one verse has fallen out.

cit.quote: ἄμεινόν ἐστι – πάγον προσίζειν.
It is better to sit near the hill.
ὅμως ἄμεινον — · ἀλκῆς λαθέσθαι τῆσδε μηδαμῶς ποτέ.
Nevertheless it is better — never to forget this strength.

sense.def: I do not care for, I neglect.

cit.quote: καὶ τὸ μαμελεῖν (sic scripsi pro μὴ ἀμελεῖν, quod est in Μ, sed eraso α) μάθε.
And learn to be careless (I wrote this for μὴ ἀμελεῖν [not to be careless], which is in M, but with the alpha erased).
τῶνδε μάμελεϊν (hic quoque et 773 μὴ ἀμελεῖν Μ) θεῶν,
to be careless of these gods (here too and at 773 M has μὴ ἀμελεῖν [not to be careless])
φρόνει μὲν ὡς ταρβοῦσα μἀμελεῖν θεῶν.
Think, as one fearing, not to be careless of the gods.
Κύπριδος δ᾽ οὐκ ἀμελεῖ θεσμὸς ὅδ᾽ εὔφρων.
This kindly ordinance does not neglect Cypris.
τάχυνε δ, ὡς ἄμεμπτος ὦ χρόνου.
Hurry, so that I may be blameless in respect of time.
τέρμον άμεμπτον (sic Herm. pr. ἀμέμπτων) πρὸς ἅπαντα.
a blameless end (thus Hermann, previously ἀμέμπτων [of blameless ones]) in all things.
πράξας ἀμέμπτως.
having acted blamelessly.
γείνατο παῖδ᾽ ἀμεμφή.
She bore a blameless child.
ἔστι γὰρ πλοῦτός γ᾽ ἀμεμφής.
For wealth at least is blameless.
ἀμεμφή τόνδ᾽ ἐτεινάτην λόγον.
They stretched out this blameless word.
cit.note: Sic Hermannus pro ἀμομφητονδετινατον λόγονa blameless ... word .
Thus Hermann for ἀμομφητονδετινατον λόγον [a blameless ... word].

cit.quote: διαλλακτῆρι δ᾽ οὐκ ἀμεμφία φίλοις.
But for friends there is no blamelessness in the reconciler.
cit.note: Recte schol. μέμφονται δὲ οἱ φίλοι αὐτῶν τὸν διαλλακτῆρα σίδηρον ὡς μηδετέρῳ χαρισάμενονtheir friends blame the reconciling iron as having favored neither side .
Correctly the scholiast: μέμφονται δὲ οἱ φίλοι αὐτῶν τὸν διαλλακτῆρα σίδηρον ὡς μηδετέρῳ χαρισάμενον [their friends blame the reconciling iron as having favored neither side].

cit.quote: Σύν τ᾽ εὐκλείᾳ καὶ ἀμηνίτῳ βάξει.
With good repute and a report not causing anger.
χειμῶν Ἀχαιῶν οὐκ ἀμήνιτον θεοῖς
a storm of the Achaeans not without the anger of the gods
cit.note: tempestatem non sine deorum ira ortam.
a storm not arisen without the anger of the gods.

cit.quote: ἐπεί σ᾽ ἔθηκε Ζεὺς ἀμηνίτως δόμοις κοινωνὸν εἶναι χερνίβων.
Since Zeus placed you without anger to be a partner in the lustral waters of the house.
cit.note: ἀμηνίτοιςwithout anger Auratus.
ἀμηνίτοις [without anger] Auratus.

form.gloss: to be at a loss, to be without resources

cit.quote: ὥστ᾽ ἀμηχανεῖν ὅποι τράποιντο.
so as to be at a loss where to turn.
ἀμηχανῶ — εὐπάλαμον μέριμναν ὅπα τράπωμαι.
I am at a loss — where to turn my resourceful thought.
νῦν γὰρ ἐξ αἰνιγμάτων ἐπαργέμοισι θεσφάτοις ἀμηχανῶ.
For now I am at a loss amid riddles and dark oracles.
τέρμα δ᾽ ἀμηχανῶ.
But I am at a loss for the end.
ἀμηχανῶ δέ.
But I am at a loss.
ἰδὼν δ᾽ ἀμηχανοῦντά σ᾽ ὁ Ζεὺς οἰκτερεῖ.
And Zeus, seeing you at a loss, pities you.
πολλάκι δ᾽ ἐν κακοῖσι τὸν ἀμάχανον (sic scripsi pro ἀμήχανον) — ὀρθοι.
Often in troubles the helpless one (I wrote this for ἀμήχανον [helpless]) — he raises up.

sense.def: qui efugi vel averti nulla ratione potest.
which can by no means be escaped or averted.

cit.quote: ἀμηχάνοις δύαις.
with helpless miseries.
[ἀμηχάνοισι δυσπραξίαις.]
[with helpless misfortunes.]
δεινός γὰρ εὑρεῖν κατ' ἀμηχάνων πόρους.
For he is clever at finding ways out of helpless situations.
ἀμήχανον βόσκημα πημονῆς.
a helpless pasture of misery.
ἀμήχανον τεύχημα (τέχνημα Nauckius) καὶ δυσέκδυτον,
a helpless contrivance (Nauck: τέχνημα [artifice]) and hard to escape,
cit.note: de quo schol. Eur. Or. 25 ἡ γὰρ Κλυταιμνήστρα χιτῶνα ΰφανεν (Αγαμέμνονι) οὔτε ταῖς χερσὶν οὔτε τὴ κεφαλῇ ἔκδυσιν ἔχονταfor Clytemnestra wove a tunic (for Agamemnon) that had no way out for the hands or the head .

about which the scholiast on Eur. Or. 25: ἡ γὰρ Κλυταιμνήστρα χιτῶνα ΰφανεν (Αγαμέμνονι) οὔτε ταῖς χερσὶν οὔτε τὴ κεφαλῇ ἔκδυσιν ἔχοντα [for Clytemnestra wove a tunic (for Agamemnon) that had no way out for the hands or the head].

cit.quote: ἴδεσθ᾽ Ἀτρειδὰν τὰ λοιπ᾽ ἀμηχάνως (scribendum ἀμαχάνως) ἔχοντα.
See the son of Atreus in the rest helplessly (should be written ἀμαχάνως [helplessly]) situated.
τάδε ἀμηχάνως ἔχει (sic Butlerus pro ἐμοί).
these things are helpless (thus Butler for ἐμοί [to me]).
κναπτόμενοι δ᾽ ἁλὸς αἰνὰ | σκύλλονται πρὸς ἀναύδων παίδων τᾶς ἀμιάντου.
And being carded by the dread salt sea, they are torn by the voiceless children of the undefiled one.
cit.note: Sic emendavi quod in M legitur γναπτόμενοι δ᾽ ἁλὶ δεινὰbeing carded by the salt sea, dread things —, de quo pluribus dixi in Philologo vol. 13 p. 480. Absurdum est αμιάντουof the undefiled one sine ἁλοςof the salt sea dici, quod omitti non poterat, addi vero ἁλιby the salt sea ubi non opus erat.

Thus I emended what is read in M: γναπτόμενοι δ᾽ ἁλὶ δεινὰ — [carded by the sea, terrible things —], about which I have said more in Philologus vol. 13 p. 480. It is absurd for ἀμιάντου [undefiled] to be said without ἁλός [of the sea], which could not be omitted, but to add ἁλί [by the sea] where it was not needed.

entry.note: [vitiose pro ἄμαλαsheaves , quod v.]
[erroneously for ἄμαλα [sheaves], which see]

cit.quote: οἶμαι βοὴν ἄμικτον ἐν πόλει πρέπειν.
I think an unsociable cry is fitting in the city.
πτερύγων θοαῖς ἁμίλλαις.
with swift contests of wings
ἀκέλευστος άμισθος ἀοιδά.
unbidden, unpaid song
λύπη ἄμισθος.
unpaid grief
οἷος Ἀμίστρης ἠδ᾽ Αρταφρένης.
such as Amistres and Artaphrenes.

sense.note: Sed Pers. 320 in initio trimetri Ἀμίστρις,Amistris, ubi ἈμηστριςAmestris Brunckius.
But at Pers. 320 at the beginning of the trimeter it is Ἀμίστρις [Amistris], where Brunck has Ἀμηστρις [Amestris].

sense.def: (for ἀναμίγνυμι [to mix in]) I mix in.

cit.quote: μέλαινα δ᾽ ἀμμεμίζεται στονόεσσα πλαγά.
and a black, groaning blow is mixed in.
cit.note: Sic correxi quod est in M ἂνif (in aὖagain mutatum) μεμίζεταιwill be mixed .
Thus I corrected what is in M: ἂν [if] (changed to αὖ [again]) μεμίζεται [will be mixed].

entry.note: ] Λαν. ἄμμιγα ν [mixed] see under νὰ ἀναμίξ [to mix in].

cit.quote: οὐδ᾽ ἀμνημονῶ.
nor am I unmindful.
έχθροξένοις τε καὶ θεῶν ἀμνήμασι.
to enemies and to those unmindful of the gods.
τῶν μεγάλων πεδίων ἀμοίρους.
without a share of the great plains.
παλλεύκων δὲ πέπλων ἄμοιρος μούνα ἐτύχθην.
but without a share of white-robed garments, I alone was born.
cit.note: Sic postulante metro emendavi pro ἄμοιρος ἄκληρος ἐτύχθηνI was born without a share, without a lot , sublato glossemate ἄκληροςwithout a lot , addito vero quod sensus postulat μούναalone .

Thus I emended, as the meter demanded, for ἄμοιρος ἄκληρος ἐτύχθην [I was born without a share, without a lot], removing the gloss ἄκληρος [without a lot] and adding what the sense requires, μούνα [alone].

sense.note: [Ib. 890 γ᾽ ἀμοίρουat least without a share corruptum ex γαμόρῳto the landowner , quod v.]
[At line 890 γ᾽ ἀμοίρου [at least without a share] is corrupt from γαμόρῳ [to the landowner], which see]

cit.quote:
ἱερᾶς νυκτὸς
ἀμολγόν.
the darkness of the holy night.

entry.note: [vitiose pro αμεμφή τόνδthis blameless one '. V. ἀμεμφήςblameless .]
[erroneously for ἀμεμφή τόνδ' [this blameless one]. See ἀμεμφής [blameless].]

cit.quote: ὅμως δ᾽ ἄμομφον ὄντα σ' αἱροῦμαι πόλει.
Nevertheless, though you are blameless, I choose you for the city.
πρὸς ὑμῶν πῶς τιθεῖσ᾽ ἄμομφος ;
How am I to be considered blameless by you?

sense.def: who has nothing to be blamed for

cit.quote: λέγειν δ᾽ ἄμομφον όντα τοὺς πέλας κακῶς πρόσω δικαίων.
to speak ill of one's neighbors, though blameless, beyond what is just.
cit.note: Sic Robortellus pro άμορφονshapeless .
Thus Robortellus for ἄμορφον [shapeless].

sense.note: Pro ἐμόςmy dixerunt tragici ubi syllaba prima longa opus erat, de quo v. quae dixi in Lexico Sophocleo p. 26.
The tragedians used it for ἐμός [my] when the first syllable needed to be long, on which see what I said in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 26.

cit.quote: τὸν ἀμόν νυν ἀντίπαλον εὐτυχεῖν θεοὶ δοῖεν.
May the gods grant that my adversary now prosper.
ὦ πανδάκρυτον ἀμὸν Οἰδίπου γένος.
O my much-wept race of Oedipus.
κροτητὸν ἀμὸν καὶ πανάθλιον κάρα.
my head, beaten and all-wretched.
έκατι δ᾽ ἀμᾶν χερῶν.
by the will of our hands.
δι᾽ ἀμὸν γάμον.
because of my marriage.
ἀμὸν ἀρχαῖον γένος.
my ancient race.

sense.note: Ineptae illatum in M Eum. 440 ἑστίας ἁμῆς πέλας,near my hearth, quasi quintus pes trimetri spondeo opus habeat. Recte ἐμῆςmy in apogr. Recte vero ib. 311, ubi in Μ ἐπινωμᾷ στάσις ἅμαthe faction distributes together legitur, restitutum est ἀμάour , nisi quis ἁμάour , quod pro ἡμετέραour dictum sit, malit cum Cantero: qua significatione tragicos ἁμόςour dixisse valde incertum est, ut ostendi in Lexico Sophocleo. ἁμόςour ubique M.

It was wrongly inserted in M at Eum. 440: ἑστίας ἁμῆς πέλας [near my hearth], as if the fifth foot of the trimeter needed a spondee. Correctly ἐμῆς [my] in the copies. But correctly at line 311, where in M ἐπινωμᾷ στάσις ἅμα [the faction distributes together] is read, it has been restored to ἀμά [our], unless one prefers ἁμά [our], which is said for ἡμετέρα [our], with Canter: in which sense it is very uncertain that the tragedians used ἁμός [our], as I showed in the Lexicon Sophocleum. ἁμός [our] everywhere in M.

cit.quote: ᾤοντ᾽ ἀμοχθὶ πρὸς βίαν τε δεσπόσειν.
They thought they would rule without toil and by force.
παλαιᾶς ἀμπέλου γάνος τόδε.
this delight of the ancient vine.
μάχλον ἄμπελον.
luxuriant vine.
cit.note: V. μάχλοςluxuriant .
See μάχλος [luxuriant].

cit.quote: ἀτιμίαν γε παιδὸς ἀμφὶ σώματι ἐσθημάτων κλύουσαν, ἥ νιν ἀμπέχει.

entry.note: || ἁπλάκημαa fault et ἀπλακεῖνto have erred interdum dixerunt tragici ubi syllaba prima brevi opus erat. Semel Aeschylus Eum. 934 τὰ γὰρ ἐκ προτέρων ἀπλακήματαFor the faults from earlier times Sic Pauwius pro ἀμπλακήματαfaults .

The tragedians sometimes said ἁπλάκημα [a fault] and ἀπλακεῖν [to have erred] where the first syllable needed to be short. Once Aeschylus Eum. 934 τὰ γὰρ ἐκ προτέρων ἀπλακήματα [for the faults from earlier times]. Thus Pauwius for ἀμπλακήματα [faults].

necessity surrounding the city,
cit.note: ubi schol. τὴν ἐκ διαφόρων πόλεων ἀνάγκην, ὅ ἐστι πόλεμον· ἐκ διαφόρων γὰρ πόλεων ἦσαν οἱ Ἕλληνες.the necessity from different cities, that is, war; for the Greeks were from different cities. quocum parum apte comparat ἀμφιμάτορας κόρουςchildren of different mothers Euripidis Andr. 465, de quo v. s. v. ἀμφιμήτωρof different mother . Recte Blomfieldus necessitatem urbi circumdatam intelligit, sc. quum ab hostibus obsidione capta esset, ut ἀμφιτειχῆ λεώνthe people around the walls Aeschylus dixit Sept. 290 populum moenia obsidentem.

where the scholiast explains it as the necessity from different cities, that is, war; for the Greeks were from different cities. With which he compares, not very aptly, ἀμφιμάτορας κόρους [children of different mothers] of Euripides Andr. 465, about which see under ἀμφιμήτωρ [of different mother]. Blomfield rightly understands it as necessity surrounding the city, namely when it was besieged by enemies, as Aeschylus said ἀμφιτειχῆ λεών [the people around the walls] Sept. 290, the people besieging the walls.

entry.note: particula potentialis, cuius de vi et significatione recte et dilucide praecipit Apollonius de syntaxi 3, 6 p. 205, 3 τὰ γεγονότα τῶν πραγμάτων ὁ σύνδεσμος ἀναιρεῖν θέλει, περιστάνων αὐτὰ εἰς τὸ δύνασθαι, ἔνθεν καὶ δυνητικός εἴρηται. τὸ μὲν γὰρ ἔγραψα ἢ τὸ ἔγραφον ἢ τὸ ἐγεγράφειν ἢ ἀπὸ μέρους γεγονότα ἐστὶν, ἢ καὶ ἔκπαλαι γεγονότα· ἔνθεν προσέρχεται τοῖς δυναμένοις τὴν ὕλην αὐτοῦ παραδέξασθαι, ἔγραφον ἄν, ἔγραψα ἂν, ἐγεγράφειν ἄν· οὐ μὴν τῷ γράφω ἢ γράψω· οὐ γὰρ παρώχηται, ἵν᾽ ἐγχωρήσῃ καὶ ἡ ἐκ τοῦ συνδέσμου ἀναίρεσις μὲν τοῦ γεγονότος, ἐπαγγελία δὲ τοῦ ἐσομένου.The conjunction wishes to cancel the actuality of the events, turning them into potentiality, whence it is also called 'potential'. For 'I wrote' or 'I was writing' or 'I had written' are either partially actualized or long since actualized; hence it attaches to those capable of receiving its material: 'I would be writing', 'I would have written', 'I would have written'; but not to 'I write' or 'I will write'; for it is not past, so that the cancellation of the actual by the conjunction and the promise of the future may be possible. Multo copiosior explanatio est, sed erroribus non libera, grammatici in Bekkeri Anecd. p. 126-128. Est autem haec particula ubique verbo adiuncta aut expresso aut ex praecedentibus intelligendo. De temporibus verborum et modis quibuscum construi potest haec sunt tenenda:

a potential particle, about whose force and meaning Apollonius in On Syntax 3, 6 p. 205, 3 correctly and clearly teaches: “the conjunction wishes to do away with the actual occurrence of events, turning them into possibility, whence it is also called ‘potential’. For ‘I wrote’ or ‘I was writing’ or ‘I had written’ are either partially completed or completed long ago; therefore it attaches to those capable of receiving its material: ‘I would be writing’, ‘I would have written’, ‘I would have written’; but not to ‘I write’ or ‘I will write’; for it is not past, so that the conjunction’s removal of the actual occurrence and promise of the future may be possible.” A much fuller explanation, but not free from errors, is that of the grammarian in Bekker’s Anecdota p. 126-128. This particle is always attached to a verb, either expressed or understood from the preceding. Regarding the tenses and moods of verbs with which it can be constructed, the following must be noted:

sense.note: Construitur cum imperfecto vel aoristo in apodosi post enuntiationem condicionalem.
It is constructed with the imperfect or aorist in the apodosis after a conditional clause.

sense.note: De optativo notandum nunquam ἄνwould cum eo coniungi ubi reapse est optantis, quaeque optandi fere significationem habent πῶς ἄνhow would et τίς ἄνwho would cum optativo coniuncta interrogantis esse, non optantis, quorum exempla v. s. v. πῶςhow et τίςwho . Non raro ἂνwould cum optativo coniungitur significatione imperativi.

Regarding the optative, it must be noted that ἄν is never joined with it where it is truly a wish; and expressions that have roughly the force of wishing, πῶς ἄν [how would] and τίς ἄν [who would], when joined with the optative, are those of someone asking, not wishing; for examples see under πῶς and τίς. Not rarely ἄν is joined with the optative with the force of an imperative.

sense.note: Frequentissimus usus particulae est cum optativo potentiali coniunctae in oratione minus quam quae indicativo sine v exprimitur confidenti. Ac primo quidem post vel ante enuntiationem condicionalem, expressam per εἰif cum optativo,

The most frequent use of the particle is when joined with the potential optative in a statement less confident than that expressed by the indicative without it. And first, after or before a conditional clause expressed by εἰ with the optative,

sense.note: Cum coniunctivo non coniungitur nisi praemisso pronomine, ut ὃς ἂνwhoever et quae ab eo ducuntur, aut particula, ut ὅπως, εῦτε, ἕως, ἡνίκα, πρίν, ἔς τεwhen, until, while, when, before, until , neque unquam postponitur coniunctivo, sed necessario praecedit.

It is not joined with the subjunctive unless a pronoun is placed before it, such as ὃς ἂν [whoever] and words derived from it, or a particle, such as ὅπως [in order that], εὖτε [when], ἕως [until], ἡνίκα [when], πρίν [before], ἔς τε [until], and it is never postponed after the subjunctive, but necessarily precedes it.

|| ἄνα [up] undergoes apocope in Suppl. 350 ἂμ πέτραις [on the rocks] and 550 Λύδιά τ᾽ ἂγ γύαλα [and Lydian glens], as Hermann corrected for metrical reasons instead of τε γύαλα [and glens], and in compounds ἀγκαλέομαι [I call upon], ἄγκρισις [judgment], ἀλλύτας [unloosed], άμβόαμα [I cry aloud], ἀμβοάω [I cry aloud], ἀμμίγνυμι [I mix], ἀμπέμπω [I send up], ἀμπίπτω [I fall upon], ἀμφαίνω [I show], ἀμφέρω [I carry about]. ἀνδαίω [I kindle], ἀντέλλω [I rise], ἀντολή [rising], ἀντρέπω [I overturn], and δυσάγκριτος [hard to judge].

τίς ὁ κραιπνῷ ποδὶ πηδήματος εὐπετοῦς ἀνάσσων;
who is it that leaps with swift foot of nimble leap?
cit.note: Quod per κρατῶνruling explicat Thomas Mag. Recte Turnebus ἀναίσσωνleaping up , nisi quod ἀνάσσωνleaping up scribere debebat.
Which Thomas Magister explains by κρατῶν [ruling]. Correctly Turnebus ἀναίσσων [leaping up], except that he should have written ἀνάσσων [leaping up].

cit.quote: ἅπαξ θανόντος οὔτις ἔστ᾽ ἀνάστασις.
once a man is dead, there is no resurrection.
πόλεων ἀναστάσεις.
destructions of cities.
άλωσιν Ἰλίου τ᾿ ἀνάστασιν.
the capture and destruction of Troy.
ἀναστατήρα Καδμείων χθονός.
destroyer of the land of the Cadmeans.
Τροίας, ἀναστατῆρας.
destroyers of Troy.
Ιλίου ἀναστάτης.
destroyer of Ilium.
δίπαις τοί σ᾿ ἐπιτύμβιος θρήνος ἀναστενάζει.
the twofold tomb-lament groans for you.
ὡς πόλλ᾽ ἀμαυρᾶς ἐκ φρενός μ' ἀναστένειν.
how many things from my dim mind make me groan.
τί δήτ' ἐγὼ κάτοικτος ὡδ᾽ ἀναστένω;
why then do I, pitiable, groan thus?

sense.note: [De 408 v. s. στένωto groan .]
[On 408 see στένω [to groan].]

sense.def: to turn back, to turn in the opposite direction

cit.quote: ἀτὰρ φράσον μοι τοῦτ᾽ ἀναστρέψας πάλιν.
but tell me this, turning back again.
και με βαθεῖα κηλὶς ἐκ βυθῶν ἀναστρέφει.
and a deep stain from the depths turns me back.
Κωρυκὶς πέτρα κοίλη, φίλορνις, δαιμόνων ἀναστροφή.
the Corycian rock, hollow, bird-loving, turning-place of the gods.
πτώματ᾽ οὐκ ἀνασχετά.
falls not to be endured.
θρέμματ᾽ οὐκ ἀνασχετά
creatures not to be endured.
κακοὶ γὰρ εὖ πράσσοντες οὐκ ἀνασχετοί.
for the wicked, when they prosper, are not to be endured.
Ἀἴγυπτος Δήμητρος ἀντέλλει στάχυν.
Egypt makes the corn of Demeter rise.
ταρφὺς ἀντέλλουσα θρίξ.
thick hair rising.
τρέφουσ᾽ ἀνατί
nourishing without harm
cit.note: Sic scripsi pro ανατείwithout harm : de quo v. Lexicon Soph Ρ. 37.
Thus I wrote for ανατεί [without harm]: on which see Lexicon Sophocles p. 37.

sense.def: s. ἀνάτλημιto endure (etsi neutra forma usi sunt veteres, sed aoristo solo ἔτληνI endured quum verb simplicis tum compositorum) perfero, sustineo.
see ἀνάτλημι [to endure] (although the ancients used neither form, but only the aorist ἔτλην [I endured] of both the simple and compound verbs) to endure, to sustain.

cit.quote: πολύθρηνον αἰῶνα, φίλον πολιτῶν μέλεον αἷμ ἀνατλᾶσα.
a much-lamented life, enduring the pitiful blood of her dear citizens.
πῶς δῆτ᾽ ἄνατος ἦσθα Λοξίου κότῳ;
How then were you unharmed by the wrath of Loxias?
εἴη δ ἄνατον πρᾶγμα τοῦτ᾽ ἀστοξένων.
May this matter be without harm to the strangers.
ἄνατον φυγάν.
an unharmed exile
ὅπως ἄνατα ταῦτα ἐκτελευτήσει.
so that these things may be accomplished without harm.
δδε Καδμείων ἤρυξε πόλιν μἀνατραπῆναι.
This man caused the city of the Cadmeans to be overturned.
cit.note: Sic scripsi pro μὴ ἀνατραπῆναιnot to be overturned .
Thus I wrote for μὴ ἀνατραπῆναι [not to be overturned].

cit.quote: μή μέγας πλοῦτος (δαίμων Heimsoethius) κονίσας οὔδας ἀντρέψῃ ποδὶ ὄλβον.
lest great wealth (a divinity, according to Heimsoeth) having stirred up the dust overturn prosperity with its foot.
μηδὲν ἐν φάει (δέει Auratus) καρδίαν (φάει καρδίας legisse videtur scholiasta) ἀνατρέφων.
nourishing nothing in the light (fear, according to Auratus) in the heart (the scholiast seems to have read 'in the light of the heart').
δωμάτων γὰρ εἱλόμαν ἀνατροπάς.
For I chose the overturnings of the house.
εἰς ἀναύγητον μολεῖν Ἅιδην.
to go to dark Hades.

sense.note: Forma Dorica
Doric form

cit.quote: ἀναυδάτῳ μένει.
with unspeakable force.
αἰθερία κόνις με πείθει φανεῖσ᾽, ἄναυδος σαφής ἔτυμος ἄγγελος.
The dust in the air, appearing, persuades me, a voiceless, clear, true messenger.
ὁρῶ κόνιν, ἄναυδον ἄγγελον στρατοῦ.
I see dust, a voiceless messenger of the army.
ἁλὸς σκύλλονται πρὸς ἀναύδων παίδων (i. e. ἰχθύων) τᾶς ἀμιάντου.
They are torn by the sea, by the voiceless children (i.e., fish) of the undefiled one.
οὔτ᾽ ἄναυδος οὔτε σοι δαίων φλόγα.
neither voiceless nor kindling a flame for you.
ὁρᾷς δίκην ἄναυδον.
You see voiceless justice.
ὃς ἀστενακτὶ θύννος ὡς ἠνέσχετο ἄναυδος.
who, like a tunny, endured without groaning, voiceless.
χαλινῶν ἀναύδῳ μένει.
with the voiceless force of the reins.
cit.note: Schol, τῷ ἀναύδῳ μένει τῶν χαλινῶν τῶν μὴ ἐώντων αὐτὴν λαλεῖνwith the voiceless force of the reins that do not allow her to speak .
Scholiast: τῷ ἀναύδῳ μένει τῶν χαλινῶν τῶν μὴ ἐώντων αὐτὴν λαλεῖν [with the voiceless force of the reins that do not allow her to speak].

cit.quote: ἐξέφθινθ᾽ αἱ τρίσκαλμοι νᾶες ἄναες ἄναες,
The three-banked ships perished, ships without ships, without ships.
cit.note: i.e. naves quae non amplius naves sunt: ubi deleto altero avaeç addidi oloî.
i.e., ships that are no longer ships: where, having deleted the second avaeç, I added oloî.

cit.quote: βοὰν ἀμφαίνω.
I raise a cry.
cit.note: Scriptura incerta nec certior Hermanni coniectura Ch. 815 ἀμφανεῖto reveal pro ἄλλα φανεῖother things will appear .
The reading is uncertain, nor is Hermann's conjecture at Ch. 815 ἀμφανεῖ [to reveal] for ἄλλα φανεῖ [other things will appear] more certain.

cit.quote: ἀναφαίνεται δ᾽ ὁ βλάπτων.
The one who harms is revealed.
έτοιμότερα γέλωτος ἀνέφερον λίβη.
They brought libations more ready for laughter.
καὶ τόδ᾽ ἀμφέρειν γένοιτ᾽ ἂν ἄχθος αἱματοσταγές φόνῳ,
And this burden, dripping with blood, would be brought upon us by the murder.
cit.note: i. e. hoc quoque nobis propter caedem illam evenit, ut exp. Hermannus. ἂν φέρεινto bring Turnebus, αὖ φέρεινto bring again Blomfieldus.
i.e., this too happens to us because of that murder, as Hermann explains. ἂν φέρειν [to bring] Turnebus, αὖ φέρειν [to bring again] Blomfield.

cit.quote: ἀναφυγάς κακῶν.
escapes from evils.
πέμπουσι δ᾽ ἀνδαίοντες φλογὸς μέγαν πώγωνα.
They send, kindling the great beard of flame.
Ἀνδραίμονος γένεθλον (Andromacha).
the offspring of Andraemon (Andromache).
τὰ μὲν — ἔθρυπτ᾽ ἄνωθεν ἀνδρακὰς καθημένοις.
the things — were broken from above upon those sitting man by man.
θυμὸς ἀνδρείᾳ φλέγων.
spirit blazing with courage.
ἐν ἀνδρείᾳ στέγῃ.
in a manly dwelling.
οὐ τοῦτον ἐκ γῆς τῆσδε χρῆν σ᾽ ἀνδρηλατεῖν;
Should you not have banished this man from this land?
ἀδελφὸν ἠνδρηλάτησεν ἐκ πόλεώς τε καὶ δόμων.
He banished his brother from the city and from his home.
οὐ φημ᾽ Ὀρέστην σ᾽ ἐνδίκως ἀνδρηλατεῖν.
I say that you are not justly banishing Orestes.
ἀνδρηλάτην φυγῇ τὸν αὐτόν τόνδε τίσασθαι τρόπον.
to punish this same man in the same way, as a banisher into exile.
γυναικὸς ἀνδρόβουλον ἐλπίζον κέαρ.
expecting the manly-counselling heart of a woman.

sense.note: ἀνδρόβουλος γυνήa woman with manly counsel apud Phrynichum in Bekk. Anecd. p. 19, 23 fortasse ex hoc loco. Simile est quod Hesychius annotavit ἀνδρολήμηνman-spirited (recte ἀνδρόλημονman-spirited Meinekius Philol. vol. 13 p. 516): ἀνδρὸς ἔχουσαν λῆμαhaving the spirit of a man .

ἀνδρόβουλος γυνή [a woman with manly counsel] in Phrynichus in Bekker's Anecdota p. 19, 23 perhaps from this passage. Similar is what Hesychius noted: ἀνδρολήμην [man-spirited] (correctly ἀνδρόλημον [man-spirited] according to Meineke Philol. vol. 13 p. 516): ἀνδρὸς ἔχουσαν λῆμα [having the spirit of a man].

cit.quote: πειραὶ (πεῖραι Portus) κοπάνων ἀνδροδαΐκτων.
attempts of man-slaying cleavers.
ἀνδροδάϊκτον ἀκούων- κόπον.
hearing the man-slaying toil.
ἀνδροθνῆτας Ἰλίου φθοράς
man-slaying destructions of Ilium
cit.note: Troiae eversionem cum virorum caede coniunctam.
the destruction of Troy joined with the slaughter of men.

cit.quote: ἀνδροκμῆτα πέλεκυν.
man-slaying axe.
μόχθοις ἀνδροκμήσι.
with man-slaying toils.
ἀνδροκμήτας — τύχας.
man-slaying fortunes.
ἀνδροκμής λοιγός.
man-slaying destruction.
πικρόκαρπον ἀνδροκτασίαν τελεῖν αἵματος οὐ θεμιστοῦ.
to accomplish bitter-fruited slaughter of men with unlawful blood.
ἀνδροκτονοῦσα πατέρ᾽ ἐμὸν κατέκτανεν.
she killed my father, slaying a man.
ἀνδρολέτειραν νόσον, ῥίψοπλον ἄταν.
man-destroying plague, shield-casting ruin.
μηδ᾽ εἰς Ἑλένην κότον ἐκτρέψης, ὡς ἀνδρολέτειρ ἀξύστατον ἄλγος ἔπραξεν.
do not turn your wrath upon Helen, saying that she, a man-destroyer, wrought unbearable grief.
ἀνδρόπαις ἀνήρ.
a man who is a boy.
ἀνδρο πλήθεια στρατού.
abundance of men of the army.

form.gloss: place where a man is slain

sense.def: place where a man is slain

cit.quote: ἀνδροσφαγεῖον (sic Dobraeus) καὶ πεδορραντήριον,
man-slaying place (thus Dobree) and ground-sprinkling,
cit.note: ubi M ἀνδρὸς σφάγιον (σφαγεῖονa man's victim (slaughter-house) pr.) καὶ πέδονand the ground (v ex p facto) ῥαντήριονsprinkling . Simile est ανδροκτονεῖονman-slaying place , de quo dixit Phrynichus in Bekk. Anecd. p. 28, 9.

where M has ἀνδρὸς σφάγιον [a man's victim] (σφαγεῖον [slaughter-house] pr.) καὶ πέδον [and the ground] (v made from p) ῥαντήριον [sprinkling]. Similar is ανδροκτονεῖον [man-slaying place], about which Phrynichus spoke in Bekker's Anecdota p. 28, 9.

cit.quote: νεανίδων ἐπηράτων ἀνδροτυχεῖς βιότους.]
lives of lovely maidens that obtain husbands.
τὸν ἀνδροφόντην, τὸν πόλεως ταράκτορα.
the man-slayer, the disturber of the city.
πατρὸς κατ᾽ ἀνδρῶνας εὐτραπέζους.
through the well-tabled men's halls of my father.
εἰς ἀνδρῶνας εὐξένους δόμων.
into the hospitable men's halls of the house.

sense.def: efuse (ἐκκεχυμένωςpoured forth Hesych.), i. e. sine more.
without restraint (ἐκκεχυμένως [poured forth] Hesych.), i.e. without custom.

cit.quote: φεύγειν ἀνέδην διὰ κῦμα ἅλιον.
to flee without restraint through the briny wave.
[τί σοι φάμενος ἢ τί ῥέξας τύχοιμ᾽ ἂν καθ᾽ ἓν οὐρίσας, ἔνθα σ' ἔχουσιν εὐναί?]
[What could I say or do to meet you, having set my course one by one, where your bed holds you?]
cit.note: [ubi Μ ἄνκαθενM: from above , superscripto ab correctore é, i. e. έκαθενfrom there , ut ἄγκαθενfrom above scribendum videri posset, quod olim coniecit Hermannus, si ἂνperhaps abesse posset. Litterae igitur καθενdown , nisi corruptae sunt, καθ᾿ ἕνone by one scribendae sunt, quod pro καθάπαξonce for all dici potuit.]

[where M has ἄνκαθεν [from above], with é written above by a corrector, i.e. έκαθεν [from there], so that ἄγκαθεν [from above] might seem to be written, which Hermann once conjectured, if ἂν [perhaps] could be absent. Therefore the letters καθεν [down], unless they are corrupt, are to be written καθ᾿ ἕν [one by one], which could be said for καθάπαξ [once for all].]

cit.quote: ἐπασσυτεροτριβῆ τὰ χερὸς ὀρέγματα ἄνωθεν ἀνέκαθεν,
the frequent-rubbed stretchings of the hand from above, from above,
cit.note: ubi notanda sunt coniuncta synonyma ἄνωθενfrom above et ἀνέκαθενfrom above .
where the conjoined synonyms ἄνωθεν [from above] and ἀνέκαθεν [from above] are to be noted.

cit.quote: ἀνέκαθεν βαρυπεσῆ καταφέρω ποδός ἀκμάν.
from above I bring down the heavy-falling edge of my foot.
cit.note: Sic postulante metro Pearsonus correxit quod est in Μ ἄγκαθενM: from above cum syncope, de qua diximus s. v. ἄγκαθενfrom above .
Thus, with the meter demanding it, Pearson corrected what is in M, ἄγκαθεν [from above], with syncope, about which we have spoken under the word ἄγκαθεν [from above].

cit.quote: ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἀνεκτόν.
but it is not bearable.

sense.def: servile, unworthy of a free man

cit.quote: κοίταν τάνδ᾽ ἀνελεύθερον.
this unworthy bed.
[ οὔτ᾽ ἀνελεύθερον οἶμαι θάνατον τῷδε γενέσθαι.]
[nor do I think that death was unworthy for him.]
cit.note: Quae verba ex versibus 1494 1518 ficta recte delevit Seidlerus.
Which words, fabricated from verses 1494 and 1518, Seidler rightly deleted.

cit.quote: ποδαπόν όμιλον τόνδ᾽ ἀνελληνόστολον προσφωνούμεν;
What foreign crowd is this, not dressed in Greek fashion, that we address?
τήνδ' ἀνέλπιστον φυγήν.
this unhoped-for flight.
πτανά τε καὶ πεδοβάμονα κἀνεμοέντων αἰγίδων φράσαι κότον,
to tell the wrath of winged and ground-walking creatures and of windy aegises,
cit.note: ubi κἀνεμόεντ᾽ ἂνand windy would recte correxit Blomfieldus.
where Blomfield rightly corrected κἀνεμόεντ᾽ ἂν [and windy would].

cit.quote: ἀγρίων ἀνέμων.
of wild winds.
ἀνέμων πνεύματα πάντων.
the blasts of all winds.
όμβροφόροισιν ἀνέμοις.
with rain-bearing winds.
ἀνέμων ἀήματα.
the blasts of winds.
ἔνθ᾽ οὔτε μίμνειν ἄνεμος οὔτ᾽ ἐκπλεῖν ἐᾷ.
where neither does the wind allow to remain nor to sail out.
ἐπεὶ δ᾽ ἀνῆλθε λαμπρὸν ἡλίου φάος.
But when the bright light of the sun had risen.

sense.note: [Ch. 536 ἀνῆλθονwent up corruptum ex ἀνῆθονbloomed . V. ἀναίθωto kindle .]
[Ch. 536 ἀνῆλθον [went up] corrupt from ἀνῆθον [bloomed]. See ἀναίθω.]

cit.quote: ἄνευ δορός.
without spear
οὐκ ἄνευ θεῶν τινός.
not without some god
ἄνευ χαλινῶν.
without bridles
ἄνευ τ᾽ ὀχημάτων χλιδῆς τε τῆς πάροιθεν.
without chariots and the former luxury
ἄνευ κακῶν.
without evils
ἄνευ δίκας.
without justice
ἄνευ φθόνου.
without envy
ἄνευ φόβου.
without fear
ἄνευ λύρας.
without lyre
ἄνευ Διός.
without Zeus
ἄνευ πολιτῶν· ἄνευ δὲ πενθημάτων.
without citizens; and without mourning
οὐκ ἄνευ δίκης.
not without justice
ἄνευ βοτῆρος.
without a shepherd
ἄνευ δορός.
without spear
ἄνευ δίκας.
without justice
ἄνευ μητρός.
without mother
ἄνευ σέθεν.
without you
ἄνευ σέθεν.
without you
οὐκ ἄνευ δήμου,
not without the people,
ἄνευ λύπης.
without grief
ἄνευ κλητῆρος.
without a summoner
ὧν ἀνευρήσει (sic Porsonus pro ἂν εὐρήσῃ) φόνον.
whose murder he will discover (thus Porson for ἂν εὐρήσῃ)
ἄκουε δ᾽ ἀν' οὓς ἔχων,
Listen, holding up your ears,
cit.note: i. e. ἄνω τὸ οὓς ἔχωνholding the ear upward , ut exp. grammatici in annot. indicati.
i.e. holding the ear upward, as the grammarians cited in the note explain.

cit.quote: πολλὰ γὰρ τὰ πρὶν κακὰ ἠνειχόμεσθα.
For we endured many former evils.
ἀλλ᾽ οὔτι πω τοιόνδε πῆμ᾽ ἀνεσχόμην.
But never yet have I endured such a calamity.
τῶν δ᾽ ἀρειφάτων ἐγὼ πρεπτῶν ἀγώνων οὐκ ἀνέξομαι τὸ μὴ οὐ τήνδ᾽ ἀστύνικον ἐν βροτοῖς τιμᾶν πόλιν.
Of the glorious contests of the slain I will not endure not to honor this city, victorious among mortals.
οὐκ ἐς φθόρον σιγῶσ᾽ ἀνασχήσει τάδε;
Will you not endure these things in silence to your ruin?
μόνης γάρ, οἶδα, σοῦ κλύων ἀνέξεται.
For I know that she will endure hearing from you alone.
καλουμένη δὲ φοιτὰς ἠνεσχόμην.
And being called a wanderer I endured.
ὃς ἀστενακτὶ θύννος ὡς ἠνέσχετο ἄναυδος.
Who, like a tunny, endured without groaning, speechless.
cit.note: Sic Iacobsius pro ηύχετοprayed , quod est ap. Athen. 7 p. 303 c.
Thus Jacobs for ηύχετο [prayed], which is in Athenaeus 7 p. 303 c.

cit.quote: συγγενῆ γάμον ἀνεψιῶν.
the kindred marriage of cousins
λέγοιτ' ἂν ὢν ἄνη τις.
one might say that there is some accomplishment.
ανηβῆσαι.
to grow young again
ἀνήκεστον πάθος.
an incurable suffering
ὦ θάνατε παιὰν μόνος γὰρ εἶ σὺ τῶν ἀνηκέστων κακῶν ἰατρός.
O death, healer, for you alone are the physician of incurable evils.

cit.note: ubi v. annot.
where see the note.

cit.quote: ἀνηκουστεῖν δὲ τῶν πατρὸς λόγων οἷόν τε πῶς;
But how is it possible to disobey the words of your father?

sense.def: (Doric ἀνάλιος) lacking the light of the sun

cit.quote: ἄντρων ἐν μυχοῖς ἀνηλίοις.
in the sunless recesses of caves
τὰν ἀνάλιον, πάνδοκον εἰς ἀφανῆ τε χέρσον.
the sunless, all-receiving land to the unseen
ἀνήλιοι, βροτοστυγεῖς δνόφοι.
sunless, mortal-hating darknesses
ἀναλίῳ (sic scripsi pro ἀνηλίῳ) λάπα.
with sunless (thus I wrote for ἀνηλίῳ) torch
ἀνήμεροι γὰρ οὐδὲ πρόσπλατοι ξένοις.
For they are savage and not approachable to strangers.
χθόνα ἀνήμερον τιθέντες ἡμερωμένην.
making the land savage that had been tamed
βρωτῆρας αἰχμὰς σπερμάτων ἀνημέρους.
eaters of the savage spears of seeds

entry.note: [a brevi, sed producto in formis epicis et lyricis ἀνέρος ἀνέρι ἀνέρα ἀνέρες ἀνέρων ἀνέραςman (genitive singular), man (dative singular), man (accusative singular), men (nominative plural), men (genitive plural), men (accusative plural) , quibus interdum in melicis usi sunt tragici. Aeschyli unum est exemplum in versu cretico Suppl. 426 γνῶθι δ᾽ ὕβριν ἀνέρωνknow the insolence of men .]

[from a short vowel, but lengthened in epic and lyric forms ἀνέρος ἀνέρι ἀνέρα ἀνέρες ἀνέρων ἀνέρας [of a man, to a man, a man, men, of men, men], which the tragedians sometimes used in lyric passages. Aeschylus has one example in a cretic verse Suppl. 426 γνῶθι δ᾽ ὕβριν ἀνέρων [know the insolence of men].]

sense.note: De homine mortali
Of a mortal human

cit.quote: λέγω κατ᾽ ἄνδρα, μὴ θεὸν, σέβειν ἐμέ.
I say to honor me as a man, not as a god.
μισήματ᾽ ἀνδρῶν καὶ θεῶν Ὀλυμπίων.
objects of hatred for men and Olympian gods

sense.note: Plene ἀνὴρ θνητόςa mortal man
Fully ἀνὴρ θνητός [mortal man]

cit.quote: τίς ἀνὴρ θνατὸς ἀλύξει;
What mortal man will escape?
οὔποτε θνατῶν τὰν Διὸς ἁρμονίαν ἀνδρῶν παρεξίασι βουλαί.
never will the counsels of men transgress the harmony of Zeus
cit.note: Sic ego correxi quod in M legitur οὔποτε τὰν Διὸς ἁρμονίαν θνατῶν παρεξίασι βουλαί.never will the counsels of mortals transgress the harmony of Zeus
Thus I corrected what is read in M: οὔποτε τὰν Διὸς ἁρμονίαν θνατῶν παρεξίασι βουλαί [never will the counsels of mortals transgress the harmony of Zeus].

cit.quote: ὡς μήτε θεῶν μήτε τις ἀνδρῶν τοῖσδ᾽ ἐγεγήθει,
so that neither any of the gods nor any of men rejoiced at these things,
cit.note: ubi ἀνδρῶνof men restitui pro ανοσman (corrupt form) (i. e. ἄνθρωποςhuman being ), quod est in M, ab correctore in ἄλλοςanother mutatum.
where I restored ἀνδρῶν [of men] for ανοσ (i.e. ἄνθρωπος [human]), which is in M, changed by a corrector to ἄλλος [other].

sense.note: De viro quatenus feminae oppositus est
Of a man insofar as he is opposed to a woman

cit.quote: ἀνὴρ γυνή τε χὤτι τῶν μεταίχμιον.
man and woman and whatever is between them

cit.note:
Verbis ἀνθρωποειδὲς θηρίον ὕδατι συζῶνa human-shaped beast living in water grammaticus interpretatus est verba poetae quae ab Phrynicho in
lemmate posita exciderunt et haec fere fuisse videntur, ἀνθρωπόμορφον κῆτος ἐξ ἁλὸς φανένa human-shaped sea-monster appearing from the sea . de quo pluribus dixi in Philologo vol. 12 p. 189 et 17 p. 720 collato versu quem ex Euripide attulit Plut. Mor. p. 22ο κήτος θοάζον ἐξ Ἀτλαντικής ἁλόςa sea-monster speeding from the Atlantic sea , quem ex Andromeda sumtum esse novimus ex scholio ad Eurip. Οrest. 335 ab me edito vol. 2 p. 111, 22 ed. Οxon. ubi verba κῆτος θοάζονa sea-monster speeding ex Andromeda afferuntur.

With the words ἀνθρωποειδὲς θηρίον ὕδατι συζῶν [a human-shaped beast living in water] the grammarian interpreted the poet's words which had fallen out of the lemma in Phrynichus, and these seem to have been approximately: ἀνθρωπόμορφον κῆτος ἐξ ἁλὸς φανέν [a human-shaped sea-monster appearing from the sea]. I have discussed this at greater length in Philologus vol. 12 p. 189 and 17 p. 720, comparing the verse which Plutarch cites from Euripides, Mor. p. 22: κήτος θοάζον ἐξ Ἀτλαντικής ἁλός [a sea-monster speeding from the Atlantic sea], which we know was taken from the Andromeda from the scholium on Euripides Orest. 335, edited by me, vol. 2 p. 111, 22 of the Oxford edition, where the words κῆτος θοάζον [a sea-monster speeding] are quoted from the Andromeda.

cit.quote: Τυφώνα θοῦρον, πᾶσιν ὃς ἀνέστη θεοῖς.
Typhon the raging, who rose up against all the gods.
cit.note: Sic Wunderlichius p. 27 pro αντέστηopposed , sed perversa structura verborum ὃς ἀνέστη συρίζων φόνον πᾶσιν θεοῖς σμερδναῖσι γαμφηλαῖσιwho rose up hissing slaughter against all the gods with terrible jaws . Dativi πᾶσιν θεοῖςto all the gods ab ἀνέστηrose up pendent. Ita Homerus Il. 23, 634 πὺς μὲν ἐνίκησα Κλυτομήδεα, Ηνοπος υἱόν, | Αγκαῖον δὲ πάλη Πλευρώνιον, ὅς μοι ἀνέστη.In boxing I defeated Clytomedes, son of Enops, and in wrestling Ancaeus of Pleuron, who rose up against me. quae ubi affert Aristides vol. 2 p. 503 in libro quodam Florentino pari errore ἀντέστηopposed scriptum est.

Thus Wunderlich p. 27 for αντέστη [opposed], but the structure of the words is perverse: ὃς ἀνέστη συρίζων φόνον πᾶσιν θεοῖς σμερδναῖσι γαμφηλαῖσι [who rose up hissing slaughter against all the gods with terrible jaws]. The datives πᾶσιν θεοῖς [to all the gods] depend on ἀνέστη [rose up]. Thus Homer Il. 23, 634 πὺς μὲν ἐνίκησα Κλυτομήδεα, Ηνοπος υἱόν, | Αγκαῖον δὲ πάλη Πλευρώνιον, ὅς μοι ἀνέστη [In boxing I defeated Clytomedes, son of Enops, and in wrestling Ancaeus of Pleuron, who rose up against me]. When Aristides quotes this in vol. 2 p. 503, in a certain Florentine manuscript ἀντέστη [opposed] is written with the same error.

cit.note: [ καὶ νύκτα ταύτην ἣν λέγεις ἐπ᾽ ἀσπίδος ἄστροισι μαρμαίρουσαν οὐρανοῦ κυρεῖν τάχ᾽ ἂν γένοιτο μάντις ἡ ἄνοιά τινιand this night which you speak of, gleaming with stars on the shield, might soon be a prophet of heaven to someone, the folly . Sic M, quod ἡ ἀνοίαthe folly scripsit corrector, de quo schol. παροξυτόνως Αττικῶς ἀντὶ τοῦ ἄνοια· διὰ δὲ τὸ μέτρον ἐξέτεινενwith acute accent on the penult, in Attic fashion, instead of folly; and for the sake of the meter he lengthened it , quae annotatio, ut aliae plures, haud dubie ab ipso scripta est διορθωτῇto the corrector postquam in textu ἀνοίαfolly correxerat, non animadversa veteris interpolatoris fraude, qui quum non intellexisset subiectum verbi esse νύξnight , quod verbis καὶ νύκτα ταύτην ἣν λέγειςand this night which you speak of continetur metri causa per attractionem dictis pro καὶ ἡ νύξ αὕτη ἣν λέγειςand this night which you speak of , inepte scripsit ἡ ἄνοιαthe folly (vel ἀνοίαfolly ) addiditque τινίto someone , ab hoc loco prorsus alienum. Ego, ut sensus postulabat, restitui τάχ᾽ ἂν γένοιτο μάντις οἷα πείσεταιsoon might become a prophet of what he will suffer . In scholio antiquiore, nulla habita illius ἡ ἀνοία τινίthe folly to someone ratione, haec recte sic explicantur, τάχα προμαντεύεται τῷ φοροῦντι ὅτι χωρήσει ὑπό νύκταsoon it prophesies to the bearer that he will advance under cover of night .]

[καὶ νύκτα ταύτην ἣν λέγεις ἐπ᾽ ἀσπίδος ἄστροισι μαρμαίρουσαν οὐρανοῦ κυρεῖν τάχ᾽ ἂν γένοιτο μάντις ἡ ἄνοιά τινι [And this night which you speak of, gleaming with stars on the shield, might soon be a prophet of heaven to someone, the folly]. Thus M, where the corrector wrote ἡ ἀνοία [the folly], about which the scholium says: παροξυτόνως Αττικῶς ἀντὶ τοῦ ἄνοια· διὰ δὲ τὸ μέτρον ἐξέτεινεν [with acute accent on the penult, in Attic fashion, instead of ἄνοια [folly]; and for the sake of the meter he lengthened it], which annotation, like many others, was undoubtedly written by the corrector himself after he had corrected ἀνοία [folly] in the text, not noticing the fraud of the old interpolator, who, not understanding that the subject of the verb is νύξ [night], which is contained in the words καὶ νύκτα ταύτην ἣν λέγεις [and this night which you speak of], said for metrical reasons by attraction instead of καὶ ἡ νύξ αὕτη ἣν λέγεις [and this night which you speak of], foolishly wrote ἡ ἄνοια [the folly] (or ἀνοία [folly]) and added τινί [to someone], which is utterly alien to this passage. I, as the sense demanded, restored τάχ᾽ ἂν γένοιτο μάντις οἷα πείσεται [soon might become a prophet of what he will suffer]. In the older scholium, taking no account of that ἡ ἀνοία τινί [the folly to someone], these words are correctly explained thus: τάχα προμαντεύεται τῷ φοροῦντι ὅτι χωρήσει ὑπό νύκτα [soon it prophesies to the bearer that he will advance under cover of night].]

Schol. ἐναντία φαίνεται τὰ θεῶν, οἷον ἀντικειμένους ἡμῖν ὁρῶ τοὺς θεούς [the things of the gods appear opposite, as if I see the gods opposed to us]. In M' ἐν ὄμμασι τ᾽ ἀνταῖα [and hostile in the eyes] (i.e., τἀνταΐα [the hostile things]), whence in some copies ὄμμασί τ᾿ ἀνταῖα [and hostile in the eyes].

cit.quote: ἀνταία: ἐναντία, ἱκέσιος. Αἰσχύλος Σεμέλη (fr. 236).
ἀνταία [hostile]: opposite, suppliant. Aeschylus in Semele (fr. 236).
ἀντάκουσον ἐν μέρει.
Hear in turn.

form.gloss: to raise a war-cry in answer

cit.quote: ὄρθιον δ᾽ ἅμα ἀντηλάλαξε νησιώτιδος πέτρας ἠχώ.
and at once the echo of the island rock raised a shrill cry in answer.
άνδρα δ᾽ ἀντηλλάξατο
and he exchanged a man
ὁ τῶν θεῶν τύραννος - κακαῖσὶ ποιναῖς ταῖσδέ μ' ἀντημείψατο.
the tyrant of the gods has repaid me with these evil punishments.
cit.note: Sic ex apogr. pro ἐξημείψατοhe exchanged , quod est in M.
Thus from the copy, for ἐξημείψατο [he exchanged], which is in M.

cit.quote: παθών κακῶς κακοῖσιν ἀντημείβετο.
having suffered evil, he repaid with evils.
πῶς δ᾽ οὐ τὸν ἐχθρὸν ἀνταμείβεσθαι κακοῖς;
How is it not right to repay an enemy with evils?

sense.def: occurro alicui rei, incido in aliquid.
I meet with something, I fall in with something.

cit.quote: ἀγρίας ἁλὸς ἀντήσαντες.
having met with the wild sea.
Ἀργείον ἀντήσας (ἀνστήσας M in textu) στόλον.
having met the Argive expedition (ἀνστήσας M in text).
ὅστις ἀνταποκτενεῖ.
whoever will kill in turn.
[τρόπον τὸν αὐτὸν ἀνταποκτεῖναι λέγων.]
[saying that he killed in the same manner in return.]
κοὐδὲν ἀντειπεῖν ἔχω.
and I have nothing to say against.

cit.note: Futurum
Future
cit.quote: τεθνάναι δ᾽ οὐκέτι ἀντερῶ θεοῖς.
but I will no longer speak against the gods about dying.
τῶν ἀντερώντων ἱμέρῳ πεπληγμένος.
struck by the desire of those who love in return.

sense.def: I resist, I withstand an attack.

cit.quote: τὰ πρῶτα — ῥεῦμα Περσικοῦ στρατοῦ ἀντεῖχεν.
at first the stream of the Persian army held out.
σεμνοί τε θᾶκοι δαίμονές τ᾿ ἀντήλιοι.
and august seats and gods facing the sun.

sense.note: In aliorum scriptorum codicibus interdum ἀνθήλιοςfacing the sun scriptum contra regulam grammaticorum, de qua v. Lobeck. ad Soph. Ai. p. 295 ed. tertiae.
In the manuscripts of other writers sometimes ἀνθήλιος [facing the sun] is written contrary to the rule of the grammarians, about which see Lobeck on Soph. Ai. p. 295 of the third edition.

sense.def: who is in place of a man.

cit.quote: ψῆγμα δυσδάκρυτον ἀντήνορος σποδοῦ.
a tearful grain of dust in place of a man.
ἀντηρέτας ἐχθροῖσι.
as adversaries to enemies.
τούτῳ σοφούς τε κἀγαθοὺς ἀντηρέτας πέμπειν ἐπαινῶ.
I advise sending wise and good men as adversaries against him.
δορός γε τῷδ᾽ ἀντηρέτας.
as a rower against this spear.

sense.def: for, i.e. in place of someone.

cit.quote: τοῦτ᾽ ἀντ᾽ ἐκείνων τούπος αἱροῦμαι σέθεν.
I choose this word from you in return for those.
ἀντὶ δὲ φωτῶν τεύχη καὶ σποδὸς εἰς ἑκάστου δόμους ἀφικνεῖται.
And instead of men, arms and ashes come to each man's house.
ἀντὶ δὲ θρήνων ἐπιτυμβιδίων παιὰν — κομίσειεν.
And instead of funeral laments, a paean — may he bring.
βωμοῦ πατρώου δ᾽ ἄντ᾽ ἐπίξηνον μένει.
But instead of the ancestral altar, a chopping-block awaits.
cit.note: Sic recte Auratus pro ἀντεπίξηνον νεί αντεπίξεινονinstead of a chopping-block or instead of a guest , etsi contra regulam grammaticorum, qui anastrophen praepositionis avrínon admittunt.

Thus Auratus correctly for ἀντεπίξηνον νεί αντεπίξεινον [instead of a chopping-block or instead of a guest], although against the rule of the grammarians, who do not allow anastrophe of the preposition ἀντί [instead of].

cit.quote: ἀλλ᾽ εἰς ἅπαντας ἀνθ᾿ ἑνὸς τόδ᾽ ἔργον ἦν·
But this deed was done against all in return for one.
σὺ δ᾽ ἀντὶ φωνῆς φράζε καρβάνω χερί.
But you, instead of speech, indicate with barbarian hand.

sense.note: Post ἄλλοςanother
After ἄλλος [another]

cit.quote: οὔτις ἄλλος ἀντ᾿ ἐμοῦ.
No one else in my place.
ἄλλην τιν᾽ ἄτης (sic Stanleius pro στην) ἀντ᾿ ἐμοῦ πλουτίζετε.
Enrich some other ruin (thus Stanley for στην) in my place.

sense.def: in alicuius rei gratiam vel poenam.
for the sake of or as a penalty for something.

cit.quote: ἀνθ' ὧν ἀτερπῆ τήνδε φρουρήσεις πέτραν.
In return for which you will guard this joyless rock.
άχαριν χάριν ἀντ᾽ ἔργων μεγάλων ἀδίκως ἐπικρᾶναι
to impose a graceless favor unjustly in return for great deeds
ὄνειδος ἥκει τόδ᾽ ἀντ᾽ ὀνείδους.
This reproach comes in return for reproach.
ὅταν γυνὴ γυναικὸς ἀντ᾿ ἐμοῦ θάνῃ, ἀνήρ τε δυσδάμαρτος ἀντ᾽ ἀνδρὸς πέσῃ.
When a woman dies in my place for a woman, and a man ill-mated falls in place of a man.
ἀντὶ μὲν ἐχθρᾶς γλώσσης ἐχθρὰ γλῶσσα τελείσθω.
Instead of a hostile tongue, let a hostile tongue be accomplished.
ἀντὶ δὲ πληγῆς φονίας φονίαν πληγὴν Τινέτω.
And instead of a murderous blow, let him pay a murderous blow.
τὰ πάντα γάρ τις ἐκχέας ἀνθ' αἵματος ἑνὸς, μάτην ὁ μόχθος.
For someone pouring out everything in return for one blood, the toil is in vain.
ἀντ᾿ ἀγαθῶν ἀγαθοῖσι βρύοις.
May you abound with good things in return for good things.
ἀλλ᾽ Ἰφιγένειά νιν ἀσπασίως ἀντιάσασα.
But Iphigenia, welcoming him gladly.
καὶ τοῖσιν οὐδεὶς ἀντέβαινε πλὴν ἐμοῦ.
And no one opposed them except me.
ὁ τιμος ὅντιν᾽ ἀντεδεξάμην.
the honor which I received in turn.

sense.def: I give back, I give in turn.

cit.quote: ἀντιδοῦναι τοῖσι πέμπουσιν τάδε στέφη.
to give in return to those who send these garlands.
τὰς ὁμοίας ἀντίδος βλάβας (λαβάς Canterus) λαβεῖν.
to receive equal harms (Canter: handles) in return.
ἀλλ᾽ ἀντιδοῦναι δεῖ σ᾽ ἀπὸ ζῶντος ῥοφεῖν ἐρυθρὸν ἐκ μελέων πέλανον.
But you must give in return to drink red libation from living limbs.
χάρματα δ' ἀντιδιδοῖεν κοινοφιλεῖ διανοίᾳ.
May they give joys in return with friendly mind.
Πριάμου μέγας ἀντίδικος, Μενέλαος ἄναξ.
Priam's great adversary, lord Menelaus.

form.gloss: serving as a slave in place of another

sense.def: holding the place of a slave.

cit.quote: κἀγὼ μὲν ἀντίδουλος.
And I, in place of a slave.
ἵππων ὄνων το ὀχεῖα καὶ ταύρων γονάς δοὺς ἀντίδουλα.
giving the mounts of horses, asses, and the offspring of bulls as slaves in return.
καὶ τὸ Κισσίων πόλισμ' ἀντίδουπον ᾄσεται.
And the city of the Cissians will sing in echo.
βόα νυν ἀντίδουπά μοι.
Shout now in echo to me.
τοὺς κτανόντας ἀντικατθανεῖν δίκην,
that the killers die in turn as justice,
cit.note: post quae verba versum excidisse, cuius sensus fuerit τíνοντας ὧν ἔδρασαν ἀξίαν κακῶνpaying the worthy penalty for the evils they did , animadvertit Weilius. In marg. M adscriptum γρ. ἀντικατακτανεῖνvariant: to kill in turn .

after which words Weil noticed that a verse had fallen out, whose sense would have been τίνοντας ὧν ἔδρασαν ἀξίαν κακῶν [paying the worthy penalty for the evils they did]. In the margin of M is written γρ. ἀντικατακτανεῖν [variant: to kill in turn].

cit.quote: ἄλγησον ἧπαρ ἐνδίκοις ἀνείδεσιν, τοῖς σώφροσιν γὰρ ἀντίκεντρα γίγνεται.
Grieve your heart with just reproaches, for to the prudent they become goads.

cit.note: Adiective
As an adjective
cit.quote: ἄλγη προφωνῶν ἀντίκεντρα καρδίᾳ.
uttering pains as goads to the heart.

sense.def: proper name Anticlea, mother of Ulysses,

cit.quote: ἐγὼ δ᾽ ὅπως μὲν ἄντικρυς τάδ᾽ αἰνέσω.
But I, how plainly I will praise these things.
ἔκτεινα τὴν τεκοῦσαν — ἀντικτόνοις ποίναῖσι φιλτάτου πατρός.
I killed the mother — with avenging penalties for my dearest father.
οἱ δ᾽ ἀντέλαμψαν καὶ παρήγγειλαν πρόσω.
And they flashed back and passed the word forward.
μνήμην ποτ᾽ ἀντίμισθον ηὕρετ᾽ ἐν λιταῖς.
he once found a recompense of memory in prayers.
ὕπνου τόδ᾽ ἀντίμολπον ἐντέμνων ἄκος,
cutting this remedy that is the opposite of sleep,
cit.note: i. e. remedium, quod canendo somnum pellit.
i.e. a remedy that by singing drives away sleep.

form.gloss: to win a victory in return

sense.def: to win a victory in return

cit.quote: εἴπερ κρατηθείς γ᾽ ἀντινικῆσαι θέλεις.
if indeed, having been defeated, you wish to win in return.
τίς ἂν τοῖσδ᾽ ἀντιωθῆναι θέλοι;
Who would wish to be opposed to these?
τὸν ἀντίον δὲ τοῖσδ᾽ ἀποστέργω λόγον.
I reject the opposing word to these.
σέβομαι δ᾽ ἀντία λέξαι.
I revere to speak in opposition.
δίεμαι δ' ἀντία φάσθαι.
I am eager to speak in opposition.

sense.def: i. q. ἰσόπαιςlike a child infanti similis.

cit.quote: δείσασα γὰρ γραὺς οὐδὲν, ἀντίπαις μὲν οῦν.
For an old woman is nothing to fear; rather, she is like a child.
μηδάμ᾽ ὁ πάντα νέμων θεῖτ᾽ ἐμᾷ γνώμᾳ κράτος ἀντίπαλον Ζεύς.
May Zeus, who allots everything, never set power opposed to my will.
τὸν ἀμόν νῦν ἀντίπαλον εὐτυχεῖν θεοὶ δοῖεν.
May the gods grant my adversary now to prosper.
δάϊος ἀντιπάλοις.
hostile to adversaries
τὸν ἀντιπενθῆ σταλαγμόν.
the equally grieving drop
cit.note: Schol. ἰσοπενθῆ, ὅμοια δρῶντα οἷς πέπονθαequally grieving, doing things similar to what I have suffered . In apogr. pluribus in ἀντιπαθῆsuffering in return corruptum.
Schol. ἰσοπενθῆ [equally grieving], ὅμοια δρῶντα οἷς πέπονθα [doing things similar to what I have suffered]. In several copies corrupted to ἀντιπαθῆ [suffering in return].

cit.quote: σκιρτᾷ δ᾽ ἀνέμων πνεύματα πάντων εἰς ἄλληλα στάσιν ἀντίπνουν ἀποδεικνύμενα,
The blasts of all winds leap against each other, displaying opposing strife,
cit.note: ubi deleto ἀποδεικνύμεναbeing displayed , pro quo Aeschylus aut aliud verbum ab consonante incipiens aut nullum posuerat, ἀντίπνοονblowing opposite scripsi cum Kiehlio.
where, having deleted ἀποδεικνύμενα [being displayed], for which Aeschylus had either another word beginning with a consonant or none, I wrote ἀντίπνοον [blowing opposite] with Kiehl.

cit.quote: μή τινας ἀντιπνόους Δαναοῖς χρονίας ἐχενηίδας αὔρας (sic scripsi pro ἀπλοίας) τεύξῃ.
lest you create for the Danaans some long-lasting opposing winds that hold ships back (thus I wrote for ἀπλοίας [lack of sailing]).
ἀντιποιν᾿ ὡς τίνης ματροφόνου δύας.
as you pay requital for the mother-murdering miseries.
cit.note: Sic Salmasius et Casaubonus pro ἀντιποίνους τείνης (ειyou stretch out requitals (ει , i. e. τείνειςyou stretch out , superscripto ab διορθωτή, τίνηςcorrector, you pay apogr.) μητροφόνας δύαςmother-murdering miseries , quod est in M.

Thus Salmasius and Casaubon for ἀντιποίνους τείνης (ει [you stretch out], i.e. τείνεις [you stretch out], with ει written above by the corrector, τίνης [you pay] in the copy) μητροφόνας δύας [mother-murdering miseries], which is in M.

cit.quote: ŵy ἀντίποινα παῖς ἐμὸς πράξειν δοκῶν.
Alas, my son, thinking to exact requital.

cit.note: De locis trans mare sitis
Of places situated across the sea
cit.quote: εἰς ἀντίπορον γείτονα χώραν.
to the opposite neighboring land
διχῆ δ᾽ ἀντίπορον γαῖαν ἐν αἴσᾳ διατέμνουσα.
and cutting the opposite land in two by fate

form.gloss: to build as a defense against

[to build as a defense against. Eum. 691 in the verses of the interpolator πόλιν νεόπτολιν τήνδ' ὑψίπυργον ἀντεπύργωσαν τότε [they then built this high-towered new city as a defense].]

cit.quote: νικᾷ τὸ κέρδος, πῆμα δ᾽ οὐκ ἀντιρρέπει.
Gain wins, but pain does not weigh equally against it.
cit.note: Sic αντίρροποςweighing equally pro ισόρροποςequally balanced dicitur.
Thus αντίρροπος [weighing equally] is said for ισόρροπος [equally balanced].

form.gloss: to weigh equally, to be of equal weight

sense.def: ex aequo libro, pari pondere sum.
to weigh equally, to be of equal weight

cit.quote: ὡς τοῖσδε καὶ δὶς ἀντισηκῶσαι ῥοπή.
so that the balance may weigh equally against these even twice.

form.gloss: to draw in the opposite direction, to hold back

sense.def: to draw in the opposite direction, to hold back

cit.quote: ορμώμενον δὲ μηδαμῶς μὲ ἀντισπάσης.
Do not in any way hold me back as I rush on.

entry.note: [adversarius. Sept. 520 in versu interpolatoris εἰκὸς δὲ πράξειν ἄνδρας ὧδ᾽ ἀντιστάτας.it is likely that men thus opposed will act. ἀντηρέταςrowers against apogr. nonnulla, ut dixerat Aeschylus locis s. h. v. indicatis.]

[adversary. Sept. 520 in the verse of the interpolator εἰκὸς δὲ πράξειν ἄνδρας ὧδ᾽ ἀντιστάτας [it is likely that men thus opposed will act]. ἀντηρέτας [rowers against] in some copies, as Aeschylus had said in the places indicated under this word.]
[Suppl. 882 vitiose pro ἀμφίστροφοςturned both ways , quod v.]
[Suppl. 882 incorrectly for ἀμφίστροφος [turned both ways], which see.]

cit.quote: τίν᾽ ἀντιτάξεις τῷδε;
Whom will you set against this man?
τῶνδ᾽ ἀντιτάξω προστάτην πυλωμάτων.
I will set a defender of the gates against these.
ἐχθρόξενον πυλωρὸν ἀντιτάξομεν.
We will set a hostile gatekeeper against them.

form.gloss: to exact punishment in return, to repay

sense.def: to exact punishment in return, to repay

cit.quote: ἐπεύχεται ἐμῆς ἀγωγῆς ἀντιτίσασθαι φόνον.
he prays to exact punishment for the murder of my carrying off.
cit.note: ἀντιτίσεσθαιto exact punishment in return Blomfieldus.
ἀντιτίσεσθαι [to exact punishment in return] Blomfield.

cit.quote: τὸν ἀντίτολμον παρβάταν.
the daring transgressor
τὸν Διὸς ἀντίτυπον ἔχοντ᾽ – ἐν σάκει δέμας,
having the form of Zeus's adversary on his shield,
cit.note: eum qui in scuto expressam habet figuram eius, qui Iovis est adversarius. Sic haec interpretatur Wellauerus eodemque sensu ἀντίτυπονopposing per ἐναντίονcontrary exp. schol., quod probari posset, nisi in stropha (v. 481) creticus responderet εὐτυχεῖνto prosper . Quamobrem τὸν Ζηνός ἀντίπνουνthe one who breathes against Zeus conieci, quod aptum Typhoo epitheton est.

one who has on his shield the figure of him who is the adversary of Zeus. Thus Wellauer interprets it, and in the same sense the scholiast explains ἀντίτυπον [opposing] by ἐναντίον [contrary], which could be approved, unless in the strophe (v. 481) a cretic responded to εὐτυχεῖν [to prosper]. For this reason I conjectured τὸν Ζηνός ἀντίπνουν [the one who breathes against Zeus], which is a fitting epithet for Typhoeus.

cit.quote: ἄγουσά τ᾽ ἀντίφερνον Ἰλίῳ φθοράν.
bringing as a dowry destruction to Ilium.

sense.def: qui pro caede rependitur, caedem compensans.

cit.quote: ἀντιφόνων ἐκ θανάτων ἀραί
curses from deaths that requite murder
cit.note: mortis mutua caede effectae.
of death brought about by mutual slaughter

cit.quote: ἀντιφόνους ἄτας
disasters that requite murder
cit.note: mutuarum caedium calamitates.
calamities of mutual slaughters

form.gloss: to sound in answer, to reply

sense.def: to sound in answer, to reply

cit.quote: οὐδ᾽ ἀντιφωνεῖς, ἀλλ᾽ ἀποπτύεις λόγους;
Do you not answer, but spit out words?
τὸν Ιξίονα οἱ μὲν Ἀντίονος γενεαλογοῦσιν, ὡς Αἰσχύλος (fr. 88).
cit.note: Aeschylum Ἀντίονος παῖson of Antion dixisse coniecit Hermannus.

cit.quote: ἐγὼ δὲ τὴν παροῦσαν ἀντλήσω τύχην.
But I will drain out the present fortune.
τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἄλλα τλημόνως ἤντλουν κακά.

cit.note: Figurate
Figuratively
cit.quote: πόλις ἄντλον οὐκ ἐδέξατο.
