but you will not be able to choose any stone from the earth.
Νεῖλος – γαῖάν (γάνος Hermannus) κυλίνδει πνευμάτων ἐπομβρίᾳ.
the Nile rolls the land (Hermann: γάνος [brightness]) with a rainstorm of winds.

sense.note: Neptunum γαιήοχονearth-holding vel γεήοχονearth-holding dixerunt Homerus, Hesiodus, Pindarus aliique: quod nomen grammatici alii γαῖαν ἔχονταholding the earth , alii γαῖαν ὀχοῦνταcarrying the earth significare crediderunt, nonnulli γαίονταrejoicing (gaudentem) ὄχοιςin chariots , quod non est verisimile cuiquam veterum in mentem venisse, ut frustra defensum sit ab Doederleinio in Glossario Homerico et Nitzschio in Philologo vol. 3 p. 10. Accedit quod γαιάοχοςearth-holding aliorum quoque numinum epitheton est, quibus nihil cum curribus est negotii: ut incredibile sit poetas γαιήοχονearth-holding ita dixisse ut modo ab γαîαearth modo ab γαίεινto rejoice derivandum esset. Collatis igitur quae de hoc epitheto dicta sunt in Thes, vol. 1, 2 p. 2315 et vol. 2 p. 490 (ubi Ἐρεχθέος γαιηόχουof Erechtheus the earth-holder addendum ex inscr. in acropoli ab Rossio reperta), non dubitandum quin γαιάοχοςearth-holding sit ὁ γαῖαν ἔχωνthe one holding the earth .

Homer, Hesiod, Pindar and others called Neptune γαιήοχον [earth-holding] or γεήοχον [earth-holding]: some grammarians believed this name to mean γαῖαν ἔχοντα [holding the earth], others γαῖαν ὀχοῦντα [carrying the earth], some γαίοντα [rejoicing] ὄχοις [in chariots], which is not likely to have occurred to any of the ancients, so that it was defended in vain by Doederlein in his Homeric Glossary and by Nitzsch in Philologus vol. 3 p. 10. Add to this that γαιάοχος [earth-holding] is also an epithet of other deities who have nothing to do with chariots: so it is incredible that the poets used γαιήοχον [earth-holding] in such a way that it would have to be derived sometimes from γαîα [earth], sometimes from γαίειν [to rejoice]. Therefore, comparing what has been said about this epithet in Thes. vol. 1, 2 p. 2315 and vol. 2 p. 490 (where Ἐρεχθέος γαιηόχου [of Erechtheus the earth-holder] is to be added from an inscription found by Ross on the acropolis), there is no doubt that γαιάοχος [earth-holding] is ὁ γαῖαν ἔχων [the one holding the earth].

cit.note: De Neptuno Aeschylus
Aeschylus, about Neptune
cit.quote: Ποσειδὰν ὁ γαιάοχος.
Poseidon the earth-holder.

cit.note: De Iove terrae imperium tenente
About Jupiter holding dominion over the earth
cit.quote: γαιάοχε παγκρατές Ζεῦ.
earth-holding, all-powerful Zeus.
πιστὰ τεκμήρι᾽, ἃ γαιονόμοισιν ἄελπτά περ ὄντα φανεῖται,
trustworthy proofs, which to the earth-dwellers, though unexpected, will appear.
cit.note: ubi M τεκμήρια τά τ' (τά τ᾽the proofs which in litura duaram litterarum, quarum prior non τ᾽which fuit) ἀνόμοια οἶδ᾽ ἄελπταunlike, unexpected -, quae correxit Hermannus.
where M has τεκμήρια τά τ' [the proofs which] (τά τ᾽ [the which] in an erasure of two letters, of which the first was not τ᾽) ἀνόμοια οἶδ᾽ ἄελπτα [unlike, unexpected], which Hermann corrected.

cit.quote: τὸν γάϊον (sic Wellauerus pro τὸν ταιον. ἀγραῖον apud grammaticos ad fr. 229 indicatos), τὸν πολυξενώτατον Ζῆνα τῶν κεκμηκότων.

γαΐα κόνις
earth dust
cit.note: pro χθονία κόνιςearthly dust ex Hesychio.

cit.quote: βοός τ᾽ ἀφ᾿ ἁγνῆς λευκὸν εὔποτον γάλα.
and from a holy cow, white milk good to drink.
ὥστ᾽ ἐν γάλακτι θρόμβον αἵματος σπάσαι.
so as to draw a clot of blood in milk.
θρόμβῳ δ᾽ ἔμιξεν αἵματος φίλον γάλα.

οὔλοισιν ἐξήμελξας εὐτραφὲς γάλα.

form.gloss: calm of the sea; improperly of a calm mind

sense.def: maris tranquillitas. Improprie de animo tranquillo

μετὰ πολλῶν δὲ γάμων.
after many marriages.
σμερδναῖσι γαμφηλαῖσι συρίζων φόνον.
hissing slaughter with terrible jaws.
γαμψωνύχων τε πτῆσιν οἰωνῶν.
and the flight of birds with hooked talons.

sense.note: Aeschylus transitive dixit, celebrandi, ut videtur, significatione.
Aeschylus used it transitively, with the meaning, as it seems, of celebrating.

cit.quote: ἴτε μὰν ἀστυάνακτας μάκαρας θεοὺς γανάοντες.
come, celebrating the blessed gods who rule the city.
cit.note: Sic Hermannus, cuius v. annot., correxit pro γανάεντεςshining , comparandum cum Homerico γανόωντεςshining , quod splendentes significat.
Thus Hermann, whose note see, corrected for γανάεντες [shining], to be compared with Homeric γανόωντες [shining], which means shining.

cit.quote: θεοῖς λάφυρα ταῦτα τοῖς καθ᾿ Ἑλλάδα δόμοις ἐπασσάλευσαν ἀρχαῖον γάνος.
They nailed up these spoils to the gods in the halls throughout Greece, an ancient delight.
ἀμφὶ κρηναῖον γάνος.
around the spring's brightness
cit.note: (ut ap. Lycophr. 247)
(as in Lycophron 247)

cit.quote: παλαιᾶς ἀμπέλου γάνος τόδε.
this is the brightness of an old vine
cit.note: (ut ap. alios in Thes, indicatos vol. 2 p.517)
(as in others cited in the Thesaurus, vol. 2 p. 517)

cit.quote: χαίρουσαν οὐδὲν ἦσσον ἢ διοσδότῳ γάνει (sic Porsonus pro διόσ-νότῳ γᾶν εἰ) σπορητός.
rejoicing no less than in Zeus-sent brightness (thus Porson for διόσ-νότῳ γᾶν εἰ) the sowing
τάδε τοι χώρᾳ τἠμῇ προφρόνως ἐπικραινομένων γάνυμαι.
I rejoice in these things being accomplished favorably for my land.

sense.def: the same as δάπεδον [ground], soil, earth

cit.quote: πρὸς Μολοσσὰ γάπεδα,
to the Molossian plains,
cit.note: ubi Μ δάπεδαM δάπεδα [grounds] vitiato metro: nam δάπεδονground syllaba prima correpta dicitur. Eodem errore apud Lycophr. 617 τοῦ τειχοποιοῦ γαπέδων Ἀμοιβέωςof the wall-building grounds of Amoebeus codices non pauci δαπέδωνgrounds . Recte igitur γάπεδαgrounds Aeschylo restituit Porsonus ad Euripidis Orest. v. 324, qua forma tragici interdum usi sunt ubi δάπεδονground metrum non ferret, servato Dorico ἄλφαalpha , ut in γάμορος γάϊος γαπόνος γάποτος γατόμος δάϊος νάϊοςlandowner, of the earth, farmer, earth-drunk, earth-cutting, hostile, of a temple aliisque vocabulis fecerunt, de quo disertum est Stephani Byzantii testimonium s. ν. Γῆ: λέγεται καὶ γήπεδον (τὸ πρὸς τοῖς οἴκοις ἐν πόλει κηπίον), ὅπερ οἱ τραγικοὶ διὰ τοῦ ἃ φασὶ δωρίζοντεςunder Γῆ: it is also called γήπεδον (the garden by the houses in the city), which the tragedians say with alpha, Doricizing . ubi quae de significatione vocabuli dicit cavendum est ne quis ad tragicos referat, quos non est verisimile usquam de hortulis ante aedes sitis esse locutos. Dixerunt illi haud dubie γάπεδονground nunquam aliter quam ut γῆς πέδονplain of earth significaret. Alterius significationis exempla antiquissima apud Platonem et Aristotelem reperiuntur, qualia in mente habuit Phrynichus quum de usu vocabuli diceret quae in Bekkeri Anecd. p. 32, 1 leguntur, ab Stephano Byzantio quoque, etsi omisso Phrynichi nomine, apposita post verba supra ab me allata, Glossa Hesychii γάπεδα: ἀγροικικαὶ οἰκίαιgrounds: rustic dwellings etsi ex prosae orationis scriptore aliquo Dorico sumta esse potest, tamen probabilius videtur eam ad tragicos spectare, adiuncta quae ab tragicorum usu aliena est interpretatione.

where M has δάπεδα [grounds] with the meter corrupted: for δάπεδον [ground] is said with the first syllable short. By the same error in Lycophron 617 τοῦ τειχοποιοῦ γαπέδων Ἀμοιβέως [of the wall-building grounds of Amoebeus] not a few manuscripts have δαπέδων [grounds]. Therefore Porson rightly restored γάπεδα [grounds] to Aeschylus in his note on Euripides' Orestes v. 324, a form which the tragedians sometimes used where δάπεδον [ground] would not fit the meter, preserving the Doric alpha, as they did in γάμορος γάϊος γαπόνος γάποτος γατόμος δάϊος νάϊος [landowner, of the earth, farmer, earth-drunk, earth-cutting, hostile, of a temple] and other words, about which the testimony of Stephanus of Byzantium is explicit under the entry Γῆ: λέγεται καὶ γήπεδον (τὸ πρὸς τοῖς οἴκοις ἐν πόλει κηπίον), ὅπερ οἱ τραγικοὶ διὰ τοῦ ἃ φασὶ δωρίζοντες [it is also called γήπεδον (the garden by the houses in the city), which the tragedians say with alpha, Doricizing]. Where what he says about the meaning of the word must be cautioned not to refer to the tragedians, whom it is not likely ever spoke about little gardens situated before houses. They undoubtedly said γάπεδον [ground] never otherwise than to mean γῆς πέδον [plain of earth]. The most ancient examples of the other meaning are found in Plato and Aristotle, such as Phrynichus had in mind when he said about the use of the word what is read in Bekker's Anecdota p. 32, 1, also appended by Stephanus of Byzantium, although omitting Phrynichus' name, after the words cited by me above. The gloss of Hesychius γάπεδα: ἀγροικικαὶ οἰκίαι [grounds: rustic dwellings] although it could be taken from some Doric prose writer, nevertheless seems more probably to refer to the tragedians, with an interpretation attached that is foreign to the usage of the tragedians.

cit.quote: γαπότους δ᾽ ἐγὼ τιμὰς προπέμψω τάσδε νερτέροις θεοῖς.
I will send forth these earth-drunk honors to the nether gods.
γάποτον χύσιν.
earth-drunk libation.
γαπότους χοάς.
earth-drunk drink-offerings.

entry.note: γάρfor interpositum sententiae cuius causam continet
γάρ [for] inserted in a sentence whose cause it contains

cit.quote: στέλλων στρατιὰν Ἑλένης ἕνεκ᾽, οὐ γάρ σ᾽ ἐπικεύσω, κάρτ᾽ ἀπομούσως ήσθα γεγραμμένος.
Sending an army for Helen's sake—for I will not conceal it from you—you were very unmusically written.
ἐγὼ δ᾽, ἐποικτείρω γὰρ, οὐ θυμώσομαι

ἐμοὶ δ᾽, ἀνάγκαν γὰρ ἀμφίπτολιν θεοὶ προσήνεγκαν · ἐκ γὰρ οἴκων cet.
But to me, for the gods have brought necessity that surrounds the city; for from the house ...
λέξω, κελεύεις γὰρ, τὸν ἐκ φρενός λόγον.
I will speak, for you command it, the word from my heart.
καὶ νῦν Ὀρέστης, ἦν γὰρ εὐβόλως ἔχων, ἔξω κομίζων cet.
And now Orestes, for he was well-aimed, carrying out ...
ἐγὼ δ᾽, ἄγει γὰρ αἷμα μητρῷον, δίκας μέτειμι.
But I, for my mother's blood drives me, will pursue justice.
καὶ μὴν, φιλῶ γὰρ, ἀβδέλυκτ᾿ ἐμοὶ τάδε,

cit.note: nisi φιλῶ γε κἀβδέλυκτ᾽I love and not loathsome scribendum cum Bekkero.
unless φιλῶ γε κἀβδέλυκτ᾽ [I love and not loathsome] is to be written with Bekker.

entry.note: γάρfor intra breve spatium iteratur ubi sententia quae rationi reddendae serviit confirmanda est, raro in eodem versu, ut
γάρ [for] is repeated within a short space where the sentence which served to give a reason is to be confirmed, rarely in the same verse, as

For you will not persuade him at all; for he is not easily persuaded.

entry.note: frequentius in duobus pluribusve versibus sese subsequentibus, ut Pr. 294-296, Sept. 336 338, Pers. 168 169, 669 670 aliisque inter exempla supra indicata. Sed Ag. 559 εὐναὶ γὰρ ἦσαν δαΐων πρὸς τείχεσιν · ἐξ οὐρανοῦ γὰρ κἀπὸ γῆς λειμώνιαι δρόσοι κατεψάκαζονFor there were beds of enemies near the walls; for from heaven and from earth meadowy dews were sprinkling down , alterum γάρfor recte in dé mutavit Pearsonus.

more frequently in two or more verses following one another, as Pr. 294-296, Sept. 336 338, Pers. 168 169, 669 670 and others among the examples indicated above. But Ag. 559 εὐναὶ γὰρ ἦσαν δαΐων πρὸς τείχεσιν · ἐξ οὐρανοῦ γὰρ κἀπὸ γῆς λειμώνιαι δρόσοι κατεψάκαζον [for there were resting-places of the enemy against the walls; for from heaven and from earth meadow dews kept sprinkling down], Pearson rightly changed the second γάρ [for] to dé.
γάρfor in respondendo non raro refertur ad sententiam cogitatione supplendam, ut
γάρ [for] in replying is not rarely referred to a sentence to be supplied in thought, as

cit.quote: HD. ἀεί γε δὴ νηλὴς σὺ καὶ θράσους πλέως. ΚΡ. ἄκος γὰρ οὐδὲν τόνδε θρηνεῖσθαι μότην,
HD. Always indeed you are pitiless and full of boldness. KR. For there is no remedy in lamenting this man in vain.
cit.note: i. e. recte dicis: nihil enim prosunt querelae.

cit.quote: τί νιν (τὴν τέχνην) στυγεῖς: πόνων γὰρ — οὐδὲν αἰτία τέχνη.
Why do you hate it (the art)? For the art is not to blame for any of the toils.
cit.note: ubi sententia interrogativa τί νιν στυγεῖςWhy do you hate it? ; par est affirmativae μάτην νιν στυγεῖςYou hate it in vain .
where the interrogative sentence τί νιν στυγεῖς; [why do you hate him?] is equivalent to the affirmative μάτην νιν στυγεῖς [you hate him in vain].

entry.note: Frequentissimus particulae usus est in sententiis interrogativis, non raro post ἢor vel oὐnot vel post pronomina et particulas interrogativas, τίς τί ποῖος ποῦ πῆ πῶςwho? what? of what kind? where? in what way? how? , positae, in quibus ipsis quoque exemta interrogatione explicandi vim retinet. Sic ἢ γὰρor for – Pr. 745 757 974. Ag. 1366. οὐ γὰρfor not — Pr. 987. Pers. 798. πότερα γὰρwhether for - Pers. 239. Ag. 630. ποῦ γὰρwhere for – Eum. 427. πῶς γὰρhow for – Ag. 634 1374. Ch. 187. Eum. 607 652. τίνα γὰρwhom for – Sept 771. τί γὰρwhat for – Pr. 519 1056. Ag. 272 601 1139 1239 1486. Ch. 48 388 880. Eum. 211 678. Fr. 174. πῶς γὰρ οὐhow for not ; Ch. 754. || In optando. εἰ γὰρif for — Pr. 152. Ch. 345. εἴθε γὰρif only for – Sept. 566.

The most frequent use of the particle is in interrogative sentences, not rarely after ἢ [or] or oὐ [not] or after interrogative pronouns and particles, τίς [who] τί [what] ποῖος [of what kind] ποῦ [where] πῆ [in what way] πῶς [how], placed, in which themselves too, when the interrogation is removed, it retains its explanatory force. Thus ἢ γὰρ [or for] – Pr. 745 757 974. Ag. 1366. οὐ γὰρ [not for] — Pr. 987. Pers. 798. πότερα γὰρ [whether for] - Pers. 239. Ag. 630. ποῦ γὰρ [where for] – Eum. 427. πῶς γὰρ [how for] – Ag. 634 1374. Ch. 187. Eum. 607 652. τίνα γὰρ [whom for] – Sept 771. τί γὰρ [what for] – Pr. 519 1056. Ag. 272 601 1139 1239 1486. Ch. 48 388 880. Eum. 211 678. Fr. 174. πῶς γὰρ οὐ; [how for not?] Ch. 754. || In wishing. εἰ γὰρ [if for] — Pr. 152. Ch. 345. εἴθε γὰρ [would that for] – Sept. 566.

Ag. 1630. οἱ μὲν γὰρ 326. τοὶ μὲν γὰρfor some on the one hand 326. for some on the one hand Sept. 295. οὓς μὲν γὰρfor whom on the one hand Ag. 433. τὰ μὲν γὰρfor some things on the one hand 1056. Ch. 278 748. Eum. 222. εἰ μὲν γὰρfor if on the one hand Sept. 4. Suppl. 472. ἦν μὲν γὰρfor there was on the one hand fr. 178. πρῶτα μὲν γὰρfor first on the one hand Pr. 1016. πολλὰ μὲν γὰρfor many things on the one hand Pers. 459 707. κρατοῦσα μὲν γὰρfor ruling on the one hand Sept. 189 ὅ τε γὰρfor the one who and Ag. 76. θεοῦ τε γὰρfor of the god and Sept. 427. λευκοῖς τε γὰρfor with white [ones] and fr. 114. καὶ παῖδα γάρand a child for Ag. 1040. ἀλλ᾽ εἰσορῶ γὰρbut for I see Pr. 941. ἀλλὰ διπλῆς γαρbut for of a double Ch. 375 ἐκ τοῦ γὰρfor from the Ag. 1478. ἐν ἀγγέλῳ γὰρfor in a messenger Ch. 773 ἐφ᾽ ἄρματος γὰρfor upon a chariot fr. 32. ἀπὸ στρατείας γὰρfor from an expedition Eum. 631. κατ᾿ ἀρχῆς γὰρfor according to the beginning Suppl. 485. τίν᾿ ἀνδρῶν γὰρfor which of men Sept. 771. χάριν τροφᾶς γὰρfor thanks of nourishment Ag. 729. μόνος θεῶν γὰρfor alone of the gods fr. 156. θεὸς θεῶν γὰρfor god of gods Pr. 29. βροτοὺς θρασύνει γὰρfor it emboldens mortals Ag. 222. Quarto loco positum est ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ Διὸς γὰρbut for from Zeus Eum. 797. τὸ μὴ θέμις γὰρfor the not lawful [thing] Ch. 641. τὸ μὴ φρονοῦν γὰρfor the not thinking [thing] 753.

We said above that the particle γάρ [for] is never placed at the beginning of a sentence, but is usually attached to the first or second word, and indeed it is very often attached to the second when it is closely connected with the first, as ὁ μὲν γάρ [for he on the one hand], ἐφ᾽ οἷς γάρ [for on which], and the rest of this kind, especially after nouns with articles. Thus τὸ σὸν γὰρ ἄνθος [for your flower] Pr. 7. ὁ λωφήσων γὰρ [for the one who will relieve] 27. τὰν Διὸς γὰρ [for the of Zeus] 905. τούς προδότας γὰρ [for the traitors] 1068. τὸν φθίμενον γάρ [for the dead man] Sept. 336. τὰ δεσποτῶν γὰρ [for the masters'] Ag. 32. τῶν πολυκτόνων γὰρ [for the murderous] 461. τὸ δυσσεβὲς γὰρ [for the impious] 758. τὴν κάτω γὰρ [for the below] 871. τὸ μόρσιμον γὰρ [for the fated] Ch. 103. τοὺς φιλτάτους γὰρ [for the dearest] 234. τὰ πάντα γὰρ [for all things] 520. τοῖς σώφροσιν γὰρ [for the prudent] Eum. 136. οὑπιρρέων γὰρ [for the one flowing upon] 853. τοῦ γηγενούς γάρ [for the earth-born] Suppl. 250. τοῖς ἥσσοσιν γὰρ [for the weaker] 489. ὁ μὲν γάρ [for he on the one hand] Sept. 511. Ag. 1630. οἱ μὲν γὰρ [for they on the one hand] 326. τοὶ μὲν γὰρ [for these on the one hand] Sept. 295. οὓς μὲν γὰρ [for whom on the one hand] Ag. 433. τὰ μὲν γὰρ [for these things on the one hand] 1056. Ch. 278 748. Eum. 222. εἰ μὲν γὰρ [for if on the one hand] Sept. 4. Suppl. 472. ἦν μὲν γὰρ [for there was on the one hand] fr. 178. πρῶτα μὲν γὰρ [for first on the one hand] Pr. 1016. πολλὰ μὲν γὰρ [for many things on the one hand] Pers. 459 707. κρατοῦσα μὲν γὰρ [for ruling on the one hand] Sept. 189. ὅ τε γὰρ [for the and] Ag. 76. θεοῦ τε γὰρ [for and of the god] Sept. 427. λευκοῖς τε γὰρ [for and with white] fr. 114. καὶ παῖδα γάρ [for even a child] Ag. 1040. ἀλλ᾽ εἰσορῶ γὰρ [but for I see] Pr. 941. ἀλλὰ διπλῆς γαρ [but for of double] Ch. 375. ἐκ τοῦ γὰρ [for from this] Ag. 1478. ἐν ἀγγέλῳ γὰρ [for in a messenger] Ch. 773. ἐφ᾽ ἄρματος γὰρ [for on a chariot] fr. 32. ἀπὸ στρατείας γὰρ [for from an expedition] Eum. 631. κατ᾿ ἀρχῆς γὰρ [for from the beginning] Suppl. 485. τίν᾿ ἀνδρῶν γὰρ [for which of men] Sept. 771. χάριν τροφᾶς γὰρ [for thanks for nurture] Ag. 729. μόνος θεῶν γὰρ [for alone of the gods] fr. 156. θεὸς θεῶν γὰρ [for god of gods] Pr. 29. βροτοὺς θρασύνει γὰρ [for it emboldens mortals] Ag. 222. In fourth position is placed ἀλλ᾽ ἐκ Διὸς γὰρ [but for from Zeus] Eum. 797. τὸ μὴ θέμις γὰρ [for what is not lawful] Ch. 641. τὸ μὴ φρονοῦν γὰρ [for what is not thinking] 753.

γὰρfor cum aliis particulis ubi consociatur, has vel praecedit, ut γὰρ δήfor indeed et γὰρ οὖνfor therefore , vel sequitur, ut ἀλλὰ γάρ, καὶ γάρ, μὲν γάρ, τοι γάρbut for, and for, on the one hand for, indeed for , de quibus suis locis dictum est.

When γάρ [for] is combined with other particles, it either precedes them, as γὰρ δή [for indeed] and γὰρ οὖν [for therefore], or follows them, as ἀλλὰ γάρ [but for], καὶ γάρ [and for], μὲν γάρ [on the one hand for], τοι γάρ [indeed for], about which it has been said in their own places.

cit.quote: καὶ τὸν ἰχθύων γάρον.
and the fish sauce of the fish.
σαίνων τε γαστρὸς ἀνάγκαις.
and fawning under the constraints of the belly.
οὔτ᾽ ἄροτρον οὔτε γατόμος τέμνει δίκελλ᾽ ἄρουραν.

cit.note: De forma syllabae primae Dorica diximus s. v. γάπεδονground .
On the Doric form of the first syllable we have spoken under γάπεδον [ground].

sense.note: Huius particulae usum hunc esse ut vel ἔμφασινemphasis vel μείωσινdiminution exprimat, observarunt Apollonius in Bekk. Anecd. p. 517, 24 et scholiasta Dionysii Thracis ib. p. 838, 10. 971, 13. Similiter Eustathius p. 969 extr. etsi in eo errans quod rem apud poetas interdum παραπληρωματικόνexpletive esse et hiatus vitandi causa (πρὸς βύσιν χασμωδίαςto fill up a gaping ) usurpari credidit, quae etiam Demetrii Triclinii aliorumque infimae aetatis grammaticorum opinio fuit, quiversus poetarum scenicorum non paucos, ubi aut brevem syllabam producere aut hiatum, quem antiquiorum librorum scriptura praeberet, corrigere vellent: qui errores interdum cum prosodiae ignoratione coniuncti sunt, cuiusmodi est quod particulis ἄγανtoo much et λίανexceedingly non raro ye addiderunt, quum syllabam alteram pro brevi haberent. Particula Latina quae Graecae prorsus conveniat non exstat: saepe tamen Latinis vocabulis certe, quidem, saltem, quippe apte reddi potest. Collocatur autem ita ut vocabulo, in quo vis sententiae cernitur, adiungatur, nisi quod articulo et substantivo vel adiectivo addita plerumque media inter articulum et nomen ponitur. Exempla Aeschylea secundumgenera vocabulorum disposuit Wellauerus: quae passim correcta apponimus. Nonnulla in his sunt in quibus re non ei vocabulo, ad quod potissimum pertinet, adiunctum, sed propter metri necessitatem transpositum est nullo sententiae detrimento, quum re non solum id cui adiunctum est vocabulum, sed totam senteutiam afficiat.

That the use of this particle is to express either emphasis or diminution has been observed by Apollonius in Bekker's Anecdota p. 517, 24 and the scholiast on Dionysius Thrax ibid. p. 838, 10. 971, 13. Similarly Eustathius p. 969 end, although he errs in believing that among the poets it is sometimes expletive and used to avoid hiatus (πρὸς βύσιν χασμωδίας [for the avoidance of a gaping of sound]), which was also the opinion of Demetrius Triclinius and other grammarians of the lowest age, who corrupted not a few verses of the scenic poets where they wanted either to lengthen a short syllable or to correct a hiatus which the reading of the older books presented: which errors are sometimes combined with ignorance of prosody, of which sort is that they not rarely added γε to the particles ἄγαν [too much] and λίαν [excessively], since they considered the second syllable short. There is no Latin particle which exactly corresponds to the Greek one: yet often it can be suitably rendered by the Latin words certe, quidem, saltem, quippe. It is placed so that it is attached to the word in which the force of the sentence is perceived, except that when added to an article and a substantive or adjective it is generally placed between the article and the noun. Wellauer arranged the Aeschylean examples according to the kinds of words: which we present here with corrections throughout. Among these there are some in which it is not attached to the word to which it especially belongs, but is transposed on account of metrical necessity without any loss of meaning, since it affects not only the word to which it is attached but the whole sentence.

entry.note: γεat least in responsionibus sententiae servit vel confirmandae vel accuratius definiendae

cit.quote: ΧΟ. καὶ νῦν φλογωπὸν πῦρ ἔχουσ᾽ ἐφήμεροι; ΠΡ. ἀφ᾽ οὗ γε πολλὰς ἐκμαθήσονται τέχνας
CHORUS: And now do they possess flaming fire, being creatures of a day? PROMETHEUS: From which at least they will learn many arts.
ΧΟ. τούτων ἄρα Ζεύς ἐστιν ἀσθενέστερος; ΠΡ. οὔκουν ἂν ἐκφύγοι γε τὴν πεπρωμένην.
CHORUS: Is Zeus then weaker than these? PROMETHEUS: He could not at least escape his appointed fate.
ΠΡ. ἐπεὶ προθυμεῖ, χρὴ λέγειν · ἄκουε δή. ΧΟ. μήπω γε —.
PROMETHEUS: Since you are eager, I must speak; listen then. CHORUS: Not yet at least—.
ΧΟ. ἢ γάρ τι λοιπὸν τῇδε πημάτων ἐρεῖς; ΠΡ. δυσχείμερόν γε πέλαγος ἀτηρᾶς δύης.
CHORUS: Will you then speak of some further suffering for her? PROMETHEUS: Yes, a stormy sea of ruinous misery.
ΙΩ. ἢ πρὸς δάμαρτος ἐξανίσταται θρόνων; ΠΡ. ἣ τέξεταί γε παῖδα φέρτερον πατρός.
IO: Or will he be driven from his throne by his wife? PROMETHEUS: Yes, she will bear a son mightier than his father.
ΙΩ. ἢ ἐμὸς παῖς σ᾽ ἀπαλλάξει κακῶν; ΠΡ. τρίτος γε γένναν πρὸς δέκ᾽ ἄλλαισιν γοναῖς.
IO: Or will my son release you from your troubles? PROMETHEUS: Yes, the third in descent after ten other generations.
ΧΟ. καὶ προσδοκᾶν χρὴ Ζηνὶ δεσπόσειν τινά; ΠΡ. καὶ τῶνδέ γ᾽ ἕξει δυσλοφωτέρους πόνους.
CHORUS: And must we expect that someone will rule over Zeus? PROMETHEUS: Yes, and he will have toils even more grievous than these.
ΧΟ. οὐ γὰρ πᾶν στράτευμα -- περᾷ᾿ τὸν Ἕλλης πορθμόν –; ΔΑ. παῦροί γε πολλῶν.
CHORUS: Did not the whole army cross the strait of Helle? DARIUS: Yes, a few out of many.
ΧΟ. ἔρως πατρώας τῆσδε γῆς σ᾽ ἐγύμνασεν; ΚΗ. ὥστ᾽ ἐνδακρῦσαί γ᾽ ὄμμασιν χαρᾶς ὕπο.
CHORUS: Did love for your native land exercise you? HERALD: Yes, so that my eyes were filled with tears of joy.
ΒΑ. μὴ καὶ λόγος τις Ζῆνα μιχθῆναι βροτῷ; ΧΟ. κἄκρυπτά γ᾽ Ἥρας ταῦτα ταμπαλάγματα.
KING: Is there not also a story that Zeus had intercourse with a mortal? CHORUS: Yes, and these are the hidden wrestlings of Hera.
ΧΟ. καὶ Ζεύς γ᾽ ἐφάπτωρ χειρὶ φιτύει γόνον,
CHORUS: And Zeus, the one who lays hold, with his hand begets offspring,
cit.note: ubi alterius personae versus qui praecesserat excidit.
where the verse of the other person which had preceded has fallen out.

entry.note: γεat least cum aliis coniunctum particulis vel praecedit vel sequitur, ex quo genere sunt γε μὲν δή, γε μέντοι, γε μήν, ἀλλὰ γε, ἀλλὰ μήν γε, ἀτὰρ – γε, δέ γεat least indeed, at least however, at least truly, but at least, but indeed at least, but – at least, and at least et δὲ γε, καὶ γε, καὶ μὴν γε, μέντοι γεand at least, and at least, and indeed at least, however at least et aliae. De his omnibus sub illis dictum est particulis, quibuscum re coniunctum est, et plura exempla reperiuntur in locis supra appositis. Male vero οὐκ ἄν γnot at least ' in apographis quibusdam est Ag. 340, in aliis simplex οὐκ ἄνnot (nam in M haec pars fabulae excidit), rectam vero scripturam οὔ τἄνnot at least restituit Hermannus.

γε [at least] joined with other particles either precedes or follows, of which kind are γε μὲν δή [at least indeed], γε μέντοι [at least however], γε μήν [at least truly], ἀλλὰ γε [but at least], ἀλλὰ μήν γε [but truly at least], ἀτὰρ – γε [but – at least], δέ γε and δὲ γε [and at least], καὶ γε [and at least], καὶ μὴν γε [and truly at least], μέντοι γε [however at least] and others. About all these it has been said under those particles with which it is actually joined, and more examples are found in the passages cited above. But wrongly οὐκ ἄν γ' [not at least] is in some copies at Ag. 340, in others the simple οὐκ ἄν [not], (for in M this part of the play has fallen out), but Hermann restored the correct reading οὔ τἄν [not then].

cit.note: ( versu spurio )
(in a spurious verse)
cit.quote: ἄτην γε μείζω καὶ μέγ᾽ ἐμπλήσας γόμου .

cit.note: Sic M , ubi γε μείζωat least greater haud dubie ex γεμίζωνfilling corruptum , ut ex scholiastae annotatione colligi potest τοῦ Διὸς ἐμπιπλῶντος καὶ γεμίζοντος ἄτης τὸν γόμονof Zeus filling and loading the cargo with ruin , unde Turnebus ἄτηςruin et γόμονcargo . ]

Thus M, where γε μείζω [at least greater] is undoubtedly corrupted from γεμίζων [filling], as can be gathered from the scholiast's annotation τοῦ Διὸς ἐμπιπλῶντος καὶ γεμίζοντος ἄτης τὸν γόμον [of Zeus filling and loading the cargo with ruin], whence Turnebus read ἄτης [ruin] and γόμον [cargo].

sense.def: res qua quid impletum est , fartum .

cit.note: γεμόντωνbeing full glossema ad φλεόντωνteeming ( in M in φλεγόντωνburning corruptum ) adscriptum , quod delevit Hermannus . ]

(in elegy)
