τόν . τριπάχυιον δαíμονα γέννας τῆσδε κικλήσκων
Calling upon the three-cubit divinity of this family.
μέγαν οἴκοις τοῖσδε δαíμονα καὶ βαρύμηνιν αἰνεῖς .
You praise a great divinity for this house, and one heavy in wrath.

cit.note: Vocativus
vocative
cit.quote: ὦ στυγνὲ δαῖμον .
O hateful divinity.
ὦ δυσπόνητε δαῖμον .
O divinity hard to deal with.
ὦ δαῖμον .
O divinity.
δαῖμον , ὃς ἐμπίτνεις δώμασι .
Divinity, who falls upon the house.

sense.def: Apud Homerum δήϊοςhostile : tragici vero ut γάϊοςof the earth et νάϊοςof a ship , ita dάϊοςhostile quoque dixerunt ( in dᾷοςhostile (contracted) contractum apud Aeschylum locis infra indicandis et composito δαϊόφρωνhostile-minded ) , servarunt vero litteram Ionicam in ἀδῇος δηοῦν δηάλωτοςunhostile, to ravage, capturable . Significatio apud eosdem duplex est , hostilis et miser . Prioris exempla apud Aeschylum sunt

In Homer δήϊος [hostile]; but the tragedians, like γάϊος [of the earth] and νάϊος [of a ship], also said δάϊος (contracted to δᾷος in Aeschylus in the places indicated below and in the compound δαϊόφρων [hostile-minded]), but they kept the Ionic letter in ἀδῇος δηοῦν δηάλωτος [unhostile, to ravage, capturable]. Its meaning among them is twofold: hostile and wretched. Examples of the former in Aeschylus are

cit.quote: δάϊον τέρας .
A hostile portent.
δάϊος στρατός .
A hostile army.
στρατῷ δαΐῳ .
To a hostile army.
πυρὶ δαΐω .
With hostile fire.
ἄνια κακά , νεόκοτα καὶ δάϊα .
Grievous evils, novel and hostile.
δάαν Ἑλλάδα χώραν .
The hostile land of Hellas.
cit.note: Thus from the copy (δαΐαν [hostile]) for δίαν [divine].

cit.quote: δαΐων ( sic scripsi pro δηίων ) πρὸς τείχεσιν .
Of hostile men (thus I wrote for δηίων [of enemies]) against the walls.
ἐπ᾿ ἀνδρὶ δᾴοισιν ( δηΐοισιν Μ ) ἐπικότῳ σέβας .
Against a man hostile (δηΐοισιν Μ [hostile in M]) in wrath, reverence.
μαστίκτορος δαΐου δαμίου .
Of a hostile public scourger.
γάμον δυσάνορα δάϊον .
A marriage that is ill for the husband, hostile.

cit.note: Formidabilis significatione ( ut Hesychius daΐhostile a per φοβεράfearful explicat ) dictum est
In the sense of formidable (as Hesychius explains δαΐα [hostile] by φοβερά [fearful]) it is said
cit.quote: δάϊος ἀντιπάλοις .
Hostile to adversaries.

cit.note: Numero plurali δάϊοιhostile ones substantive dictum hostes significat ,
In the plural number δάϊοι [hostile ones] used substantively means enemies.
cit.quote: πάντως ἄρηξον δαΐων ἅλωσιν .
In every way ward off the capture by enemies.
λάφυρα δάων .
Spoils of enemies.
στυγναὶ δ᾽ Ἀθᾶναι δάοις .
Hateful Athens to enemies.

sense.def: The other meaning is wretched, ruined.

cit.quote: Πέρσαις δάοις .
To the Persians, enemies.
ὠωὼ δάων .
Alas, enemies.
δαΐα πάντολμε μᾶτερ δαΐαις ἐν ἐκφοραῖς ἔτλης ἀνοíμωκτον ἄνδρα θεῖναι .
Wretched, all-daring mother, in wretched funeral rites you dared to lay out your husband without lamentation.

sense.note: V. δαϊκτήρslayer .
See δαϊκτήρ [slayer].

sense.def: ( contractum ex ΔάειραDaeira , de quo v . Thes . vol . 2 p . 847 ) est Proserpinae nomen , de quo v . schol . Apoll . Rh . 3 , 847 , cuius verba apposuimus fr . 275 .
(contracted from Δάειρα [Daeira], on which see Thes. vol. 2 p. 847) is a name of Proserpina, on which see schol. Apoll. Rh. 3, 847, whose words we have quoted in fr. 275.

sense.note: Huius vocabuli duo tantum casus usitati sunt daï et dáïv : de quibus v . Thes . vol . 2 p . 866. Dativo post Homerum , qui ἐν δαΐ λυγρῇin destructive battle dixit , usus est Aeschylus

Of this word only two cases are in use, δαΐ [in battle] and δάϊν [battle (accusative)]: on which see Thes. vol. 2 p. 866. In the dative after Homer, who said ἐν δαΐ λυγρῇ [in destructive battle], Aeschylus used it

cit.quote: πολυφθόρους ἐν δαΐ ,
In destructive battle,
cit.note: ubi in apogr . pluribus δαΐδιwith a torch .
where in several copies δαΐδι [with a torch].

cit.quote: δαῖτ᾿ ἀκέλευστος ἔτευξεν .
He prepared a feast unbidden.
τὴν μὲν Θυέστου δαῖτα παιδείων κρεῶν Ξυνήκα .
I understood the feast of Thyestes on the flesh of his children.
παρέσχε δαῖτα παιδείων κρεῶν .
He provided a feast of children's flesh.
οὕτω γὰρ ἄν σοι δαῖτες ἔννομοι βροτῶν κτιζοίατο .
For thus lawful feasts of mortals would be established for you.

cit.note: de aquila cor Promethei comedente
of the eagle eating the heart of Prometheus
cit.quote: ἄκλητος ἕρπων δαιταλεὺς πανήμερος .
Uninvited, creeping, a feaster all day long.
δαίων φλόγα .
Kindling a flame.
πῦρ καὶ φῶς ἐπ᾿ ἐλευθερίᾳ δαίων .
Kindling fire and light for freedom.
καὶ ζῶν με δαίσεις .
And you will feast on me alive.

form.gloss: to bite oneself, to torment oneself

sense.def: ( forma media ) mordeo me , ango me .
(middle form) I bite myself, I torment myself.

cit.quote: στένε καὶ δακνάζου .
Groan and torment yourself.

sense.note: Verbum alibi non lectum .
A verb not read elsewhere.

cit.quote: δακὼν δὲ στόμιον ὡς νεοζυγής πώλος .
Biting the bit like a newly yoked colt.
πρὸ τῶν τοιούτων χρὴ λόγων δάκνειν στόμα
Before such words one must bite one's tongue.
σήπειν θιγοῦσ᾽ ἂν ἄλλον οὐ δεδηγμένον . ]
It would rot another by touching, though not bitten.

sense.note: Improprie rebus tribuitur .
It is attributed improperly to things.

cit.quote: λόφοι δὲ κώδων τ᾽ οὐ δάκνουσ᾽ ἄνευ δορός .
Crests and bells do not bite without the spear.
καὶ τόδ᾽ ἀμφέρειν δόμοις γένοιτ᾽ ἂν ἄχθος αἱματοσταγές φόνῳ τῷ πρόσθεν ἑλκαίνοντι καὶ δεδηγμένῳ ,
And this blood-dripping burden would be brought upon the house, with the former murder festering and having been bitten.
cit.note: ubi recte , ut videtur , Bambergerus ἑλκαίνουσι καὶ δεδηγμένοιςthey fester and have been bitten , quae librarius in numerum singularem mutavit propter praecedens τῷ πρόσθενthe one before .

where correctly, as it seems, Bambergerus [reads] ἑλκαίνουσι καὶ δεδηγμένοις [they fester and have been bitten], which the copyist changed to the singular number because of the preceding τῷ πρόσθεν [the one before].
De rebus animum pungentibus ,
Of things that prick the mind,
cit.quote: μάλιστα δ ' ήδε συμφορὰ δάκνει .
But most of all this misfortune bites.
ταύτην τοιαύτην εἶπον , ὡς δηχθῇ λεώς .
I said this about her, that the people might be bitten.

cit.note: δακώνhaving bitten Hirschig . pro δράκωνserpent , quod v . ]
δακών [having bitten] Hirschig for δράκων [serpent], which see.

cit.quote: ποντίοις δάκεσι δὸς βοράν .
Give him as food to the sea beasts.
θηρὸς ἐχθίστου δάκους εἰκὼ φέροντα .
Bearing the likeness of a most hateful beast, a monster.
πόλιν διημάθυνεν Ἀργεῖον δάκος .
The Argive monster destroyed the city.
τί νιν καλοῦσα δυσφιλές δάκος τύχοιμ᾽ ἄν ; ]
What hateful monster could I call her and hit the mark?
νεογενὲς δάκος .
A newborn monster.
ὅπη μέλλει τις οἴσεσθαι δάκρυ πρὸς τῶν κλυόντων .
Where someone is likely to bring tears upon the hearers.
δάκρυ λείβοντες .
Shedding tears.
δάκρυ μὴ κατασχεῖν .
Not to hold back tears.
ἵετε δάκρυ καναχές .
Pour forth a resounding tear.
διαμυδαλέοις δάκρυσι κόλπους τέγγουσι .
They wet their bosoms with streaming tears.
σὺν δάκρυσιν ἰάπτων .
Hurling with tears.
λέκτρα δ᾽ ἀνδρῶν πόθῳ πίμπλαται δακρύμασιν .
The beds are filled with tears from longing for their husbands.
δακρυογόνον ῎Αρη .
Ares who causes tears.
ἐμοῖσὶν ὄσσοις ὁμίχλα προσῇξε πλήρης δακρύων .
A mist full of tears rushed upon my eyes.
ἴτω δάκρυα .
Let tears flow.
χαρά μ᾽ ὑφέρπει δάκρυον ἐκκαλουμένη .
Joy creeps upon me, calling forth a tear.
δακρύων βίον ἀμβλωπὸν παρέχουσαι .
Providing a life dimmed by tears.
δακρύων δ᾽ ἀποστάζει πένθιμον αἰδῶ .
A mournful shame drips from tears.

sense.note: Quum δάκρυtear et δάκρυσιwith tears poetae non videantur dixisse nisi propter metri necessitatem , sequitur genitivum δακρύωνof tears ad δάκρυονtear potius esse referendum quam ad δάκρυtear .

Since the poets do not seem to have said δάκρυ [tear] and δάκρυσι [with tears] except for metrical necessity, it follows that the genitive δακρύων [of tears] should be referred to δάκρυον [tear] rather than to δάκρυ [tear].

form.gloss: causing tears to fall, causing tears

sense.def: causing tears to fall, causing tears

cit.quote: πάθεα μέλεα – δακρυοπετή .
Sufferings, cares, causing tears.
δακρυσίστακτον ἀπ᾿ ὄσσων ῥαδινῶν δ᾽ εἰβομένα ῥέος .
A stream dripping with tears from the eyes, flowing from the slender ones.
δακρυτός ἐλπὶς σπέρματος σωτηρίου .
A lamentable hope of saving seed.
δακρυχέων ἐκ φρενός .
Shedding tears from the heart.

sense.note: Hoc participio tam masculino quam feminino δακρυχέουσαshedding tears non raro usi sunt epici veteres , ut aliis participiis similiter compositis : quod non animadverterunt recentiores , velut Nonnus , qui δακρυχέεινto shed tears et δακρυχέεσκεhe used to shed tears dixit .

The old epic poets used this participle, both masculine and feminine δακρυχέουσα [shedding tears], not rarely, as with other similarly compounded participles: which the more recent poets did not notice, such as Nonnus, who said δακρυχέειν [to shed tears] and δακρυχέεσκε [he used to shed tears].

cit.quote: οὔθ᾽ ὑπολείβων οὔτε δακρύων ,
Neither dripping nor weeping,
cit.note: ubi οὔτε δακρύωνnor weeping recte delere videtur Paleius .
where Paleius seems rightly to delete οὔτε δακρύων [nor weeping].

cit.quote: πῶς σε δακρύσω ;
How shall I weep for you?
δακρύω δ᾽ ὑφ᾽ εἱμάτων ,
I weep beneath my garments,
cit.note: scriptura propter improbabilem metri formam suspecta .
the reading is suspect because of an improbable metrical form.

cit.quote: τοιοῦτα χαίρειν καὶ δακρύεσθαι πάρα .
It is possible to rejoice and weep at such things.

form.gloss: pointed at with the finger, famous

sense.def: pointed at with the finger, famous

cit.quote: δακτυλοδείκτων ( sic Schuetzius pro daκτυλοδεικτῶν , quod Casaubonus in δακτυλόδεικτον mutaverat ) δ᾽ οὔτις ἀπειπών εἴργει μελάθρων .
But no one, forbidding, keeps me from the halls of those pointed at with the finger (thus Schuetzius for δακτυλοδεικτῶν, which Casaubonus had changed to δακτυλόδεικτον).
ὁ μὲν ἐν χερσὶν βόμβυκας ἔχων , τόρνου κάματον , δακτυλόδικτον πίμπλησι μέλος ,
He, holding in his hands the silkworm's cocoon, the work of the lathe, fills the finger-pointed melody.
cit.note: i . e . cum digitorum iactu . δακτυλόδικτονfinger-pointed apud Hesychium lemma sine interpretatione .
i.e. with a throwing of the fingers. δακτυλόδικτον [thrown with the fingers] in Hesychius is a lemma without interpretation.

cit.quote: καταίθουσα παιδὸς δαφοινὸν δαλὸν ἥλικα .
burning the blood-red firebrand, the age-mate of her child.
φρόνημα τοῦ θανόντος οὐ δαμάζει πυρὸς μαλερὰ γνάθος .
The spirit of the dead man the fierce jaw of fire does not subdue.
εὗτε πτόλις δαμασθῇ .
when the city is subdued.
μὴ πόλις δαμασθῇ .
lest the city be subdued.
στρατός δαμασθεὶς ναΐοισιν ἐμβολαῖς .
the army subdued by naval assaults.

cit.note: οὐ δαμάζεταιis not subdued vitiose pro οὐδάμ᾽ ἅζεταιnever reverences . V. ἅζομαιto stand in awe of . ]
οὐ δαμάζεται [is not subdued] is corrupt for οὐδάμ᾽ ἅζεται [never reverences]. See ἅζομαι [to stand in awe of].

sense.def: Aorist passive ἐδάμην (as if from the unused present form δάμνημι).

cit.quote: πληγείς θεοῦ μάστιγι παγκοίνῳ ᾿δάμη .
struck by the god's all-scourging whip, he was subdued.
ἄλλον ἐν πόνοις δαμέντ᾽ ἀδαμαντοδέτοις .

ἐπικότοισι μήδεσι δαμεῖσα .

θηλυκτόνῳ Ἄρει δαμέντων .
of those subdued by woman-slaying Ares.
δαμέντος φύλακος εὐμενεστάτου .

δολίῳ μόρῳ δαμείς .
subdued by a treacherous fate.
οὕτω δαμῆναι .
thus to be subdued.

sense.note: Alia aoristi forma est δμηθῆναιto be subdued , cuius imperativo δμηθήτωlet him be subdued usus est Homerus , participii forma Dorica δμαθείςhaving been subdued aliquoties est apud Euripidem , semel apud Aeschylum

Another aorist form is δμηθῆναι [to be subdued], whose imperative δμηθήτω [let him be subdued] Homer uses; the Doric participial form δμαθείς [having been subdued] occurs several times in Euripides, once in Aeschylus.

cit.quote: δμαθέντες μεγάλως πλαγαῖσι ποντίαισιν .
subdued greatly by sea-borne blows.
λυκοδίωκτον ὡς δάμαλιν .
like a heifer chased by wolves.
ἄγαγες Ἡσιόναν πιθὼν δάμαρτα κοινόλεκτρον .
you led Hesione, persuading her to be your wife, sharing your bed.
ἢ πρὸς δάμαρτος ἐξανíσταται θρόνων ;
or is he roused from his throne by his wife?
ἡ Διὸς κλεινή δάμαρ .
the glorious wife of Zeus.
Ἥρα τελεία , Ζηνὸς εὐναία δάμαρ .
Hera the fulfiller, the wedded wife of Zeus.
δάμναται οὐρανίαν γένναν .
the heavenly race is subdued.
ἰὼ πόλεως ἀγοὶ πρόμοι , δάμναμαι .
Alas, leaders and champions of the city, I am subdued.

Danaids, daughters of Danaus; this was the title of a tragedy by Aeschylus (fr. 40-42b). The chorus of Danaids is in the Suppliants.

one woman destroying the lives of many Danaan men.
δοριλυμάντους Δαναῶν μόχθους .
the spear-wasted toils of the Danaans.

sense.note: Huius nominis formae Graecae sunt quattuor , prima et usitatissima ΔαρεῖοςDareios , secunda ΔαριαῖοςDariaios , ab librariis plerumque ΔαρειαῖοςDareiaios scripta , apud Xen . H. Gr . 2 , 1,8 et 9 et in excerptis ex Ctesia apud Photium Bibl . p . 38-43 , tertia ΔαριήκηςDariēkēs , quam memorat Strabo 16 p . 785 , quarta ΔαριάνDarian ( correpta syllaba media ) , qua ter usus est Aeschylus ,

There are four Greek forms of this name: the first and most common Δαρεῖος [Dareios], the second Δαριαῖος [Dariaios], usually written Δαρειαῖος [Dareiaios] by scribes, in Xen. H. Gr. 2, 1, 8 and 9 and in the excerpts from Ctesias in Photius Bibl. p. 38-43, the third Δαριήκης [Dariēkēs], which Strabo 16 p. 785 mentions, the fourth Δαριάν [Darian] (with the middle syllable shortened), which Aeschylus used three times,

Why Darian thus ... etc.,

where Aa-ρεῖος Μ [Dareios M], but the meter demands what I restored as Δαριάν [Darian],

to the long-lived gods

For the thick and shady paths of the mind extend.
cit.note: ubi schol . πυκνοὶ γάρ εἰσιν οἱ τῶν πραπίδων αὐτοῦ τοῦ Διὸς πόροιfor the paths of the mind of Zeus himself are dense . Accentum δαῦλοςdaulos probasse Pausaniam annotavit Eustathius p . 274 , 24 1654 , 27. όξυτόνωςwith an acute accent scriptum ab Herodiano apud Arcad . p . 53 , 6 .

where the schol. says: πυκνοὶ γάρ εἰσιν οἱ τῶν πραπίδων αὐτοῦ τοῦ Διὸς πόροι [for the paths of the mind of Zeus himself are dense]. Eustathius p. 274, 24 1654, 27 noted that Pausanias approved the accent δαῦλος [daulos]. It is written with an acute accent by Herodian in Arcad. p. 53, 6.

cit.quote: δαφνηφόροις βουθύτοισι τιμαῖς .
with laurel-bearing, ox-sacrificing honors.
καταίθουσα παιδὸς δαφοινὸν δαλὸν ἥλικα ,
burning the bloody firebrand of her child, of the same age,
cit.note: i . e . torrem sanguinarium , ut exp . Schuetzius .
i.e. a bloody firebrand, as Schuetz explains.

cit.quote: δαφοινὸς ἀετός .
a blood-red eagle.

sense.note: V. Thes . vol . 2 p . 924 .
See Thes. vol. 2 p. 924.

sense.def: autem , sed , vero . Huius particulae , ut fortioris particulae ἀλλάbut , de qua supra diximus p . 19 , duplex vis est , altera adversativa , qua posterior sententia priori vel negativae vel affirmativae opponitur , altera qua transitus ab alia sententia ad aliam efficitur ( unde inter συνδέσμους μετάβασιν ποιουμένουςconjunctions making a transition numeratur , ab Apollonio de synt . p . 128 , 10 ( 123 , 5 Bekk . ) et σύνδεσμος μεταβατικόςtransitional conjunction appellatur ab scholiasta Dionysii Thracis p . 958 , 15 ) una aliqua vel pluribus deinceps sententiis per δέand/but illatis , non tam oppositionis faciendae quam orationis continuandae et nectendae causa , ut apud Latinos autem , et ita quidem ut praecedentibus aliquid vel explicandi vel confirmandi rationisque reddendae causa adiungatur , cuiusmodi locis quum saepe non minus aptae sint καίand et γάρfor particulae , δέand/but non raro pro his particulis positum esse multi olim crediderunt interpretes in locis qualis est

but, however, indeed. This particle, like the stronger particle ἀλλά [but], which we discussed above on p. 19, has a double force: one adversative, by which the following sentence is opposed to the preceding one, whether negative or affirmative; the other by which a transition is made from one sentence to another (whence it is counted among the conjunctions that make a transition, by Apollonius in his Syntax p. 128, 10 (123, 5 Bekk.) and is called a transitional conjunction by the scholiast on Dionysius Thrax p. 958, 15), when one or more sentences are introduced in succession by δέ [but/and], not so much for the sake of opposition as for continuing and connecting the discourse, as in Latin autem, and indeed in such a way that something is added to what precedes for the sake of explaining, confirming, or giving a reason; in such passages, since καί [and] and γάρ [for] are often no less suitable, many interpreters once believed that δέ [but/and] was often used in place of these particles in passages such as

cit.quote: τῶν δ᾽ εἴ τί σοι ψέλλόν τε καὶ δυσεύρετον , ἐπανδίπλαζε καὶ σαφῶς ἐκμάνθανε · σχολὴ δὲ πλείων ἢ θέλω πάρεστί μοι ,
And if any of these things is stammering and hard to find, repeat it and learn it clearly; I have more leisure than I want.
cit.note: ubi σχολή γάρfor there is leisure dici poterat , sed non minus aptum est σχολή δέbut there is leisure otium autem - . de quo usu dixit Hermannus ad Viger . p . 675.
where σχολή γάρ [for leisure] could have been said, but σχολή δέ [but leisure] is no less apt. Hermann discussed this usage in his notes on Viger, p. 675.

sense.note: Huius autem generis quum infinita sit apud scriptores quosvis exemplorum copia , quae omnia in Lexicis enumerare inutilis sit diligentiae , nos de centenis Aeschyleis unius fabulae Promethei exempla producemus , quorum similia non pauciora in reliquis fabulis reperiri videbit qui perlustrare volet . Sic igitur

Since, however, the supply of examples of this kind is infinite in any writers you please, and to enumerate them all in lexicons would be a useless diligence, we shall produce examples from the hundred Aeschylean instances in the single play Prometheus, of which no fewer similar ones will be found in the remaining plays by anyone who wishes to examine them. Thus, then,

cit.quote: ὡς ἂν διδαχθῇ τὴν Διὸς τυραννίδα στέργειν , φιλανθρώπου δὲ παύεσθαι τρόπου .
so that he may be taught to love the tyranny of Zeus and to cease from his human-loving ways.
6 ἐγὼ δ᾽ δ᾽ ἄτολμός εἰμι συγγενή θεὸν δῆσαι βίᾳ πάντως δ᾽ ἀνάγκη τῶνδέ μοι τόλμαν σχεθεῖν .
But I am too timid to bind a kindred god by force; yet in every way I must summon courage for this.
ἵν᾿ οὔτε φωνὴν οὔτε του μορφὴν βροτῶν ὄψει · σταθευτὸς δ᾽ ἡλίου φοίβη φλογί χροιᾶς ἀμείψεις ἄνθος · ἀσμένῳ δέ σοι ἡ ποικιλείμων νὺξ ἀποκρύψει φάος · ἀεὶ δὲ τοῦ παρόντος ἀχθηδὼν κακοῦ τρύσει σε .

where you will see neither the voice nor the form of any mortal; but scorched by the bright flame of the sun, you will change the bloom of your skin; and welcome to you will be the night with its embroidered robe hiding the light; and always the burden of your present evil will wear you down.
τήνδε φρουρήσεις πέτραν – οὐ κάμπτων γόνυ · πολλοὺς δ᾽ ὀδυρμοὺς – φθέγξει .
You will guard this rock, not bending your knee; and you will utter many laments.
ξύμφημ᾿ · ἀνηκουστεῖν δὲ τῶν πατρὸς λόγων οἷόν τε πῶς ;
I agree; but how is it possible to disobey the words of my father?
ἄκος γὰρ οὐδὲν τόνδε θρηνεῖσθαι μάτην · σὺ δὲ τὰ μηδὲν ὠφελοῦντα μὴ πόνει μάτην .
For there is no remedy in lamenting him in vain; do not toil in vain at things that are of no help.
χώρει κάτω · σκέλη δὲ κίρκωσον βίᾳ .
Go down; and force your legs into a circle.
σὺ μαλθακίζου · τὴν δ᾽ ἐμὴν αὐθαδίαν – μὴ ἐπίπλησσέ μοι .
You be soft; but do not reproach my stubbornness.

cit.note: ( ubi οὐ κατ᾿ ἰσχύνnot by force et δόλῳ δέbut by guile , i . e . ἀλλὰ δόλῳbut by guile , sibi opposita sunt )
(where οὐ κατ᾿ ἰσχύν [not by force] and δόλῳ δέ [but by cunning], i.e. ἀλλὰ δόλῳ [but by cunning], are opposed to each other)

cit.quote: μανίαι θάλπουσ᾽ , | οἴστρου δ᾽ ἄρδις χρίει μ᾿ ἄπυρος , κραδία δὲ φόβῳ φρένα λακτίζει , | τροχοδινεῖται δ᾽ ὄμμαθ᾽ ἑλίγδην . | ἔξω δὲ δρόμου φέρομαι λύσσης | πνεύματι μάργῳ , γλώσσης ἀκρατής · { θολεροὶ δὲ λόγοι παίουσ᾽ εἰκῆ .

Madnesses heat me, and the goad of the gadfly, fireless, anoints me; my heart kicks my mind with fear, and my eyes whirl in circles. I am carried out of the course of frenzy by a raging blast, without control of my tongue; and turbid words strike at random.
cit.note: ubi quinquies deinceps δέand/but
where δέ [but] five times in succession

sense.def: 1. δέand/but in responsione , ubi praecedentia alius personae verba continuantur ,
1. δέ [but/and] in response, where the preceding words of another person are continued,

cit.quote: ΗΦ . σῶν ὕπερ στένω πόνων . ΚΡ . σὺ δ᾽ αὖ κατοκνεῖς τῶν Διός τ᾽ ἐχθρῶν ὑπερ στένεις ;
HEPHAESTUS: I groan over your labors. KRATOS: But you shrink back and groan over the enemies of Zeus?
ἰώ μοί μοι . ΠΡ . σὺ δ ' αὖ κέκραγας – .
IO: Alas, alas! PROMETHEUS: But you cry out again—

cit.note: ubi post ea quae Orestes dixerat chorus pergit
where after what Orestes had said the chorus continues
cit.quote: γένοιτο δ᾽ οὕτως · τἄλλα δ᾽ ἐξηγοῦ φίλοις .
May it be so; but explain the rest to your friends.

cit.note: ubi Danao chorus respondet
where the chorus answers Danaus
cit.quote: πάντων δ᾽ ἀνάκτων τῶνδε κοινοβωμίαν σέβεσθε .
And revere the common altar of all these lords.

sense.def: 2. δέand/but in interrogatione positum etsi non aliter ponitur quam in sententiis extra interrogationem inter se nexis , tamen exempla nonnulla apponimus .
2. δέ [but/and] placed in a question, although it is placed no differently than in sentences connected to each other outside of a question, nevertheless we add some examples.

cit.quote: ΙΩ . κλύεις φθέγμα τᾶς βούκερω παρθένου ; ΠΡ . πῶς δ᾽ οὐ κλύω τῆς οἰστροδινήτου κόρης ;
IO: Do you hear the voice of the cow-horned maiden? PROMETHEUS: How could I not hear the gadfly-driven girl?
ΠΡ . ἥδοι᾽ ἂν , οἶμαι - . ΙΩ . πῶς δ᾽ οὐκ ἂν ἥτις – .
PROMETHEUS: You would be pleased, I think—. IO: How could I not, who—
ΙΩ . θέορτον ἢ βρότειον ( γάμον ) ; – ΠΡ . τί δ᾽ ὅντινα ;
IO: A marriage ordained by god or mortal? PROMETHEUS: What do you mean, which one?
ΧΟ . πῶς δ᾽ οὐχὶ ταρβεῖς – ; ΠΡ . τί δ᾽ ἂν φοβοίμην – ;
CHORUS: How do you not tremble—? PROMETHEUS: What would I fear—?
ποῖον δ᾽ ἀμείψεσθε γαίας πέδον τᾶσδ᾽ ἄρειον ;
What better ground of this land will you exchange for?
τί δ᾽ ἐστὶ πρᾶγμα - ;
What is the matter—?
τίνες ; τί δ᾽ εἶπας ;

τί δ᾽ ἄλλο γ᾽ ἤ πόνοι - ;

πῶς τοῦτ᾽ ἔλεξας ; τίνι τρόπῳ δὲ συμμαχεῖ ;

ποῦ δὲ φίλων ἄλλος ὄχλος , ποῦ δὲ σοὶ παραστάται ;

ποῦ δὲ Σευάλκης ἄναξ ;

πῶς δ᾽ οὔ ;

ἔστιν · τί δ᾽ οὐχí ;

πότερα δὲ – ;

ἔστιν θάλασσα · τίς δέ νιν κατασβέσει ;

τί δ᾽ ἐστὶ χρῆμα ;
What is the matter?
τίς δ᾽ ἐπιτύμβιος αἶνος – ;

μήτηρ βασιλέως , βασίλεια δ᾽ ἐμή .
Mother of the king, and my queen.
ἐμὸς πόσις , νεκρός δέ .

πιστή ξύνευνος , ναυτίλων δὲ σελμάτων ίσοτριβής .

cit.note: pro ἐμὴ δὲ μήτηρbut my mother sensus postulat ἐμή γε μήτηρmy mother at least , quod restituit Porsonus , quemadmodum ib . 841 μόρον γ᾽ Ορέστουthe fate of Orestes recte scripsit Portus pro μόρον δbut the fate ' . ]

for ἐμὴ δὲ μήτηρ [but my mother] the sense requires ἐμή γε μήτηρ [my mother at least], which Porson restored, just as at line 841 Portus correctly wrote μόρον γ᾽ Ορέστου [the fate of Orestes] for μόρον δ᾽ [but the fate].

cit.quote: ἡ κεκλημένου τέκνου τοκεὺς , τροφὸς δὲ κύματος νεοσπόρου ,
The mother of the child called hers, but nurse of the newly sown wave,

sense.note: Accurate de hoc usu δέand/but particulae , quam huiusmodi in locis interdum in te mutarunt librarii , dixit Elmsleius ad Eur . Med . 940 p . 225 πατρὸς νέαν γυναῖκα , δεσπότιν τ᾿ ἐμήνmy father's new wife, and my mistress , ubi quum γυναῖκαwoman et δεσπότινmistress de eadem persona dicta sint , necessarium erat δέand/but , quod Elmsleius restituit . Recte vero v . 17 legitur προδοὺς γὰρ αὑτοῦ τέκνα δεσπότιν τ᾽ ἐμήνfor having betrayed his own children and my mistress , quum diversi sint Iasonis liberi ab uxore .

Elmsley discussed accurately this use of the particle δέ [but], which in places of this kind copyists sometimes changed to τε [and], in his note on Euripides, Medea 940, p. 225: πατρὸς νέαν γυναῖκα, δεσπότιν τ᾿ ἐμήν [my father's new wife, and my mistress], where since γυναῖκα [wife] and δεσπότιν [mistress] are said of the same person, δέ [but] was necessary, which Elmsley restored. But correctly at line 17 is read προδοὺς γὰρ αὑτοῦ τέκνα δεσπότιν τ᾽ ἐμήν [for having betrayed his own children and my mistress], since Jason's children are different from his wife.

sense.def: 4. δέand/but post vocabulum , quod praecesserat , repetitum ( cuiusmodi in locis frequentius in priore sententiae parte μένon the one hand additur , ut s . v . μένon the one hand ostendetur )
4. δέ [but/and] repeated after a word that had preceded (in such passages μέν [on the one hand] is more frequently added in the earlier part of the sentence, as will be shown under the entry μέν)

cit.quote: αἰαῖ δαιμόνιοι , | αἰαῖ δ᾽ ἀντιφόνων – .
Alas, you gods! Alas, for the avengers—.
ἈΝ . διπλᾶ λέγειν . ΙΣ . διπλᾶ δ᾽ ὁρᾶν .
AN. To say double things. IS. To see double things.
ἐλευθεροῦτε πατρίδ᾽ , ἐλευθεροῦτε δὲ - .
Free your country, free—.
θεομήστωρ δ ' ἐκικλήσκετο Πέρσαις , θεομήστωρ δ᾽ ἔσκεν .
He was called god-counselled by the Persians, and god-counselled he was.
παροίχεται πόνος , παροίχεται δὲ – .
The toil is past, and past—.
ἄνευ πολιτᾶν ἄνακτ᾽ , ἄνευ δὲ πενθημάτων .
A king without citizens, and without mourning.
ἢ δεινὰ λέξαι , δεινὰ δ᾽ ὀφθαλμοῖς ὁρᾶν .
Terrible to say, and terrible to see with the eyes.
Ζεύς ἐστιν αἰθὴρ , Ζεὺς δὲ γῆ , Ζεὺς δ᾽ οὐρανός .

sense.def: 5. Rarius est δέand/but in apodosi post sententiam condicionalem , de quo dixi in Lexico Sophocleo p . 108. Aeschyli exempla sunt
5. δέ [but/and] is rarer in the apodosis after a conditional sentence, about which I have spoken in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 108. The examples in Aeschylus are

cit.quote: εἰ δ᾽ ἀξυνήμων οὖσα μὴ δέχει λόγον , σὺ δ᾽ ἀντὶ φωνῆς φράζε καρβάνῳ χερί .
But if you do not understand and do not accept my words, then instead of speech, make signs with your barbarian hand.
ἀλλ᾽ εἰ μὲν ἁγνόν ἐστί σοι Πειθούς σέβας σὺ δ᾽ οὖν μένοις ἄν .
But if the holy majesty of Persuasion is dear to you, then you may remain.

cit.note: Post ἐπείsince
After ἐπεί [when]
cit.quote: ἐπεὶ δ᾽ ἐπεμνησάμην ἀμειλίχων πόνων , ἀκαίρως δέ – .
But when I remembered the relentless toils, and untimely—.

cit.note: ubi δὲand/but post κρατηθείςhaving been conquered recte delevit Porsonus , nec videtur legisse scholiasta . Alio modo erratum Ag . 12 , ubi post sententiam ab εὔτ᾽ ἂν δὲbut whenever incipientem verbum excidit in apodosi positum λύζωI sob , de quo s . h . v . dicetur . ]

where Porson rightly deleted δέ [but] after κρατηθείς [having been conquered], nor does the scholiast seem to have read it. There is a different error at Agamemnon 12, where after a sentence beginning with εὔτ᾽ ἂν δὲ [but whenever] the verb λύζω [I sob] placed in the apodosis has fallen out, about which will be discussed under that word.
Post ὡςas
After ὡς [as]
cit.quote: ὡς δὲ πλῆθος ἐν στενῷ νέων | ἤθροιστ᾽ , ἀρωγὴ δ᾽ οὔτις ἀλλήλοις παρῆν , | αὐτοὶ δ᾽ ὑφ᾽ αὑτῶν ἐμβόλοις χαλκοστόμοις παίοντο - ,
But when the crowd of ships was gathered in the narrow strait, and no help was at hand for one another, and they themselves were struck by their own bronze-beaked rams—,
cit.note: ubi structura mutata postremis verbis αὐτοὶ δὲ παίοντοbut they themselves were struck praecedentia ἀρωγή – παρῆνhelp—was present continuantur , omissa verborum ὡς δὲ ἤθροιστοbut when it had gathered apodosi .

where with a change of construction the preceding words ἀρωγή – παρῆν [help – was present] are continued by the final words αὐτοὶ δὲ παίοντο [but they themselves were struck], the apodosis of ὡς δὲ ἤθροιστο [but when they had gathered] being omitted.

sense.def: 6. In sententiis per μένon the one hand et de sibi oppositis saepe eadem vel similia iteranturvocabula . Deinde μένon the one hand et δέand/but saepe post longa intervalla sibi respondent . Denique in diverbiis non raro particulae μένon the one hand , qua prior usa erat persona , δέand/but respondet in alterius personae verbis . Quorum omnium exempla s . v . μένon the one hand sunt allata . Arctior haec sententiarum per μένon the one hand et δέand/but coniunctio quum non sit necessaria , nihil causae est cur in locis ubi solum in altera sententiae parte δέand/but positum est , μένon the one hand in priore sententiae parte omissum esse dicatur , licet apte addi potuisset , velut

6. In sentences opposed to each other by μέν [on the one hand] and δέ [but/and], the same or similar words are often repeated. Furthermore, μέν [on the one hand] and δέ [but/and] often correspond to each other after long intervals. Finally, in dialogues the particle μέν [on the one hand], which the first speaker had used, is not infrequently answered by δέ [but/and] in the words of the other speaker. Examples of all these are given under the entry μέν. Since this close connection of sentences by μέν [on the one hand] and δέ [but/and] is not necessary, there is no reason why in passages where δέ [but/and] is placed only in the second part of the sentence, μέν [on the one hand] should be said to have been omitted in the first part, although it could have been suitably added, for example

cit.quote: Σύμφημ ' , ἀνηκουστεῖν δὲ τῶν πατρὸς λόγων οἱόν τε πῶς :
I agree—but how is it possible to disobey the words of a father?

sense.note: ΝοNo n magis μένon the one hand omissum esse dici potest ubi vel contraria sibi opponuntur per solum δέand/but , vel idem aut simile in utraque sententiae parte vocabulum positum est , etsi huiusmodi in locis frequentissimum est μὲν – δέon the one hand—on the other hand , ut exempla s . v . μένon the one hand allata docent .

Nor can μέν [on the one hand] be said to be omitted where either opposites are set against each other by δέ [but] alone, or the same or similar word is placed in each part of the sentence, although in such places μὲν – δέ [on the one hand – but on the other] is very frequent, as the examples cited under the word μέν show.

sense.def: 7. Collocatio particulae δέand/but usitatissima est post primum vocabulum , vel post secundum , si duo priora arcte cohaerent , ut articulus vel praepositio cum nomine , pronomine , adiectivo , participio .

7. The most usual position of the particle δέ [but/and] is after the first word, or after the second, if the first two are closely connected, such as an article or preposition with a noun, pronoun, adjective, or participle.
sense.note: Sic post articulum et substantivum vel adiectivum
Thus after the article and a substantive or adjective

τοὺς σοὺς δέ .

τὰ πρὶν δέ .

After adverbs and particles with another word

sense.def: [ Ag . 976 vitiose pro δεῖμαfear , quod v . ]

shaken by dreams and night-wandering terrors.
τοιοῖσδε πάσας εὐφρόνας ὀνείρασι | συνειχόμην δύστηνος , ἔς τε δὴ πατρὶ · | ἔτλην γεγωνεῖν νυκτίφαντ᾽ ὀνείρατα .
In such nightly visions I was held, wretched one, and especially for my father; I dared to cry out night-appearing dreams.
cit.note: Pro νυκτίφαντappearing by night ' in apographis scriptum est νυκτίφοιτ᾽roaming by night , quod verum videtur . Porro non est verisimile Aeschylum ὀνείραταdreams scripsisse quum modo praecesserit ὀνείρασιdreams . Recte igitur , ut opinor , Nauckius ( in Bulletin de l'Académie de Pétersbourg a . 1860 p . 241 ) νυκτίφοιτα δείματαnight-roaming terrors restituit , quod apud Lycophronem legitur v . 225 , qui fortasse huncipsum Aeschyli locum est imitatus . ]

For νυκτίφαντ' [appearing by night] in the copies is written νυκτίφοιτ᾽ [roaming by night], which seems correct. Furthermore, it is not likely that Aeschylus wrote ὀνείρατα [dreams] when ὀνείρασι [dreams] has just preceded. Therefore, rightly, as I think, Nauck (in Bulletin de l'Académie de Pétersbourg a. 1860 p. 241) restored νυκτίφοιτα δείματα [night-roaming terrors], which is read in Lycophron v. 225, who perhaps imitated this very passage of Aeschylus.

cit.note: Huc referendum erit

cum metri vitio legitur

There is a place where the terrible (Hermann: αὖ [again]) and the overseer of the mind fears while sitting,
cit.note: ubi Dobraeus δεῖ μένεινit is necessary to remain , quod fortasse legit scholiasta , qui annotavit οὐ πανταχὴ τὸ δεινὸν ἀπεῖναι φρενῶνδεῖnot everywhere should the terrible be absent from the mind , cuius scholii initium fortasse fuerunt verba nunc scholio ad v . 530 adiecta ἔσθ᾽ ὅπη δέουςthere is a place where fear , quae Weilius cum scholio superiore sic coniungit ἔσθ᾽ ὅπη δέους ὄφελος καὶ οὐ πανταχήthere is a place where fear is useful and not everywhere cet . Ad horum verborum similitudinem versus compositi sunt interpolatoris 701 702 καὶ μὴ τὸ δεινὸν πᾶν πόλεως ἔξω βαλεῖν · τίς γὰρ δεδοικὼς μηδὲν ἔνδικος βροτῶνand not to cast all fear out of the city; for who of mortals, fearing nothing, is just? ;

where Dobree has δεῖ μένειν [it is necessary to remain], which perhaps the scholiast read, who noted οὐ πανταχὴ τὸ δεινὸν ἀπεῖναι φρενῶν δεῖ [it is not everywhere necessary that the terrible be absent from the mind], the beginning of which scholium perhaps were the words now attached to the scholium on v. 530, ἔσθ᾽ ὅπη δέους [there is a place where of fear], which Weil connects with the previous scholium thus: ἔσθ᾽ ὅπη δέους ὄφελος καὶ οὐ πανταχή cet. [there is a place where fear is useful and not everywhere etc.]. In imitation of these words the verses of the interpolator 701-702 were composed: καὶ μὴ τὸ δεινὸν πᾶν πόλεως ἔξω βαλεῖν · τίς γὰρ δεδοικὼς μηδὲν ἔνδικος βροτῶν; [and not to cast all fear out of the city; for who of mortals, fearing nothing, is just?]

[for αἱματοσταγές [dripping with blood], which see]

sense.note: Haec prima est significatio adiectivi a δέοςfear derivati , quod de hominibus dicitur et de rebus : unde multiplex prodit vocabuli de omni fere graviorum malorum genere usus , cui expri nendo saepissime apta sunt Latina vocabula gravis et vehemens et alia magis specialia quae scriptorum locis interpretandis adhibuit Stephanus in Thesauro vol . 2 p . 953 954 , velut atrox , indignus , immanis . Non raro de hominibus dicitur qui alios mentis facultatibus superant , vel de eo quod magnam vim exserit , ut

This is the first meaning of the adjective derived from δέος [fear], which is said of persons and of things: whence arises a manifold use of the word for almost every kind of more serious evils, for expressing which the Latin words gravis [heavy] and vehemens [violent] and other more specific ones are very often suitable, which Stephanus used in interpreting passages of writers in his Thesaurus vol. 2 p. 953-954, such as atrox [fierce], indignus [unworthy], immanis [monstrous]. Not rarely it is said of persons who surpass others in mental faculties, or of that which exerts great force, as

cit.quote: τὸ συγγενές τοι δεινὸν ἥ θ᾽ ὁμιλία ,

cit.note: et similiter
and similarly

καὶ μὴ τὸ δεινὸν πᾶν πόλεως ἔξω βαλεῖν . ]

στυγεῖ δὲ δεῖπνον ἀετῶν .

λάκτισμα δείπνου ξυνδίκως τιθεὶς ἀρᾷ .

I do not refuse to be a meal for birds.
ἄριστα , δεῖπνα , δόρπα θ᾽ αἱρεῖσθαι τρίτα .
To choose breakfast, dinner, and supper as the third.
σπευδομένα θυσίαν νεικέων τέκτονα σύμφυτον αἰνῶν , οὐ δεισήνορα ,
Hastening a sacrifice, praising the inborn maker of strife, not fearing her husband.
cit.note: quod Schuetzius interpretatur , e quo iurgia domestica et odium coniugis virum non metuentis .
which Schuetz interprets, from which domestic quarrels and hatred of a wife not fearing her husband.

cit.quote: τρίτος γε γένναν πρὸς δέκ᾽ ἄλλαισιν γοναῖς .
third in lineage, upon ten other generations.
ἐς τριακάδας δέκα ναῶν .
into ten thirties of ships.
εἰ δέκ᾽ ἤματα στοιχηγοροíην .
if I were to recount ten days in order.
τρίτον γὰρ ὄντα μ᾽ ἐπὶ δέκ᾽ ἀθλίῳ πατρὶ συνεξελαύνει ,
for being third upon ten, he drives me out together with my wretched father.
cit.note: ubi vitiosum est ἐπὶ δέκ᾽upon ten .
where ἐπὶ δέκ᾽ [upon ten] is corrupt.

cit.quote: δεκὰς δ᾽ ἦν τῶνδε χωρὶs ἔκκριτος .
and there was a chosen group of ten apart from these.
δέκατον μὲν ἔτος τόδε .
this is the tenth year.
δεκάτῳ ( δεκάτου Wunderus ) σε φέγγει τῷδ᾽ ἀφικόμην ἔτους .
in the tenth (Wunder: δεκάτου [of the tenth]) year I have arrived at this light.
Nestoris navis δεκέμβολος
the ship of Nestor, fitted with ten beaks

form.gloss: receiver, acceptor, one who takes something upon oneself

sense.def: receptor , acceptor , qui aliquid in se recipit .
receiver, acceptor, one who takes something upon oneself

cit.quote: ὑπέστης αἵματος δέκτωρ νέου .
you undertook to be the receiver of fresh blood.

form.gloss: one who records on tablets, mindful

sense.def: one who records on tablets, mindful

cit.quote: δελτογράφῳ δὲ πάντ᾽ ἐπωπᾷ φρενí .
and he oversees all things with a tablet-writing mind.
ἣν ἐγγράφου σὺ μνήμοσιν δέλτοις φρενών .
which you inscribe on the mindful tablets of your heart.

form.gloss: I note down for myself on tablets, I commit to memory

sense.def: in tabulis mihi noto , memoriae trado .
I note down for myself on tablets, I commit to memory

cit.quote: τάμ᾽ ἔπη δελτουμένας .
my words being recorded on tablets.
δελφινοφόρον πόντου πεδίον .
the dolphin-bearing plain of the sea.
cit.note: Sic cod . Ven . , nisi quod falso accentu δελφινόφορονdolphin-bearing . in aliis est δελφίνορονdolphin-bearing vel δελφινόρον . δελφινοφόρονdolphin-bearing iam Barnesius correxerat .
Thus the Venice codex, except that it has the false accent δελφινόφορον [dolphin-bearing]. In others it is δελφίνορον or δελφινόρον. Barnes had already corrected it to δελφινοφόρον [dolphin-bearing].

form.gloss: Delphus, son of Apollo and Celaeno, from whom the city of Delphi took its name

sense.def: Delphus , Apollinis et Celaenus filius , a quo nomen accepit urbs Delphorum .
Delphus, son of Apollo and Celaeno, from whom the city of Delphi took its name

cit.quote: Δελφός τε χώρας τῆσδε πρυμνήτης ἄναξ .
and Delphus, the lord who governs this land.
σὸν δέμας εἰσιδούσᾳ .
having seen your body.
ἀχρεῖον καὶ παράορον δέμας .
a useless and useless body.
κρύψει δέμας τὸ σόν .
he will hide your body.
ῥίψειε δέμας τοὐμόν .
may he cast away my body.
τοῦ χθονίου δέμας δαίμονος .
the body of the nether god.
λαμπρόν ἔκκρουστον δέμας .
a shining, beaten body.
πτήξας δέμας παρεῖχε .
he crouched and offered his body.
φράξαντες εὐχάλκοις δέμας ὅπλοισι .
having fenced their bodies with bronze armor.
πτεροφόρον δέμας .
a winged body.
χαλκηλάτῳ πλάστιγγι λυμανθὲν δέμας . ]
a body destroyed by a bronze-wrought scale.
πρέποντα βουθόρῳ ταύρῳ δέμας .
a body fitting for a bull that feeds on oxen.
καλοῖσι λουτροῖς ἐκλελουμένος δέμας .
his body washed in fair baths.

sense.def: In periphrasi frequens apud Sophoclem et Euripidem , semel apud Aeschylum ,
Frequent in periphrasis in Sophocles and Euripides, once in Aeschylus,

cit.quote: κτανεῖν σ᾽ ἔπεισα μητρῷον δέμας .
I persuaded you to kill your mother's body.

cit.note: De avibus in nido residentibus
Of birds sitting in the nest
cit.quote: δεμνιοτήρη πόνον ὀρταλίχων ὀλέσαντες .
having lost the bed-keeping toil of their chicks.
μὴ περιώδυνος μηδὲ δεμνιοτήρης .
neither in pain nor bed-keeping.
δενδροπήμων δὲ μὴ πνέοι βλάβα .
may no tree-harming harm blow.
δενδρῶτις ὥρα .
tree-covered season.
cit.note: Sic Hermannus pro δένδρων τιςsome of the trees , quod legitur apud Athen . 13 p . 600 а .
Thus Hermann for δένδρων τις [some of the trees], which is read in Athenaeus 13 p. 600 a.

form.gloss: I greet someone with raised right hand, I offer prayers to someone

sense.def: dextra sublata aliquem saluto , alicui preces fundo .
I greet someone with raised right hand, I offer prayers to someone

cit.quote: θεοῖσι πρῶτα δεξιώσομαι .
first I will greet the gods.
τὸ δεξιὸν μὲν πρῶτον εὔτακτον κέρας .
first the right wing, well ordered.
τῆσδε δεξιᾶς χερós ἔργον .
the work of this right hand.
οἵτινές τε δεξιοὶ φύσιν εὐωνύμους τε .
and those who are right by nature and those who are left.
δεξιὰ μὲν , κατάμομφα δὲ φάσματα φαίνων .
showing right but blameworthy omens.

form.gloss: of good name or omen, right

sense.def: of good name or omen, right

cit.quote: χερσὶ δεξιωνύμοις ἔφριξεν αἰθήρ .
the air bristled with right-named hands.
cit.note: Per δεξιοῖςright exp . schol .
Explained by the scholiast through δεξιοῖς [right].

cit.quote: ἐπεὶ δέος παλαιόν σοι φρενῶν ἀνθίσταται .
since ancient fear of your mind stands against you.
εἶλε δ᾽ ἐμὰς φρένας δέος ,
and fear seized my heart,
cit.note: ubi verba φρένας δέοςfear of the mind in M omissa supplevi : de quo v . quae in Praef . ed . Lips . quintae dixi p . XXXIV .
where I supplied the words φρένας δέος [fear in the mind] omitted in M: on which see what I said in the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. XXXIV.

cit.quote: τίς δὲ μηδὲν ἐν φάει καρδίαν ἀνατρέφων ,
who, nurturing his heart in no light,
cit.note: ubi ineptum est φάειin light , aptum vero déeι , quod coniecit Auratus . φάει καρδίαςin the light of the heart legisse videtur schol . , qui exp . λαμπρότητι , ὀρθότητι φρενώνby the brightness, uprightness of mind . Post καρδίανheart una excidit syllaba , nisi tribracho qui in versu strophico legitur 516 ἢ τεκοῦσα νεοπαθήςor having borne a new grief formam non solutam opposuit poeta : unde ἔτ᾽ ἀνατρέφωνstill nurturing coniecit Hermannus .

where φάει [in light] is inappropriate, but déeι is fitting, which Auratus conjectured. The scholiast seems to have read φάει καρδίας [in the light of the heart], who explains it as λαμπρότητι, ὀρθότητι φρενών [by the brightness, uprightness of mind]. After καρδίαν [heart] one syllable has fallen out, unless the poet opposed an unresolved form to the tribrach which is read in the strophic verse 516 ἢ τεκοῦσα νεοπαθής [or having borne a new grief]: whence Hermann conjectured ἔτ᾽ ἀνατρέφων [still nurturing].

cit.quote: Ηφαιστοτυκές δέπας
a cup forged by Hephaestus
cit.note: de coeli rubore dictum , in quem immergitur sol occidens .
said of the redness of the sky, into which the setting sun is plunged.

cit.quote: φονίου δέργμα δράκοντος .
the murderous glance of a serpent.
ἐξ ἐλευθέρου ἀποιμώζουσα φιλτάτων μόρον .
lamenting from a free throat the fate of her dearest ones.
πολλὰς ἄνωθεν ἀρτάνας ἐμῆς δέρης ἔλυσαν .
they released many nooses from above my neck.
μαντεία περὶ δέρη στέφη .
prophetic garlands around my neck.
ξιφουλκῷ χειρὶ πρὸς δέρην τεμών .
with sword-drawn hand cutting at the throat.

sense.def: ( cum perfecto δέδορκαI have seen praesentis significationem habente et aoristis ἐδέρχθηνI was seen et ἔδρακονI saw ) cerno , video .
(with the perfect δέδορκα having present meaning and the aorists ἐδέρχθην and ἔδρακον) I see, perceive.

cit.quote: δέρκεται πλέον τι τοῦ πεφασμένου .
he sees something more than what has been revealed.
δέρκου θέαμα .
look at the sight.
φρίσσω δέ σε δερκομένα .
I shudder as I look at you.
δερκομένοισι καὶ δυσομμάτοις .
to those who see and to those with poor eyesight.
πρόχειρα ψάλια δέρκεσθαι πάρα .
it is possible to see the ready bits.
οἷον δέδορκεν ἄτα .
what ruin has seen.
πυκνοῖς ὄσσοις δεδορκώς τοὺς ἐμοὺς κατὰ στίβους .
having seen with many eyes along my paths.
ὁ χρησμὸς οὐκέτ᾽ ἐκ καλυμμάτων ἔσται δεδορκώς .
the oracle will no longer be seen from behind veils.
δεδορκὸς ὄμμα .
a seeing eye.
λεόντων ὡς ῎Αρη δεδορκότων .
like lions that have seen Ares.
ἀλαοῖσι καὶ δεδορκόσιν .
to the blind and to those who see.

cit.note: Improprie de re quae auditu percipitur
Improperly of a thing that is perceived by hearing
cit.quote: κτύπον δέδορκα .
I see a sound.

cit.note: Suspectum est quod
It is suspected that
cit.quote: πᾶσα γὰρ Τροία δέδορκεν Ἕκτορος τύχης διαί ,
for all Troy has seen the fate of Hector,
cit.note: ubi Bernhardyus déδουπενit thudded coniecit .
where Bernhardy conjectured déδουπεν [it thudded].

cit.quote: τί γὰρ γυναικὶ τούτου φέγγος ἥδιον δρακεῖν ;
for what light is sweeter for a woman to see than this?
δεινὰ δ᾽ ὀφθαλμοῖς δρακεῖν .
terrible things to see with the eyes.
οὐδ᾽ ἐδέρχθης ὀλιγοδρανίαν ἄκικυν .
you did not see the feeble weakness.
δέρχθηθ᾽ οἵαις αἰκίαισιν διακναιόμενος τὸν μυριετῆ χρόνον ἀθλεύσω .
see with what outrages I am worn down, struggling through my endless time.
δέρχθητ᾽ , ἐσίδεσθε .
look, behold.
σήψει παλαιὸν δέρμα .
it will rot the old skin.
ὕμνον δ᾽ ἀκούσει τόνδε δέσμιον σέθεν .
you will hear this binding hymn of yours.
ὕμνος ἐξ Ἐρινύων δέσμιος φρενών .
a hymn from the Erinyes, binding the mind.
cit.note: ubi de carmine dictum est quo Furiae Orestem se quasi constricturas et in potestatem suam redacturas esse minantur , ut monuit Schuetzius .
where it is said of the song by which the Furies threaten to bind Orestes and bring him under their power, as Schuetz pointed out.

cit.quote: δεσμὸν ἀεικῆ .
an unseemly bond.
οἵῳ δεσμῷ προσπαρτός .
nailed to what bond.
δεσμὸς δὲ καὶ τὸ γῆρας αἵ τε νήστιδες δύαι διδάσκειν ἐξοχώταται .
bond and old age and fasting pains are most excellent teachers.
δεσμὸν ἀθλίῳ πατρί .
a bond for my wretched father.
δεσμοῦ τε πάθος τόδ᾽ ἐποψόμενοι .
to see this suffering of bondage.
ἀδαμαντίνων δεσμῶν ἐν ἀρρήκτοις πέδαις .
in unbreakable fetters of adamantine bonds.
ὑπαιθρίοις δεσμοῖσι προσπεπαρμένος .
nailed in open-air bonds.
δεσμοῖς ἀλύτοις ἀγρίως πελάσας .
bringing him savagely into unloosable bonds.
πρὶν ἂν ἐξ ἀγρίων δεσμῶν χαλάση .
before he loosens from the wild bonds.
τῶνδέ σ᾽ ἐκ δεσμῶν ἔτι λυθέντα .
you still being released from these bonds.
πλὴν ἐὰν ἐγὼ ἐκ δεσμῶν λυθῶ .
unless I am released from bonds.
λῦσαί με δεσμῶν τῶνδε .
to release me from these bonds.
δεσμῶν ἄριστος .
best of bonds.
δεσμοὺς ἀεικεῖς καὶ δύας ἐκφυγγάνω .
I escape unseemly bonds and pains.

sense.note: Numeri pluralis forma ἑτερόκλιτος δεσμάheteroclite bonds , de qua v . Thes . vol . 2 p . 1010.
The heteroclite plural form δεσμά [bonds], on which see Thes. vol. 2 p. 1010.

cit.quote: ούκουν ἐπείξει τῷδε δεσμὰ περιβαλεῖν ;
will you not hasten to cast bonds around him?
ὧδε δεσμὰ φυγγάνω .
Thus I escape the bonds.
πρὶν ἂν χαλασθῇ δεσμὰ λυμαντήρια .
before the bonds of ruin are loosened.
Ἑλλησπόντον ἱρὸν δοῦλον ὡς δεσμώμασιν ἤλπισε σχήσειν ῥέοντα .
He hoped to hold the sacred Hellespont, flowing as a slave, with bonds.
ὁρᾶτε δεσμώτην με δύσποτμον θεόν .
You see me, a prisoner god, ill-fated.
cit.note: unde haec tragoedia inscripta Προμηθεὺς δεσμώτηςPrometheus Bound .
whence this tragedy is entitled Prometheus Bound [Προμηθεὺς δεσμώτης].

cit.quote: ᾤοντ᾽ ἀμοχθὶ πρὸς βίαν τε δεσπόσειν .
They thought they would rule without toil and by force.
πῶς δή ; διδαχθεὶς τοῦδε δεσπόσω λόγου .
How so? Taught by this word I shall be master.
πῶς γὰρ ἐλπίσω ἀστῶν τιν᾽ ἄλλον τῆσδε δεσπόζειν φόβης ;
For how shall I expect any other of the citizens to rule over this land?

cit.note: Cum dativo construxisse videtur
He seems to have constructed it with the dative
ubi nunc legitur
where now is read
cit.quote: καὶ προσδοκᾶν χρὴ δεσπόσειν Ζηνός τινα ;
And must one expect that someone will rule over Zeus?
cit.note: ubi apographa multa Διόςof Zeus , quod probandum foret , nisi dubitari posset an Aeschylus scripserit καὶ προσδοκᾶν χρὴ Ζηνὶ δεσπόσειν τινάand one must expect that someone will rule over Zeus , ne versus ex tribus partibus aequalibus compositus esset , verbo δεσπόζεινto rule cum dativo constructo , ut ἄρχεινto rule interdum cum dativo construitur et ab Aeschylo ipso constructum est in hac fabula ν . 945 δαρόν γὰρ οὐκ ἄρξει θεοῖςline 945: for he will not rule the gods for long , pariterque ἐπιδεσπόζεινto rule over Pers . 241 τίς δὲ ποιμάνωρ ἔπεστι κἀπιδεσπόζει στρατῷwho is the shepherd-commander who is in charge and rules over the army? ; ubi nihil causae est cur dativus στρατῷthe army (dative) ( in apographis multis in στρατοῦof the army (genitive) mutatus ) propter verbum praecedens ἔπεστιis in charge positus esse putetur .

where many copies have Διός [of Zeus], which would be acceptable, unless it could be doubted whether Aeschylus wrote καὶ προσδοκᾶν χρὴ Ζηνὶ δεσπόσειν τινά [and one must expect that someone will rule over Zeus], lest the verse be composed of three equal parts, with the verb δεσπόζειν [to rule] constructed with the dative, as ἄρχειν [to rule] is sometimes constructed with the dative and was constructed by Aeschylus himself in this play at line 945 δαρόν γὰρ οὐκ ἄρξει θεοῖς [for he will not rule the gods for long], and likewise ἐπιδεσπόζειν [to rule over] in Persians 241 τίς δὲ ποιμάνωρ ἔπεστι κἀπιδεσπόζει στρατῷ [who is the shepherd-commander who is in charge and rules over the army?]; where there is no reason why the dative στρατῷ [the army] (changed in many copies to στρατοῦ [of the army]) should be thought to be used because of the preceding verb ἔπεστι [is in charge].
Cum accusativo coniunxit Euripides Herc . f . v . 20
Euripides connected it with the accusative in Hercules Furens line 20
cit.quote: τὴν ὑψίπυργον τήνδε δεσπόζων πόλιν ,
ruling this high-towered city,
cit.note: quod ipsum quoque unicum est exemplum , etsi poetam nihil impediebat quominus scriberet τῆς ὑψιπύργου τῆσδε δεσπόζων πόλεωςruling this high-towered city .
which itself is also a unique example, although nothing prevented the poet from writing τῆς ὑψιπύργου τῆσδε δεσπόζων πόλεως [ruling this high-towered city].

cit.quote: ὦ δέσποινα .
O mistress.
δεσποίνης χάριν .
for the sake of the mistress.
δέσποινα πεντήκοντα Νηρήδων χοροῦ .
mistress of the chorus of fifty Nereids.
δέσποιν᾽ Ἑκάτη .
mistress Hecate.
δέσποινα νύμφη δυσχίμων ὀρῶν ἄνάξ .
mistress nymph, lord of the wintry mountains.
δεσποσίῳ ξὺν ὕβρει .
with masterly insolence.

sense.note: Vocabulum ex hoc uno loco cognitum et Eustathio p . 846 , 13 , qui δεσπόσιοιbelonging to masters pro δεσπόσυνοιof masters dictum annotavit , i . e . δοῦλοι τραφέντες ἐν οἰκίαις δεσποτῶνslaves raised in the houses of masters , vernae .

A word known from this one passage and from Eustathius p. 846, 13, who noted that δεσπόσιοι [belonging to masters] is said for δεσπόσυνοι [of masters], i.e. δοῦλοι τραφέντες ἐν οἰκίαις δεσποτῶν [slaves raised in the houses of masters], home-born slaves.

cit.quote: δεσποσύνοισιν ἀνάγκαις .
by masterly constraints.
δεσποσύνων δόμων .
of the master's house.

form.gloss: to be ruled by a master

sense.def: to be ruled by a master

cit.quote: τὸν πρὸς ἄλλης δεσποτούμενον χερός .
the one ruled by another's hand.
μήτ᾽ ἀνάρχετον βίον μήτ μήτε δεσποτούμενον αἰνέσῃς .
May you praise neither a life without a ruler nor one ruled by a master.
τὸ μήτ᾽ ἄναρχον μήτε δεσποτούμενον . ]
the neither unruled nor ruled by a master.
τοιῶνδε δεσπότης μαντευμάτων .
master of such prophecies.
ὄμμα γὰρ δόμων νομίζω δεσπότου παρουσίαν .
For I consider the presence of the master the eye of the house.
τῷ μολόντι δεσπότη ἐμῷ .
to my master who has come.
ὀλομένῳ δεσπότα .
to the doomed master.
μή νυν σὺ ταῦτ᾽ ἄγγελλε δεσπότου στύγει .
Do not report these things to the master's hatred.
οἴμοι πανοίμοι δεσπότου τελουμένου .
Alas, all-alas, the master is being accomplished.
τῶνδε δεσπότη δόμων .
to the master of this house.
κύνες διημάθυνον ἄνδρα δεσπότην .
the dogs tore apart the man, the master.

cit.note: Vocativus δέσποταmaster regum compellatio
The vocative δέσποτα [master] is an address to kings
cit.quote: δέσποτα δεσποτᾶν ( sic scripsi pro δεσπότου ) φάνηθι .
Master of masters (thus I wrote for δεσπότου [of the master]), appear.
μέλειν πάρεστι , δέσποτα .
It is possible to care, master.
κλύε σέβας , ὦ δέσποτ᾽ , ἐξ ἀμαυρᾶς φρενός .
Hear my reverence, O master, from a dimmed mind.

cit.note: Numero plurali
In the plural number
cit.quote: τὰ δεσποτῶν γὰρ εὖ πεσόντα θήσομαι .
For I will make the fortunes of my masters fall well.
ἀρχαιοπλούτων δεσποτῶν πολλή χάρις .
Great is the gratitude for masters rich from ancient times.
δεσποτών θανάτοισι .
By the deaths of masters.
ματαίοισι δεσποτᾶν τύχαις .
With vain fortunes of masters.
εὐχὰῖς δὲ σώζοις δεσπότας παιωνίαις .
May you save your masters with healing prayers.
ἃ πρὶν μολεῖν δεῦρ᾽ ἐкмеμόχθηκε .
What you toiled at before coming here.

cit.note: et sic cum verbo μολεῖνto come
and thus with the verb μολεῖν [to come]
cum ἐλθεῖνto come
with ἐλθεῖν [to come]
κατελθεῖν [to come down]
cum ἄγεινto lead
with ἄγειν [to lead]
cum πέμπεινto send
with πέμπειν [to send]
et aliis
and others
cit.quote: πρὸς δῶμα δεῦρ᾽ ἀστοῖσι κηρύσσειν βοήν .
To proclaim a shout to the citizens here at the house.
ὥσπερ δεῦρ᾽ ἀπεζύγην πόδα .
Just as I unyoked my foot here.
ἐπεὶ δὲ πρᾶγμα δεῦρ᾽ ἐπέσκηψεν τόδε .
But when this matter fell upon us here.
δεῦρ᾽ ἴτε .
Come here.
δεῦρο δ᾽ ἐξοκέλλεται .
And here it runs aground.
τὰ δ᾽ ἄλλα τούτῳ δεῦρ᾽ ἐποπτεῦσαι λέγω .
And the rest I bid you oversee here for this man.
καὶ δεῦρό γ᾽ ἀεὶ τὴν τύχην οὐ μέμφομαι .
And indeed up to this point I do not blame my fortune.
Γηρυὼν ὁ δεύτερος .
Geryon the second.
δευτέραν ( sc . πληγήν ) πεπληγμένος ,
struck with a second (sc. blow),
cit.note: ubi praecesserat πέπληγμαι καιρίαν πληγήνI have been struck a fatal blow .
where πέπληγμαι καιρίαν πληγήν [I have been struck a fatal blow] had preceded.

cit.quote: τὸν δεύτερον δὲ τόνδε πενθητήριον .
and this second one, the mourning one.
δεύτερον τεκμήριον .
second proof
ἣ δὴ τὸ μητρὸς δευτέρα τόδ᾽ ἕζετο μαντεῖον .
She who indeed sat as the second oracle of her mother.
μάραινε δευτέροις διώγμασιν .
quench with second pursuits.
τὴν δευτέραν δὲ κρᾶσιν ἥρωσιν νέμω .
And the second libation I assign to the heroes.

sense.def: δεύτερον [second] adverbially, in the second place, after

sense.def: [ cum perf . δέδεγμαιI have received , aoristo ἐδεξάμηνI received et futuro δέξομαιI will receive ] Propria verbi significatio est accipio quod alter dat , diciturque non solum de rebus quae in manus sumi possunt , sed etiam de hominibus quos quis recipit et de rebus quibusvis , factis et dictis quae alter in alterum confert .

[with perfect δέδεγμαι [I have received], aorist ἐδεξάμην [I received], and future δέξομαι [I will receive]] The proper meaning of the verb is 'I receive what another gives', and it is said not only of things that can be taken in the hands, but also of people whom one receives and of any things, deeds and words that one person confers upon another.

sense.def: De huius particulae usu lectu digna est H. Helleri disputatio in Philologo vol . 8 p . 277-308 . quocum fere consentientes Baeumleinius ( Untersuchungen über die griechischen Partikeln ) p . 98 et qui exempla Aristophanea collegit Wehrius in Quaestionibus Aristophaneis I p.51 , varium huius particulae usum eo redire observarunt ut res aliqua manifesta esse significetur visque vel unius cui adiuncta est vocabuli vel totius sententiae urgeatur : neque enim ubique cum primario coniungitur vocabulo , quod in versibus poetarum saepe per metrum non licebat . Particula Latina quae ei ubique respondeat nulla est , sunt vero plures quae pro diversa locorum ratione interpretandae ei adhiberi possint , quorum plurimis aptum est iam . Particulam cum aliis quibusdam particulis coniunctam encliticam fieri inanis grammaticorum quorundam opinio fuit , ab Eustathio memorata p . 143 , 22 et ubi de vῦνδηindeed coniunctim scribendo agit p . 174 .

On the use of this particle, the discussion by H. Heller in Philologus vol. 8 p. 277-308 is worth reading. Agreeing with him for the most part, Baeumlein (Investigations on Greek Particles) p. 98 and Wehr, who collected Aristophanic examples in Quaestiones Aristophaneae I p. 51, observed that the varied use of this particle comes down to this: that some matter is indicated as evident, and the force either of the single word to which it is attached or of the whole sentence is emphasized. For it is not always joined to the primary word, which in the verses of poets was often not allowed by the meter. There is no Latin particle that corresponds to it everywhere, but there are several which can be used to interpret it according to the different nature of the passages, of which 'iam' is suitable for most. The opinion of some grammarians, mentioned by Eustathius p. 143, 22 and where he deals with writing νῦν δή [now indeed] as one word p. 174, that the particle when joined with certain other particles becomes enclitic, was groundless.
sense.note: Exempla Aeschylea ab Wellauero collecta haec sunt :

cit.quote: τί δῆθεν αὐτοῖς ὄνομα θήσονται βροτοί ,
What name forsooth will mortals give them?
cit.note: ubi nunc ex libro optimo Paris . restitutum τί δῆτ᾽ ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖςwhat then upon them – . ]
where now from the best Paris manuscript has been restored τί δῆτ᾽ ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς – [what then upon them –].

cit.quote: ὁδοιπόρων δήλημα χωρίτης δράκων .
a rustic serpent, a destruction for travelers
λιπὼν δὲ λίμνην Δηλίαν τε χοιράδα .
leaving the lake and the Delian rock
ὡς κάρτα μοι σαφῶς ἐδήλωσας κακά .
How clearly you have revealed evils to me.
τί τῶνδ᾽ ἂν εἴποις ώστε δηλώσαι φρενί ;
What of these things could you say so as to make it clear to my mind?
δημηγόρους δ᾽ ἤκουσεν εὐπιθεῖς στροφὰς δῆμος Πελασγών .
The people of the Pelasgians heard persuasive public speeches.
οὔτιν᾿ ἐφ᾽ αἵματι δημηλασίαν φήφῳ πόλεως γνωσθεῖσαι .
no exile for blood, decided by the vote of the city

form.gloss: driven out by the people, exiled

sense.def: populo s . patria eiectus , in exsilium actus .
driven out by the people or fatherland, sent into exile

cit.quote: ἄτιμον εἶναι ξὺν φυγῇ δημηλάτῳ .
to be dishonored with exile driven by the people.

sense.note: φυγὴν δημήλατονexile driven by the people exilium dicit a populo decretum . Adiectivum alibi non lectum ex hoc loco annotavit Steph . Βyz . s . ν . δῆμοςν. δῆμος [the people] , per ὁ ἀπὸ ( ὑπὸὁ ἀπὸ (ὑπὸ [the one from (by]) Meinekius ) τοῦ δήμου ἐλαθεὶτοῦ δήμου ἐλαθεὶ [driven by the people] s interpretatus .

φυγὴν δημήλατον [exile driven by the people] means exile decreed by the people. The adjective, not read elsewhere, Stephanus of Byzantium noted from this passage under the word δῆμος [people], interpreting it as ὁ ἀπὸ (ὑπὸ Meineke) τοῦ δήμου ἐλαθεὶς [the one driven from (by) the people].

cit.quote: φερέσβιον Δήμητρος ἀντέλλει στάχυν .
the life-giving ear of Demeter rises.
μήλων τε βοσκὰς καὶ βίον Δημήτριον .
pasture of sheep and Demetrian livelihood.

sense.note: Frequentius Δημήτριος καρπόςDemetrian fruit dicitur , in codicibus saepe ΔημήτρειοςDemetreios scriptum : de quo v . Thes . vol . 2 p . 1071 .
More frequently Δημήτριος καρπός [Demetrian fruit] is said, in manuscripts often written Δημήτρειος [Demetreios]: on which see Thes. vol. 2 p. 1071.

cit.quote: κτήνη πρόσθε τὰ δημιοπληθῆ ,
the cattle before, the publicly abundant ones,
cit.note: i . e . copiosas olim opes publicas .
i.e. formerly abundant public wealth.

cit.quote: μέλεσθέ θ᾽ ἱερῶν δημίων .
and you care for the public sacrifices.
πόλει μὲν ἕλκος ἓν τὸ δήμιον τυχεῖν .
for the city to have one public wound.
δι᾽ ὤτων φρενός τε δαμίας περαῖνον .
passing through the ears and the public mind.
ποίοισι βωμοῖς χρώμενος τοῖς δημίοις ;
using which public altars?

cit.note: δαμαίωνof the public ( cum a super w ) et 879 δαμίανpublic vitiose pro δαναιᾶνof the long-lived . V. δηναιόςlong-lived . ]
δαμαίων [of the public] (with a super w) and 879 δαμίαν [public] corruptly for δαναιᾶν [of the long-lived]. See δηναιός.

cit.quote: καὶ δώματ᾽ ἐστὶ πολλὰ μὲν τὰ δήμια .
and there are many public houses.

sense.def: τὸ δήμιονthe public thing res publica , imperium .
τὸ δήμιον [the public thing] the state, the government.

cit.quote: σύ τοι πόλις , σὺ δὲ τὸ δήμιον .
you are the city, you are the public thing.
τὸ δήμιον , τὸ πτόλιν κρατύνει .
the public thing, which rules the city.

sense.note: Utrobique Doricam restitui formam δάμιονpublic (Doric) , servatam in M Ch . 56 .
In both places I restored the Doric form δάμιον [public], preserved in M Ch. 56.

form.gloss: with public clamor, spread by public rumor

sense.def: cum clamore populi coniunctus , populi ore et sermone iactatus .
joined with the clamor of the people, tossed about by the mouth and speech of the people.

cit.quote: δημόθρους ἀναρχία .
public-voiced anarchy.
φήμη γε μέντοι δημόθρους μέγα σθένει .
yet public rumor has great strength.
τόδ᾽ ἐπέθου θύος δημοθρόους τ᾿ ἀράς .
you offered this sacrifice and public curses.
cit.note: ubi reliquae formae Doricae δαμοθρόουςwith public clamor (Doric) postulant .
where the remaining Doric forms δαμοθρόους [with public clamor] demand.

cit.quote: δημόθρους τ᾽ ἔχειν ἀράς .
and to have public curses.

sense.note: Adiectivum apud alios non lectum , nisi quod Tzetza Exeg . 11. p . 62 , 22 δημόθρουν κανόνpublic rule øregulam trivialem dixit . Idem fere de tribus proximis adiectivis dicendum est δημόκραντοςratified by the people ( ab verbo κραίνειν ) δημόπρακτος δημορριφήςto accomplish) done by the people, cast out by the people , quae ipsa quoque apud Aeschylum solum leguntur .

An adjective not read in other authors, except that Tzetzes Exeg. 11. p. 62, 22 called δημόθρουν κανόν [public rule] a trivial rule. The same is to be said about the three following adjectives δημόκραντος [ratified by the people] (from the verb κραίνειν [to accomplish]) δημόπρακτος [done by the people] δημορριφής [cast out by the people], which also are read only in Aeschylus.

cit.quote: δημοκράντου δ᾽ ἀρᾶς τίνει χρέος .
he pays the debt of a curse ratified by the people.
τοιάδε δημόπρακτος ἐκ πόλεως μία ψῆφος κέκρανται .
such a vote, done by the people, has been decided by the city.

sense.def: thrown or cast out by the people.

cit.quote: δημορριφεῖς – λευσίμους ἀράς .
cast out by the people – curses of stoning.
λευστήρα δήμου δ᾽ οὔτι μὴ φύγῃ μόρον .
and may he not escape the fate of stoning by the people.
δήμου προβούλοις .
to the people's counselors.
τραχύς γε μέντοι δῆμος ἐκφυγὼν κακά .
yet the people, having escaped evils, are harsh.
Βακτρίων δ᾽ ἔρρει πανώλης δῆμος .
and the whole people of the Bactrians perishes.
οὐκ ἄνευ δήμου τάδε πράξαιμ᾽ ἄν .
I would not do these things without the people.
ὑμῖν δ᾽ ἂν εἴη δῆμος εὐμενέστερος .
and the people would be more kindly to you.
δήμου δέδοκται παντελή ψηφίσματα .
the people have decreed full measures.
δήμου κρατοῦσα χεὶρ ὅποι πληθύεται .
the ruling hand of the people, wherever it prevails.
δῆμος Πελασγών .
the people of the Pelasgians.
τοὶ δ᾽ ἀνὰ γᾶν Ἀσίαν δὴν οὐκέτι περσονομοῦνται .
and they no longer are ruled by Persians throughout the land of Asia for long.
cit.note: ubi ἈσιηνάνAsian vel ἈσιανάνAsian coniecit Meinekius . Probabilius θήνindeed coniicias , ut dixi in Thes . vol . 4 p . 364 .
where Meineke conjectured Ἀσιηνάν [Asian] or Ἀσιανάν [Asian]. More probably you would conjecture θήν [indeed], as I said in Thes. vol. 4 p. 364.

cit.quote: αἱ Φορκίδες ναίουσι δηναιαὶ κόραι .
the Phorcides, long-lived maidens, dwell.
δηναιῶν θρόνων .
of long-lived thrones.

sense.note: Forma Dorica
Doric form

cit.quote: τιμᾶν δαναιᾶν
to honor the long-lived
cit.note: restituta ab L. Dindorfio in Thes . vol . 2 p . 885. In M loco priore τιμῶν δαμαίωνhonors of the public cum.a. super ῶνῶν et.a. super wv ab διορθωτῇto the corrector scripto , loco altero τιμᾶν δαμίανto honor the public (goddess) .

restored by L. Dindorf in Thes. vol. 2 p. 885. In M in the former place τιμῶν δαμαίων [honors of the public] with a. over ῶν and a. over wv written by a corrector, in the latter place τιμᾶν δαμίαν [to honor the public].

cit.quote: δηξίθυμον ἔρωτος ἄνθος .
the heart-biting flower of love

cit.note: Hoc a quibusdam illatum
This was introduced by some
cit.quote: γοᾶται δὲ δήποθεν κατάπτυστον ,
and the land laments from somewhere, abominable,
cit.note: ubi in Μ δὴ ποθειM δὴ ποθει [indeed longs for] ( sic sine accentu ) . γοᾶται δὲ γᾶς πάθοςthe land laments its suffering Hermannus . ]
where in M δὴ ποθει [indeed longs for] (thus without accent). γοᾶται δὲ γᾶς πάθος [the land laments its suffering] Hermannus.

cit.quote: Τροίαν ἑλόντες δήποτε .
having taken Troy at some time
καὶ μήτε δῆρις ῥυσίων ἐφάψεται .
and may no strife over reprisals touch them.
ἢ καὶ σὺ νίκην τήνδε ( τῆσδε Auratus ) δήριος τίεις ;
Or do you also pay honor to this victory (this victory Auratus) of strife?
cit.note: ubi notanda Ionica genitivi forma , in δήρεωςof strife mutata a Bothio .
where the Ionic form of the genitive is to be noted, changed to δήρεως [of strife] by Bothius.

sense.def: profecto . Huius particulae idem fere usus est qui dήor particulae , sed ut graviorem quam illa exprimat asseverationem .
indeed. The use of this particle is almost the same as that of the particle δή, but it expresses a stronger assertion than that.

cit.quote: οὐ δήτα .
not indeed.
μὴ δῆτα .
not indeed.
ἢ δῆτ᾽ ἂν εἴη πανδίκως ψευδώνυμος Δίκη .
or indeed Justice would be truly called by a false name.
αὐτὸς δ᾽ ἀναλοῖ δῆτα δύσποτμον γένος .
and he himself indeed destroys the ill-fated race.
οἳ δῆτ᾽ ὀρθῶς ὤλοντο .
who indeed perished justly.
ἴυγγά μοι δῆτ᾽ ἀγαθῶν ἑτάρων ὑπομιμνήσκεις .
you remind me indeed of the spell of good companions.
ἰὼ δῆτα ναὶ ναί .
ah indeed, yes, yes.
καὶ τὰς προπομποὺς δῆτα τάσδε λοιδορεῖς .
and indeed you abuse these escorts.
ἣν δῆτ᾽ Ἀχαιῶν ἄκτορές τε καὶ πρόμοι – ἔνειμαν .
which indeed the leaders and chiefs of the Achaeans allotted.
ἴδοιτο δῆτ᾽ ἄνατον φυγὰν ἱκεσία Θέμις .
may Themis see indeed the unharmed flight of the suppliant.

sense.def: in responsione , repetito quo alter usus erat vocabulo .
in response, repeating the word which the other had used.

cit.note: ( post alterius verba ἑλόντες μέλεοι σὺν ἀλκᾷhaving taken, wretched, with strength )
(after the other's words ἑλόντες μέλεοι σὺν ἀλκᾷ [having taken, wretched, with strength])
cit.quote: μέλεοι δῆτα .
wretched indeed.
τετυμμένοι δῆτα .
struck indeed.
ὁμόσποροι δῆτα .
of the same seed indeed.

cit.note: ἀπώλεσεν δῆταhe destroyed indeed corruptum ex ὤλεσε δὴ τόδεhe destroyed this indeed , ut s . v . δήindeed diximus . ]
ἀπώλεσεν δῆτα [he destroyed indeed] corrupted from ὤλεσε δὴ τόδε [he destroyed this indeed], as we said under δή.

cit.quote: ἴδοιτο δῆτα .
may she see indeed.
συγγνοῖτο δῆτα .
may he pardon indeed.
ποῖ δῆτα κρανεῖ ;
where indeed will it end?
πότερα δῆτ᾽ ἐγὼ ποτιπέσω βρέτη δαιμόνων ;
whether indeed shall I fall upon the images of the gods?
ποῦ δῆθ᾽ ὁ τίμος ;
where indeed is the honor?
πῶς δῆτ᾽ ἂν εἰπὼν κεδνὰ τἀληθῆ τύχοις ;
how indeed could you speak good things and hit upon the truth?
πῶς δῆτ᾽ ἄνατος ήσθα Λοξίου κότῳ ;
how indeed were you unharmed by the wrath of Loxias?
τί δῆτα μέλλεις ;
why indeed do you delay?
τί δῆτ᾽ ἐμοὶ Ζῆν κέρδος ;
what indeed is the gain of life to me?
τί δῆτ᾽ ἐμαυτῆς καταγέλωτ᾽ ἔχω τάδε ;
why indeed do I have these mockeries of myself?
τί δῆτ᾽ ἐγὼ κάτοικτος ὧδ᾽ ἀναστένω ;
why indeed do I, pitiable, lament thus?
τί δῆτα πρὸς ταῦτ᾽ ἄλοχος ἰσχυρὰ Διός ;
what indeed is the strong wife of Zeus to these things?
καὶ πρὸς τί δῆτα τυγχάνω κατευγμάτων ;
and for what indeed do I happen to be praying?

sense.def: per . Cum genitivo spatii vel loci quem quis vel quid permeat .
through. With the genitive of space or place through which someone or something passes.

cit.quote: στείχει δ᾽ ἴουλος ἄρτι διὰ παρηΐδων .
and the down goes just now through the cheeks.
ἱκνεῖται λόγος διὰ στηθέων .
the word comes through the breast.
βέβακεν ῥίμφα διὰ πυλᾶν .
he has gone swiftly through the gates.
παραλλάξασα διὰ χερῶν βέβακεν ὄψις .
the vision has passed through the hands and gone.
δι᾽ ὤτων φρενός τε δαμίας περαῖνον .
through the ears and the mind of the public, accomplishing.
δι᾽ ὤτων δὲ συντέτραινε μῦθον .
and through the ears pierce the word.
ἐλῶσι γάρ σε καὶ δι ' ἠπείρου μακρᾶς .
for they will drive you through the long mainland.
πᾶσαν αἰαν , ἧς δί᾽ ἁγνὸς ἔρχεται Στρυμών .
the whole land through which the holy Strymon flows.
δι᾽ ἄστεως στείχουσι .
they walk through the city.
δι᾿ αἴας μηλοβότου Φρυγίας .
through the sheep-pasturing land of Phrygia.
δι᾽ ὀρῶν Κιλίκων .
through the mountains of the Cilicians.
οἳ διὰ χώρας θελεμὸν πῶμα χέουσιν .
who through the land pour a soothing drink.

sense.note: Pro ἐνin cum dativo saepe ponitur in locutione διὰ χειρὸς ἔχεινto hold in hand et similibus , quae collectae sunt in Thes . vol . 2 p . 1100. et in Lexico Soph . p . 117 .
It is often used for ἐν with the dative in the expression διὰ χειρὸς ἔχειν [to have in hand] and similar ones, which are collected in Thes. vol. 2 p. 1100 and in the Lexicon Soph. p. 117.

cit.quote: φλέγει δὲ λαμπὰς διὰ χερῶν .
and the torch blazes through their hands.
διὰ χερός βέλος φλέγων .
a blazing missile through the hand.
πότερα γάρ το-Ξουλκὸς αἰχμὴ διὰ χερῶν αὐτοῖς πρέπει ;
for does the drawn spear point through their hands befit them?
ἱκετηρίας – σεμνῶς ἔχουσαι διὰ χερῶν εὐωνύμων .
holding suppliant branches solemnly in their left hands.
βαθεῖαν ἄλοκα διὰ φρενός καρπούμενος .
reaping a deep furrow through the mind.

sense.def: de tempore dictum per quod quid fit vel durat
said of time through which something happens or lasts

cit.quote: ἀλκὰ δι᾽ ὀλίγου .
strength through a short time.
διὰ μακροῦ χρόνου .
through a long time.
οἷαι δι᾿ αἰῶνος τύχαι ,
such fortunes through all time.
cit.note: ubi sensus et metrum διαίμονες τύχαιbloody fortunes vel aliud huius mensurae vocabulum postulat .
where the sense and meter require διαίμονες τύχαι [bloody fortunes] or another word of this measure.
Recte vero δι ' αἰῶνοςthrough all time
Correctly indeed δι' αἰῶνος [through eternity]
cit.quote: τὸν δι᾽ αἰῶνος χρόνον .
the time through all eternity.
δι᾽ αἰῶνος δ᾽ ἰυγμοῖσι βόσκεται κέαρ .
and through all time the heart is fed with wailings.
δι᾿ αἰῶνος δὲ τὸν πρὶν ὄλβον ἕρματι προσβαλών δίκας .
and through all time, having cast his former prosperity upon a support of justice.
δι ' ( sic recte Hermannus pro Ζεύς ) αἰῶνος κρέων ἀπαύστου .
through (thus rightly Hermann for Zeus) unceasing eternity ruling.
δι ' αἰῶνος μακροῦ πάνολβον .
through long eternity all-blessed.

sense.def: διάthrough cum genitivo personae vel rei per quam quid fit
διά with the genitive of the person or thing through which something happens

cit.quote: διὰ θεῶν πόλιν νεμόμεθ᾽ ἀδάματον .
through the city of the gods we dwell, unconquered.
δι᾽ ὧν αἰνομόροις , δι ' ὧν νεῖκος ἔβα .
through which to the ill-fated, through which strife came.
δι ' εὐωνύμων τετυμμένοι .
struck through the left sides.
φρυκτωρῶν δία πεισθεῖσα .
persuaded by means of beacon-fires.
δι ' ἆς τοι γένος εὐχόμεθ᾽ εἶναι γᾶς ἀπὸ τᾶσδ᾽ ἔνοικοι .
through whom we boast to be the race of this land, its inhabitants.
cit.note: Sic Poisonus pro δίαςthrough .
Thus Poisonus for δίας [of the goddess].

sense.def: διάthrough cum genitivo rationem significans qua quid fit
διά with the genitive signifying the reason by which something happens

cit.quote: διὰ δίκας πᾶν ἔπος ἔλακον .
through justice I uttered every word.
πικροὶ γὰρ κοὐ διὰ ζόης ἀτμοί .
for bitter are the vapors, and not through life.
τὸν πᾶσι θεοῖς δι᾽ ἀπεχθείας ἐλθόντα .
who came into hatred with all the gods.
διὰ μάχης ἥξω τέλους .
I will come through battle to the end.
ὡς μάθητε διὰ τέλους τὸ πᾶν .
so that you may learn the whole matter through to the end.
διὰ τέλους δέ σοι φύλαξ ἐγγὺς παρεστώς .
and through to the end a guard stands near you.
τοὺς σοὺς δὲ πόνους χρήζω διὰ παντὸς ἀκοῦσαι .
and I desire to hear your toils throughout.
cit.note: διὰ τέλους , διὰ παντόςthrough to the end, throughout ad finem usque , omnino .
διὰ τέλους, διὰ παντός [through to the end, through all] to the end, altogether.

cit.quote: πάνυ θήσειν Ἀγαμεμνονίων οἴκων ὄλεθρον διὰ παντός .
that he will utterly bring about the destruction of the house of Agamemnon throughout.
νικᾷ δ᾽ ἀγαθῶν ἔρις ἡμετέρα διὰ παντός .
and our strife of good things prevails throughout.
βίοτον διὰ παντὸς ( sic Heathius pro διὰ πάντ᾽ ) ἄτιμος ἀμείψει ( ἀμειψεται M , quod correxit Erfurdtius ) .
throughout life (thus Heath for διὰ πάντ᾽) dishonored you will change (M has ἀμειψεται, which Erfurdt corrected).

sense.def: διάthrough per , cum accusativo . De loco quem quis pervadit
διά through, with the accusative. Of the place which someone traverses

cit.quote: ὃς ἀεὶ δι᾽ Ἀχέροντ᾽ ἀμείβεται .
who always crosses through Acheron.
περᾷ κρυσταλλοπῆγα διὰ πόρον .
crosses the ice-bound passage.
φεύγειν ἀνέδην διὰ κῦμ᾽ ἅλιον .
to flee unhindered through the sea wave.
δι᾽ ἁλίρρυτον ἄλσος – ἀλαθείς .
through the sea-washed grove – wandering.
οἶκτος δ᾽ οὔτις ἦν διὰ στόμα .
and no pity was in their mouths.
ἱέντα πύρπνοον διὰ στόμα λιγνὺν μέλαιναν .
sending through the mouth fire-breathing black smoke.
λέγει δὲ τοῦτ᾽ ἔπος διὰ στόμα .
and he speaks this word through his mouth.

sense.def: διά with the accusative, on account of.

cit.quote: διὰ τὴν λίαν φιλότητα βροτῶν .
because of the excessive love of mortals.
δι᾽ ἔριν αἱματόεσσαν .
through bloody strife.
δι ' ὠμὰν ἔριν ,
through cruel strife.
cit.note: ut Hermannus pro αιωμαναιρεινto lift up .
as Hermannus for αιωμαναιρειν.

cit.quote: δι᾽ αἵματ᾽ ἐκποθένθ᾽ ὑπὸ χθονὸς τροφοῦ .
through blood drunk up by the nurturing earth.
δι᾽ ὀργάν .
through anger.
δι᾽ ἀμὸν γάμον .
through my marriage.
διὰ δ᾽ Ἰαόνων χέρας
and through the hands of the Ionians
cit.note: corrupte pro ήδ᾽ Ἰαόνων χέρεςand the hands of the Ionians , quod restitui . ]
corruptly for ήδ᾽ Ἰαόνων χέρες [and the hands of the Ionians], which I restored.

cit.quote: διὰ χερί ποτε λαχεῖν κτήματα ,
to obtain possessions by lot through the hand.
cit.note: i . e . διαλαχεῖνto obtain by lot .
i.e. διαλαχεῖν [to divide by lot].

cit.quote: πηδαλίων δία .
through the rudders.
φρυκτωρῶν δία πεισθεῖσα .
persuaded by means of beacon-fires.
πᾶσαν αἰαν , ἧς δί᾽ ἁγνὸς ἔρχεται Στρυμών .
the whole land through which the holy Strymon flows.

sense.def: pro διάthrough , quod cum similibus comparandum est formis καταί παραί ὑπαίdown along, beside, under , aliquoties dixit Aeschylus .
for διά, which is to be compared with similar forms καταί, παραί, ὑπαί, Aeschylus said several times.

cit.quote: ἀλλοτρίας διαὶ γυναικός .
for the sake of another man's wife.
κακῶν γὰρ διαί .
for the sake of evils.

sense.note: Utrobique in Μ διάM: through , sed διαίfor the sake of priore loco grammaticus in Crameri Anecd . Oxon . vol . 1 p . 119 , 14 , altero Hermannus .
In both places M has διά, but διαί in the former place the grammarian in Cramer's Anecdota Oxoniensia vol. 1 p. 119, 14, in the latter Hermann.

cit.quote: πολλὰ τλάντος γυναικὸς διαί .
for the sake of a woman who endured much.
διαὶ Διὸς παναιτίου .
through Zeus, the cause of all.
διαὶ ( sic Schuetzius pro διὰ ) βίου .
through (thus Schuetz for διὰ) life.

sense.note: Sed
But

cit.note: vitiose in M.
faultily in M.
cit.quote: Ἀἰγίσθου διαι ( sine accentu )
for the sake of Aegisthus (without accent)

cit.note: quod schol . exp . δάκρυε τὸ ἀτύχημαweep for the misfortune . Sed quaeritur quomodo metri vitium tollendum sit , quum de synecphonesi cogitari nequeat , neque ἴαιν᾽ ἴαινεwarm, warm scribi cum Heimsoethio ( p . 352496 ) possit , quod verbum non de rebus tristibus , sed de laetis dici solet . Aeschylus igitur si verbo διαίνωto wet, moisten usus est , de quo vix dubitari potest , quum chorus Xerxi respondeat διαίνομαι γοεδνὸς ὤνI am wet with tears, being mournful et 1065 Xerxes iterum διαίνου δ᾽ ὄσσεwet your eyes dicat , et chorus v . 258 αἰαῖ , διαίνεσθε , Πέρσαι τόδ᾽ ἄχος κλύοντεςalas, wet yourselves, Persians, hearing this grief , ubi scholiasta pariter per δακρύετεweep explicat , nihil relinquitur quam ut δίαιν δίαινεwet, wet scribatur . Simili apocope παῦstop pro παθεsuffer dictum esse cognoscitur ex Photio p . 403 , 4 , unde Aristophani Equit . 821 restitutum est παῦ παῦ᾽ οὗτοςstop, stop, you , ubi libri violato metro παῦ᾽ οὑτοσίstop, this fellow . Ceterum sponte intelligitur apocopen hanc ibi tantum locum habere ubi idem verbum repetatur . Itaque Aeschylus et Aristophanes recte dicere potuerunt δίαιν δίαινεwet, wet et παῦ παῦεstop, stop , non potuissent simpliciter δίαινwet et παῦstop , quod non probatur formula ἄλευ δᾶavoid, O earth , de qua dixi s . v . ἀλεύωto avoid .

which the scholiast explains as δάκρυε τὸ ἀτύχημα [weep for the misfortune]. But the question is how the metrical fault is to be removed, since synizesis cannot be considered, nor can ἴαιν᾽ ἴαινε [warm, warm] be written with Heimsoeth (p. 352496), because that verb is usually said of joyful, not sad, things. Therefore, if Aeschylus used the verb διαίνω [to wet, moisten], about which there can scarcely be doubt, since the chorus answers Xerxes διαίνομαι γοεδνὸς ὤν [I am wet with tears, being mournful] and at 1065 Xerxes again says διαίνου δ᾽ ὄσσε [wet your eyes], and the chorus at v. 258 αἰαῖ, διαίνεσθε, Πέρσαι τόδ᾽ ἄχος κλύοντες [alas, wet yourselves, Persians, hearing this grief], where the scholiast likewise explains it by δακρύετε [weep], nothing remains but to write δίαιν δίαινε [wet, wet]. That a similar apocope παῦ [stop] is used for παθε [suffer] is known from Photius p. 403, 4, whence in Aristophanes Knights 821 παῦ παῦ᾽ οὗτος [stop, stop, you] has been restored, where the manuscripts, with the meter violated, have παῦ᾽ οὑτοσί [stop, this fellow]. Moreover, it is self-evident that this apocope has a place only where the same verb is repeated. Thus Aeschylus and Aristophanes could rightly say δίαιν δίαινε [wet, wet] and παῦ παῦε [stop, stop], but they could not simply say δίαιν [wet] and παῦ [stop], which is not proven by the formula ἄλευ δᾶ [avoid, O earth], about which I have spoken s.v. ἀλεύω [to avoid].
