κεί στόμαργός ἐστ᾽ ἄγαν, αἴθων τέτακται λῆμα.
Even if he is too loud-mouthed, his spirit is fiery and steadfast.
εἰκός γε πράξειν ἄνδρας ὧδ᾽ ἀντιστάτας, εἰ Ζεύς γε Τυφῶ καρτερώτερος μάχη.
It is likely that men will act as opponents, if Zeus is stronger than Typhon in battle.
παῦροί γε πολλῶν, εἴ τι πιστεῦσαι θεῶν χρὴ θεσφάτοισιν.
Few out of many, if one must trust the oracles of the gods.
εἰ σὺ μὴ τόδ᾽ ἐννοεῖς, ἐγὼ λέγω σοι.
If you do not understand this, I tell you.
καὶ τῶνδ᾽ ὅμοιον εἴ τι μὴ πείθω.
And similar to these, if I do not persuade you.
εἰ δ᾽ ἐτητύμως μόρον τὸν αὑτῆς οἶσθα, πῶς – πατεῖς;
But if you truly know her fate, how do you tread?
τί τοῦτ᾽ ἔφευξας, εἴ τι μὴ φρενῶν στύγος;
Why did you flee from this, if not from some horror of the mind?
εἰ δὲ δυστυχῆ, βολαῖς ὑγρώσσων σφόγγος ὤλεσεν γραφήν.
But if they are unfortunate, a sponge wetting with its strokes destroyed the writing.
ὧδ᾽ ἔχει λόγος γυναικός, εἴ τις ἀξιοῖ μαθεῖν.
Thus goes the woman's story, if anyone cares to learn.
εἰ δ᾽ ἄλλο πρᾶξαι δεῖ τι βουλιώτερον, ἀνδρῶν τόδ᾽ ἐστὶν ἔργον.
But if some other, more weighty matter must be done, this is the work of men.
εἰ τοῖσιν οὖν κτείνουσιν ἀλλήλους χαλᾷς – οὐ φημι.
If then you relax your hold on those who kill each other—I do not say it.
τὸ πρᾶγμα μεῖζον εἴ (ἤ recte Porsonus) τις οἴεται τόδε βροτὸς δικάζειν.
The matter is too great, if (or as Porson rightly says) anyone thinks that a mortal judges this.
εἰ δὲ κυρεῖ τις πέλας οἰωνοπόλων — δοξάσει.
But if someone near is an augur—he will think.
ποῖ φύγωμεν Ἀπίας χθονός, κελαινὸν εἴ τι κεῦθός ἐστί που;
Where shall we flee from the land of Apia, if there is any dark hiding-place somewhere?
εἰ δέ τις μείζων χάρις, πάρεστιν | οἰκεῖν.
But if there is any greater favor, it is possible to dwell.
δίδαξον ἡμᾶς, εἴ τι μὴ βλάπτει λόγω.
Teach us, if it does not harm in speech.
εἰ δ᾽ ἔχεις εἰπεῖν ὅ τι λοιπὸν πόνων, σήμαινε.
But if you can say what remains of toils, indicate it.
σήμηνον, εἰ μή τις βλάβη.
Give a sign, if there is no harm.
εἰ ῥητὸν, φράσον.
If it is speakable, tell it.
εἴ τι σοὶ ψελλόν τε καὶ δυσεύρετον, ἐπανδίπλαζε.
If anything is stammering and hard to find for you, repeat it.
εἰ μέν τι τῇδε λοιπὸν ἔχεις γεγωνεῖν, λέγε.
If you have anything left to say here, speak.
εἰ δὲ πάντ᾽ εἴρηκας, ἡμῖν αὐ χάριν δός.
But if you have said everything, give us thanks in return.
λέξον κατάστὰς, κεἰ στένεις κακοῖς ὅμως.
Speak, standing up, even if you groan at your misfortunes.
εἰ δ᾽ ἀξυνήμων οὖσα μὴ δέχει λόγον, σὺ δ᾽ ἀντὶ φωνῆς φράζε καρβάνῳ χερί.
But if you are uncomprehending and do not accept my word, then you, instead of voice, make signs with a foreign hand.
μέμνησ' Ὀρέστου, κεί θυραῖός ἐσθ᾽ ὅμως.
Remember Orestes, even though he is away from home.
κεἰ παρ᾿ Ἑλλήνων τινὲς ἴτων πάλῳ λαχόντες.
And if some of the Greeks come, having obtained it by lot.
εἰ μιαίνεται πόλις, ξυνῇ μελέσθω λαός.
If the city is polluted, let the people be concerned in common.
νοσοῖμ᾽ ἂν, εἰ νόσημα τοὺς ἐχθροὺς στυγεῖν.
I would be sick, if sickness is to hate one's enemies.
εἰ γάρ τι κακῶν ἄκος οἶδε πλέον, μόνος ἂν θνητῶν πέρας εἴποι.
For if he knows any further remedy for evils, he alone of mortals could tell the end.
εἰ δ᾽ εὐσεβοῦσι τοὺς πολισσούχους θεοὺς οὔ τἂν ἑλόντες αὖθις ἀνθαλοῖεν ἄν.
But if they revere the gods who protect the city, they would not, after conquering, flourish again.
εἰ δὲ χρὴ τυχεῖν σωτηρίας, σμικροῦ γένοιτ᾽ ἂν σπέρματος μέγας πυθμήν.
But if salvation must be obtained, from a small seed a great stock might grow.
λέγοιτ᾽ ἂν εἴ τι δεῖ.
It would be said, if there is any need.
ἀλλ᾽ εἰ μὲν ἁγνόν ἐστί σοι Πειθοῦς σέβας — σὺ δ᾽ οὖν μένοις ἄν · εἰ δὲ μὴ θέλεις μένειν, οὐ τἂν δικαίως τῇδ᾽ ἐπιρρέποις πόλει μηνίν τινα.
But if the majesty of Persuasion is holy to you, then you might remain; but if you do not wish to remain, you would not justly bring any wrath upon this city.
εἴ τοι κρατοῦσι παῖδες Αἰγύπτου σέθεν τίς ἂν τοῖσδ᾽ ἀντιωθῆναι θέλοι;
If the sons of Aegyptus have power over you, who would wish to oppose them?
ἐγὼ γὰρ οὐκ εἰ δυστυχῶ, τοῦδ᾽ ούνεκα θέλοιμ᾽ ἂν ὡς πλείστοισι πημονὰς τυχεῖν.
For I, if I am unfortunate, would not for that reason wish that misfortunes befall as many as possible.
ἀλλ' εἰ δοκεῖ σοι ταῦθ᾽, ὑπαί τις ἀρβύλας λύοι.
But if this seems good to you, let someone loosen the sandals.
θεοῦ δὲ καὶ μήτηρ ἔφυς, εἴ τι μὴ δαίμων παλαιὸς νῦν μεθέστηκε στρατῷ.
And you were born of a goddess as mother, unless some ancient divinity has now changed sides for the army.
εἰ γάρ τι μὴ θεοῖς βεβούλευται νέον, ἴχνος τὸ πρόσθεν οὐ διαστρέψω φρενός.
For if no new thing has been decided by the gods, I will not turn aside the former track of my mind.
εἴ που πάλαι (δέδεχθε), φαιδροῖσι καὶ νῦν ὄμμασιν δέξασθε.
If you have received it long ago, receive it now with bright eyes.
κεἰ μὴ πέποιθα, τοὔργον ἔστ᾽ ἐργαστέον.
And if I do not trust it, the deed must still be done.

sense.def: 3. Cum futuro, sequente in apodosi indicativo vel imperativo.
3. With the future, followed in the apodosis by the indicative or imperative.

cit.quote: κεἰ μή τις ἀρχῆς τῆς ἐμῆς ἀκούσεται –, ψῆφος κατ᾿ αὐτῶν ὀλεθρία βουλεύσεται.
And if no one will obey my authority, a destructive vote will be decided against them.
οἶδεν ὡς σφε χρὴ τελευτῆσαι μάχη, εἰ καρπὸς ἔσται θεσφάτοισι Λοξίου.
He knows that he must die in battle, if there is to be fruit from the oracles of Loxias.
ὡς, εἰ μελαίνης νυκτός ἵξεται κνέφας, Ἕλληνες οὐ μενοῖεν.
So that, if the darkness of black night comes, the Greeks would not remain.
εἴ τι δράσεις τώνδε, μὴ σχολὴν τίθει.
If you will do any of these things, do not delay.
εἰ προτέρων αἷμ᾿ ἀποτίσει ἐπικρανεῖ.
If he pays back the blood of those before, it will be revealed.
οὐχ ἡσσον εὐδάκρυτά μοι λέγεις τάδε, εἰ τῆσδε χώρας μήποτε ψαύσει ποδί.
You tell me these things no less worthy of tears, if he will never touch this land with his foot.
ἄτας – ἐξαυδώμενος, εἰ μὴ μέτειμι τοῦ πατρὸς (immo τοῦ φόνου) τοὺς αἰτίους.
Calling down ruin, if I do not pursue those responsible for my father's murder.
εἰ δ᾽ οὖν ἀμείψω βαλὸν ἕρκειον πυλῶν —, νεκρὸν θήσω.
But if I change my throw at the gate of the courtyard, I will make him a corpse.
εἴ σε μάρψει ψῆφος, ἀλλ᾽ ἐρεῖς τάχα.
If the vote seizes you, but you will speak soon.
εἰ μή τι πιστὸν τῷδ᾽ ὑποστήσεις στόλῳ.
Unless you will provide something trustworthy for this expedition.
εἰ μὲν γὰρ ὑμῖν μὴ τόδ᾽ ἐκπράξω χρέος, μίασμ᾿ ἔλεξας οὐχ ὑπερτοξεύσιμον.
For if I do not accomplish this task for you, you have spoken of a pollution not to be outshot.
εἰ μή τις ἐς ναῦν εἶσιν –, κατοικτιεῖ.
Unless someone goes to the ship, he will lament.
εἰ γάρ τιν᾽ ἑστιοῦχον ὄψομαι μόνον —, στέγην πυρώσω.
For if I see any guardian of the hearth alone, I will set the house on fire.
ἀλλ᾽ εἰ δρακόντων δυσφρόνων ἐχθίοσιν (ἐκδώσεις);
But if you will give them to enemies more hateful than hostile serpents?

sense.def: Followed in the apodosis by the optative

cit.quote: εἰ δ᾽ ὧδε τραχεῖς καὶ τεθηγμένους λόγους ῥίψεις, τάχ᾽ ἄν σου καὶ μακρὰν ἀνωτέρω θακῶν κλύοι Ζεύς.
But if you hurl such harsh and sharpened words, perhaps Zeus, seated far above you, may hear.
ἄγοιμ᾽ ἂν, εἴ τις τάσδε μὴ ᾿ξαιρήσεται.
I would lead them, unless someone will take these women away.

sense.def: 4. Cum imperfecto, sequente in apodosi imperfecto vel aoristo cum av, dicitur de re quae non est, sed esse fingitur.
4. With the imperfect, followed in the apodosis by the imperfect or aorist with ἄν, used of a thing which is not, but is imagined to be.

cit.quote: εἰ δ᾽ ἡ Διὸς παῖς παρθένος Δίκη παρῆν –, τάχ᾽ ἂν τόδ᾽ ἦν.
But if the maiden Justice, daughter of Zeus, were present, this would quickly be so.
εἰ δ᾽ ἦν τεθνηκὼς – τρισώματός τἂν Γηρυὼν ἐξηύχει.
But if he were dead, three-bodied Geryon would have boasted.
εἰ δὲ μὴ τεταγμένα Μοῖρα – εἰργε –, προφθάσασα καρδία γλῶσσαν ἂν τάδ᾽ ἐξέχει.
But if Fate had not prevented what was ordained, my heart, anticipating my tongue, would have poured out these things.
κυρεῖν λέγουσαν, ὥσπερ (ἂν ἔλεγες) εἰ παρεστάτεις.
Saying that she happens to be, as you would say if you were standing by.
εἰ δ᾽ ἣν πρεπόντως ὥστ᾽ ἐπισπένδειν νεκρῷ, τάδ᾽ ἂν δικαίως ἦν.
But if it were fitting to pour libations to the dead, these things would be just.
εἰ τοξοτευχεῖς ἦτε, κάρτ᾽ ἂν ἤκασα.
If you were armed with bows, I would have guessed very much.

sense.note: et omisso ἄνwould
and with ἄν omitted

cit.quote: καὶ τἄλλα πόλλ᾽ ἐπεικάσαι δίκαιον ἦν, εἰ μὴ παρόντι φθόγγος ἦν ὁ σημανῶν.
And it would be just to infer many other things, if there were not a voice present to indicate.

sense.def: Followed in the apodosis by the perfect

cit.quote: τραυμάτων μὲν εἰ τόσων ἐτύγχανεν –, τέτρωται.
If he had received so many wounds, he is wounded.
ὡς ὅντ᾽ ἀναστατῆρα Καδμείων χθονός, εἰ μὴ θεῶν τις ἐμποδὼν ἔστη.
As being an overthrower of the land of the Cadmeans, unless some god stood in the way.
εἴ τι φλαῦρον εἶδες, αἰτοῦ τῶνδ᾽ ἀποτροπὴν κακῶν.
If you saw anything bad, ask for the averting of these evils.
τί δ᾽ ἂν δοκεῖ σοι Πρίαμος εἰ τάδ᾽ ἤνυσεν;
What do you think Priam would have done if he had accomplished these things?
εἰ γὰρ ὑπ᾿ Ἰλίῳ κατηναρίσθης —, πολύχωστον ἂν εἶχες τάφον.
For if you had been slain beneath Ilium, you would have had a tomb heaped high with earth.

sense.def: 6. Cum optativo de re quae incertum est sit an non sit, sequente in apodosi plerumque optativo cum ἄνwould .
6. With the optative of a thing which is uncertain whether it is or is not, followed in the apodosis generally by the optative with ἄν.

cit.quote: εἴης φορητός οὐκ ἂν, εἰ πράσσοις καλῶς.
You would not be easy to bear, if you were faring well.
εἰ μὲν γὰρ εὐ πράξαιμεν, αἰτία θεοῦ · εἰ δ᾽ αὖθ᾽, ὃ μὴ γένοιτο, συμφορὰ τύχοι, Ἐτεοκλέης ἂν εἰς πολὺς κατὰ πτόλιν ὑμνοῦτο.
For if we should fare well, the credit is the god's; but if, on the other hand—which may it not happen—misfortune should befall, Eteocles alone would be much sung throughout the city.
εἰ γὰρ θανόντι νὺξ ἐπ᾿ ὀφθαλμοῖς πέσοι –, γένοιτ᾽ ἄν.
For if night should fall upon the eyes of the dead—it would be so.
εἰ γὰρ τύχοιεν –, ἡ τἂν πανώλεις παγκάκως τ᾽ ὀλοίατο.
For if they should succeed—then utterly destroyed and most miserably would they perish.

ὡς εἰ
102 μόρον φευξοίαθ᾽ Ἕλληνες κακὸν – πᾶσι στέρεσθαι κρατὸς ἦν προκείμενον.
As if the Greeks would escape an evil fate—it was set before them all to be deprived of their heads.
ἥξω λαβοῦσα πέλανον –, ἐπίσταμαι μὲν ὡς ἐπ᾿ ἐξειργασμένοις, ἀλλ᾽ ἐς τὸ λοιπὸν, εἴ τι δὴ λῷον πέλοι.
I will come bringing a libation cake—I know it is for deeds already done, but for the future, if anything better might be.
οὐδ᾽ ἂν εἰ δέκ᾽ ἤματα στοιχηγοροίην, οὐκ ἂν ἐκπλήσαιμί σοι.
Not even if I should speak for ten days in succession could I satisfy you.
εἰ μὴ στρατεύοισθ᾽ ἐς τὸν Ἑλλήνων τόπον.
Unless you march to the land of the Greeks.
cit.note: ubi apodosis πράσσοιτ᾽ ἂν ὡς ἄρισταthey would fare as best as possible supplenda ex praecedentibus alterius personae verbis.
where the apodosis πράσσοιτ᾽ ἂν ὡς ἄριστα [may he fare as well as possible] is to be supplied from the preceding words of the other person.

cit.quote: θεοῖς δ᾽ ἀναμπλάκητος εἰ μόλοι στρατός, κάμψαι – γένοιτ᾽ ἂν, εἰ πρόσπαια μὴ τύχοι κακά,
If the army should come without offense to the gods, it might turn back—if it should not encounter unforeseen evils.
cit.note: ubi εἰif in protasi duplici positum est, interposita apodosi, ut in locis Sophocleis Ai. 782. El. 582.
where εἰ is placed in a double protasis, with the apodosis interposed, as in the Sophoclean passages Ai. 782, El. 582.

cit.quote: τόν θ᾽ ὑπ᾽ Ἰλίῳ σέθεν κίνδυνον, εἴ τε δημόθρους ἀναρχία βουλὴν καταρρίψειεν.
And the danger to you beneath Ilium, whether the people's voice in anarchy might cast down the council.
πείθοι᾽ ἂν εἰ πείθοιο.
You would be persuaded if you should persuade.
χαίροιτ᾽ ἂν εἰ χαίροιτε.
You would rejoice if you should rejoice.
εἰ δέ τοι μόχθων γένοιτο τῶνδ᾽ ἅλις, δεχοίμεθ᾽ ἄν.
But if there should be enough of these toils, we would accept it.
λέγοις ἂν, εἴ τι τῶνδ᾽ ἔχοις ὑπέρτερον.
You might speak, if you have anything better than these.
μάθοιμ᾽ ἂν, εἰ λέγοι τις ἐμφανῆ λόγον.
I would learn, if someone should speak a clear word.
ἄλγη προφωνῶν ἀντίκεντρα καρδίᾳ, εἰ μή τι τῶνδ᾽ ἔρξαιμι τοὺς ἐπαιτίους.
Uttering pains as goads to my heart, unless I should do something to those responsible.
εἰ βραδύνοιμεν βοῇ.
If we should delay with the shout.
καλῶς γ᾽ ἂν ἡμῖν ξυμφέροι ταῦτ᾽, ὦ τέκνα, εἰ σοί τε καὶ θεοῖσιν ἐχθαιροίατο.
It would be well for us, my children, if they were hated by you and the gods.
κλάοις ἂν, εἰ ψαύσειας.
You would weep, if you should touch.
οὔτε πολλά τραύματ᾽ ἐν στέρνοις λαβὼν | θνήσκει τις, εἰ μὴ τέρμα συντρέχοι βίου.
Nor does anyone die from many wounds in the chest, unless the end of life should coincide.
εἴ τις ἐς νόσον πέσοι, οὐκ ἦν ἀλέξημ᾽ οὐδέν.
If anyone fell into sickness, there was no remedy at all.
κεἰ μὴ θέλοι, πυρωπὸν ἐκ Διός μολεῖν κεραυνόν.
And if he should not wish, a fiery thunderbolt from Zeus to come.

cit.note: Omisso in apodosi verbo
With the verb omitted in the apodosis
cit.quote: εἰ πάντα δ᾽ ὡς πράσσοιμεν (sic correxi vitiosum πράσσοιμ᾽ ἄν), εὐθαρσὴς ἐγώ,
But if we should do everything as we do (thus I corrected the faulty 'I would do'), I am confident.
cit.note: quod est εὐθαρσὴς ἐγὼ ἂν εἴηνI would be confident .
which is εὐθαρσὴς ἐγὼ ἂν εἴην [I would be confident].

cit.quote: εἰ δ᾽ οὖν ἀνάγκη τῆσδ᾽ ἐπιρρέποι τύχης, ἀρχαιοπλούτων δεσποτῶν πολλὴ χάρις,
But if indeed the necessity of this fortune weighs down, great is the gratitude of the ancient wealthy masters.
cit.note: i. e. χάρις ἂν εἴηthere would be gratitude .
i.e. χάρις ἂν εἴη [it would be a favor].
Cum anacolutho
With anacoluthon
cit.quote: μόχθους γὰρ εἰ λέγοιμι καὶ δυσαυλίας – σπαρνάς παρήξεις καὶ κακοστρώτους, τί δ᾽ οὐ στένοντες, οὐ λαχόντες ἤματος μέρος;
For if I should speak of the toils and the hard lodgings—the cramped and ill-strewn quarters—what part of the day did we not have groaning, not obtaining?
cit.note: ubi post εἰ λέγοιμιif I were to say sequi debebat οὐκ ἂν τέλος εὕροιμιI would not find an end , pro quo infertur τί δ᾽ οὐwhy not? – . Similiter ib. 563 ubi χειμῶνα δ᾽ εἰ λέγοι τις οἰωνοκτόνονAnd if someone should speak of the bird-killing winter et quae sequuntur, pro apodosi inferuntur verba τί ταῦτα πενθεῖν δεῖ;Why is it necessary to lament these things?

where after εἰ λέγοιμι [if I should say] there should have followed οὐκ ἂν τέλος εὕροιμι [I would not find an end], instead of which is introduced τί δ᾽ οὐ – [why not –]. Similarly at line 563 where χειμῶνα δ᾽ εἰ λέγοι τις οἰωνοκτόνον [if one should speak of a bird-killing storm] and what follows, instead of the apodosis are introduced the words τί ταῦτα πενθεῖν δεῖ; [why must we lament these things?]

sense.note: construxerunt epici, perraro tragici, quod de Sophocle observavit grammaticus in Bekkeri Anecdotis p. 144, 22: de quo dixi in Lexico Soph. p. 138. Aeschyli exempla ipsa quoque pauca sunt et partim incerta. Sic quod Pers. 791 legitur μηδ᾽ εἰ στράτευμα πλεῖον ἢ τὸ ΜηδικόνNot even if an army greater than the Median suspectum est propter πλεῖονmore . Nam veteres Attici, licet πλείων πλείονος πλείονα πλείωmore, of more, more (accusative), more (neuter) et reliqua dixerint, tamen πλέονmore potius quam πλεῖονmore dixerunt, ut incredibile sit Aeschylum hoc uno loco πλεῖον ἢmore than dixisse, quum στράτευμ' εἴη πλέονthe army would be more scribere posset. Verum ne hoc quidem Aeschylus videtur scripsisse, sed μηδ' εἰ στράτευμα πληθύοι τὸ ΜηδικόνNot even if the Median army should be numerous , cui adscriptum fuit glossema πλέον εἴηit would be more , postmodo in πλείον ἢmore than mutatum: quemadmodum passivum πληθύνεσθαιto be multiplied , cuius eadem quae intransitivi πληθύεινto multiply significatio est, in Suppl. 604 δήμου κρατοῦσα χεὶρ ὅπη πληθύνεταιThe ruling hand of the people, wherever it prevails , ab scholiasta explicatur πότερον πλείους οἱ συμμαχοῦντες ἡμῖν, ἢ ὀλίγοιWhether those fighting with us are more, or few . Nullius momenti est Suppl. 400 μὴ καὶ ποτὲ εἴπῃ λεώς, εἴ πού τι μὴ τοῖον τύχῃ,Lest the people ever say, if something should not turn out such ubi non dubitandum quin Porsonus recte scripserit τύχοιit would happen . Certius eiusdem fabulae exemplum est 91 εἰ κρανθῇ πρᾶγμα τέλειον.If the matter should be accomplished perfectly. et Eum. 234 δεινή τοῦ προστροπαίου μῆνις, εἰ προδῶ σφ᾽ ἑκών,Terrible is the wrath of the suppliant's protector, if I willingly betray them. ubi Porsonus ἢν προδῶif I betray scripsit.

The epic poets constructed it, very rarely the tragedians, as the grammarian observed about Sophocles in Bekker's Anecdota p. 144, 22: about which I have spoken in my Lexicon Sophocleum p. 138. The examples in Aeschylus are also few and partly uncertain. Thus what is read at Pers. 791 μηδ᾽ εἰ στράτευμα πλεῖον ἢ τὸ Μηδικόν [not even if an army greater than the Median] is suspect because of πλεῖον [greater]. For the ancient Attic writers, although they said πλείων πλείονος πλείονα πλείω [more, of more, more (acc.), more (neut. pl.)] and the rest, nevertheless said πλέον [more] rather than πλεῖον [more], so that it is incredible that Aeschylus in this one place said πλεῖον ἢ [more than], when he could have written στράτευμ᾽ εἴη πλέον [the army might be more]. But Aeschylus does not seem to have written even this, but μηδ᾽ εἰ στράτευμα πληθύοι τὸ Μηδικόν [not even if the Median army should increase], to which was added the gloss πλέον εἴη [might be more], later changed into πλείον ἢ [more than]: just as the passive πληθύνεσθαι [to be increased], which has the same meaning as the intransitive πληθύειν [to increase], in Suppl. 604 δήμου κρατοῦσα χεὶρ ὅπη πληθύνεται [the ruling hand of the people, in whatever direction it is increased], is explained by the scholiast as πότερον πλείους οἱ συμμαχοῦντες ἡμῖν, ἢ ὀλίγοι [whether those fighting with us are more, or few]. Of no importance is Suppl. 400 μὴ καὶ ποτὲ εἴπῃ λεώς, εἴ πού τι μὴ τοῖον τύχῃ [lest the people ever say, if perhaps something not such should happen], where there is no doubt that Porson rightly wrote τύχοι [should happen]. A more certain example from the same play is 91 εἰ κρανθῇ πρᾶγμα τέλειον [if the matter should be accomplished perfectly]. and Eum. 234 δεινή τοῦ προστροπαίου μῆνις, εἰ προδῶ σφ᾽ ἑκών [terrible is the wrath of the suppliant, if I willingly betray them], where Porson wrote ἢν προδῶ [if I should betray].

cit.quote: θήλεια γὰρ φρήν · εἰ δὲ μὴ, τάχ᾿ εἴσεται.
For the mind is female; but if not, he will soon know.
εἰ δὲ μὴ, παρ' εὐδείπνοις ἔσει ἄτιμος.
But if not, you will be without honor among those who feast well.

εἰ δὲ μὴ, —
ἱξόμεσθα.
But if not, we will come.
πότ᾽, εἰ μὴ νῦν, ἀμφὶ λιτάν᾿ ἕξομεν;
When, if not now, shall we cling to prayers?
cit.note: quae metro postulante transposuit Prienus εἰ μὴ νῦν, πότ᾽if not now, when? -.
which Prien transposed, as the meter demands, to εἰ μὴ νῦν, πότ᾽ - [if not now, when?].

cit.quote: οὐδέν ποτ᾽ εἰ μὴ ξυνθανουμένην.
Never except as one who will die with you.
κεἰ στόμαργός ἐστ᾽ ἄγαν.
Even if he is too talkative.
κεί στένεις κακοῖς ὅμως.
Even if you groan in evils, nevertheless.
κεἰ θυραῖός ἐσθ᾽ ὅμως.
Even if he is outside the door, nevertheless.
κεἰ μὴ πέποιθα.
Even if I do not trust.
ὄψει δὲ κεἴ τις ἄλλος ἤλιτεν βροτῶν.
You will see, even if any other of mortals has sinned.
εἰ γάρ μ᾽ ὑπὸ γῆν – εἰς ἀπέραντον Τάρταρον ἧκεν.
For if he had sent me beneath the earth—to boundless Tartarus.
αἰτουμένῳ μοι κοῦφον εἰ δοίης τέλος.
If you would grant me, who ask, a light fulfillment.
εἰ θείη θεὸς (sic Schuetzius correxit pro Διός) εὐ παναληθῶς.
If a god should grant (thus Schuetz corrected for 'of Zeus') well and truly.
ὅρα νυν, εἴ σοι ταῦτ᾽ ἀρωγὰ φαίνεται.
Consider now, if these things seem helpful to you.
τάχ᾽ εἰσόμεσθα τἀπίσημ᾿ ὅπη τελεῖ, εἴ νιν κατάξει χρυσότευκτα γράμματα.
Soon we shall know where the tokens lead, if the gold-wrought letters will bring him down.
εἰ δ᾽ ἐτητύμως, τίς οἶδεν;
But if truly, who knows?
Μενέλεων δὲ πεύθομαι, εἰ νόστιμός γε.
And I learn about Menelaus, whether he is returning home.
εἰ δὲ τυγχάνω οὐκ οἶδα.
But whether I happen to, I do not know.
ἰδώμεθ᾽ εἴ τι τοῦδε φροιμίου ματᾷ.
Let us see whether anything of this prelude is in vain.
τὴν μητέρ᾽ εἰπὲ πρῶτον εἰ κατέκτονας.
Tell me first whether you killed your mother.
ἐξηγοῦ δέ μοι. εἴ σφε σὺν δίκη κατέκτανον.
Explain to me whether I killed her justly.
γοεδνὰ δ᾽ ἀνθεμίζομαι δειμαίνουσα φίλους, τᾶσδε φυγᾶς εἴ τίς ἐστι κηδεμών.
I lament with mournful flowers, fearing for my loved ones, whether there is any protector of this exile.
περίφοβόν μ' ἔχει τάρβος ἐτητύμως, πολυδρόμου φυγᾶς ὄφελος εἴ τί μοι.
A terrifying fear truly holds me, whether there is any help for me in my far-wandering exile.

sense.def: 12. εἰ answered by the particle εἴτε

cit.quote: εἰ ξὺν λοχίταις, εἴτε καὶ μονοστιβῆ.
Whether with armed men, or even alone.
εἰ δικαίως εἴτε μὴ, κρῖνον δίκην.
Judge the case, whether justly or not.
εἰ δικαίως εἴτε μὴ τῇ σῇ φρενὶ δοκεῖ τόδ᾽ αἷμα, κρῖνον.
Whether justly or not, judge this blood according to your judgment.
τοὺς θανόντας εἰ θέλεις εὐεργετεῖν εἴτ᾿ οὖν κακουργεῖν, ἀμφιδεξίως ἔχει.
Whether you wish to benefit the dead or harm them, it is possible either way.
εἰα δὴ, φίλοι λοχῖται, τοὔργον οὐχ ἑκὰς τόδε.
Come on, dear comrades in arms, this task is not far off.
εἰα δὴ, ξίφος πρόκωπον πᾶς τις εὐτρεπιζέτω.
Come on, let everyone make ready his sword with hilt forward.
δακρυσίστακτον ἀπ᾿ ὄσσων ῥαδινῶν δ᾽ εἰβομένα ῥέος παρειὰν νοτίοις ἔτεγξα παγαῖς.
Dripping with tears from her slender eyes, she wet her cheek with moist streams.
cit.note: Sic Hermannus pro δακρυσίστακτον δ᾽ ἀπ᾿ ὄσσων ῥαδινῶν λειβομέναdripping with tears from her slender eyes . Eadem corruptela apud Sophoclem Ant. 527 Ισμήνη, φιλάδελφα κάτω δάκρυα λειβόμεναIsmene, shedding sisterly tears below , ubi recte Triclinius δάκρυ᾽ εἰβομένηshedding tears .

Thus Hermann for δακρυσίστακτον δ᾽ ἀπ᾿ ὄσσων ῥαδινῶν λειβομένα [dripping with tears from her slender eyes]. The same corruption in Sophocles Ant. 527 Ισμήνη, φιλάδελφα κάτω δάκρυα λειβόμενα [Ismene, shedding sisterly tears below], where Triclinius correctly has δάκρυ᾽ εἰβομένη [shedding tears].

sense.note: V. οἶδαI know .
See οἶδα [I know].

cit.quote: δαίμονά τε τὰν ἄμαχον – εἰδομέναν τοκεῦσιν.
And the unconquerable divinity, appearing like her parents.

sense.note: V. ὁράωI see .
See ὁράω [I see].

cit.quote: οὔτ᾽ εἶδος οὔτε θυμὸν οὔθ᾽ ὅπλων σχέσιν μωμητός.
Not blameworthy in form, nor in spirit, nor in the bearing of his arms.
κάτοπτρον εἴδους χαλκός ἐστ᾽, οἶνος δὲ νοῦ.
Bronze is a mirror of the form, but wine of the mind.

sense.note: Schol. Hom. Od. 4, 366 Εἰδοθέη: ἀπὸ τῆς εἰδήσεως καὶ ἐπιστήμης τοῦ πατρὸς τὸ ὄνομα. καὶ Αἰσχύλος δὲ ἐν ΠρωτεῖEidothea: the name comes from the knowledge and understanding of her father. And Aeschylus in Proteus (fr. 210) Εἰδοθέαν αὐτὴν καλεῖcalls her Eidothea . Etym. Gud. p. 316, 30 ex cod. Paris. 2638 correctum, κερδώ: ὑποκοριστικῶς, ὡς παρ᾿ Αἰσχύλῳ ἡ Εἰδὼ καὶ Ὑψὼ ἀντὶ τοῦ Εἰδοθέα καὶ Ὑψιπύληkerdo: as a diminutive, as in Aeschylus Ido and Hypso instead of Eidothea and Hypsipyle . Conf. Bekkeri Anecd. p. 857, 9. et schol. Aristoph. Eq. 1065 (1068.) Ex his colligi potest Aeschylum non ΕἰδοθέανEidothea dixisse, quod tradit schol. Homeri, sed ΕἰδώIdo .

Schol. Hom. Od. 4, 366 Εἰδοθέη: ἀπὸ τῆς εἰδήσεως καὶ ἐπιστήμης τοῦ πατρὸς τὸ ὄνομα. καὶ Αἰσχύλος δὲ ἐν Πρωτεῖ [Eidothea: the name comes from the knowledge and understanding of her father. And Aeschylus in Proteus] (fr. 210) Εἰδοθέαν αὐτὴν καλεῖ [calls her Eidothea]. Etym. Gud. p. 316, 30 corrected from cod. Paris. 2638, κερδώ: ὑποκοριστικῶς, ὡς παρ᾿ Αἰσχύλῳ ἡ Εἰδὼ καὶ Ὑψὼ ἀντὶ τοῦ Εἰδοθέα καὶ Ὑψιπύλη [kerdo: as a diminutive, as in Aeschylus Ido and Hypso instead of Eidothea and Hypsipyle]. Cf. Bekker's Anecdota p. 857, 9 and schol. Aristoph. Eq. 1065 (1068). From these it can be gathered that Aeschylus did not say Eidothea, as the Homeric scholium reports, but Ido.

cit.quote: εἴδωλον ῎Αργου γηγενοῦς.
The phantom of earth-born Argus.
ὁμιλίας κάτοπτρον, εἴδωλον σκιᾶς.
A mirror of companionship, a phantom of a shadow.

sense.def: tertia optativi εἴηνI would be persona pluralis, quae in adverbium transiit, quod Latine reddi potest esto, age.
third person plural of the optative εἴην, which has become an adverb, which can be rendered in Latin as esto, age.

cit.quote: εἶεν, ἀκούω.
Well then, I hear.
cit.note: ubi notandum εἶενwell then in initio trimetri pro spondeo positum, in formula, ut videtur, solenni. Eodem modo apud Aristophanem Pac. 663 εἶεν, ἀκούω · ταῦτ᾽ ἐπικαλεῖς; μανθάνωWell then, I hear; do you call these things? I understand. . Nam sic libri optimi et scholiasta, deteriores εἶέν γ', ἀκούωWell then, I hear .

where it should be noted that εἶεν [well then] is placed at the beginning of a trimeter as a spondee, in what seems to be a solemn formula. In the same way in Aristophanes Pac. 663 εἶεν, ἀκούω · ταῦτ᾽ ἐπικαλεῖς; μανθάνω [well then, I hear; do you bring these charges? I understand]. For thus the best manuscripts and the scholiast, the inferior ones εἶέν γ', ἀκούω [well then, I hear].

cit.quote:
εἶεν, φίλιαι δμωΐ
δες οἴκων.
Well then, dear maidservants of the house.
εἶεν · τόδ᾽ ἐστὶ τἀνδρὸς ἐκφανές τέκμαρ.
Well then; this is the man's clear proof.

sense.note: Construitur cum indicativo temporum praeteritorum ubi de rebus agitur quae optandae fuissent, sed quae non contigerunt, cum optativo de rebus quae optandae sint et contingere possint.

It is constructed with the indicative of past tenses when it concerns things that should have been wished for but did not happen, and with the optative when it concerns things that may be wished for and can happen.

cit.quote: εἴθ᾿ ὄφελεν, Ζεῦ, κἀμὲ θανάτου κατὰ μοῖρα καλύψαι.
Would that, Zeus, he had covered me too in death's allotted fate.
εἴθε μ᾿ ἐδέξω.
Would that you had received me.
εἴθ᾽ εἶχε φωνὴν ἔμφρονα.
Would that it had a voice of understanding.
εἴθ᾽ ἀνὰ πολύρυτον ἁλμήεντα πόρον διώλου.
Would that I might perish along the much-flowing briny strait.
εἴθε γὰρ θεοὶ τούσδ᾽ ὀλέσειαν ἐν γᾷ.
Would that the gods might destroy these men in the land.

cit.note: in apogr. εἴθ᾽ εἴηwould that it were pro εἰ θείηif he should place .
in the copies εἴθ᾽ εἴη [would that it were] for εἰ θείη [if he should place].

cit.quote: ἤκασεν δέ τις τὸ δεινὸν αὐ Λημνίοισι πήμασιν.
Someone compared the terrible thing to the Lemnian woes.
οὐδ᾽ αὐτε Γοργείοισιν εἰκάσω τύποις.
Nor will I compare them to Gorgon shapes.

sense.def: to attain by comparing or conjecturing

cit.quote: τίν᾿ ἐκ τῶνδ᾽ εἰκάσαι λόγος πάρα;
What word is there to conjecture from these things?
οὐκ ἔχοιμ᾽ ἂν εἰκάσαι τάδε.
I would not be able to conjecture these things.
Ἀμαζόνας, εἰ τοξοτευχεῖς ἦτε, κάρτ᾽ ἂν ἤκασα ὑμᾶς.
Amazons, if you were armed with bows, I would certainly have compared you.
δαίμονος ἐχθρὸν εἴκασμα.
the hateful image of a divinity.
οὐδ᾽ εἴκεις κακοῖς.
Nor do you yield to evils.
εἴκουσ᾽ ἀνάγκῃ τῇδε.
Yielding to this necessity.
μέμνησο δ' εἴκειν
Remember to yield
ἔφυρον εἰκὴ πάντα.
They mixed everything rashly.
θαλεροὶ δὲ λόγοι παίουσ᾽ εἰκῆ στυγνῆς πρὸς κύμασιν ἄτης.
But luxuriant words strike rashly against the waves of hateful ruin.
εἰκός γε πράξειν ἄνδρας ὧδ᾽ ἀντιστάτας.
It is likely that men who stand against them will act thus.
ὡς κομπάσαι τῷδ᾽ εἰκός ἡλίου φάει.
As it is fitting for him to boast in the light of the sun.
δόμοις δὲ ταῦτα καὶ Κλυταιμνήστρᾳ μέλέιν εἰκὸς μάλιστα.
It is most fitting that these things be a concern for the house and for Clytemnestra.
τὸν τεκόντα δ᾽ εἰκὸς εἰδέναι.
It is fitting that the father knows.
λέοντος ἄντρον αἱματορρόφου οἰκεῖν τοιαύτας εἰκός.
It is fitting that such women dwell in the den of a blood-drinking lion.
ἀπουσίᾳ μὲν εἶπας εἰκότως ἐμῇ.
You spoke fittingly about my absence.
νέμων εἰκότως ἄδικα μὲν κακοῖς, ὅσια δ᾽ ἐννόμοις.
Distributing fittingly unjust things to the bad, and holy things to the lawful.
ἐχθίστου δάκους φέροντα.
bearing the most hateful beast.

sense.note: Athen. 8 p. 262f τὰς δὲ τοιαύτας εὐωχίας Αἰσχύλοςsuch feasts Aeschylus (fr. 410) καὶ Εὐριπίδης εἰλαπίνας ἀπὸ τοῦ λελαπάχθαιand Euripides call feasts from to have been devoured . Est vocabulum poeticum, frequens apud Homerum numero et singulari et plurali.

Athenaeus 8 p. 262f: "Such feasts Aeschylus (fr. 410) and Euripides call εἰλαπίνας [feasts] from λελαπάχθαι [to have been devoured]." It is a poetic word, frequent in Homer in both singular and plural.

cit.quote: στρόμβοι δὲ κόνιν εἱλίσσουσι.
Whirlwinds roll the dust.
αἰθὴρ κοινὸν φάος εἱλίσσων.
The ether rolling its common light.
τοῦ περὶ πᾶσάν θ᾽ εἱλισσομένου χθόν᾿ ἀκοιμήτῳ ῥεύματι παῖδες πατρὸς Ὠκεανοῦ.
The children of father Oceanus, who rolls around the whole earth with sleepless stream.
εἰλλόμενον,
being shut in
cit.note: quod per εἰργόμενονbeing shut in exp. Hesychius et Simplicius ad Aristot. p. 505, 19.
which Hesychius and Simplicius on Aristotle p. 505, 19 explain by εἰργόμενον [being shut in].

sense.note: Bothii coniectura pro Νειλοθερής Suppl. 70, quod v.

cit.quote: πλοῦτον εἵματος κακόν.
the evil wealth of a garment.
δακρύω δ᾽ ὑφ᾽ εἱμάτων.
I weep beneath my garments.
μηδ' εἵμασι στρώσασ᾽ ἐπίφθονον πόρον τίθει.
Do not spread with garments and make the path enviable.
κηκίδα παγκαίνιστον, εἱμάτων βαφάς.
a fresh-made ooze, the dyeing of garments.
πολλῶν πατησμὸν δ᾽ εἱμάτων ἂν ηὐξάμην.
I would have prayed for the trampling of many garments.

sense.note: Ag. 948 εἱματοφθορεῖν Franzii coniectura pro σωματοφθορεῖν, quod v.

form.gloss: to go, but the present indicative has the meaning of the future 'I will go' and is often joined with the futures of other verbs

sense.def: eo, sed indicativo praesentis significationem futuri ibo habente et saepe cum aliorum verborum futuris coniuncto
to go, but the present indicative has the meaning of the future 'I will go' and is often joined with the futures of other verbs

cit.quote: καὶ νῦν ἐγὼ μὲν εἶμι καὶ πειράσομαι.
And now I will go and try.
πρὸς αὐτὸ δ᾽ εἶμι τέρμα σῶν πλανημάτων.
I will go to the very end of your wanderings.
τούτοις πεποιθὼς εἶμι ξυστήσομαι αὐτός.
Trusting in these things I will go and stand with them myself.

κεῖνος
δ᾽ ὁ τάλας ἄγοος – εἶσι.
But that wretched man, unwept, goes.
ἡμεῖς μὲν ἴμεν καὶ συνθάψομεν.
We will go and help bury him.
ἀλλ᾽ εἶμι καὶ πειράσομαι.
But I will go and try.
εἰμ᾿ ἐς δόμων μέλαθρα.
I will go to the roof of the house.
ἀλλ᾿ εἶμι καν δόμοισι κωκύσουσα.
But I will go and wail in the house.
ἀλλ᾽ εἶμι καὶ σοῖς ταῦτα πείσομαι λόγοις.
But I will go and obey your words.
χαλεποῦ γὰρ ἐκ πνεύματος εἶσι χειμών.
For from a harsh wind comes a storm.
εἰ μή τις ἐς ναῦν εἶσιν.
Unless someone goes to the ship.
εἶσ'
You will go.
cit.note: corruptum ex ὥστ᾽so that .
corrupted from ὥστ᾽ [so that].

cit.quote: μελάναιγις οὐκ εἶσι δόμους Ἐρινύς.
The black-robed Erinys will not go to the house.
ἴθι ἱκοῦ,
Go, come,
cit.note: ubi metro postulante ἔλθ᾽ ἱκοῦcome, go restitui.
where the meter demanding it I restored ἔλθ᾽ ἱκοῦ [come, arrive].

cit.quote: πρὸς δόμους δ᾽ ἴθι.
But go to the house.
ἴθ᾽, ὦ τάλαινα.
Go, wretched woman.
ἴτω κατ᾿ οὐρον.
Let it go with a fair wind.
ἴτω δάκρυα. ἴτω γόος.
Let tears go. Let lamentation go.
τὸ μὴ μάταιον δ᾽ ἐκ σεσωφρονισμένων ἴτω προσώπων.
Let what is not vain go from prudent faces.
ἴτ᾽ ἴτε πάντες ώδε
Go, go, all of you, here
cit.note: (ὧδεhere ego addidi).
(I added ὧδε [thus]).

cit.quote: ὦ παίδες Ἑλλήνων ἴτε.
O children of the Greeks, go.
ἴτ᾽ ἐς φθόρον πεσόντε.
Go, falling to ruin.
πρὸς φῶς ἱερὸν τῶνδε προπομπῶν ἴτε.
Go to the holy light of these escorts.
δεῦρ᾽ ἴτε.
Come here.
ἴτε μὰν, ἀστυάνακτες.
Go, indeed, lords of the city.
ἴτων πάλῳ λαχόντες.
Let those chosen by lot go.
ἰοῦσα πράξω.
I will go and do it.
ἄγγελλ᾿ ἰοῦσα.
Go and announce it.
ἰόντ᾽ αἰνέσατ' ἐκ δόμων.
Praise them as they go from the house.
ἰόντ᾽ ἐκ τῶνδε δόμων ἄλλην γενεὰν τρίβειν.
As they go from this house to wear down another race.
δεινά τοι λέγεις ἰόντων τοῖς τεκοῦσι φροντίσαι.
You speak terrible things, that those who go should care for their parents.
corrupte ἰοῦσαν,
corruptly going
cit.note: ubi metrum postulat vocabulum quod cretici mensuram habuit.
where the meter demands a word that has the measure of a cretic.

sense.note: De huius verbi formis, quas accurate tractavit Veitchius p. 199-202, haec sunt notanda.
Concerning the forms of this verb, which Veitch has accurately treated on p. 199-202, the following are to be noted.

1. Formae praesentis vel ὀρθοτονούμεναιbeing accented on the ultima sunt vel, excepta secunda εἰif , encliticae: de quo infra dicetur. Usitatissimae sunt prima, secunda et tertia numeri singularis persona, εἰμίI am (vel cum elisione εἴμ'), εῖ, ἐστίI am, you are, he/she/it is . Persona tertia non solum elisionem admittit, sed etiam aphaeresin (velut ποῦ ᾿στιwhere is ) vel crasin (velut κἀστίand is et μοὐστίto me is ex καὶ ἐστίand is et μοι ἐστίto me is contracta). Numeri dualis ἐστόνyou two are unum exemplum est Ch. 207 δύ᾽ ἐστὸν τώδε περιγραφὰ ποδοῖνthese are two outlines of feet , plura vero exempla nnmeri pluralis ἐσμέν ἐστέ εἰσίwe are, you are, they are .

1. The forms of the present are either orthotone or, except for the second person singular εἰ [you are], enclitic: about which more will be said below. The most common are the first, second, and third person singular, εἰμί [I am] (or with elision εἴμ᾽ [I am]), εῖ [you are], ἐστί [he/she/it is]. The third person not only admits elision, but also apheresis (as ποῦ ᾿στι [where is]) or crasis (as κἀστί [and is] and μοὐστί [to me is] contracted from καὶ ἐστί and μοι ἐστί). Of the dual ἐστόν [they two are] there is one example, Ch. 207 δύ᾽ ἐστὸν τώδε περιγραφὰ ποδοῖν [these are two outlines of feet], but more examples of the plural ἐσμέν [we are], ἐστέ [you are], εἰσί [they are].
2. Imperativi singularis personae secundae ἴσθιbe! tria apud Aeschylum sunt exempla, pauca tertiae ἔστωlet it be , duo numeri pluralis ἔστεbe! , de quo v. p. 104a.
2. Of the second person singular imperative ἴσθι [be] there are three examples in Aeschylus, a few of the third person ἔστω [let him/her/it be], two of the plural ἔστε [be], about which see p. 104a.
3. Optativi εἴην εἴης εἴηI would be, you would be, he/she/it would be et tertiae personae pluralis exempla plura sunt.
3. Of the optative εἴην [I would be], εἴης [you would be], εἴη [he/she/it would be], and the third person plural there are several examples.

4. Coniunctivi et participii ὤνbeing formae sunt eaedem quae apud alios omnes, nisi quod dualis exempla nulla sunt. Infinitivi εἶναιto be formae epicae ἔμμενto be unum est exemplum apud Sophoclem Ant. 623, nullum apud Aeschylum.

4. The forms of the subjunctive and the participle ὤν [being] are the same as in all other authors, except that there are no examples of the dual. Of the infinitive εἶναι [to be], there is one example of the epic form ἔμμεν [to be] in Sophocles Ant. 623, none in Aeschylus.

5. Imperfecti personae primae propria Atticorum forma est ἢor , de qua dixi in Thes. vol. 3 p. 262 et quod ad Sophoclem attinet in Lex. Soph. p. 1415. Eius duo sunt apud Aeschylum exempla Ag. 1637 a Porsono restitutum pro ň, et Ch. 523 in composito παρῆhe/she/it was present , quod Porsonus restituit pro πάρειyou are present . Reliquarum personarum exempla sunt ἦσθα ἦνyou were, he/she/it was (epicum ἔσκενhe/she/it was semel Pers. 656) et ἦμεν ἦτε ἦσανwe were, you were, they were .

5. The first person singular of the imperfect has the Attic form ἢ [I was], which I discussed in Thes. vol. 3 p. 262 and, as far as Sophocles is concerned, in Lex. Soph. p. 1415. There are two examples in Aeschylus: Ag. 1637, restored by Porson for ň, and Ch. 523 in the compound παρῆ [I was present], which Porson restored for πάρει [you are present]. Examples of the other persons are ἦσθα [you were], ἦν [he/she/it was] (the epic form ἔσκεν [he/she/it was] once, Pers. 656), and ἦμεν [we were], ἦτε [you (pl.) were], ἦσαν [they were].

6. Futuri personae primae ἔσομαιI will be nulla sunt apud Aeschylum exempla. Personae secundae ἔσειyou will be terminatio Attica nusquam servata in M, qui constanter ἔσῃyou will be praebet, et sic plerumque in aliis quoque verbis ἢor pro ei. Tertia persona ἔσταιhe/she/it will be satis frequens: ἔσεταιhe/she/it will be vero quod in M legitur Pers. 121, corruptum est ex ᾄσεταιhe/she/it will be , quod restituit Burneius. Infinitivus ἔσεσθαιto be about to be est in versu interpolatoris Pr. 835.

6. There are no examples of the first person singular of the future ἔσομαι [I will be] in Aeschylus. The second person singular ending ἔσει [you will be] is nowhere preserved in M, which consistently offers ἔσῃ [you will be], and similarly in other verbs it often has ἢ for ei. The third person singular ἔσται [he/she/it will be] is quite frequent; but the form ἔσεται [he/she/it will be] which is read in M at Pers. 121 is a corruption of ᾄσεται [he/she/it will sing], which Burney restored. The infinitive ἔσεσθαι [to be about to be] is in the interpolated verse Pr. 835.

Exempla verbi εἰμίI am ab Wellauero collecta quum pleraque omnia ita sint comparata ut non sit operae pretium verba quibuscum coniuncta leguntur
104 tur exscribi, solis versuum numeris indicamus, secundum temporum et modorum ordinem digesta. Duo autem distinguenda sunt horum exemplorum genera. Nam εἰμίI am vel verbum est substantivum, quod esse, i. e. exstare, aliquid significat et praedicatum in se ipso continet, vel copula est quam logici vocant, quae praedicati alicuius accessionem requirit. Copula ubi est, praesentis indicativi personarum omnium, una excepta secunda εἰif , accentus inclinatur (secundum grammaticorum doctrinam, quam exposuerunt Hermannus de emend. rat. gr. Gr. p. 84 seqq. et Buttmannus Gramm. Gr. vol. 1 p. 552) ubi praecedens vocabulum ita est comparatum ut accentus in id reiici possit, velut ἕτοιμός εἰμι, ἕτοιμός ἐστιI am ready, he/she/it is ready , servetur vero ubi non potest reiici, velut σώφρων εἰμί, σώφρων ἐστίI am prudent, he/she/it is prudent . Praeterea tertiam personam ἐστίhe/she/it is grammatici (ab Fischero in Annot, ad Welleri Gramm. vol. 1 p. 294 indicati) retracto accentu ἔστινhe/she/it is scribendam esse praecipiunt in initio sententiae, in interrogatione, post dictiones ἀλλbut ' et τοῦτ᾽this (ubi altera syllaba elisa est), εἰ, καί, μή, οὐκ, ὡς, μέν, ὅτιif, and, not, not, as, indeed, that , et in formulis ἔστιν ὅς, ἔστιν ὅτε, ἔστιν ὅπου, ἔστιν ὅπως, ἔστιν ὡςthere is someone who, there is a time when, there is a place where, there is a way how, there is a way in which et similibus: quae leges satis accurate servatae sunt in codicibus et verae haud dubie sunt de formulis modo memoratis et de particulis accentu carentibus εἰ, οὐκ ετώςif, not truly , parum probabiles vero et idonea ratione destitutae de ceteris ἀλλ᾽, τοῦτ᾽, καί, μή, μέν. ὅτιbut, this, and, not, indeed, that , quod Buttmannus quoque partim animadvertit.

The examples of the verb εἰμί [I am] collected by Wellauer, since most of them are of such a kind that it is not worth the trouble to write out the words with which they are read in connection, we indicate by line numbers alone, arranged according to the order of tenses and moods. Two classes of these examples, however, must be distinguished. For εἰμί [I am] is either a substantive verb, which signifies to be, i.e. to exist, something, and contains the predicate in itself, or it is the copula, as logicians call it, which requires the addition of some predicate. Where it is a copula, in the present indicative of all persons, with the single exception of the second person εἶ [you are], the accent is thrown back (according to the doctrine of the grammarians, which Hermann in his work on the emendation of Greek grammar p. 84 ff. and Buttmann in his Greek Grammar vol. 1 p. 552 have expounded) when the preceding word is of such a kind that the accent can be thrown back upon it, as ἕτοιμός εἰμι [I am ready], ἕτοιμός ἐστι [he is ready], but it is retained where it cannot be thrown back, as σώφρων εἰμί [I am prudent], σώφρων ἐστί [he is prudent]. Moreover, the grammarians (cited by Fischer in his notes on Weller's Grammar vol. 1 p. 294) prescribe that the third person ἐστί [he/she/it is] should be written with the accent drawn back, ἔστιν [he/she/it is], at the beginning of a sentence, in a question, after the words ἀλλ' [but] and τοῦτ' [this] (where the second syllable has been elided), εἰ [if], καί [and], μή [not], οὐκ [not], ὡς [as], μέν [indeed], ὅτι [that], and in the formulas ἔστιν ὅς [there is someone who], ἔστιν ὅτε [there is a time when], ἔστιν ὅπου [there is a place where], ἔστιν ὅπως [there is a way in which], ἔστιν ὡς [there is a sense in which] and the like: which rules are observed with sufficient accuracy in the manuscripts and are undoubtedly true regarding the formulas just mentioned and the particles without accent εἰ [if], οὐκ [not], ὡς [as], but are hardly probable and lack a suitable reason regarding the others ἀλλ' [but], τοῦτ' [this], καί [and], μή [not], μέν [indeed], ὅτι [that], as Buttmann also in part has noticed.

sense.def: verbum substantivum, esse vel exstare significans
substantive verb, meaning to be or to exist

Futuri ἔσομαιI will be persona secunda ἔσειyou will be constanter ἔσῃyou will be scripta Sept. 68. Ag. 1410, 1633. Ch. 484. Suppl. 460. ἔσταιhe/she/it will be Pr. 189, 623, 908. Ag. 1179, 1249. Eum. 550, 854, 865. [Infinitivus ἔσεσθαιto be going to be Pr. 835.]

Of the future ἔσομαι [I will be], the second person ἔσει [you will be] is consistently written ἔσῃ [you will be] at Sept. 68, Ag. 1410, 1633, Ch. 484, Suppl. 460. ἔσται [he/she/it will be] at Pr. 189, 623, 908, Ag. 1179, 1249, Eum. 550, 854, 865. sense.def: εἰμίI am cum participiis verborum coniunctum periphrasi servit (quod σχῆμα ΧαλκιδικὸνChalcidian form appellat Lesbonax p. 179): de quo allatis poetarum prosaeque orationis scriptorum exemplis dictum est in Thesauro vol. 3 p. 258.

εἰμί [I am] joined with participles of verbs serves as a periphrasis (which Lesbonax p. 179 calls the Chalcidian figure): about which, with examples from poets and prose writers, it is discussed in the Thesaurus vol. 3 p. 258.

cit.quote: στέρεσθαι - ἣν προκείμενον.
to be deprived of - which was set before.
ἐκείνων εἴ τις ἐστὶν ἐμπνέων.
if any of those is breathing.
φεύγων Ορέστης ἐστίν.
Orestes is in exile.
ἔστ᾽ ἀναγκαίως ἔχον.
it is necessarily so.
οἵας ἑορτῆς ἔστ᾽ ἀπόπτυστοι θεοῖς στέργηθρ᾽ ἔχουσαι.
what kind of feast they have, loathsome to the gods, with their offerings.
αἰδόμενός τις ἔστω.
let someone be ashamed.
ἤλπιζον εἶναι μαντικῇ βρύον τέχνη.
I hoped that he was abounding in the prophetic art.

cit.note: in apographis τί δ' ἐστὶ πρᾶγμα νεόκοτον πόλει παρόνWhat strange thing is present for the city? , ubi παρόνbeing present ab correctore illatum pro πλέονmore , cuius facilior correctio foret πέλονbeing , nisi aptius esset πάλινagain , quod ego conieci.

in the copies τί δ' ἐστὶ πρᾶγμα νεόκοτον πόλει παρόν [what strange thing is present to the city], where παρόν [being present] was introduced by a corrector for πλέον [more], whose easier correction would be πέλον [being], unless πάλιν [again] were more fitting, which I have conjectured.

cit.quote: εἰ δ᾽ ἦν τεθνηκώς.
but if he were dead.
ἔσται δεδορκώς.
he will be seeing.
πάντα γ᾽ ἔστ᾽ ἐκεῖνα διαπεπραγμένα.
all those things have been accomplished.
ὡς ἕκαστος ἦν τεταγμένος.
as each had been stationed.
ἔργον ἐστὶν ἐξειργασμένον.
the deed has been done.
ἀπομούσως ἦσθα γεγραμμένος.
you were written unmusically.
εἴπερ ἐστὶ μὴ -- κεκτημένη.
if indeed she is not - possessed.
ἣν τετμημένος.
which he had cut.
ἐστὶν ἡμῖν τοῦτο προστεταγμένον.
this has been enjoined upon us.
ἐστὶν ἐσφραγισμένος.
he is sealed.
πολλῶν τάδ᾽ ἡμῖν ἐστιν ἠξιωμένα.
these things have been deemed worthy by us of many things.
ταῦτ᾽ οὐ πίναξίν ἐστιν ἐγγεγραμμένα.
these things are not written on tablets.
τίν᾿ αὐδὴν τήνδε γηρυθεῖσ᾽ ἔσει;
what voice will you utter?
τίς οὖν ὁ λύσων σ᾽ ἐστίν;
who then is the one who will release you?
αὐτὸς ἦν ὁ μαρτυρῶν.
he himself was the witness.
τίς ἦν ὁ θέλξας;
who was the one who charmed?
αὐτός ἐστιν ὁ κτανών.
he himself is the killer.

sense.def: cum genitivo dicitur originis significandae causa, addita vel omissa praepositione
it is said with the genitive to indicate origin, with the preposition added or omitted

cit.quote: ἀνδρῶν τάδ᾽ ἐστὶ, σφάγια καὶ χρηστήρια θεοῖσιν ἔρδειν.
it is for men to perform these sacrifices and oracles to the gods.
οὔτοι γυναικός ἐστιν ἱμείρειν μάχης.
it is not for a woman to desire battle.
τοῦ δρῶντός ἐστι καὶ τὸ βουλεῦσαι πέρι.
it is the doer's part also to plan.
οὐκ ἂν Ἀργείων τόδ' εἴη φῶτα προσσαίνειν κακόν.
it would not be like Argives to fawn upon a base man.
ἀνδρῶν γάρ έστιν ἐνδίκων τε καὶ σοφῶν ἐν τοῖς κακοῖσι μὴ τέθυμῶσθαι θεοῖς.
for it is the part of just and wise men not to rage against the gods in misfortunes.
διχῶς ἐπράθην ὢν ἐλευθέρου πατρός.
I was sold twice, though I was from a free father.
κάρτα δ᾽ εἰμὶ τοῦ πατρός.
and I am very much my father's.
φυσίζουν γένος, τὸ δὴ Ζηνός ἐστιν ἀληθῶς.
the life-giving race, which is truly Zeus's.
Τροίαν Ἀχαιῶν οὖσαν.
Troy, which belonged to the Achaeans.

sense.def:
Cum dativo coniungitur habendi significatione,
105 diciturque non solum de rebus quas quis habere et possidere potest, sed etiam de cogitationibus et consiliis.
It is joined with the dative in the sense of having, and it is said not only of things which one can have and possess, but also of thoughts and plans.

cit.quote: Ὠκεανοῦ φίλος ἐστὶ βεβαιότερός σοι.
Oceanus is a more steadfast friend to you.
ἔσται δὲ θνητοῖς εἰσαεὶ λόγος μέγας.
and there will be a great story for mortals forever.
ἔστι θεοῖς δ᾽ ἔτ᾿ ἰσχὺς καθυπερτέρα.
but the gods still have superior strength.
cit.note: Sic M a m. antiqua correctus pro θεοῦof a god . Praeterea rectius post ἔστιis (ita est) interpungitur.
Thus M, corrected by an ancient hand from θεοῦ [of a god]. Moreover, it is more correctly punctuated after ἔστι [it is] (so it is).

cit.quote: εἰ καρπὸς ἔσται θεσφάτοισι Λοξίου.
if there will be fruit for the oracles of Loxias.
πάντα γὰρ τὰ κέδν᾽ ἐν ὑμῖν ἐστί μοι βουλεύματα.
for all good counsels are in you for me.
ἀργύρου πηγή τις αὐτοῖς ἐστί.
there is a certain fountain of silver for them.
προτοῦ μὲν αἰδὼς ἣν ἐμοὶ λέγειν τάδε.
before, there was shame for me to say these things.
ὡς νόμος βροτοῖς ἐστί.
as is the custom for mortals.
οὐκ εἰσὶ δόξαι τῶνδε πημάτων ἐμοί.
there are no expectations of these sufferings for me.
ἄγος μὲν εἴη τοῖς ἐμοῖς παλιγκότοις.

ἀσφάλεια δ᾽ ἢ δι᾽ ἄστεως στείχουσι.

εὔφημον εἴη τοὔπος εὐφημουμένη.

sense.def: ἔστινis sequente infinitivo significat fieri aliquid posse, vel copiam rei alicuius fieri, licere
ἔστιν [it is] followed by an infinitive means that something can happen, or that there is opportunity for something, or that it is permitted

θάλασσα δ᾽ οὐκέτ᾽ ἣν ἰδεῖν.

φθογγὰς ἀκούειν ἔστι.

οὐκ ἔστι λαθεῖν ὄμματα φωτός.

ὅδ᾽ ἐστὶ κάρτ᾿ ἰδεῖν ὁμόπτερος.
this one is very much to be seen as winged.
τοῖς τοιούτοις οὔτε κρατῆρος μέρος εἶναι μετασχεῖν.

πολυπλάνητα δ᾽ ἦν ἰδεῖν ὀρέγματα.

ἔστιν [it is] with a relative pronoun or adverb in the formulas οὐκ ἔστιν ὅστις [there is no one who], οὐκ ἔσθ᾽ ὅπου [there is no place where]

sense.def: siquidem, addito interdum ye, vel nullo vel uno duobusve vocabulis interpositis. Construitur cum indicativo praesentis, perfecti, futuri.
if indeed, sometimes with ye added, either with no word or one or two words interposed. It is construed with the indicative present, perfect, future.

cit.quote: δεῖξον, εἴπερ οἶσθα.

εἴπερ τις, εἰδώς γ᾽ εὐ τόδ᾽ ἐξεῖπον τέλος.

εἴπερ ἐστὶ μὴ – φωνὴν βάρβαρον κεκτημένη.

καν τοῖς ἐμοῖς ἄρ᾽, εἴπερ ἔν γε τοῖσι σοῖς.
And in mine, if indeed in yours.
τί δὴ πύλαισι τὸν ἱκέτην ἀπείργετε, Αἴγισθος εἴπερ οἶδεν ἔκδημός περ ὤν;

τρίτον τόδ᾽ ἐκπέραμα δωμάτων καλῶ, εἴπερ φιλόξεν᾽ ἐστὶν, Αἰγίσθου βίαν.

τὰς ὁμοίας ἀντίδος λαβάς λαβεῖν, εἴπερ κρατηθείς γ᾿ ἀντινικῆσαι θέλεις.

τόνδ᾽ ἀμυναθοῦ ψόγον, εἴπερ – ἡσαι.

sense.def: Cum imperfecto ubi de re agitur contra ac fingitur se habente
With the imperfect when the matter is dealt with contrary to what is pretended

cit.quote: εἴπερ γ᾿ ἀπ᾿ ἐχθροῦ κρατὸς ἦν τετμημένος.

εἴπερ γ᾽ ἀπ᾿ ἀρχῆς πραγμάτων κοινωνὸς ἦν.

εἴπερ κακὸν φέροι τις αἰσχύνης ἄτερ, ἔστω,
If someone bears evil without shame, let it be.
cit.note: ubi φέρειbrings apogr. multa.
where φέρει [brings] many copies.

cit.quote: ἄγοις ἂν, εἴπερ εὐσεβὴς πίθοι λόγος.
You would lead, if indeed a pious word should persuade.
Δίκη δ᾽ ὁμαίμων κάρτα νιν προστέλλεται εἵργειν τεκούση μητρὶ πολέμιον δόρυ.
Justice of kindred blood greatly commands him to keep away the hostile spear from his mother who bore him.
ἀνδρὸς ἐχθαίρουσ᾽ ὕβριν εἴρξει νεοσσῶν ὡς δράκοντα δύσχιμον.
Hating the man's violence, she will keep him away from her young like a hostile serpent.
εἴργων γὰρ ἐχθροὺς θάνατον εἵλετ᾽ ἐν πόλει,
For keeping enemies away, he chose death in the city.
cit.note: ubi στυγῶνhating est in M, recte ab Wakefieldo in στέγωνcovering mutatum, cuius glossema est εἴργωνkeeping away , quod legitur in apogr.
where στυγῶν [hating] is in M, rightly changed by Wakefield to στέγων [covering], whose gloss is εἴργων [keeping away], which is read in the copies.

cit.quote: ἐχυροῖς ἕρκεσιν εἴργειν ἄμαχον κύμα θαλάσσας.
To keep away the irresistible wave of the sea with strong barriers.
εἰ δὲ μὴ τεταγμένα μοῖρα μοῖραν ἐκ θεῶν εἶργε μὴ πλέον φέρειν.
But if the appointed fate from the gods did not prevent fate from bringing more.
δακτυλοδείκτων δ᾽ οὔτις ἀπειπὼν εἴργει μελάθρων.
No one of those pointed at by fingers, having forbidden, keeps me away from the halls.
λέκτρων, ὧν θέμις εἴργει.
Of the marriage bed, which custom keeps away.
ἄλγος γυναιξὶν ἀνδρὸς εἴργεσθαι.
It is a grief for women to be kept away from their husband.
ἀπὸ χώρων ποταμῶν τ᾽ ἐργομένα,
Being kept away from the lands and rivers.
cit.note: ubi Victorius εἰργομέναbeing kept away , Hermannus ἀπὸ χλωρῶν πετάλων ἐγρομέναrising from green leaves . Per διωκομένηbeing pursued exp. schol.
where Victorius has εἰργομένα [being kept away], Hermannus ἀπὸ χλωρῶν πετάλων ἐγρομένα [rising from green leaves]. The scholiast explains it by διωκομένη [being pursued].

cit.quote: ἔθηκε πᾶσιν εἰρήνην φίλοις.
He made peace for all his friends.
Ετεοκλέης ἂν εἰς πολὺς κατὰ πτόλιν ὑμνοῖτο,
Eteocles, one man among many throughout the city, would be hymned.
cit.note: ubi πολύςmany supra versum scriptum est in M. Conieci πᾶσαν εἷς κατὰ πτόλινone man throughout the whole city .
where πολύς [much] is written above the line in M. I conjectured πᾶσαν εἷς κατὰ πτόλιν [one throughout the whole city].

cit.quote: φέρει δ᾽ ὑφ᾽ αὑτῇ φῶτα Καδμείων ἕνα.
And she carries beneath her one man of the Cadmeans.
ἄλλ᾽ εἰς ἅπαντας ἀνθ᾽ ἐνὸς τόδ᾽ ἔργον ἦν.
But this deed was done by all in return for one.
εἷς ἀνὴρ πλεῖστον πόνον ἐχθροῖς παρασχών.
One man having caused the greatest toil to his enemies.
ἐξ ἑνὸς ῥόθου.
From one rush.
ἕν᾽ ἄνδ᾽ ἁπάσης Ἀσίδος μηλοτρόφου ταγεῖν.
To lead one man of all sheep-nurturing Asia.
πάντες ἑνὶ πιτύλῳ.
All with one stroke.
μία τὰς πολλὰς ψυχὰς ὀλέσασα.
One woman having destroyed many lives.
μία πολλῶν ἀνδρῶν ψυχὰς ὀλέσασα.
One woman having destroyed the lives of many men.
ἐκ μιᾶς ὁδοῦ.
From one road.
δημόπρακτος ἐκ πόλεως μία ψῆφος κέκρανται.
A single vote, publicly exacted from the city, has been decided.
οἵδε ναὸς ἐκ μιᾶς πέσον.
These fell from one ship.
πολλῶν ῥαγεισῶν ἐλπίδων μιᾶς τυχών.
Having obtained one hope after many had been shattered.
νηδύος μιᾶς ἄπο.
From one womb.
ἐν μιᾷ πληγῇ.
In one blow.
ἡμέρᾳ μιᾷ.
In one day.
μιᾷ φρενί.
With one mind.
πόλει μὲν ἕλκος ἓν τὸ δήμιον τυχεῖν.
For the city to suffer one public wound.
ἓν μὲν τόδ᾽ ἤδη τῶν τριῶν παλαισμάτων.
This is already one of the three wrestling bouts.
πάταγος οὐχ ἑνὸς δορός.
The clash is not of one spear.
οὐκ ἔστιν ὅστις πλὴν ἑνὸς κείραιτό νιν,
There is no one except one who could shear him.
cit.note: Sic Dobraeus pro πλὴν ἐμοῦexcept me .
Thus Dobree for πλὴν ἐμοῦ [except me].

cit.quote: τὰ πάντα γάρ τις ἐκχέας͵ ἀνθ᾽ αἵματος ἑνός.
For someone pouring out everything in return for one blood.
πολλοὶ γὰρ εἰς ἓν συμπίτνουσιν ἵμεροι.
For many desires fall together into one.
τοὺς δ᾽ ἕν τι ποιεῖν, τοὺς δὲ μή τι δρᾶν λέγων.
Saying that some should do one thing, and others should do nothing.

sense.note: [Incertum est καθ᾿ ἕνone by one ib. 316 pro καθάπαξonce for all dictum, de quo dixi s. v. ἀνέκαθενfrom the beginning .]
[It is uncertain whether καθ᾿ ἕν [one by one] at line 316 is said for καθάπαξ [once for all], about which I have spoken under the word ἀνέκαθεν [from the beginning].]
εἶone (variant spelling) c pro εἷςone Canter. Eum. 200.
εἶ for εἷς [one] Canter, Eum. 200.

Huius praepositionis (ut dixi in Lexico Sophocleo p. 145) duplex inde ab antiquissimis temporibus scriptura fuit, εἰςinto et ἐςinto , de quibus quae grammatici Graeci tradiderunt etsi non sufficiunt, duae tamen eorum supersunt observationes non inutiles. Earum altera est Helladii apud Photium Bibl. p. 573, 10 ὅτι ἀναλογώτερον ἀντὶ μὲν τῆς εἰς προθέσεως τὸ ἐς λέγειν, ἀντὶ δὲ τῆς ἐξ τὸ ἐκ· πᾶσα γὰρ πρόθεσις βραχυκαταληκτεῖν θέλειthat it is more regular to say ἐς [into] instead of the preposition εἰς [into], and ἐκ [out of] instead of ἐξ [out of]; for every preposition wants to end in a short vowel . et p. 535, 2 ὅτι οἱ Ἀττικοὶ κατά τι πάτριον ἔθος οὐ χρῶνται τῇ ει διφθόγγῳ ἐν τῷ λέγειν ἐς κόρακας ἢ ἐς μακαρίαν, ἀλλ᾽ ἄνευ τοῦ διχρόνου ἐκφωνοῦσι τὴν πρόθεσιν· ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων καὶ μετὰ τοῦ διχρόνου καὶ χωρὶς τοῦ διχρόνου τὴν πρόθεσιν λέγουσινthat the Athenians, according to some ancestral custom, do not use the diphthong ει in saying ἐς κόρακας [to the crows] or ἐς μακαρίαν [to blessedness], but pronounce the preposition without the long vowel; but in all other cases they say the preposition both with and without the long vowel . altera est grammatici (in Ἐπιμερισμοῖς Ὁμήρουin the Epimerisms of Homer ) in Crameri Anecd. Oxon. vol. 1 p. 172, 3 ἐς πρόθεσις παρὰ τῷ ποιητῇ συμφώνου μὲν ἐπιφερομένου ἐκβάλλειν τὸ ἰῶτα λέγεται, φωνήεντος δὲ ἐπιφερομένου φυλάττει. “ἀλλ᾽ ἐς μὲν ΜενέλαονThe preposition ἐς [into] in the poet is said to drop the iota when a consonant follows, but to keep it when a vowel follows. “ἀλλ᾽ ἐς μὲν Μενέλαον [but to Menelaus] (Od. 3, 317).” “ἐσβάντες κνήμας τ᾽ ἠδὲ λόφονἐσβάντες κνήμας τ᾽ ἠδὲ λόφον [having gone into the greaves and the crest] (Il. 10, 573).” “εἰς Ἀγαμέμνονα δίονεἰς Ἀγαμέμνονα δῖον [to godlike Agamemnon] (Il. 7, 312).” “εἰς ἐμὰ δέμνια βάντεεἰς ἐμὰ δέμνια βάντε [having gone into my bed] (Od. 8, 296, ubi nunc recte τὼ δ᾽ ἐς δέμνια | βάντε).” μάχεται τὸ ‘οἵδ᾽ αἰψ᾽ εἴσβαινοντὼ δ᾽ ἐς δέμνια | βάντε [and the two having gone into the bed]).” This conflicts with ‘οἵδ᾽ αἴψ᾽ εἴσβαινον [these quickly went in] (Od. 9, 103),” εἰ μὴ ἄρα οὐκ ἦν παράθεσις, ἀλλὰ σύνθετον· ἀμφίβολον τὸ “εἰς ὄρος ἡ εἰς κῦμαunless perhaps it was not a prepositional phrase but a compound; ambiguous is “εἰς ὄρος ἢ εἰς κῦμα [to the mountain or to the wave] (Il. 6, 347).” ἀναγινώσκεται γὰρ καὶ ἐς κῦμαfor it is also read ἐς κῦμα [to the wave] .” Inscriptionum auctoritate nihil proficitur, quum utriusque scripturae exempla praebeant parumque sibi constent, de quo dixit L. Dindorfius in Thesauro vol. 3 p. 298, et inscriptionum postea ab Rhangabe aliisque editarum eadem sit inconstantia. Idem de codicibus dicendum, in quibus etsi utraque scriptura
106 ita alternat ut scriptores ipsi temere modo εἰςinto modo ἐςinto scripsisse videantur, tamen in summa inconstantia sanioris rationis vestigia relicta sunt, quibus si adhibeantur grammaticorum quas modo memoravi observationes et indicia in metris poetarum scenicorum posita, normae nonnullae quibus utriusque formae usus regatur inveniri posse videntur. 1. Poetarum tragicorum exempla triplicis sunt generis: in aliis enim metrum postulat εἰςinto , in aliis ἐςinto , in aliis utramque formam fert. Et apud Aeschylum quidem εἰςinto metro postulante legitur in senariis Pr. 236 361 1028. Sept. 255 1050. Pers. 183 326. Ag. 510 1207. Ch. 299 680 712. Eum. 763. Suppl. 882. Fr. 165 196 236, in trochaico versu Pers. 230, in anapaestis Pr. 191 1074 1078. Ag. 1464, in canticis Pr. 689, (ubi in dochmio εἰςinto pro ἐςinto restitui ex apogr. pro ἐς ἀκοὰν ἐμάνἐς ἀκοὰν ἐμάν [to my hearing] ), in antispastis Sept. 860. Suppl. 538, in Ionicis Pers. 67 97, in glyconeis Ag. 384 435. Ch. 612. Eum. 364, in versu iambico-cretico Suppl. 103. Contra ἐςinto metro necessarium est in senariis Pr. 2 302 387. Pers 833. Ag. 737. Eum. 56 459 851. Suppl. 330. Fr. 252, in anapaestis Pers. 2, in dochmio Sept. 240. Idem de verbis cum εἰςinto compositis dicendum, quae omnia sub εἰσinto - posuimus, etsi metrum modo εἰςinto modo ἐςinto postulat. Tertii vero generis par fere utriusque formae exemplorum numerus est in M, posito ante litteras consonantes, quum in praepositione simplici tum in verbis cum ea compositis, modo εἰςinto modo ἐςinto , velut ἐσβέβηκε ἐσθορεῖν ἐσκόμιζεἐσβέβηκε [has gone in], ἐσθορεῖν [to leap in], ἐσκόμιζε [was bringing in] , rarum vero es ante litteras vocales sine metri necessitate positum. 2. Aristophanem ceterosque poetas comicos satis constat forma ἐςinto nusquam usos esse postulante metro, nisi ubi tragicorum aut verba repeterent aut sermonem imitarentur: quo Elmsleius inductus ἐςinto ab comicorum usu prorsus alienum et ubique ante vocales pariter ac consonantes εἰςinto scribendum esse iudicabat, cui opinioni non solum Helladii, haud dubie antiquiore auctore usi, observatio supra memorata, sed etiam codicum auctoritas obstat. Nam codices Aristophanis, quorum in rebus orthographicis fides aliquanto maior est quam codicum per quos tragicorum fabulae propagatae sunt, formam es in praepositione simplici verbisque cum ea compositis toties ante litteras consonantes praebent ut exemplorum prope idem atque alterius formae numerus sit. 3. His igitur indiciis inter se collatis ego in annot. Oxon. ad Arist. Ach. 242 vol. 3 p. 385, hanc proposui regulam “discrimen inter εἰςinto et ἐςinto apud comicos hoc intercedit ut εἰςinto ante vocales, ἐςinto ante consonantes litteras scribatur. Ab hac lege tragicorum usus ita tantum recedit, ut ἐςinto etiam ante vocalem dicatur ubi metri necessitas postulat.” Assensi mihi sunt Meinekius in Aristophanis editione Lipsiensi a. 1860 aliique, dissentiunt alii, quibus nihil aliud relinquitur quam ut librariorum exemplum sequentes ab scriptoribus veteribus temere modo εἰςinto modo ἐςinto scriptum fuisse credant. Nec quod quibusdam placuit ab regula mea, etiamsi in universum vera esse possit, tamen vocabula quaedam, ut εἰσφοράcontribution, tax , quod sic in inscriptionibus constanter scriptum reperitur, vel genera vocabulorum, velut ἐπεισπίπτειν, ἐπεισφέρεινἐπεισπίπτειν [to fall upon in addition], ἐπεισφέρειν [to bring in addition] et alia huiusmodi bicomposita, exemta esse videri, magnam veri speciem habet, quum nec ratio huius discriminis appareat et exemplorum numerus perexiguus sit. Scriptorum ipsorum utrum tanta fuerit diligentia ut ab regulis quas sibi scripserant nusquam desciscerent neque aut casu aut euphoniae gratia εἰςinto etiam ante consonantes et, quod minus credibile est, ἐςinto sine metri necessitate ante vocales ponerent, sciri non potest, quum codices fidem sibi ipsi abrogent non solum inconstantia sua, sed etiam εἰςinto et ἐςinto interdum contra metri legem illatis. Ad euphoniam vel metri elegantiam quod attinet, valde incerta quorundam opinio est in senariis, et praesertim in dipodia tertia, ἐς Ἴλιον, ἐς αὔριον, ἐς ὕστερον, ἐσείδομενἐς Ἴλιον [to Ilium], ἐς αὔριον [until tomorrow], ἐς ὕστερον [for later], ἐσείδομεν [we saw] et reliqua omnia huiusmodi probabiliora esse quam quae spondeum praebent εἰς Ἴλιον, εἰς αὔριον, εἰς ὕστερον, εἰσείδομενεἰς Ἴλιον [to Ilium], εἰς αὔριον [until tomorrow], εἰς ὕστερον [for later], εἰσείδομεν [we saw] .

Of this preposition (as I said in my Lexicon Sophocleum p. 145) there was from the earliest times a twofold spelling, εἰς [into] and ἐς [into], about which what the Greek grammarians have handed down, though not sufficient, yet two of their observations survive that are not useless. One of them is that of Helladius in Photius' Bibliotheca p. 573, 10: ὅτι ἀναλογώτερον ἀντὶ μὲν τῆς εἰς προθέσεως τὸ ἐς λέγειν, ἀντὶ δὲ τῆς ἐξ τὸ ἐκ· πᾶσα γὰρ πρόθεσις βραχυκαταληκτεῖν θέλει [that it is more analogical to say ἐς instead of the preposition εἰς, and ἐκ instead of ἐξ; for every preposition wants to end in a short syllable]. And p. 535, 2: ὅτι οἱ Ἀττικοὶ κατά τι πάτριον ἔθος οὐ χρῶνται τῇ ει διφθόγγῳ ἐν τῷ λέγειν ἐς κόρακας ἢ ἐς μακαρίαν, ἀλλ᾽ ἄνευ τοῦ διχρόνου ἐκφωνοῦσι τὴν πρόθεσιν· ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων καὶ μετὰ τοῦ διχρόνου καὶ χωρὶς τοῦ διχρόνου τὴν πρόθεσιν λέγουσιν [that the Athenians, according to some ancestral custom, do not use the diphthong ει in saying ἐς κόρακας [to the crows] or ἐς μακαρίαν [to blessedness], but pronounce the preposition without the long vowel; but in all other cases they say the preposition both with and without the long vowel]. The other is that of the grammarian (in the Epimerismi Homeri) in Cramer's Anecdota Oxoniensia vol. 1 p. 172, 3: ἐς πρόθεσις παρὰ τῷ ποιητῇ συμφώνου μὲν ἐπιφερομένου ἐκβάλλειν τὸ ἰῶτα λέγεται, φωνήεντος δὲ ἐπιφερομένου φυλάττει [the preposition ἐς in the poet is said to drop the iota when a consonant follows, but to keep it when a vowel follows]. “ἀλλ᾽ ἐς μὲν Μενέλαον (Od. 3, 317).” [but to Menelaus] “ἐσβάντες κνήμας τ᾽ ἠδὲ λόφον (Il. 10, 573).” [having gone up onto the shins and the ridge] “εἰς Ἀγαμέμνονα δίον (Il. 7, 312).” [to noble Agamemnon] “εἰς ἐμὰ δέμνια βάντε (Od. 8, 296, ubi nunc recte τὼ δ᾽ ἐς δέμνια | βάντε).” [going into my bed] μάχεται τὸ ‘οἵδ᾽ αἰψ᾽ εἴσβαινον (Od. 9, 103),” [the phrase 'these quickly went on board' conflicts] εἰ μὴ ἄρα οὐκ ἦν παράθεσις, ἀλλὰ σύνθετον· ἀμφίβολον τὸ “εἰς ὄρος ἡ εἰς κῦμα (Il. 6, 347).” [unless it was not a juxtaposition but a compound; the phrase 'to the mountain or into the wave' is ambiguous] ἀναγινώσκεται γὰρ καὶ ἐς κῦμα.” [for it is also read as 'into the wave']. The authority of inscriptions is of no help, since they offer examples of both spellings and are inconsistent, as L. Dindorf said in the Thesaurus vol. 3 p. 298, and the inscriptions later published by Rhangabe and others show the same inconsistency. The same must be said of the manuscripts, in which although both spellings alternate so much that the writers themselves seem to have written now εἰς now ἐς at random, yet in the midst of this inconsistency traces of a sounder principle remain, from which, if the observations of the grammarians I just mentioned and the indications found in the meters of the scenic poets are applied, some rules can be found by which the use of each form is governed. 1. The examples in the tragic poets are of three kinds: in some the meter requires εἰς, in others ἐς, in others either form is allowed. And in Aeschylus indeed, when the meter requires εἰς, it is read in the senarii Pr. 236 361 1028. Sept. 255 1050. Pers. 183 326. Ag. 510 1207. Ch. 299 680 712. Eum. 763. Suppl. 882. Fr. 165 196 236, in the trochaic verse Pers. 230, in the anapaests Pr. 191 1074 1078. Ag. 1464, in the lyrics Pr. 689, (where in a dochmiac I restored εἰς for ἐς from the apograph for ἐς ἀκοὰν ἐμάν [to my hearing]), in the antispasts Sept. 860. Suppl. 538, in the Ionic verses Pers. 67 97, in the glyconics Ag. 384 435. Ch. 612. Eum. 364, in the iambic-cretic verse Suppl. 103. On the other hand, ἐς is required by the meter in the senarii Pr. 2 302 387. Pers 833. Ag. 737. Eum. 56 459 851. Suppl. 330. Fr. 252, in the anapaests Pers. 2, in the dochmiac Sept. 240. The same must be said of verbs compounded with εἰς, which we have all placed under εἰσ-, although the meter sometimes requires εἰς, sometimes ἐς. But of the third kind, the number of examples of each form is almost equal in M, when placed before consonants, both in the simple preposition and in verbs compounded with it, now εἰς now ἐς, for example ἐσβέβηκε [has entered], ἐσθορεῖν [to leap in], ἐσκόμιζε [was bringing in], but rarely is ἐς placed before vowels without metrical necessity. 2. It is well established that Aristophanes and the other comic poets never used the form ἐς when the meter required it, except where they were repeating the words of the tragedians or imitating their style: led by this, Elmsley judged that ἐς was entirely foreign to the usage of the comic poets and that εἰς should be written everywhere, before vowels as well as consonants, an opinion which is opposed not only by the observation of Helladius mentioned above, who no doubt used an older authority, but also by the authority of the manuscripts. For the manuscripts of Aristophanes, whose reliability in orthographic matters is somewhat greater than that of the manuscripts through which the plays of the tragedians have been transmitted, offer the form ἐς in the simple preposition and in verbs compounded with it so often before consonants that the number of examples is almost the same as that of the other form. 3. Therefore, comparing these indications with each other, I proposed in my Oxford annotation on Arist. Ach. 242 vol. 3 p. 385 the following rule: "the distinction between εἰς and ἐς in the comic poets is that εἰς is written before vowels, ἐς before consonants. The usage of the tragedians departs from this rule only in that ἐς is also said before a vowel where metrical necessity demands." Meineke in his Leipzig edition of Aristophanes of 1860 and others agreed with me, but others disagree, who have no alternative but to follow the example of the scribes and believe that the ancient writers wrote now εἰς now ἐς at random. Nor does the opinion that some have held, that certain words, such as εἰσφορά [tax], which is found consistently written thus in inscriptions, or classes of words, such as ἐπεισπίπτειν [to fall upon], ἐπεισφέρειν [to bring in upon], and other such double compounds, are exempt from my rule, even if it could be true in general, have much appearance of truth, since the reason for this distinction is not apparent and the number of examples is very small. Whether the writers themselves had such great care that they never departed from the rules they had set for themselves, and never placed εἰς before consonants either by chance or for the sake of euphony, and, what is less credible, never placed ἐς before vowels without metrical necessity, cannot be known, since the manuscripts discredit themselves not only by their inconsistency, but also by sometimes introducing εἰς and ἐς against the law of the meter. As for euphony or metrical elegance, the opinion of some is very uncertain that in senarii, and especially in the third dipody, ἐς Ἴλιον [to Ilium], ἐς αὔριον [to tomorrow], ἐς ὕστερον [to later], ἐσείδομεν [we saw] and all such forms are more probable than those which offer a spondee, εἰς Ἴλιον [to Ilium], εἰς αὔριον [to tomorrow], εἰς ὕστερον [to later], εἰσείδομεν [we saw].

Praepositiones εἰςinto et ἐνin , quibus in lingua Latina una respondet in, apud Graecos sic differunt ut εἰςinto (ut in cum accusativo) motum in locum, ἐνin (ut in cum ablativo) quietem in loco significet, et ita quidem utraque ut saepe non ipse qui nominatur locus, sed vicinia loci intelligatur.

The prepositions εἰς and ἐν, to which in Latin one word in corresponds, differ among the Greeks in that εἰς (like in with the accusative) signifies motion into a place, and ἐν (like in with the ablative) rest in a place, and indeed both often in such a way that not the place itself that is named, but the vicinity of the place is understood.

cit.quote: χθονὸς μὲν εἰς τηλουρὸν ἥκομεν πέδον, Σκύθην ἐς οἶμον, ἄβροτον εἰς ἐρημίαν.
We have come to a far-off land, to a Scythian path, to an untrodden wilderness.
εἰς ἀπέραντον Τάρταρον ἡκεν.
He came to boundless Tartarus.
εἰς ἀρθμὸν ἐμοὶ καὶ φιλότητα – ἥξει.
He will come to a bond of friendship with me.
ἐς θρόνον καθέζετο.
He sat down on the throne.
τὴν σιδηρομήτορα ἐλθεῖν ἐς αἷαν
to come to the iron-mother land
φρένας γὰρ εἰς αὐτὰς τυπείς.
struck in the very mind
σαφῶς μ᾽ ἐς οἶκον σὸς λόγος στέλλει πάλιν.
Your word clearly sends me back home.
ἐς νόσον πεσών.
having fallen into sickness
εἴ τις εἰς νόσον πέσοι
if someone should fall into sickness
δυστέκμαρτον εἰς τέχνην ὥδωσα θνητούς.
I thrust mortals into a hard-to-interpret art.
πωλεύμεναι ἐς παρθενῶνας τοὺς ἐμούς.
going about into my chambers
ἔς τε Πυθὼ κἀπὶ Δωδώνης πυκνοὺς θεοπρόπους ἴαλλεν.
He sent frequent envoys to Pytho and to Dodona.
οὐπώποτ᾽ ηὔχουν ξένους μολεῖσθαι λόγους ἐς (εἰς recte apogr.) ἀκοὰν ἐμάν.
I never boasted that foreign words would come to my hearing.
ἐς μεσημβρινὴν βῆναι κέλευθον.
to go on the midday journey
οὗτός σ᾽ ὁδώσει τὴν τρίγωνον ἐς χθόνα.
This man will guide you to the triangular land.
ἐς ταυτὸν ἐλθὼν τῶν πάλαι λόγων ἴχνος.
coming to the same track of old words
ἐς τάσδε σαυτὸν πημονὰς καθώρμισας.
You have brought yourself into these troubles.
ἄψορρον ἥξεις ἐς φάος.
You will return to the light.
εἰς ἀναύγητον μολεῖν ῞Αιδην.
to go to sunless Hades
ἔς τε κελαινὸν Τάρταρον ἄρδην ῥίψειε δέμας.
and may he hurl his body headlong into black Tartarus
Ζεὺς ὑμᾶς εἰς ἀπρόοπτον πῆμ᾽ εἰσέβαλεν.
Zeus has cast you into unforeseen ruin.
εἰς ἀπέραντον δίκτυον ἄτης ἐμπλεχθήσεσθε.
You will be entangled in a boundless net of ruin.
ἔς τ᾽ ἐπάλξεις καὶ πύλας πυργωμάτων ὁρμᾶσθε πάντες.

ταυροσφαγούντες ἐς μελάνδετον σάκος.

οὐκ ἐς φθόρον σιγῶσ᾽ ἀνασχήσει τάδε;
Will you not endure these things in silence to your ruin?
τρέψον εἰς ἐχθροὺς βέλος.
Turn your weapon against the enemy.
εἰς ἑπτατειχεῖς ἐξόδους τάξω μολών.
I will go and station myself at the seven-gated exits.
ἐς οὐρανὸν πέμπει.
He sends to heaven.
Ἀργείοισι Καδμείους ἅλις ἐς χεῖρας ἐλθεῖν.
It is enough for the Argives to come to blows with the Cadmeans.
πανδόκον εἰς ἀφανή τε χέρσον.
to a land that receives all and is unseen
ἐπεὶ κατῆλθες ἐς πόλιν.
since you came down to the city
τῶν οἰχομένων Ἑλλάδ᾽ ἐς αἶαν.
of those who have gone to the land of Hellas
πεπέρακεν μὲν ὁ – στρατὸς εἰς ἀντίπορον γείτονα χώραν.
the army has crossed to the opposite neighboring land
παράγει βροτὸν εἰς ἄρκυας ῎Ατα.
Ruin leads a mortal into her nets.
εἰς ὄψιν μολεῖν.
to come into sight
ἐσθλά σοι πέμπειν – γῆς ἔνερθεν ἐς φάος.
to send good things to you from beneath the earth to the light
εὐτ᾽ ἂν εἰς οἴκους μόλωμεν.
when we come home
ἐς ναῦν ἐχώρει.
he went to the ship
ἐς μάχην ὁρμῶντες.
rushing into battle
ῥέπουσαν ἐς τὰ μάσσονα.
inclining to the greater side
διεκπερῶμεν ἔς τε Φωκέων χθόνα.
we pass through to the land of the Phocians
ἔς τε (ἠδὲ Robort.) Μακεδόνων χώραν ἀφικόμεσθα.
and we arrived at the land of the Macedonians
προπέμπετ᾽ ἐς δόμους.
escort him to the house
ἐς γᾶν προπίτνοντες.
falling to the ground
πέμψατ᾽ ἔνερθεν ψυχὴν ἐς φῶς.
send up the soul from below to the light
ἐς δὲ παῖδ᾽ ἐμὸν Ζεὺς ἐπέσκηψεν τελευτὴν θεσφάτων.
Zeus has laid upon my son the fulfillment of the oracles.
εἰ μὴ στρατεύοισθ᾽ ἐς τὸν Ἑλλήνων τόπον.
unless you march to the land of the Greeks
ἐς τὰ νῦν πεπραγμένα βλέψαντα,
looking at what has now been done
cit.note: ut ἰδέσθαι εἰςἰδέσθαι εἰς [to look upon] dixit Suppl. 103 ἰδέσθω δ᾽ εἰς ὕβρινἰδέσθω δ᾽ εἰς ὕβριν [let him look upon the outrage] . [Sed Ch. 232 ἰδοῦ — εἰς δὲ θήρειον γραφήν, εἰς δὲἰδοῦ — εἰς δὲ θήρειον γραφήν, εἰς δὲ [look — and at the beastly painting, and at] ex ἠδὲand corruptum, quod restituit Turnebus.]

as he said ἰδέσθαι εἰς [to look upon] Suppl. 103 ἰδέσθω δ᾽ εἰς ὕβριν [let him look upon the outrage]. [But Ch. 232 ἰδοῦ — εἰς δὲ θήρειον γραφήν [behold — and into the beastly writing], εἰς δὲ is corrupted from ἠδὲ, which Turnebus restored.]

cit.quote: ἐλθοῦσ᾽ ἐς οἴκους.
having come home
αἰακτὸς ἐς δόμους κίε.
he went lamenting to the house
κρόκου βαφὰς δ᾽ ἐς πέδον χέουσα.
pouring saffron dyes to the ground
Ἀτρειδῶν ἐς τόδε σκήπτει στέγος φάος.
the light of the Atreidae falls upon this house
λακτίσαντι μέγαν Δίκας βωμὸν εἰς ἀφάνειαν.
having kicked the great altar of Justice into oblivion
ἐλθὼν ἐς δόμον τὸν Ἀτρειδᾶν.
having come to the house of the Atreidae
σποδὸς εἰς ἑκάστου δόμους ἀφικνεῖται.
ashes arrive at each man's house
ἰάπτων μηκέτ᾽ εἰς ἡμᾶς βέλη.
hurling no more arrows at us.
ἐλθεῖν ἐς Ἰλίου πόλιν.
to go to the city of Ilium.
ἐς αἱματηρὸν τεῦχος ψήφους ἔθεντο.
they cast votes into the blood-stained urn.
ἐς μέλαθρα καὶ δόμους ἐφεστίους ἐλθών.
having come to the halls and the hearth-homes.
ἐς δῶμ᾽ ἄελπτον ὡς ἂν ἡγῆται Δίκη.
to an unexpected house, as Justice may lead.
εἰμ᾿ ἐς δόμων μέλαθρα.
I go to the halls of the house.

a leafy branch came to the house.
πεσεῖν ἐς τὸ μὴ τελεσφύρον.
to fall into that which brings no fulfillment.
τέκνων εἰς ἔργον ἠλθέτην.
they came to the deed of their children.
ἴτ᾿ ἐς φθόρον πεσόντε.
go, having fallen to ruin.
ἀπήγαγ᾽ ἐς τοιάσδε θανασίμους τύχας.
he led away to such deadly fortunes.
μηδ᾽ εἰς Ἑλένην κότον ἐκτρέψης.
do not turn your wrath against Helen.
ἐς τόνδ᾽ ἐνέβης ξὺν ἀληθείᾳ χρησμόν.
you have entered upon this oracle with truth.
ἥκω γὰρ εἰς γῆν τήνδε.
for I have come to this land.
εἰς ταὐτὸ συμβαίνουσι τοῖς ἐμοῖς στίβοις.
they meet in the same place as my steps.
εἰς ὄψιν ἥκεις.
you have come into sight.
τὸ μητρὸς ἐς σε μοι ῥέπει στέργηθρον.
my mother's love inclines toward you.
πολλοὶ γὰρ εἰς ἓν συμπίτνουσιν ἵμεροι.
for many desires fall together into one.
φονίας σταγόνας χυμένας ἐς πέδον.
murderous drops poured on the ground.
ἐς φάος μολών.
having come into the light.
στείχοντα – ἐς ῎Αργος κίεις.
going – you go to Argos.
ἄγ᾿ αὐτὸν εἰς ἀνδρῶνας.
lead him into the men's quarters.
τεκοῦσα γάρ μ' ἔρριψας ἐς τὸ δυστυχές.
for having borne me, you cast me into misfortune.
οὔτοι σ᾽ ἀπέρριψ᾽ εἰς δόμους δορυξένους.
I did not cast you away into a house of foreign spears.
ἔμολε δ᾽ ἐς δόμον.
he came to the house.
ταραγμὸς ἐς φρένας πίτνει.
confusion falls upon my mind.
ἐς τήνδε γαῖαν ἦλθε.
he came to this land.

κόσμος οὔτε πρὸς θεῶν ἀγάλματα φέρειν δίκαιος οὔτ᾽ ἐς ἀνθρώπων στέγας.
an ornament not fit to bring to the statues of the gods nor to the dwellings of men.
εἰς ἄγκρισιν ἐλθεῖν.
to come to a reckoning.
μολὼν ἐς οἶκον.
having come to the house.
ἐς ἀλλόφυλον ἐλθοῦσαι χθόνα.
having come to a foreign land.
κέλσειν ἐς ῎Αργος.
to land at Argos.
ἐς βυθὸν μολεῖν.
to go into the deep.
παλαιὸν δ᾽ εἰς ἴχνος μετέσταν.
they moved to the old track.
ἐς γῆν ἐνεγκεῖν.
to bring to the land.
ἐς νύκτ᾿ ἀποστείχοντος ἡλίου.
as the sun departs into night.
κί᾽ ἐς δόρυ.
go to the spear.

unless someone goes to the ship.
γυναικῶν ἐς πόλιν δοκεῖς μολεῖν.
you think you are going to a city of women.
οὐ μάλ᾽ ἐς μακράν (ἄπει);
not far off (will you go?).
ἥκουσ᾽ ἐκ σκότου τόδ᾽ ἐς φάος.
I have come from darkness into this light.
ἐς ὑψίκρημνον Ἱμέραν τ᾽ ἀφικόμην.

εἰς μελανίππου προφυγὼν ἱερᾶς | νυκτὸς ἀμολγόν.
having fled to the dark of the holy night of the black-horsed.

a tearing comes over the top of my head.
ἥξεις δὲ Λιγύων εἰς ἀτάρβητον στρατόν.
you will come to the fearless army of the Ligurians.
ἔπεμψεν ἐς δόμους.
he sent to the house.

εἰς ῞Αιδου μολεῖν.
to go to Hades.
ἁπλοῦς οἶμος εἰς ῞Αιδου φέρει.
a single path leads to Hades.
ἐς δ᾽ ὑμᾶς ἐρῶ μύθον.
I will speak a word to you.

sense.def: De actione versus s. contra aliquem directa
Of action directed toward or against someone

cit.quote: τὸν ἐξαμαρτόντ᾽ εἰς θεούς.
the one who sinned against the gods.
εἰς ἄλληλα | στάσιν ἀντίπνουν ἀποδεικνύμενα.
showing opposing strife against each other.
ἀλλ᾽ εἰς ἅπαντας ἀνθ᾽ ἑνὸς τόδ᾽ ἔργον ἦν.
but this deed was against all in place of one.

sense.def: εἰςinto in locutionibus adverbiorum significationem habentibus
εἰς [into] in expressions having adverbial meaning

cit.quote: ὑμῖν τῇδέ τ᾽ ἐς κοινὸν φράσω.
I will tell you and her in common.
πᾶσι δ᾽ ἐς κοινὸν λέγω.
I say to all in common.

sense.note: Frequens ἐς τὸ πᾶνἐς τὸ πᾶν [for the whole, altogether] , i. e. πάντωςin every way, altogether vel παντελῶςcompletely, utterly prorsus, omnino, cuius exempla v. s. v. πᾶςall, every .
Frequent is ἐς τὸ πᾶν [to the whole], i.e. πάντως or παντελῶς, utterly, altogether, for examples see under πᾶς.

sense.def: εἰςinto eo sensu quo Latine quod attinet dicitur
εἰς [into] in the sense in which Latin says 'as regards'

cit.quote: ἐς τὰ πάνθ᾽ ὁμῶς βίαιος.
violent in all things alike.
πρῶτος εἰς εὐψυχίαν.
first in courage.
τελεῖται δ᾽ ἐς τὸ πεπρωμένον.
it is accomplished to what is fated.
τὰ δ᾽ ἐς τὸ σὸν φρόνημα μέμνημαι κλύων.

ἐς τριακάδας δέκα ναῶν.
to thirty tens of ships.
ἐς τόδ᾽ ἡμαμ εὐ ῥέπει θεός,
to this day the god inclines well.
cit.note: i. e. usque hunc diem.
i.e. up to this day.

it remains for a third lifetime.
ἐς τὸ λοιπόν.
for the future.
καλὰ ἐς τὸν πολὺν φίλοισι καρποῦσθαι χρόνον.
