καὶ τὰς ἀγχιάλους ἐκράτυνε μεσάκτους ( νήσους )
And he made strong the sea-girt islands in the middle (islands).
καὶ τὰς ε τὰς εὐκτεάνους, κατὰ κλῆρον Ἰαόνιον πολυάνδρους | Ελλάνων ἐκράτυνε σφετέραις φρεσίν
And the wealthy, populous islands, by the Ionian allotment, he made strong with his own mind.
cit.note: ubi metrum ἐκράτειhe ruled postulat, quod coniecit Hermannus, si recte habet σφετέραιςtheir own .
where the meter demands ἐκράτει [he ruled], which Hermann conjectured, if σφετέραις [their own] is correct.

cit.quote: κράτος τ᾿ ἰσόψυχον ἐκ γυναικῶν καρδιόδηκτον ἐμοὶ κρατύνεις
And you strengthen for me a power equal in life, heart-biting, from women.
κρατύνεις βωμὸν ἑστίαν χθονός
You strengthen the altar, the hearth of the land.
ὑπ᾿ ἀρχᾶς δ᾽ οὔτινος θοάζων τὸ μεῖον κρεισσόνων ( sic Turnebus pro κρεῖσσον ὢν ) κρατύνειν οὔτινος ἄνωθεν ἡμένου σέβει κάτω
Under no one's rule, hastening the lesser to rule over the stronger (thus Turnebus for κρεῖσσον ὢν [being stronger]), he reveres no one seated above, below.
cit.note: Sic Hermannus pro κρατύνειhe rules .
Thus Hermann for κρατύνει [he rules].

cit.quote: τὸ δάμιον, τὸ πτόλιν κρατύνει
The public thing, which strengthens the city.
χεῖρας κρεῶν πλήθοντες οἰκείας βορᾶς
Filling their hands with meat of their own kindred feast.
τὴν μὲν Θυέστου δαῖτα παιδείων κρεῶν ξυνῆκα
I understood the feast of Thyestes, of children's flesh.
παρέσχε δαῖτα παιδείων κρεῶν
He provided a feast of children's flesh.
τῶν κρεισσοτέκνων δ᾽ ἀπ᾿ ( δ᾽ ἀπ᾿ metro postulante delevit Blomfieldus ) ὀμμάτων ἐπλάγχθη
And from the eyes of his stronger children (Blomfield deleted δ᾽ ἀπ᾿ [but from] as the meter demanded) he was driven astray.
cit.note: Vocabulum suspectum. κυρσοτέκνωνof children to be met Hermannus, quod significet privavit se oculis qui liberis occursuri erant.
A suspect word. Hermann proposed κυρσοτέκνων [of children to be met], which would mean he deprived himself of eyes that were going to meet his children.

cit.quote: κρεισσόνων ἐμοῦ θεῶν ( sic scripsi pro κρεισσόνων θεῶν ἔρως ) ἄφυκτον ὄμμα προσδράκοι με
May the inescapable eye of gods stronger than me (thus I wrote for κρεισσόνων θεῶν ἔρως [love of stronger gods]) look upon me.
cit.note: ubi κρείσσονεςthe stronger ones oppositi sunt Oceano, inferioris ordinis deo. κρείττονεςthe stronger ones de diis dictum ab Aeschylo ΑἰτναίαιςAetnaeae ( fr. 7 ) memorat Hesychius.
where κρείσσονες [the stronger ones] are opposed to Oceanus, a god of lower rank. Hesychius records that κρείττονες [the stronger ones] was used of the gods by Aeschylus in the Aetnaeae (fr. 7).

cit.quote: κεραυνοῦ κρείσσον᾽ εὑρήσει φλόγα
He will find a flame stronger than lightning.
οὕτω δ᾽ Ατρέως παῖδας ὁ κρείσσων ἐπ᾿ Ἀλεξάνδρῳ πέμπει ξένιος Ζεύς
Thus the stronger Zeus, god of guests, sends the sons of Atreus against Alexander.
τὸ μεῖον κρεισσόνών κρατύνειν
The lesser to rule over the stronger.
ἀλλ᾽ ἔστι φήμη τοὺς λύκους κρείσσους κυνῶν εἶναι
But there is a saying that wolves are stronger than dogs.
cit.note: ubi Μ κρείσσωνM: stronger , superscripto ουςstronger (acc. pl.) : unde Hermannus φήμη κρείσσονας λύκους κυνῶνreport that wolves are stronger than dogs .
where M has κρείσσων [stronger], with ους [stronger (acc. pl.)] written above: hence Hermann proposed φήμη κρείσσονας λύκους κυνῶν [report that wolves are stronger than dogs].

cit.quote: ὕψος κρεῖσσον ἐκπηδήματος
A height too great for leaping.
τὸ μὴ μαθεῖν σοι κρεῖσσον ἢ μαθεῖν τάδε
It is better for you not to learn than to learn these things.
κρεῖσσον γὰρ εἰσάπαξ θανεῖν ἢ τὰς ἁπάσας ἡμέρας πάσχειν κακῶς
For it is better to die once for all than to suffer every day.
κρεῖσσον γὰρ οἶμαι τῇδε λατρεύειν πέτρᾳ ἢ πατρὶ φῦναι Ζηνὶ πιστὸν ἄγγελον
For I think it is better to serve this rock than to be born the trusted messenger of father Zeus.
κρεῖσσον δὲ πύργου βωμός
An altar is stronger than a tower.
τὸ μὴ γενέσθαι δ᾽ ἐστὶν ἢ πεφυκέναι κρεῖσσον κακῶς πράσσοντα
It is better not to be born than, having been born, to fare badly.
εὔχου τὰ κρείσσω
Pray for better things.
ταῦτα μὲν, ὦ παῖ, κρείσσονα χρυσοῦ – φωνεῖς
These things, my child, you say are better than gold.

sense.def: adiectivum a κρέκεινto strike the lyre ductum, quod de cithara pulsanda dicitur: hinc cantatus
an adjective derived from κρέκειν [to strike the lyre], which is said of playing the cithara: hence sung

cit.quote: ἅμα δὲ κρεκτὸν γοατὰν νόμον θήσομεν πόλει
And together we shall set a sung nomos of wailers for the city.
cit.note: Sic Hermannus pro ὁμοῦ κρεκτὸν γοήτων ( γοητῶν Μwoven together with wailers a m. rec. ) νόμον μεθήσομεν πόλειwe shall release a strain for the city . Est vocabulum alibi non lectum, nisi quod Hesychius annotavit θρεκτοῖσι νόμοις ἀντὶ τοῦ τροχαίοις, Σοφοκλῆς Ὀδυσσεῖ μαινομένῳ. ἔνιοι δὲ κρεκτοῖςθρεκτοῖσι νόμοις [with woven strains] instead of τροχαίοις [trochaic], Sophocles in Odysseus Mad; but some read κρεκτοῖς [woven] , et recte quidem, si quid loci Aeschylei similitudini tribuendum est.

Thus Hermann for ὁμοῦ κρεκτὸν γοήτων [together a sung (nomos) of wailers] (γοητῶν [of wailers] M by a later hand) νόμον μεθήσομεν πόλει [we shall release a nomos for the city]. The word is not found elsewhere, except that Hesychius noted θρεκτοῖσι νόμοις [with struck nomoi] instead of τροχαίοις [trochaic], Sophocles in Odysseus Mad; but some read κρεκτοῖς [struck], and rightly so, if any weight is to be given to the similarity of the Aeschylean passage.

cit.quote: οἰόφρων κρεμάς γυπιὰς πέτρα
solitary-minded, hanging on the vulture's rock
cit.note: Falsum in M accentum κρέμας γυπίαςhanging vulture's rock correxit Hermannus.
Hermann corrected the false accent in M, κρέμας γυπίας [hanging vulture's rock].

cit.quote: κρεμαστὰ τόξα πίτυος ἐκ μελανδρύου
bows hung from a dark-leaved pine
cit.note: Sic Hermannus pro κρεμάσασα τόξονhaving hung the bow , quod est ap. schol. Hom. Od. 14, 12 κρεμάσας τόξονhaving hung the bow ap. Eustath. p. 1748, 57.
Thus Hermann for κρεμάσασα τόξον [having hung the bow], which is in the scholium on Homer, Od. 14, 12; κρεμάσας τόξον [having hung the bow] in Eustathius p. 1748, 57.

cit.quote: τὰς ἀνάνδρους κρεοβόρους ( sic anonymus Butleri pro κρεοβρότους, quod etiam κρεοβότους esse potest ) Ἀμαζόνας
the unwomanly flesh-eating (thus Butler's anonymous scholar for κρεοβρότους [flesh-devouring], which could also be κρεοβότους [flesh-grazing]) Amazons

form.gloss: to cut up meat, to mangle

sense.def: to cut up meat, to mangle

cit.quote: κρεοκοποῦσι δυστήνων μέλη
they cut up the limbs of the wretched

entry.note: Alterum huius verbi exemplum est apud Euripidem Cycl. 358 κρεοκοπεῖν μέλη ξένωνto cut up the limbs of strangers .
Another example of this verb is in Euripides, Cycl. 358 κρεοκοπεῖν μέλη ξένων [to cut up the limbs of strangers].

cit.quote: κρεουργὸν ἦμαρ εὐθύμως ἄγειν δοκῶν
thinking to pass a day of feasting cheerfully
cit.note: diem festum, quo convivis carnes distribuuntur.
a feast day, on which meats are distributed to the guests.

sense.def: Creon, son of Menoeceus, king of Thebes

cit.quote: Μεγαρεὺς Κρέοντος σπέρμα
Megareus, seed of Creon
Ζεὺς δι᾽ αἰῶνος κρέων ἀπαύστου
Zeus, ruling through unending time
ὕπερθ᾽ ὀμμάτων κρημναμενᾶν νεφελᾶν
above the eyes, hanging clouds
ἀμφὶ κρηναῖον γάνος
around the spring's water
Λέρνης τε κρήνην
and the spring of Lerna
cit.note: Sic Canterus pro Λέρνης ἄκρην τεand the height of Lerna .
Thus Canter for Λέρνης ἄκρην τε [and the height of Lerna].

cit.quote: Νύμφαις κρηνιάσιν
to the nymphs of the springs
cit.note: Sic Meinekius pro κρήναισινwith springs , pro quo etiam κρηναίαιςof springs scribi potest.
Thus Meineke for κρήναισιν [with springs], for which also κρηναίαις [of springs] can be written.

cit.quote: κοὐδέπω κακῶν κρηπὶς ὕπεστιν
and not yet is there a foundation of evils
ἐγὼ γένος μέν εἰμι Κρὴς ἀρχέστατον
I am by birth a Cretan of most ancient lineage

sense.def: was the title of a play by Aeschylus

cit.quote: Κρητικοῖς χρυσοκμήτοισιν ὅρμοις
with Cretan necklaces wrought of gold
τόνδ᾽ ἐν ῥοθοῦντι κριβάνῳ θήσω
I will place this in a roaring oven
cit.note: Sic correxi quod apud Athen. 9 p. 375d legitur νοθοῦντιspurious .
Thus I corrected what is read in Athenaeus 9 p. 375d as νοθοῦντι [spurious].

cit.quote: κριθῶντα πῶλον
a colt neighing
οὐ πίνοντας ἐκ κριθῶν μέθυ
not drinking strong drink made from barley
οὐκ εὔκριτον τὸ κρίμα
the judgment is not easy to decide

form.gloss: to separate, choose; to prefer; to decide, judge

cit.quote: κρίνασα δ᾽ ἀστῶν τῶν ἐμῶν τὰ βέλτατα
having chosen the best of my citizens
ἀπὸ δ᾽ αὐτε ξουθὸς ἱππαλεκτρυών | στάζει κριθέντων ( sic Hermannus pro κηρόθεν τῶν ) φαρμάκων πολὺς πόνος
and from it the tawny horse-cock | drips much toil of chosen drugs (thus Hermann for κηρόθεν τῶν [from wax])
κρίνω δ᾽ ἄφθονον ὄλβον
I judge abundant wealth
κρῖνε σέβας τὸ πρὸς θεῶν
judge the reverence due to the gods
ἔργον δ᾽ ἐν κύβοις ῎Αρης κρινεῖ
and Ares will decide the work with dice
δύσμαχα δ᾽ ἔστι κρίναι
and it is hard to decide
κρίνω σε νικᾶν
I judge you to be victorious
κρίνε δ᾽ εὐθεῖαν δίκην
and judge a straight justice
κρῖνον δίκην
judge the case
εἰ δικαίως εἴτε μὴ τῇ σῇ φρενὶ δοκεῖ τόδ᾽ αἷμα κρῖνον
whether justly or not, judge this blood according to your own mind
πρώτας δίκας κρίνοντες αἵματος χυτοῦ
judging first cases of shed blood
ἐμὸν τόδ᾽ ἔργον, λοιθίαν κρῖναι δίκην
this is my task, to judge the final case
πῶς ἀγὼν κριθήσεται ;
how will the contest be decided?
κἂν ἰσόψηφος κριθῇ
even if the vote is equal
κἄκρινα πρῶτος ἐξ ὀνειράτων ἃ χρὴ ὕπαρ γενέσθαι
and I first judged from dreams what must come to pass in waking
cit.note: de somniis interpretandis.
about interpreting dreams.

cit.quote: εὐ δὲ πανταχή τελεῖν σοι τῶνδε κρίνομεν πέρι
and we judge that all these things will turn out well for you
ὑμεῖς δὲ φαύλως αὔτ᾽ ἄγαν ἐκρίνατε
but you judged these things too lightly
κρίνω δέ τοι νιν ὥστε συγκόλλως ἔχειν
and I judge him so as to hold together
οὕτως ἀπαλλάσσουσιν ἐν θεῶν κρίσει
thus they depart in the judgment of the gods
μή μ ' αἱροῦ κριτήν
do not choose me as judge
εὔνους γ᾽ ὁ πρῶτος τῶνδ᾽ ἐνυπνίων κριτής
kindly indeed is the first judge of these dreams
cit.note: De somniorum interprete.
about an interpreter of dreams.

cit.quote: κροκόβαπτον ποδὸς εὔμαριν ἀείρων
lifting a saffron-dyed shoe of the foot
ἐπὶ δὲ καρδίαν ἔδραμε κροκοβαφής σταγών
And upon his heart ran a saffron-dyed drop
κρόκου βαφὰς δ᾽ ἐς πέδον χέουσα
pouring to the ground the dye of saffron
ὦ Κρόνιε παῖ
O son of Cronus

cit.bibl: Ioannes Lydus de mensibus p. 274 ed. Has.
cit.note: τὴν τότε μὲν λεγομένην Κρονίαν, νῦν δὲ Ἱερὰν πόλιν ὡς Ἰσίγονος καὶ Αἰσχύλοςthe city then called Cronia, but now Hierapolis, as Isigonus and Aeschylus (fr. 10) ἐν τῇ Αἴτνῃin the Aetna ( i. e. ταῖς Αἰτναίαις ) παραδιδόασινthe Aetnaeae) record .
the city then called Cronia, but now Hierapolis, as Isigonus and Aeschylus (fr. 10) in the Aetna (i.e. the Aetnaeae) record.

cit.quote: Κρόνου παῖ
son of Cronus
θέλοντες ἐκβαλεῖν ἕδρας Κρόνον
wishing to cast Cronus from his throne
τὸν παλαιγενῆ Κρόνον
ancient Cronus
αὐτὸς δ᾽ ἔδησε πατέρα πρεσβύτην Κρόνον
and he himself bound his aged father Cronus
ἔνθα ποταμὸς ἐκφυσᾷ μένος κροτάφων ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν
where the river breathes forth its might from its very temples
πυκνοῦ κροτησμοῦ τυγχάνουσ᾽ ὑπὸ πτόλιν
meeting with the dense clatter beneath the city
cit.note: i. e. ictus telorum in clypeum coniectorum.
i.e. the striking of weapons hurled against the shield.

cit.quote: κτύπῳ δ᾽ ἐπιρροθεῖ κροτητὸν ἀμὸν καὶ πανάθλιον κάρα
and with a din it resounds upon my stricken and all-wretched head
μῶν οὖν Ὀρέστου κρύβδα δῶρον ἦν τόδε ;
Was this then a secret gift from Orestes?
κακόν με καρδίαν τι περιπίτνει κρύος
some evil cold falls upon my heart
τὸ περίβαρυ κρύος ἔχειν
to have the heavy cold
κρυπταδίου μάχας δολιόφρών ποινά
the guileful punishment of a secret battle
ἐν ἀγγέλῳ γὰρ κρυπτὸς ὀρθοῦται λόγος
for in a messenger a hidden word is set upright
πολλὰ δ᾽ ἄλλα φανεῖ χρηίζων κρυπτά
and many other hidden things he will reveal, needing them
cit.note: loco corrupto, in Μ κρυπτάM κρυπτά [hidden things] vel κρυπτάνκρυπτάν [hidden] est, sed κρυπτάκρυπτά [hidden things] explicat scholiasta supra versum verbis τὰ κρυπτὰ φανερώσειτὰ κρυπτὰ φανερώσει [he will reveal the hidden things] , et in margine θέλων πολλὰ κρυπτὰ εὑρίσκειθέλων πολλὰ κρυπτὰ εὑρίσκει [wishing he finds many hidden things] .

in a corrupt passage, in M it is κρυπτά [hidden things] or κρυπτάν [hidden], but the scholiast explains κρυπτά [hidden things] above the verse with the words τὰ κρυπτὰ φανερώσει [he will reveal the hidden things], and in the margin θέλων πολλὰ κρυπτὰ εὑρίσκει [wishing he finds many hidden things].
καὶ κρυπτάκαὶ κρυπτά [and hidden things] vitiose pro κἄκρυπτακἄκρυπτα [and not hidden] : v. s. v. ἄκρυπτοςἄκρυπτος [not hidden] .
καὶ κρυπτά [and hidden things] is corrupt for κἄκρυπτα [and not hidden]: see under ἄκρυπτος [not hidden].

cit.quote: κρύψει δέμας τὸ σόν
he will hide your body
ἐχθρὰ δ᾽ ἔχοντας ἔκρυψεν
and he hid those who had enmity
ποικίλοις ἀγρεύμασιν κρύψασα
having hidden with embroidered nets

sense.def: celo cum accus. personae et rei
to conceal with accusative of person and thing

cit.quote: μήτοι με κρύψης τοῦθ᾽ ὅπερ μέλλω παθεῖν
do not hide from me this which I am about to suffer
ἔνερθε δὲ χθονός κεκρυμμέν᾿ ἀνθρώποισιν ὠφελήματα
and beneath the earth hidden benefits for mortals
ἑτοιμότερα γέλωτος ἀνέφερον λίβη, χέουσα ( sic Dobraeus pro χαίρουσα ) πολύδακρυν γόον κεκρυμμένα
they brought forth libations more ready than laughter, pouring (thus Dobraeus for χαίρουσα [rejoicing]) a much-weeping lament, hidden
cit.note: ubi κεκρυμμένονκεκρυμμένον [hidden] correxi.
where I corrected κεκρυμμένον [hidden].

cit.quote: οὐκ ἐκρύφθη, πρέπει δὲ, φῶς αίνολαμπές, σίνος
it was not hidden, but it shines, a terribly bright light, the harm
περᾷ κρυσταλλοπῆγα διὰ πόρον
he crosses the ice-bound strait
δρασμῷ κρυφαίῳ
by secret flight
κρυφαῖον ἔκπλουν
a secret sailing out
κρυφαίοις πένθεσιν παχνουμένη
being chilled by secret griefs
ναυσὶν κρυφαίως δρασμὸν εὑρόντες τινά
having found some escape secretly with ships
μηδὲ κρωσσοὺς μήτ᾽ οἰνηροὺς μήθ᾽ ὑδατηροὺς λείπειν ἀφνεοῖσι δόμοισι
nor leave pitchers, neither wine-jars nor water-jars, in wealthy houses
μέγαν τέκνοις πλοῦτον ἐκτήσω σὺν αἰχμῇ
you acquired great wealth for your children with the spear
Λυδῶν δὲ λαὸν καὶ Φρυγῶν ἐκτήσατο
and he acquired the people of the Lydians and Phrygians
τοιοῦτον ἂν κτήσαιτο φηλήτης ἀνήρ
such a thing would a thievish man acquire
κτήσεται δ᾽ ἄνευ δορὸς αὐτόν τε καὶ γῆν
and he will acquire without the spear both himself and the land

sense.def: κέκτημαικέκτημαι [I have acquired] vel ἔκτημαιἔκτημαι [I have acquired] comparavi mihi, habeo
κέκτημαι [I have acquired] or ἔκτημαι [I have acquired] I have acquired for myself, I possess

cit.quote: κοινὸν ὄμμ᾽ ἐκτημέναι
having acquired a common eye
φωνὴν βάρβαρον κεκτημένη
having acquired a barbarian voice
κοινὸν τύχη, γνώμη δὲ τῶν κεκτημένων
common is fortune, but the judgment belongs to the owners
ἄγος δὲ καὶ θανὼν κεκτήσεται
and even dead he will acquire pollution

sense.def: ὁ κεκτημένοςὁ κεκτημένος [the one who has acquired] dominus
ὁ κεκτημένος [the one who has acquired] the owner

cit.quote: τις δ᾽ ἂν φίλους ὠνοῖτο τοὺς κεκτημένους ;
who would buy friends, the owners?
καί σφε σιδαρονόμῳ διὰ χερί ποτε λαχεῖν κτήματα
and that they once obtained possessions by lot through the iron-wielding hand
διέλαχον σφυρηλάτῳ Σκύθη σιδήρῳ κτημάτων παμπησίαν
they divided by lot with the hammered Scythian iron the whole property of possessions
ἐμοιράσαντο δ᾽ ὀξυκάρδιοικτήματα
and they divided sharp-hearted possessions
πάντα δὲ πύργων κτήνη πρόσθε τὰ δημιοπληθή Μοῖρα λαπάξει
But Fate will plunder all the herds of the people before the towers.
χρημάτων κτησίων
of possessions
σταθεῖσαν κτησίου βωμοῦ πέλας
standing near the altar of the god of possessions
cit.note: Iovis Penatis epitheton, de quo v. Thes. vol. 4 p. 2035.
Epithet of Jupiter the household god, on which see Thes. vol. 4 p. 2035.

cit.quote: κτησίου Διὸς χάριν
for the sake of Zeus the protector of possessions
οὗ δὴ τὴν μακράν ἀποικίαν, Ἰοῖ, πέπρωται σοί τε καὶ τέκνοις κτίσαι
There, Io, it is fated for you and your children to found a distant colony.
τὸν τᾶς βοὸς παῖδ᾽ ἀτιμάσας, τὸν αὐτός ποτ᾽ ἔκτισεν γόνῳ
having dishonored the son of the cow, whom he himself once begot as his own offspring
εὐμενεῖ βίᾳ κτίσας
having founded with kindly force
ἐπιστρεπτὸν αἰῶ κτίσσας
having founded a life to be turned back
ὁπότερ᾽ ἂν κτίσῃς
whichever of the two you may found
μόρον κτίσαι μωμένα
seeking to bring about death
cit.note: Sic Stanleius. κτεῖναιto kill M, littera v in litura a m. rec.
Thus Stanley. κτεῖναι [to kill] M, with the letter v written over an erasure by a later hand.

cit.quote: οὕτω γὰρ ἄν σοι δαῖτες ἔννομοι βροτῶν κτιζοίατο
For in this way lawful feasts of mortals would be established for you.
πολλὰς Περσίδων μάταν ἔκτισαν εὔνιδας ( ubi metrum εὔνιδας ἔκτισσαν postulat, quod restituit Boeckhius ) ἠδ᾽ ἀνάνδρους
many Persian women they made in vain husbandless (where the meter demands εὔνιδας ἔκτισσαν [they made husbandless], which Boeckh restored) and without men
ἐλεύθερόν σε τῶνδε πημάτων κτίσει
he will make you free from these troubles
τέχνης δέ νιν Ζεὺς ἔνθεον κτίσας φρένα
Zeus, having made his mind inspired with art
χρησμοὺς τοὺς ἐμούς τε καὶ Διὸς ταρβεῖν κελεύω μηδ᾽ ἀκαρπώτους κτίσαι
I bid you to fear my oracles and those of Zeus, and not to make them fruitless.
τελευτὰς δ᾽ ἐν χρόνῳ πατὴρ ὁ παντόπτας πρευμενεῖς κτίσειεν
and in time may the all-seeing father bring about kindly endings
μήποτε – βοὰν κτίσαι μάχλον ῎Αρη
never to raise a lustful cry to Ares
τὸ δὲ καλῶς κτίμενον
the well-founded
cit.note: Sic Bambergerus pro κτάμενονslain . Frequens apud Homerum in composito ἐϋκτίμενοςwell-built .
Thus Bamberger for κτάμενον [slain]. Frequent in Homer in the compound ἐϋκτίμενος [well-built].

cit.quote: τὸ δὲ καλῶς κτίμενον ὦ μέγα ναίων στόμιον
the well-founded, O great mouth of the harbor
κτύπου γὰρ ἀχὼ χάλυβος διῇξεν ἄντρων μυχόν
For the echo of the clash of steel pierced the depths of the caves.
τοῖς πεδαρσίοις οις κτύποις πιστός
trusting in the sounds from on high
βροντῆς θ᾽ ὑπερβάλλοντα καρτερὸν κτύπον
and the mighty crash of thunder surpassing
ὅπλων κτύπος ποτιχρίμπτεται
the clash of arms approaches
cit.note: Sic correxi quod est in Μ οπλοκτύπος τί χρίμπτεταιa clash of arms approaches .
Thus I corrected what is in M: οπλοκτύπος τί χρίμπτεται [a clash of arms approaches].

cit.quote: ἀκούετ᾽ ἢ οὐκ ἀκούετ᾿ ἀσπίδων κτύπον ;
Do you hear, or do you not hear, the clash of shields?
κτύπον δέδορκα
I see the clash
δέδοικα δ᾽ ὄμβρου κτύπον δομοσφαλῆ
I fear the crash of rain that destroys houses
κτύπῳ δ᾽ ἐπιρροθεῖ κροτητὸν ἀμὸν καὶ πανάθλιον κάρα
and with a blow it strikes my head, beaten and utterly wretched
θύρας ἄκουσον ἑρκείας κτύπον
hear the knock at the courtyard door
κυάνεον δ᾽ ὄμμασι λεύσσων φονίου δέργμα δράκοντος
looking with dark blue eyes, the deadly gaze of a serpent
cit.note: ubi trisyllabum est: unde κυανοῦνdark blue Blomfieldus.
where it is trisyllabic: hence Blomfield reads κυανοῦν [dark blue].

cit.quote: κυανέη καὶ τούσδε μενέγχεας ὤλεσεν ἄνδρας Μοῖρα
dark Fate destroyed these men too, who held their spears
cit.note: syllaba prima producta, i. e. mors.
with the first syllable lengthened, i.e. death.

cit.quote: κυανώπιδες θοαὶ ( θοαὶ ego addidi ) vᾶες
dark-eyed swift ships (I added θοαί [swift])
δορυπαγεῖς δ᾽ ἔχοντες κυανώπιδας νῆας
holding spear-built dark-eyed ships

entry.note: Hoc adiectivum alibi non legitur, eodem vero sensu naves κυανόπρωροιdark-prowed (naves caeruleae apud Virgilium) dicuntur, de quibus v. Thes. vol. 4 p. 2049.
This adjective is not found elsewhere, but in the same sense ships are called κυανόπρωροι [dark-prowed] (dark ships in Virgil), on which see Thes. vol. 4 p. 2049.

cit.quote: φιλεῖ ὠδῖνα τίκτειν νὺξ κυβερνήτη σοφῷ
night loves to bring forth pain for a wise helmsman
βέβληκ᾽ Ἀχιλλεὺς δύο κύβω καὶ τέσσαρα
Achilles has thrown two dice and a four
ἔργον δ᾽ ἐν κύβοις ῎Αρης κρινεῖ
Ares will decide the matter with dice
οὔ τοι γυναιξὶ δεῖ κυδάζεσθαι
It is not fitting for you to be reviled by women
κύδιστ᾽ ἀχέων ἐπέκρανεν
he accomplished the most glorious of griefs
κύδιστ᾽ Ἀχαιῶν
most glorious of the Achaeans
ἄροισθε κύδος τοῖσδε πολίταις
win glory for these citizens
ὡς γὰρ θεὸς ναῶν ἔδωκε κῦδος Ἕλλησιν μάχης
for as a god he gave glory to the Greeks in battle

form.gloss: glorious, excelling in glory and grace

sense.def: glorious, excelling in glory and grace

cit.quote: νύμφαις κρηνιάσιν κυδραῖσι θεαῖσιν ἀγείρω
I gather for the nymphs of the springs, the glorious goddesses
μηδ᾽ ὑπ᾿ ἀνάγκας γάμος ἔλθοι Κυθερείας
May no marriage come under compulsion from Cythereia.
cit.note: quod in ΚυθέρειοςCytherean mutatum est in apogr. Guelferbytano. γάμοςmarriage ex glossemate illatum esse pro τέλοςend, fulfillment coniecit Weilius.
which was changed to Κυθέρειος [Cytherean] in the Guelferbytan copy. Weilius conjectured that γάμος [marriage] was introduced from a gloss in place of τέλος [end].

cit.quote: καὶ συναίρεσθαι Κύπριν θέλει
And he wishes to join with Cypris.
Κύπρου Πάφου τ᾽ ἔχουσα πάντα κλῆρον
Holding all the allotted land of Cyprus and Paphos.
cit.note: Quod fragmentum Archilocho recte adscribere videtur Meinekius Vind. Strabon. p. 103.
Meineke in Vind. Strabon. p. 103 seems rightly to attribute this fragment to Archilochus.

entry.note: u brevi, cum aoristo ἐκύρησαI hit upon et futuro κυρήσωI will hit upon
with short u, with aorist ἐκύρησα [I hit upon] and future κυρήσω [I will hit upon]

cit.quote: ὁρῶ κυροῦντα τόνδε τῶν ἐπαξίων
I see this man attaining what he deserves.
ταὐτοῦ κυρήσας ἐκδίκοις ἀγρεύματος
Having attained the same with avenging capture.
κυρήσει νοστίμου σωτηρίας
He will attain a homecoming of safety.
στυγερᾶς μοίρας τῆσδε κυρήσας
Having attained this hateful fate.
ἔκυρσας ὥστε τοξότης ἄκρος σκοποῦ
You hit the mark like a top archer.
οὔτοι κυρήσεις μεῖον ἀξίας σέθεν
You will not attain less than your worth.
οὐδ᾽ ἀτιμίας κυρῶ
Nor do I meet with dishonor.
πρὶν δαΐκτορος βίᾳ κάρζας γάμου κυρῆσαι
Before by the force of the slayer he attained marriage with the girl.
πικροῦ δ᾽ ἔκυρσας – μνηστῆρος
You met with a bitter suitor.
κἀγὼ πάλου δ᾽ ἔκυρσα
And I obtained by lot.
Ιαόνων ναυβατᾶν κύρσαντες οὐκ εὐτυχῶς
Having met with the Ionian sailors not fortunately.
ὁ δὲ μὴ κύρσας βαρεῶν τούτων
But he who did not meet with these heavy things.
τί νῦν ἕκατι δαιμόνων κυρῶ ;
Why now am I in the power of the gods?
κἀκεῖ κυρούντων σώμασιν τὰ πρόσφορα
And there let them provide what is fitting for their bodies.

sense.def: without a case, to attain truly

cit.quote: καὶ τόδ᾽ ἂν γένος λέγων ἐξ Ἐπάφου κυρήσαις
And speaking of this race, you would trace it from Epaphus.
Ζηλῶ σ᾽ ὁθούνεκ᾽ ἐκτὸς αἰτίας κυρεῖς
I envy you because you are free from blame.
καλῶς τὰ πλείω πόλεμος ἐκ θεῶν κυρεῖ
For the most part war from the gods turns out well.
κακὸς οὐ κεκλήσει ριον βίον εὐ κυρήσας
You will not be called bad, having fared well in life.
cit.note: quod schol. exp. εὐτυχήσας, εὖ πράξαςhaving been fortunate, having fared well . Rectius Hermannus bene te habens quod que ad vitam attinet, i. e. recte instituens vitam.
which the scholiast explains as εὐτυχήσας, εὖ πράξας [having been fortunate, having fared well]. More correctly Hermann: 'keeping yourself well as regards life', i.e. 'rightly ordering your life'.

cit.quote: τρανῷς Ἀτρείδην εἰδέναι κυροῦνθ᾽ ὅπως
Clearly to know that Atreides is attaining how.
νύκτα ταύτην ἣν λέγεις ἐπ᾿ ἀσπίδος – κυρεῖν
This night which you speak of, on the shield – to be.
κακῶν μὲν ὅστις ἔμπειρος κυρεῖ
Whoever has experience of evils.
εἰ δὲ κυρεῖ τις πέλας οἰωνοπόλων ἐγγάϊος
But if some local diviner is near.
οὑμὸς δέ πότμος οὐρανῷ κυρῶν ἄνω
But my fate, reaching to heaven above.
σεσωσμένος κυρεῖ
He is saved.
θαυμάζω δέ σε – κυρεῖν λέγουσαν
I marvel at you – saying that you are.
κυρεῖν παρασχὼν ἰταμαῖς κυσὶν ἀεροφοίτοις
Giving to bold, air-wandering dogs to be.
cit.note: inter versus Aeschyleos hunc habet, de quo v. quae s. ν. ἰταμόςunder the word ἰταμός dicta sunt.
he has this among the verses of Aeschylus, about which see what has been said under the word ἰταμός [bold].
κυρήσαςhaving attained ex glossemate illatum.
κυρήσας [having attained] introduced from a gloss.

entry.note: u longo, cum aoristo ἔκυρσαI met with, encountered , qua forma tragici utuntur ubi metrum postulat
with long u, with aorist ἔκυρσα [I hit upon], which form the tragedians use when the meter demands it

cit.quote: ὁρῶ κυροῦντα τόνδε τῶν ἐπαξίων
I see this man attaining what he deserves.
ταὐτοῦ κυρήσας ἐκδίκοις ἀγρεύματος
Having attained the same with avenging capture.
κυρήσει νοστίμου σωτηρίας
He will attain a homecoming of safety.
στυγερᾶς μοίρας τῆσδε κυρήσας
Having attained this hateful fate.
ἔκυρσας ὥστε τοξότης ἄκρος σκοποῦ
You hit the mark like a top archer.
οὔτοι κυρήσεις μεῖον ἀξίας σέθεν
You will not attain less than your worth.
οὐδ᾽ ἀτιμίας κυρῶ
Nor do I meet with dishonor.
πρὶν δαΐκτορος βίᾳ κάρζας γάμου κυρῆσαι
Before by the force of the slayer he attained marriage with the girl.
πικροῦ δ᾽ ἔκυρσας – μνηστῆρος
You met with a bitter suitor.
κἀγὼ πάλου δ᾽ ἔκυρσα
And I obtained by lot.
Ιαόνων ναυβατᾶν κύρσαντες οὐκ εὐτυχῶς
Having met with the Ionian sailors not fortunately.
ὁ δὲ μὴ κύρσας βαρεῶν τούτων
But he who did not meet with these heavy things.
τί νῦν ἕκατι δαιμόνων κυρῶ ;
Why now am I in the power of the gods?
κἀκεῖ κυρούντων σώμασιν τὰ πρόσφορα
And there let them provide what is fitting for their bodies.

sense.def: without a case, to attain truly

cit.quote: καὶ τόδ᾽ ἂν γένος λέγων ἐξ Ἐπάφου κυρήσαις
And speaking of this race, you would trace it from Epaphus.
Ζηλῶ σ᾽ ὁθούνεκ᾽ ἐκτὸς αἰτίας κυρεῖς
I envy you because you are free from blame.
καλῶς τὰ πλείω πόλεμος ἐκ θεῶν κυρεῖ
For the most part war from the gods turns out well.
κακὸς οὐ κεκλήσει ριον βίον εὐ κυρήσας
You will not be called bad, having fared well in life.
cit.note: quod schol. exp. εὐτυχήσας, εὖ πράξαςhaving been fortunate, having fared well . Rectius Hermannus bene te habens quod que ad vitam attinet, i. e. recte instituens vitam.
which the scholiast explains as εὐτυχήσας, εὖ πράξας [having been fortunate, having fared well]. More correctly Hermann: 'keeping yourself well as regards life', i.e. 'rightly ordering your life'.

cit.quote: τρανῷς Ἀτρείδην εἰδέναι κυροῦνθ᾽ ὅπως
Clearly to know that Atreides is attaining how.
νύκτα ταύτην ἣν λέγεις ἐπ᾿ ἀσπίδος – κυρεῖν
This night which you speak of, on the shield – to be.
κακῶν μὲν ὅστις ἔμπειρος κυρεῖ
whoever has experience of evils
εἰ δὲ κυρεῖ τις πέλας οἰωνοπόλων ἐγγάϊος
but if someone near the bird-seers happens to be at hand
οὑμὸς δέ πότμος οὐρανῷ κυρῶν ἄνω
but my fate, reaching its fulfillment in heaven above
σεσωσμένος κυρεῖ
is saved
θαυμάζω δέ σε – κυρεῖν λέγουσαν
I marvel at you, saying that you have met with
κυρεῖν παρασχὼν ἰταμαῖς κυσὶν ἀεροφοίτοις
having granted to the bold, air-wandering dogs to meet with
cit.note: inter versus Aeschyleos hunc habet, de quo v. quae s. ν. ἰταμόςsee ἰταμός dicta sunt.
he has this among the verses of Aeschylus, about which see what has been said under the word ἰταμός [bold].
κυρήσαςhaving met with, encountered ex glossemate illatum.
κυρήσας [having attained] introduced from a gloss.

form.gloss: having power, in whose power or decision lies

sense.def: potens, penes quem potestas 's. arbitrium est
having power, in whose power or decision lies

cit.quote: κύριός εἰμι θροεῖν ὅδιον κράτος αἴσιον ἀνδρῶν
I have the authority to proclaim the auspicious power of men on the road
ἐμῶν τε καὶ σῶν κύριος πιστωμάτων
master of my pledges and yours
ὕπνος πόνος͵ τε κύριοι συνωμόται
sleep and toil, the lords who share the oath
ματρῷον ἅγνισμα κύριον φόνου
the maternal purification that has authority over bloodshed
κύριον μένει τέλος
the appointed end awaits
χρόνῳ τοι κυρίῳ τ᾽ ἐν ἡμέρᾳ
in the appointed time and day
τί τῶνδε κυριωτέρους μένεις ;
why do you wait for those who have more authority than these?
νεανίδων τ᾽ ἐπηράτων ἀνδροτυχεῖς βιότους δότε κύρι᾽ ἔχοντες
and grant to the lovely maidens lives that bring men, having authority
cit.note: De diis nuptiarum praesidibus.
of the gods who preside over marriage.

cit.quote: ὅτε τὸ κύριον μόλῃ
when the appointed time comes
cit.note: De hora fatali.
of the fatal hour.

sense.def: Substantive κύριοςhaving power, master, lord dominus
as a substantive, κύριος [lord] means master

cit.quote: ἄγγελλε τοῖσι κυρίοισι δωμάτων
announce to the masters of the house
εἰ δὲ τυγχάνω τοῖς κυρίοισι καὶ προσήκουσιν λέγων
but if I happen to be speaking to those who have authority and are concerned

form.gloss: to butt with the head, to strike

sense.def: to butt with the head, to strike

cit.quote: ἀμφὶ νῆσον τὴν πελειοθρέμμονα νικώμενοι ( δεδουπότες ? ) κύρισσον ἰσχυρὰν χθόνα
around the island that nourishes doves, being defeated (having fallen?) they struck the strong earth with their heads
cit.note: i. e, allisi sunt ad terram, ut Brunckius interpretatur.
that is, they were dashed to the ground, as Brunck interprets.

cit.quote: τὸν πάθει μάθος θέντα κυρίως ἔχειν
who has established learning through suffering as a firm possession
δὸς τύχας, τυχεῖν δέ μοι κυρίως
grant good fortune, and grant that I may obtain it firmly
τρίτος δ᾽ ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ Κύρος
third from him, Cyrus
Κύρου δὲ παῖς
the son of Cyrus
οὐκ ἔχουσι κύρος οὐδὲν ἀμφὶ σοῦ
they have no authority at all concerning you
παιδὶ καὶ δόμοις ἐμοῖσι τήνδ᾽ ἐκύρωσας φάτιν
you ratified this utterance for my child and my house
τήνδε κυρώσων δίκην
about to decide this judgment
ὅσπερ τέτακται τήνδε κυρῶσαι δίκην
who has been appointed to decide this judgment
μάχης γὰρ δὴ κεκύρωται τέλος
for the end of the battle has been decided
ἔνισπε δ᾽ ἡμῖν ποῖ κεκύρωται τέλος
tell us where the end has been decided
ἐπειδὴ τῇδ᾽ ἐκύρωσεν φάτις ὑμῶν
since this utterance of yours has been ratified

entry.note: Hermanni coniectura Sept. 784. V. κρεισσότεκνοςhaving stronger children .
Hermann's conjecture at Sept. 784. See κρεισσότεκνος.

cit.quote: περίδρομον κύτος – κοιλογάστορος κύκλου
the encircling shield – of the hollow-bellied circle
ὄξος τ᾽ ἄλειφά τ᾽ ἐγχέας ταὐτῷ κύτει
pouring vinegar and oil into the same vessel
τῷ δ᾽ ἐναντίῳ κύτει ἐλπὶς προσήει
but in the opposite vessel hope was approaching

cit.note: κύτειvessel pro τεύχειvessel coniecit Blomf.
Blomfield conjectured κύτει [vessel] for τεύχει [vessel].

cit.quote: αἰθέρος θρόνος, πρὸς δν κύφελλ᾽ ὑδρηλὰ γίγνεται χιών
the throne of the upper air, to which watery clouds become snow
cit.note: ubi Μ πρὸς ὃν νέφη δ᾽ ὑδρηλάM πρὸς ὃν νέφη δ᾽ ὑδρηλά [to which watery clouds] ex glossemate. κύφελλαclouds ( nam numeri singularis exempla nulla sunt ) grammatici per νέφηclouds explicant. Usi sunt hoc vocabulo Callimachus et Lycophro, quorum exempla v. in Thes. vol. 4 p. 2164, haud dubie praeeuntibus antiquioribus poetis.

where M has πρὸς ὃν νέφη δ᾽ ὑδρηλά [to which watery clouds] from a gloss. κύφελλα [clouds] (for there are no examples of the singular) the grammarians explain by νέφη [clouds]. Callimachus and Lycophron used this word, examples of which see in the Thesaurus vol. 4 p. 2164, no doubt following older poets.

cit.quote: ἀκτὰς ἀμφὶ Κυχρείας
around the Cychrean shores
cit.note: i. e. circa Salaminem. Nam Κυχρεῖος εὐπάγος περὶ ΣαλαμίναΚυχρεῖος εὐπάγος περὶ Σαλαμίνα [Cychrean with good cliffs around Salamis] , et Salamis ipsa Kυχρεία εὐαυχρεία εὐα [Cychrean ...] appellata: v. Steph. Byz. s. v. ΚυχρεῖοςCychrean .

that is, around Salamis. For Κυχρεῖος εὐπάγος περὶ Σαλαμίνα [Cychrean with good cliffs around Salamis], and Salamis itself was called Kυχρεία εὐα [Cychrean ...]: see Stephanus of Byzantium s.v. Κυχρεῖος [Cychrean].

cit.quote: ἁρπαγὴν κυσίν
as plunder for the dogs
κυνὸς δίκην
in the manner of a dog
κλαγγάνεις δ᾽ ἅπερ κύων
you cry out like a dog
τετραυματισμένον γὰρ ὡς κύων νεβρόν ἐκματεύομεν
for like a dog we track the wounded fawn
ἀλλ᾽ ἔστι φήμη τοὺς λύκους κρείσσους κυνῶν εἶναι
But there is a saying that wolves are stronger than dogs.
κυσὶν δ᾽ ἔπειθ᾽ ἕλωρα – οὐκ ἀναίνομαι πέλειν
And then to be prey for dogs — I do not refuse.
κύνες διημάθυνον ἄνδρα δεσπότην
Dogs tore apart the man, their master.

entry.note: Non raro transfertur ad alia.
It is not rarely transferred to other things.

cit.quote: Ζηνὸς ἀκλαγγεῖς κύνας γρύπας φύλαξαι
Beware the silent hounds of Zeus, the griffins.
Διὸς δέ τοι πτηνός κύων δαφοινὸς ἀετός
But the winged dog of Zeus, the blood-red eagle.
πτανοῖσιν κυσί πατρός
With the winged hounds of his father.
cit.note: pariter de aquilis.
likewise of eagles.

cit.quote: γλῶσσα μισητῆς κυνός
The tongue of a hateful dog.
cit.note: de Clytaemnestra.
of Clytaemnestra.

cit.quote: φύλαξαι μητρὸς ἐγκότους κύνας
Beware the wrathful hounds of your mother.
αἵδε μητρὸς ἔγκοτοι κύνες
These are the wrathful hounds of my mother.
Σφίγγα δυσαμεριᾶν πρύτανιν κύνα πέμπει
He sends the Sphinx, the dog that presides over evil days.
γυναῖκα πιστὴν δωμάτων κύνα
A faithful wife, the watchdog of the house.
ἄνδρα ρ. 2211. τόνδε τῶν σταθμῶν κύνα
The man... this dog of the sheepfolds.
κυρεῖν παρασχών ἰταμαῖς κυσὶν ἀεροφοίτοις
Granting to meet with the bold, air-wandering hounds.
cit.note: inter versus Aeschyleos hunc habet, de quo v. s. v. ἰταμόςbold, reckless .
among the verses of Aeschylus he has this one, about which see under ἰταμός.

sense.def: dog or dog-star, name of a constellation

cit.quote: φυλλὰς σκιὰν ὑπερτείνασα σειρίου κυνός
A leafy shade stretching over the dog of Sirius.
cit.note: i. e. umbram adversus canicularis sideris aestum praetendens.
that is, holding out shade against the heat of the dog-star.

cit.quote: χαλκήλατοι κλάζουσι κώδωνες φόβον
Bronze-wrought bells ring out terror.
λόφοι δὲ κώδων τ᾽ οὐ δάκνουσ᾽ ἄνευ δορός
Crests and bells do not bite without the spear.
λιγέα κωκύματα
Shrill wailings.
οἰμωγὴ δ᾽ ὁμοῦ κωκύμασιν κατεῖχε πελαγίαν ἅλα
And a cry of lamentation together with wailings held the sea.
μή νυν — κωκυτοῖσιν ἁρπαλίζετε
Do not — you are snatching with wailings.
ὑμᾶς δὲ κωκυτοῖς ἐπανθίζειν νόμος
It is the custom for you to crown yourselves with wailings.
κῦμα Κωκυτοῦ λαχόν
Having obtained the wave of Cocytus.
ἀμφὶ Κωκυτόν τε κἀχερουσίους ὄχθους
Around Cocytus and the Acherusian banks.
ἀλλ᾽ εἶμι κὰν δόμοισι κωκύσουσ᾽ ἐμὴν Ἀγαμέμνονός τε μοῖραν
But I will go and in the house wail for my fate and that of Agamemnon.
κώλοισιν ἀμφίβληστρ᾽ ἔχει
He has nets around his limbs.
πρὸς κέντρα κῶλον ἐκτενεῖς
You will stretch your leg against the goads.
κνίση τε κώλα συγκαλυπτά
And the savor of limbs covered up.
μεθῆκεν αὑτοῦ κώλα
He let go his limbs.
σφαλερὰ τανυδρόμοις κώλα
Slippery limbs for swift runners.
δεῖ – κάμψαι διαύλου θάτερον κώλον πάλιν
It is necessary to turn the other leg of the double course back again.
cit.note: De altera parte stadii.
Of the other side of the racecourse.

cit.quote: κωλύουσαν
Hindering.
πεπωκώς – βρότειον αἷμα κῶμος ἐν δόμοις μένει
Having drunk — a revel of mortal blood remains in the house.
λεπταῖς ὑπαὶ κώνωπος ἐξηγειρόμην ῥιπαῖσι θωύσσοντος
I was awakened by the thin whirring of a gnat.
ναυβάτης τ᾽ ἀνὴρ τροποῦτο κώπην
And the sailor man handled the oar.
πᾶς ἀνὴρ κώπης ἄναξ
Every man is master of an oar.
κώπης ῥοθιάδος ξυνεμβολῇ
With the stroke of a splashing oar.
ἀγαῖσι κωπῶν
With the handles of oars.
νερτέρᾳ προσήμενος κώπῃ
Seated at the lower oar.
ἔθραυον πάντα κωπήρη στόλον
They shattered the whole oar-equipped fleet.
ἔνθα Κωρυκὶς πέτρα κοίλη
Where the hollow Corycian rock is.
cit.note: i. e. Parnassus: v. Thes. vol. 4
i.e. Parnassus: see Thesaurus vol. 4

cit.quote: ἤκουσας, ἢ οὐκ ἤκουσας, ἢ κωφῇ λέγω ;
Did you hear, or did you not hear, or am I speaking to a deaf woman?
κωφοῖς ἀϋτῶ
I shout to the deaf.
τὸ νεῖκος δ᾽ οὐκ ἐν ἀργύρου λαβῇ ἔλυσεν ( Άρης )
Ares did not resolve the quarrel by a grip on silver.
cit.note: ubi schol. ὁ Ἀρης κρίνει τὸ νεῖκος. οὐδὲ γὰρ ἄργυρον παρ᾽ ὑμῶν λαμβάνοντες εἰρηνεύσαιμεν ἄνAres decides the quarrel; for not even by taking silver from you would we make peace .
where the scholiast says: ὁ Ἀρης κρίνει τὸ νεῖκος. οὐδὲ γὰρ ἄργυρον παρ᾽ ὑμῶν λαμβάνοντες εἰρηνεύσαιμεν ἄν [Ares decides the quarrel; for not even by taking silver from you would we make peace].

entry.note: Dicitur plerumque de prehensione qua athleta adversarium prehendit, i. e. de nexu in lucta s. de nexu luctae, ut Quintilianus loquitur, ab H. Stephano memoratus: unde ad alia transfertur.

It is said mostly of the grip with which an athlete seizes his opponent, i.e. of the hold in wrestling or the wrestling hold, as Quintilian says, mentioned by H. Stephanus: whence it is transferred to other things.

cit.quote: τὰς ὁμοίας ἀντίδος λαβὰς λαβεῖν
to take equal grips in return
cit.note: Sic Canterus pro βλάβαςharms .
Thus Canterus for βλάβας [harms].

cit.quote: πνεύματι λάβρῳ
with furious blast

sense.def: procax sum in loquendo, audacter loquor
I am insolent in speech, I speak boldly

cit.quote: μηδ᾽ ἄγαν λαβροστόμει
do not speak too boldly
λαβρόσυτος ( sic Hermannus pro λαβρόσσυτος ) ἦλθον Ἥρας ἐπικότοισι μήδεσι δαμεῖσα
rushing impetuously (thus Hermannus for λαβρόσσυτος) I came, subdued by the wrathful counsels of Hera
ἀετὸς λάβρως διαρταμήσει σώματος μέγα ῥάκος
an eagle will violently tear apart a great rag of the body
λαγίναν ἐρικυμάδα φέρματι γένναν
the hare-born race of the wave
ἐδάη λαγοδαίτας πομπούς τ᾽ ἀρχᾶς
he learned of the hare-eating guides and leaders
cit.note: de aquilis.
of eagles.

sense.def: (with perfect εἴληχα and aorist ἔλαχον) I obtain by lot

cit.quote: ὡς πάλῳ λαχών ἕκα-στος αὐτῶν πρὸς πύλας ἄγοι λόχον
as each of them, having obtained by lot, would lead his company to the gates
πύλαις προσίστανται πάλῳ λαχόντες
they stand at the gates, having obtained by lot
ἴτων πάλῳ λαχόντες
let them go, having obtained by lot
ὡς τ᾿ ἐν πύλαις ἕκα-στος εἴληχεν πάλον
as each at the gates has obtained his lot
Καπανεὺς δ᾽ ἐπ᾽ Ἠλέκ-τραισιν εἴληχεν πύλαις
Capaneus has obtained the Electran gates
λέγ᾽ ἄλλον ἄλλαις ἐν πύλαις εἰληχότα
tell of another who has obtained other gates
τὸν ἐντεῦθεν λαχόντα πρὸς πύλαις λέξω
I will tell of the one who has obtained the gates from there
ἔμπας τις αὐτὴν ἄλλος ὤφελεν λαχεῖν
yet someone else should have obtained her
κύμα Κωκυτοῦ λαχόν
the wave of Cocytus having obtained
ὥστ᾽ ἴσον λαχεῖν
so as to obtain an equal share
ἔχουσι μοῖραν λαχόν-τες
they have obtained a portion
Ἑλλάδα κλήρῳ λαχοῦσα γαῖαν
having obtained the land of Hellas by lot
ὥστ᾽ ἀπαρκεῖν εὐ πραπίδων λαχόντα
so as to suffice well for those who have obtained wisdom
τί δ᾽ οὐ στένοντες οὐ λαχόντες ἤματος μέρος ;
why do we not groan, not having obtained a share of the day?
cit.note: ubi corruptum est λαχόντες. κλαίοντες ( κλάοντεςhaving obtained by lot; weeping ) Stanleius.
where λαχόντες [having obtained by lot] is corrupt. κλαίοντες (κλάοντες) [weeping] Stanley.

cit.quote: ἀλλ᾽ αἱματηρά πράγ-ματ᾿ οὐ λαχὼν σέβεις
but you revere bloody deeds, not having obtained them
πάντα γὰρ αὗται τὰ κατ᾿ ἀνθρώπους ἔλαχον διέπειν
for these obtained to manage all things among men
τὸ πᾶν τ᾽ ἐκ δαιμόνων λάθοιεν
and may they escape the whole from the gods
cit.note: ubi λάχοιενthey might obtain by lot probabilius est quam λάβοιενthey might take .
where λάχοιεν [they might obtain by lot] is more probable than λάβοιεν [they might take].

cit.quote: ἔλακε δ᾽ ἐς τὸ πᾶν ὁ Πυθοχρήστας φυγάς ( Orestes ) θεόθεν εὐ φραδαῖσιν ὡρμημένος
the Pythian-chosen exile (Orestes) drove to the whole, urged on by the gods with good counsels
cit.note:
ubi Schuetzius ἔλαχε δὴ τὸ πᾶνhe obtained the whole , alii minus probabiliter ἔλαχε δhe obtained '.
ἐς τὸ πᾶνfor the whole ( omnino, ut interpretatur Hermannus ). ἔλασεhe drove legisse videtur scholiasta qui explicat, ἤλασε δὲ εἰς τὸ τέλος τοῦ δρόμου, ὁ ἐστιν ἤνυσε τὸν ἀγῶνα · ἀφίκετο, φησὶν, εἰς τὸ τέλος τοῦ ἀγῶνοςhe drove to the end of the course, that is, he completed the contest; he arrived, he says, at the end of the contest , cui verbo ἐς τὸ πᾶνfor the whole aptius iungitur quam verbo ἔλαχεhe obtained . Quamobrem aut ἔλαχε δὴ τὸ πᾶνhe obtained the whole aut ἔλασε δ᾽ ἐς τὸ πᾶνhe drove for the whole scribendum videtur.

where Schuetz reads ἔλαχε δὴ τὸ πᾶν [he obtained the whole], others less probably ἔλαχε δ᾽ ἐς τὸ πᾶν [he obtained for the whole] (omnino, as Hermannus interprets). The scholiast seems to have read ἔλασε [he drove], who explains: ἤλασε δὲ εἰς τὸ τέλος τοῦ δρόμου, ὁ ἐστιν ἤνυσε τὸν ἀγῶνα · ἀφίκετο, φησὶν, εἰς τὸ τέλος τοῦ ἀγῶνος [he drove to the end of the course, that is, he completed the contest; he arrived, he says, at the end of the contest], which word ἐς τὸ πᾶν [for the whole] is more fittingly joined with than with the word ἔλαχε [he obtained]. Therefore either ἔλαχε δὴ τὸ πᾶν [he obtained the whole] or ἔλασε δ᾽ ἐς τὸ πᾶν [he drove for the whole] seems to be written.

cit.quote: λαγὼ δίκην Πενθεῖ καταρράψας μόρον
like a hare, having sewn up the fate of Pentheus
δίκην ἄτης λαθραίου
the penalty of secret ruin
οὐκ ἐξαίφνης οὐδὲ λαθραίως
not suddenly nor secretly
λαίλαπι χειμωνοτύπῳ
with a storm-lashed hurricane

entry.note: Est ventus violentus qui inferne sursum versus repente convolvitur: v. Thes. vol. 5 p. 41.
It is a violent wind that suddenly whirls from below upward: see Thes. vol. 5 p. 41.

cit.quote: λαιᾶς δὲ χειρὸς οἱ σιδηροτέκτονες οἰκοῦσι Χάλυβες
and on the left hand dwell the iron-working Chalybes

sense.def: Laius, father of Oedipus, king of Thebes

cit.quote: Λάϊος
Laius
Λαΐου
of Laius

sense.def: Laius, the second play of the tetralogy - the Oedipodeia
( forma Dorica pro ληΐςbooty, spoil ) praeda

cit.quote: λαΐδος ὀλλυμένας μιξοθρόου
of the spoil being destroyed with mingled cry
cit.note: De captivis, quas ληϊάδας γυναῖκαςcaptive women dixit Homerus Il. 20, 193 ληϊάδας δὲ γυναῖκας ἐλεύθερον ήμαρ ἀπούρας ήγονand they led captive women, taking away their day of freedom . Quod Hesychius interpretatur ἐκ λείας αἰχμαλώτους συλληφθείσαςcaptives taken from the spoil . Male Aeschyli scholiasta recentior λαΐδοςof the spoil pro λαοῦof the people dictum accepit, λαΐδος ἀντὶ τοῦ ληΐδος, ἤγουν τῆς πληθύος τοῦ λαοῦ, τουτέστι τῶν πολιτῶν, ὀλλυμένης καὶ διαφθειρομένηςλαΐδος instead of ληΐδος, that is, of the multitude of the people, that is, of the citizens, being destroyed and perishing .

Concerning captives, whom Homer called ληϊάδας γυναῖκας [captive women] in Il. 20, 193 ληϊάδας δὲ γυναῖκας ἐλεύθερον ήμαρ ἀπούρας ήγον [and they led captive women, taking away their day of freedom]. Hesychius interprets this as ἐκ λείας αἰχμαλώτους συλληφθείσας [captives taken from the spoil]. The later scholiast of Aeschylus wrongly took λαΐδος [of the spoil] as said for λαοῦ [of the people], λαΐδος ἀντὶ τοῦ ληΐδος, ἤγουν τῆς πληθύος τοῦ λαοῦ, τουτέστι τῶν πολιτῶν, ὀλλυμένης καὶ διαφθειρομένης [λαΐδος instead of ληΐδος, that is, of the multitude of the people, that is, of the citizens, being destroyed and perishing].

cit.quote: στολμοί τε λαίφους καὶ παραρρύσεις νεώς
the furling of the sail and the side-hangings of the ship
στείλασα λαῖφος
having furled the sail
λαῖφος ὅταν λάβη πόνος θραυομένας κεραίας
when the sail is caught by the storm, the yardarm shattering
αὔειν, λακάζειν
to shout, to cry aloud
ἴυζε καὶ λάκαζε
cry aloud and shout
λακάζει: λέληκε, βοᾷ, ἀπὸ τοῦ λακεῖν
λακάζει: it has sounded, it shouts, from λακεῖν [to have sounded]

form.gloss: to have sounded, to have cried

entry.note: V. λάσκωto sound, to cry .
See λάσκω.

cit.quote: μή – βυσσίνοις δ᾽ ἐν πέπλοις πέση λακίς
lest a rent fall upon the fine linen robes
cit.note: ubi schol. μὴ ῥῆξις πέση πέπλοιςlest a rent fall upon the robes , cui schol. Byz. addidit ἤτοι μὴ διαρρήξωσι τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτῶνthat is, lest they tear their garments .
where the scholiast has μὴ ῥῆξις πέση πέπλοις [lest a rent fall upon the robes], to which the Byzantine scholiast added ἤτοι μὴ διαρρήξωσι τὰ ἱμάτια αὐτῶν [that is, lest they tear their garments].

cit.quote: πολλάκι δ᾽ ἐμπίτνω ξὺν λακίδι λίνοισιν ἢ Σιδονίᾳ καλύπτρᾳ
often I fall with a rent in my linen or Sidonian veil
cit.note: Schol. τῷ διασχισμῷ ἐμπίπτωI fall into the rent .
The scholiast: τῷ διασχισμῷ ἐμπίπτω [I fall into the rent].

cit.quote: λακὶς χιτῶνος ἔργον οὐ κατοικτιεῖ
a rent in the tunic will not pity the work
cit.note: i. e. τὴν ἐργασίαν τοῦ χιτῶνοςthe workmanship of the tunic , ut schol. explicat.
i.e. τὴν ἐργασίαν τοῦ χιτῶνος [the workmanship of the tunic], as the scholiast explains.

cit.quote: λινοφθόροι δ᾽ ὑφασμάτων λακίδες
and the linen-destroying rents of the garments
λακίδες ἀμφὶ σώματι στημορραγοῦσι ποικίλων ἐσθημάτων
rents around the body cause the warp to flow from the embroidered robes
πρὸς κέντρα μὴ λάκτιζε
do not kick against the goads
cit.note: locutione proverbiali, qua etiam alii usi sunt et Aeschylus Pr. 323 dixit οὔκουν πρὸς κέντρα κῶλον ἐκτενεῖςwill you not stretch out your leg against the goads? : v. Thes. vol.5 p.58.
in a proverbial expression, which others also used, and Aeschylus in Pr. 323 said οὔκουν πρὸς κέντρα κῶλον ἐκτενεῖς [will you not stretch out your leg against the goads?]: see Thes. vol.5 p.58.

cit.quote: ἀνδρὶ λακτίσαντι μέγαν Δίκας βωμόν
for a man who has kicked the great altar of Justice
σύγγονον βροτοῖσι τὸν πεσόντα λακτίσαι πλέον
to kick the fallen one more, a kindred thing to mortals
κραδία δὲ φόβῳ φρένα λακτίζει
and the heart kicks the mind with fear
λάκτισμα δείπνου ξυνδίκως τιθεὶς ἀρᾷ
setting the kick of the banquet as a curse with justice
cit.note: Improprie de atroci coenae iniuria quam passus erat Thyestes.
Improperly, of the cruel outrage of the banquet which Thyestes suffered.

cit.quote: αὖθις τῶνδε κῦμα λαμβάνει
again a wave of these things seizes
ἔρως δὲ γαῖαν λαμβάνει
and love seizes the earth
λαβών νιν ( i.e. τά ψέλια ) ἀμφὶ χερσὶν ἐγκρατεῖ σθένει ῥαιστῆρι θεῖνε
taking it (i.e. the bracelets) in her hands with mighty strength she struck with a hammer
cit.note: ubi recte Stanleius correxit βαλώνhaving thrown
where Stanley rightly corrected to βαλών [having thrown]

cit.quote: καὶ τῶνδε καιρόν ὅστις ὤκιστος λαβέ
and take the opportunity of these things, whoever is quickest
ἕξουσι δ᾽ ἣν λάβωσιν ἐν ταφῇ χθονός
and they will have whatever land they receive in burial
τοὐπιτίμιον λαβεῖν
to receive the penalty
κνέφας δὲ τέμενος αἰθέρος λάβη
and darkness may seize the precinct of the upper air
ἥξω λαβοῦσα πέλανον ἐξ οἴκων ἐμῶν
I will come having taken a libation cake from my house
κόσμον ὅστις εὐπρεπής λαβοῦσ᾽ ὑπαντίαζε παιδί
taking whatever adornment is seemly she went to meet the child
λαβούσα κόσμον ἐκ δόμων
having taken adornment from the house
οἱ κατὰ χθονὸς θεοὶ λαβεῖν ἀμείνους εἰσὶν ἢ μεθιέναι
the gods beneath the earth are better at taking than at letting go
εἰ φθογγὴν λάβοι
if it should receive a voice
προ-νωπή λαβεῖν ἀέρδην
to take her headlong, lifted up
οὐ δόξαν ἂν λαβοιμι βριζούσης φρενός
I would not get the opinion of a slumbering mind
τρίμοιρον χλαῖναν ἐξηύχει λαβών
he boasted that he had taken a cloak of three portions
μελαγκέρῳ λαβοῦσα μηχανήματι
having taken it with a black-horned device
ὁ δ᾽ αὐτῶν ( τῶν κρεῶν ) αὐτίκ᾿ ἀγνοίᾳ λαβὼν ἔσθει βορὰν ἄσωτον
and he, taking some of them (the meats) at once in ignorance, eats a ruinous food
τὰς ὁμοίας ἀντίδος λαβάς ( sic Canterus pro βλάβας ) λαβεῖν
to receive equal returns of grasp (thus Canterus for βλάβας [harms])
ἄγκαθεν λαβὼν βρέτας
taking the statue in his arms
λάβε, λάβε, λάβε, λάβε, φράζου
take, take, take, take, speak
cit.note: Hoc accentu M, non λαβέtake! . Verba extra metrum posita, nisi Aeschylus scripserat Α. λαβοῦ λαβοῦ. Β. λαβοῦ λαβοῦ. Γ. φράζου, λαβοῦA. take, take! B. take, take! C. speak, take! .
With this accent M, not λαβέ [take!]. The words are placed outside the meter, unless Aeschylus wrote A. λαβοῦ λαβοῦ [take! take!]. B. λαβοῦ λαβοῦ [take! take!]. C. φράζου, λαβοῦ [speak, take!].

cit.quote: λαβούσα πτη-νὸν ἀργηστὴν ὄφιν
having taken a winged, white serpent
λαῖφος ὅταν λάβη πόνος θραυομένας κεραίας
when toil seizes the sail of the shattered yardarm
τἀπὶ χέρσου νῦν προμήθειαν λαβών αἰνῶ φυλάξαι
now taking forethought for things on land, I advise you to keep watch
κλάδους γε τούτους αἳψ᾽ ἐν ἀγκάλαις λαβών
taking these branches at once in your arms
αἰδοῖον εὑ-ρεθέντα πρόξενον λαβεῖν
to receive a revered protector when found
λαβούσα δ᾽ ἕρμα Δίον
and having taken the divine support
τὸ πᾶν τ᾽ ἐκ δαιμόνων λάβοιεν
and may they receive everything from the gods
cit.note: Sic Turnebus pro λάθοιενmay they escape notice , idque fortasse legit schol. qui ἐκ δαιμόνωνfrom the gods per παρά δαιμόνωνfrom the gods explicat, quod aptum est verbo λάβοιενmay they receive . Ego praetuli λάχοιενmay they obtain by lot .

Thus Turnebus for λάθοιεν [they might escape notice], and perhaps the scholiast read this, who explains ἐκ δαιμόνων [from the gods] by παρά δαιμόνων [from the gods], which is suited to the verb λάβοιεν [they might take]. I preferred λάχοιεν [they might obtain].

cit.quote: ἐγὼ δ᾽ ἀρωγοὺς ξυνδίκους θ᾽ ἥξω λαβών
and I will come having taken helpers and advocates
φυγάδα μάταισι πολυθρόοις βίαια δίζηνται λαβεῖν
they seek to take the exile by force with vain, many-voiced cries
θράσος λαβοῦσαι
having taken courage
οὐ γὰρ δακὼν ἀνῆκεν, ἀλλ᾽ ἐνῴκισεν δεινὴν στομώ-τὸν ἔκφυσιν ποδὸς λαβεῖν
for having bitten he did not let go, but implanted a terrible sharp-toothed growth to take hold of the foot
cit.note: ubi Valcken. λαβών, βλάβηνhaving taken, harm Schneidewinus.
where Valckenaer proposed λαβών [having taken], Schneidewin βλάβην [harm]

cit.quote: πολλά τραύματ᾽ ἐν στέρνοις λαβών
having received many wounds in the chest
λαβὼν γὰρ αὐτόθηκτον Εὐβοικὸν ξίφος
for taking a self-sharpened Euboean sword
ποίῳ λαβών σε Ζεὺς ἐπ᾿ αἰτιάματι ;
on what charge did Zeus take you?
οὔτιμὴ ληφθῶ δόλω
may I not be caught by deceit
ὡς ἂν δόλῳ κτείναντες ἄνδρα τί-μιον δόλῳ τε καὶ ληφθῶσιν ἐν ταὐτῷ βρόχῳ θα-νόντες
so that having killed a man of honor by deceit, they may also be caught by deceit and die in the same noose
cit.note: ubi Weilius ληφθέντες – θάνωσιhaving been seized – may they die .
where Weil proposed ληφθέντες – θάνωσι [having been taken – they may die]

cit.quote: τοὶ δ᾽ ἄρα πρωτομόροιο ληφθέντες ( sic ex apogr. pro λειφθέντες ) πρὸς πρὸς ἀνάγκας
and they, seized by a fate of early death (thus from the copy for λειφθέντες [left behind]) against necessity
πρός βίαν λελημμένης
seized by force
cit.note: ubi notanda perfecti forma λελημμένηςhaving been seized ( pro εἰλημμένηςhaving been seized ), cuius aliquot exempla apud Sophoclem fr. 794 οἴμοι λέλημμαιalas, I am seized ( sed ἐπείληπταιhe has been caught Ant. 732 ) ét Euripidem Ion. 1113. Bacch. 1100. Cycl. 433.

where the perfect form λελημμένης [having been seized] (for εἰλημμένης [having been seized]) is to be noted, of which there are several examples in Sophocles fr. 794 οἴμοι λέλημμαι [alas, I am seized] (but ἐπείληπται [he has been caught] Ant. 732) and Euripides Ion. 1113. Bacch. 1100. Cycl. 433.

cit.quote: τοιοίδε τοί μοι ( sic Schuetzius τοιοίδ᾽ ἕτοιμοι ) λαμπαδηφόρων νόμοι
such are the laws of the torch-bearers for me (thus Schuetzius for τοιοίδ᾽ ἕτοιμοι [such ready ones])
φλέγει δὲ λαμπὰς διὰ χερῶν ὡπλισμένη
and the torch blazes, armed in their hands
φυλάσσω λαμπάδος τὸ σύμβολον
I watch for the signal of the torch
ὀλολυγμὸν εὐφημοῦντα τῇδε λαμπάδι ἐπορθιάζειν
to raise a joyful cry with this torch
ἄλλη δ᾽ ἀλλόθεν οὐρανομήκης λαμπὰς ἀνίσχει
and another torch, reaching to heaven, rises from another place
ἰσχὺς πορευτοῦ λαμπάδος
the strength of the traveling torch
σθένουσα λαμπὰς δ᾽ οὐδέπω μαυρουμένη
and the torch, still strong, not yet dimmed
λαμπάδων φαεσφόρων
of light-bearing torches
φέγγη λαμπάδὼν σελασφόρων
the gleams of torch-bearing lights
πυριδάπτῳ λαμπάδι τερπόμεναι
delighting in the fire-devouring torch
λαμπραῖσιν ἀστραπαῖσι λαμπάδων σθένει
with bright lightnings and the strength of torches
πεδαίχμιοι λαμπάδες πεδάοροι
torches in the middle, raised on high
cit.note: De solis radiis.
Of the rays of the sun.

entry.note: V. λάπηscum, foam .
See λάπη.

cit.quote: λάμπουρις : ἡ ἀλώπηξ παρ᾽ Αἰσχύλῳ ( fr . 397 )
lampouris: the fox in Aeschylus (fr. 397)

entry.note: Aeschyli nomen omittit Hesychius. Vitiosum apud utrumque grammaticum accentum λαμπουρίςfox correxit L. Dindorfius in Thesauro vol. 5 p. 84 ex Etym. M. p. 474, 2 σεσημείωται τρίαthree are noted ( non oxytona ut alia in ουρις ) λάμπουρις, ἡ ἀλώπηξ, Τόμουρις ὄνομα πόλεως, καὶ ἵππουριςouria) lampouris, the fox, Tomuris, name of a city, and hippouris . Post Aeschylum hoc vocabulo usus est Lycophro 344 1393.

Hesychius omits the name of Aeschylus. The faulty accent λαμπουρίς [fox] in both grammarians was corrected by L. Dindorf in the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 84 from Etym. M. p. 474, 2 σεσημείωται τρία [three are noted] (not oxytone like other words in ουρις [ouria]) λάμπουρις, ἡ ἀλώπηξ [lampouris, the fox], Τόμουρις ὄνομα πόλεως [Tomuris, name of a city], καὶ ἵππουρις [and hippouris]. After Aeschylus this word was used by Lycophron 344 1393.

cit.quote: λαμπρὰ δὲ πανσέληνος ἐν μέσῳ σάκει πρέπει
The bright full moon shines in the middle of the shield
λαμπρὸς ἡλίου κύκλος
the bright circle of the sun
τοὺς φέροντας χεῖμα καὶ θέρος βροτοῖς λαμπροὺς δυνάστας, ἐμπρέποντας αἰθέρι
the bright rulers who bring winter and summer to mortals, conspicuous in the sky
λαμπρὸν ἐκπέμπων σέλας
sending forth a bright light
λαμπραῖσιν ἀστραπαῖσι λαμπάδων σέλας
with bright flashes of torchlight
λαμπρὸν ἡλίου φάος
the bright light of the sun
λαμπρὸς δ᾽ ἔοικεν ἡλίου πρὸς ἀντολὰς πνέων ἐσάξειν
he seems to be blowing brightly toward the sunrise
καί νιν ἐλευθερίας φῶς λαμπρὸν ἰδεῖν φιλίοις ὄμμασιν ἐκ δνοφερᾶς καλύπτρας
and to see the bright light of freedom with friendly eyes from the dark veil
cit.note: ubi Μ ἐλευθερίως λαμπρῶς ἰδεῖνM: to see the light of freedom brightly . Correxit Weilius.
where M has ἐλευθερίως λαμπρῶς ἰδεῖν [to see the light of freedom brightly]. Weilius corrected it.

cit.quote: ὁρῶντα λαμπρὸν ἐν σκότῳ νωμῶντ᾽ ὀφρύν
seeing a bright brow moving in the darkness
βορβόρῳ θ᾽ ὕδωρ λαμπρὸν μιαίνων οὔποθ᾽ εὑρήσεις ποτόν
and by polluting bright water with mud you will never find a drink
cit.note: de aqua pura s. limpida.
of pure or clear water.

cit.quote: λαμπρὰ μαρτύρια παρῆν
bright testimonies were present
εὕδουσα γὰρ φρὴν ὄμμασιν λαμπρύνεται
for the sleeping mind is brightened by the eyes
λαμπρῶς κοὐδὲν αἰνικτηρίως
brightly and not at all in riddles

cit.note: v. ς. ν. λαμπρόςunder λαμπρός [bright] .
see under λαμπρός [bright].

cit.quote: ὦ χαῖρε λαμπτήρ νυκτός
Hail, torch of the night
πολλοὶ δ᾽ ἀνῆθον – λαμπτῆρες ἐν δόμοισι
and many torches were lit in the house
τὰς ἀμφὶ σοὶ κλάουσα λαμπτηρουχίας ἀτημελήτους αἰέν
weeping for the torch-carrying rites around you, always neglected
μήτ᾿ ἀχρημάτοισι λάμπειν φῶς
not to shine a light for the poor
Δίκα δὲ λάμπει μὲν ἐν δυσκάπνοις δώμασιν
Justice shines in smoky houses

form.gloss: to escape notice, to be hidden

sense.def: to escape notice, to be hidden

cit.quote: οὐκ ἔστι λαθεῖν ὄμματα φωτός
it is not possible to escape the eyes of light
εὔσημον γὰρ οὐ με λανθάνει
for it does not escape my notice, being clear
νέας γυναικός οὔ με μὴ λάθη φλέγων ὀφθαλμός
the eye of a young woman, blazing, will not escape my notice
μή λάθη φύγδα βάς
lest he escape notice, having gone in flight
μήτ᾿ ἀέλπτως δορικανεῖ μόρῳ θανὼν λάθοιμι
lest I escape notice, having died unexpectedly by a spear-wrought fate

cit.note: λάθοιενthey might escape notice corrupte pro λάχοιενthey might obtain . V. λαγχάνωto obtain by lot .
λάθοιεν [they might escape notice] is corrupt for λάχοιεν [they might obtain]. See λαγχάνω [to obtain by lot].

cit.quote: μη μηδαμῶς λάθη
let it not escape notice in any way
ἀλκῆς λαθέσθαι τῆσδε μηδαμῶς ποτέ
never to forget this strength

entry.note: Idem est λήθομαιI forget , quod v.
The same is λήθομαι [I forget], which see.

cit.quote: τὸ μὴ θέμις – λὰξ πέδον ( πέδοι Hermannus ) πατούμενον
what is not lawful, trampled with the foot on the ground (Hermann: on the ground)
πάντα ταῦτα λὰξ ὁρῶ πατούμενα
I see all these things trampled underfoot
βωμὸν αἴδεσαι Δίκας μηδέ νιν κέρδος ἰδὼν ἀθέῳ ποδὶ λὰξ ἀτίσῃς
revere the altar of Justice, and do not, seeing gain, dishonor it with godless foot by trampling
λαοδάμας ῎Αρης
Ares, tamer of peoples
λαοπαθῆ σέβῶν ἁλίτυπά τε βάρη
revering the people-suffering and sea-beaten burdens
cit.note: Vocabulum corruptum. Metrum postulat νεοπαθέαnewly suffering , quod coniecit Paleius, aut aliud huius mensurae vocabulum.
The word is corrupt. The meter requires νεοπαθέα [newly suffering], which Paleius conjectured, or another word of this measure.

cit.quote: λαοπόροις τε μαχαναῖς
with people-passing devices
ἀπρόσοιστος γὰρ ὁ Περσᾶν στρατὸς ἀλκίφρων τε λαός
for the army of the Persians is unapproachable and the people valiant
λέλυται γὰρ λαὸς ἐλεύθερα βάζειν
for the people are freed to speak freely
λαὸς πᾶς καιτέφθαρται δορί
the whole people has been destroyed by the spear
Λυδῶν δὲ λαὸν καὶ Φρυγῶν ἐκτήσατο
he acquired the people of the Lydians and Phrygians
Ἰάνων λαὸς οὐ φυγαίχμας
the people of the Ionians, not fleeing from the spear
μετ᾿ ἄλλων δουρικμῆτι λαῷ
with other spear-skilled people
ξυνῇ μελέσθω λαὸς ἐκπονεῖν ἄκη
let the people be concerned to work out remedies in common
ὅθεν καλεῖν | Κουρῆτα λαὸν ἤνεσαν
from where they approved calling the people Curetes

sense.def: in the plural λαοί [peoples] assembled men

cit.quote: μερόπεσσι λαοῖς
to mortal peoples
λαοὺς συγκαλῶν ἐγχωρίους
calling together the local people
βάξει λαῶν τῶν ἑγχώρων
by the report of the local people
ῥεῖ πολὺς ὅδε λεὼς πρόδρομος ἱππότας
This great people flows forth, a vanguard of horsemen
λευκοπρεπής λεώς
white-complexioned people
cit.note: Thus I emended for ὁ λεύκασπις λαὸς εὐτρεπής [the white-shielded ready people] (or εὐπρεπής [comely]).

cit.quote: τὸν ἀμφιτειχῆ λεών
the people around the walls
πᾶς γὰρ ἱππηλάτας καὶ πεδοστιβὴς λεώς
For all the horse-driving and land-treading people
πάντα ναυτικὸν λεών
all the naval people
Περσικός λεώς
Persian people
Ἀχαιικός λεώς
Achaean people
ἀσπιδηφόρος λεώς
shield-bearing people
μολόντο μολόντα δ᾽ αὐτὸν κάρτα τιμαλφεῖ λεώς
let them come, and when he comes, the people honor him greatly
τὸν Ἀργεῖον λεών
the Argive people
ὡς δηχθῇ λεώς
so that the people may be bitten
Ἀττικὸς ( ἀστικός , ut v . 997 , Hermannus ) λεώς
Attic (or urban, as at v. 997, Hermann) people
πολισσούχος λεώς
city-protecting people
χαίρετ᾽ ἀστικὸς λεώς
farewell, urban people
μὴ καὶ ποτε εἴπῃ λεώς
lest ever the people say
κατ᾿ ἀρχῆς γὰρ φιλαίτιος λεώς
for from the beginning the people are fond of blame
Ἀργεῖος λεώς
Argive people
τὸν οὔποτ᾽ αὐχοῦντ᾿ ἰδὼν ἀμαχάνοις δύαις λαπαδνόν
seeing him never boasting, weak in helpless miseries
cit.note: Sic Musgravius pro λέπαδνονyoke-strap . Huius formae unum hoc est exemplum: frequentius inde ab Homero άλαπαδνόςweak .
Thus Musgravius for λέπαδνον [yoke-strap]. Of this form there is only this one example: more frequent from Homer onward is άλαπαδνός [weak].

form.gloss: to empty out; hence to plunder, to sack

sense.def: properly to empty out; hence to plunder, to sack

entry.note: Per ἐκκενοῦνto empty out explicant Athenaeus 8 p. 362f. Hesychius aliique grammatici in Thes. indicati vol.5 p. 109.
They explain it by ἐκκενοῦν [to empty out]: Athenaeus 8 p. 362f., Hesychius and other grammarians indicated in the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 109.

cit.quote: ὡρκωμότησαν ἢ πόλει κατασκαφὰς θέντες λαπάξειν ἄστυ Καδμείων βίᾳ
they swore an oath that they would sack the city of the Cadmeans by force, laying waste to it
cit.note: ubi schol. ἐκκενώσειν, ἀπὸ τοῦ λαπάθουto empty out, from the dock .
where the scholiast has ἐκκενώσειν, ἀπὸ τοῦ λαπάθου [to empty out, from the dock].
iidem verbis.
the same in words.

cit.quote: πάντα δὲ πύργων κτήνη Μοῖρ᾽ ἀλαπάξει
and Fate will sack all the flocks from the towers
cit.note: ubi Triclinius Μοῖρα λαπάξειFate will sack , qua forma tragici fortasse non sunt usi nisi metro postulante, quemadmodum ἀμαυροῦνto weaken , ubi metrum ferret, alteri formae μαυροῦνto weaken praetulisse videntur. Accedit ad haec quod ἀλαπάζωto sack forma est Homerica.

where Triclinius has Μοῖρα λαπάξει [Fate will sack], a form which the tragedians perhaps did not use except when the meter demanded it, just as they seem to have preferred ἀμαυροῦν [to weaken] to the other form μαυροῦν [to weaken] when the meter allowed. Add to this that ἀλαπάζω [to sack] is a Homeric form.

cit.quote: ἀναλίῳ λάπᾳ
in sunless slime
cit.note: Sic Wieselerus pro λάμπαι ( λάμπαmoulds (mould) Canterus ), ut apud alios quoque scriptores plerumque λάμπηmould scribitur, de quo v. Thes. vol. 5 p. 82 et 111. ubi v. quae de propria vocabuli significatione dicta sunt ὁ παχὺς ἀφρὸς ὁ ἐπιπολάζων τῷ οἴνῳ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ὑγροῖςthe thick foam that floats on wine and other liquids .

Thus Wieseler for λάμπαι [moulds] (λάμπα [mould] Canterus), since in other writers too it is usually written λάμπη [mould], on which see the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 82 and 111, where see what is said about the proper meaning of the word: ὁ παχὺς ἀφρὸς ὁ ἐπιπολάζων τῷ οἴνῳ καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις ὑγροῖς [the thick foam that floats on wine and other liquids].

cit.quote: Λασθένους βίαν
the force of Lasthenes

form.gloss: to utter a sound, to speak, to cry out

sense.def: to utter a sound, to speak, to cry out

cit.quote: ὀλολυγμὸν ἄλλος ἄλλοθεν κατὰ πτόλιν ἔλασκον
one from one place, another from another, they raised a cry throughout the city
κάκιον ἄλλο πῆμα λάσκοντας δόμοις
uttering another evil woe upon the house

sense.def: Aoristus est λακεῖνto have cried out
The aorist is λακεῖν [to have cried out]

cit.quote: ἔλακον ἀξόνων βριθομένων χνόαι
the naves of the heavy-laden axles creaked
τοιόσδ᾽ ὁ κόμπος οὐκ αἰσχρὸς ὡς γυναικὶ γενναίᾳ λακεῖν
such boasting is not shameful for a noble woman to utter
περίφρονα δ᾽ ἔλακες
you uttered proud words
ἀωρόνυκτον ἀμβόαμα μυχόθεν ἔλακε
from the depths it uttered a cry in the dead of night
κριταί τε τῶνδ᾽ ὀνειράτων θεόθεν ἔλακον
and the judges of these dreams spoke from the gods
διὰ δίκας ( κάδ δίκαν Hermannus ) πᾶν ἔπος ἔλακον
they uttered every word through justice (or according to justice, Hermann)

sense.def: Perfecti λέλακαI have cried out ( syllaba media producta ) unum est exemplum
Of the perfect λέλακα [I have cried out] (with the middle syllable lengthened) there is one example

cit.quote: πρόπασα δ᾽ ἤδη στονόεν λέλακε χώρα
and already the whole land has cried out in grief

entry.note: V. ΛητογενήςLeto-born .
See Λητογενής [Leto-born].
V. ΛητώLeto .
See Λητώ [Leto].

cit.quote: τῇδε λατρεύειν πέτρα
to serve this rock
τῆς σῆς λατρείας τὴν ἐμὴν δυσπραξίαν — οὐκ ἂν ἀλλάξαιμ᾽ ἐγώ
I would not exchange my misfortune for your servitude
οἴκησις δὲ καὶ δι-πλῆ πάρα · τὴν μὲν Πελασγὸς, τὴν δὲ καὶ πόλις δι-δοῖ, οἰκεῖν λάτρων ἄτερθεν
And there is a dwelling, a double one: one part Pelasgus, the other the city gives, to live without hired servants.
cit.note: ubi vitiosum accentum λατρῶνof hired servants correxit L. Dindorfius in Thes. vol. 5 p. 132. Per μισθόςwages explicant Aristophanes Byz. apud Eustath. p. 1246, 9 aliique grammatici in Thes. indicati. Proprie haud dubie de mercede dictum fuit quae servo datur.

where L. Dindorf corrected the faulty accent λατρῶν [of hired servants] in the Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 132. Aristophanes of Byzantium in Eustathius p. 1246, 9 and other grammarians cited in the Thesaurus explain it as μισθός [wages]. Properly it was no doubt said of the pay given to a slave.

cit.quote: λάφυρα δάων
spoils of the enemy
λαφύροις δῶμα κοσμήσει πατρός
he will adorn his father's house with spoils
θεοῖς λάφυρα ταῦτα δόμοις ἐπασσάλευσαν
they hung up these spoils for the gods in their temples
τάφων πατρώων λαχαί
allotments of ancestral tombs

entry.note: Apud Hesychium est paroxytonum λάχη: λῆξις, ἀποκλήρωσιςallotments: allotment, assignment by lot . Oxytonum convenit regulae Herodiani apud Arcadium p. 115, 19. Ceterum inepta est scholiastae interpretatio αἱ σκαφαί · ὡς τὸthe digging, as in ( Homeri Od. 24, 241 ) “ φυτὸν ἀμφελάχαινενhe dug around the plant . ”

In Hesychius it is paroxytone λάχη [allotments]: λῆξις, ἀποκλήρωσις [allotment, assignment by lot]. The oxytone form agrees with Herodian's rule in Arcadius p. 115, 19. Moreover, the scholiast's interpretation αἱ σκαφαί [the digging] is foolish, as in Homer Od. 24, 241 "φυτὸν ἀμφελάχαινεν [he dug around the plant]."

cit.quote: μόριμον λάχος πιμπλάντων ( emendavi περαίνων, cuius glossema fuit πιμπλάνων, corruptum in πιμπλάντων ) χεροῖν
filling their fated lot with their hands (I emended περαίνων [accomplishing], of which πιμπλάνων [filling] was a gloss, corrupted into πιμπλάντων [filling])
ἐν δὲ τῷ τρίτῳ λάχει
and in the third lot
λάχη τὰ κατ᾿ ἀνθρώπους
the lots that befall mortals

sense.def: office which fell to someone by lot

cit.quote:
τοῦτο γὰρ λάχος διανταία Μοῖρ᾽ ἐπέκλωσεν ἐμπέ
δως ἔχειν
for this lot did piercing Fate spin to hold steadfastly
γιγνομέναισι λάχη τάδ᾽ ἐφ᾽ ἁμὶν ἐκράνθη
for those being born these lots were fulfilled upon us
ἀτίετα διόμεναι λάχη
pursuing unhonored lots

sense.def: part which fell to someone by lot

cit.quote: τῶν αἰχμαλώτων χρημάτων λάχος μέγα
a great share of the captive spoils
αὕτη δίπους λέαινα συγκοιμωμένη λύκῳ
this two-footed lioness, sleeping with a wolf
λέαινα ἠριγένεια
a lioness, early-born
γεμίζων λέβητας εὐθέτους
filling well-made cauldrons
δολοφόνου λέβητος τύχαν σοι λέγω
I tell you the fortune of the murderous cauldron
λέβητος χαλκέου πλευρώματα
the sides of the bronze cauldron
τὸν μὲν τρίπους ἐδέξατ᾽ οἰκεῖος λέβης
the household cauldron received him as a tripod

entry.note: Construitur cum accusativo vel cum infinttivo, vel cum accusativo et infinitivo, vel addito vel omisso dativo personae cui aliquid dicitur. Vulgaris huius usus exempla secundum fabularum ordinem disposita ' haec sunt.

It is constructed with the accusative or with the infinitive, or with the accusative and infinitive, with the dative of the person to whom something is said either added or omitted. Examples of this common usage arranged according to the order of the plays are these.

cit.quote: ἀλγεινὰ μέν μοι καὶ λέγειν ἐστὶν τάδε
These things are painful for me even to say.
οὔτ᾽ ἐμοὶ λέγειν καθ᾽ ἡδονὴν, σοί τ᾽ ἄλγος
neither is it pleasant for me to say, nor is it grief for you.
ἀρχαῖ᾽ ἴσως σοὶ φαίνομαι λέγειν τάδε
Perhaps I seem to you to be saying ancient things.
καὶ γὰρ εἰδυίαισιν ἂν ὑμῖν λέγοιμι
for I would speak even to you who know.
λέξω δέ
but I will speak
λέξω τορῶς σοι πᾶν
I will tell you everything clearly.
λέγ᾽ ἥντιν᾽ αἰτεῖ
say what she asks
χρὴ λέγειν
it is necessary to say
αὐτῆς λεγούσης τὰς πολυφθόρους τύχας
as she herself tells her many-destroying fortunes
καὶ λέγουσ᾽ αἰσχύνομαι
And I am ashamed to say
τί χρὴ δρῶντ᾽ ἢ λέγοντα δαίμοσιν πράσσειν φίλα
What must one do or say to win the favor of the gods?
λέγ᾽, ἐκδίδασκε
Speak, instruct me
τοιοῦτο μέν σοι τοῦτο φρούριον λέγω
Such a fortress I tell you this is
λέγε
Speak
ἃ βούλομαι λέγω
I say what I wish
καὶ σὲ δ᾽ ἐν τούτοις λέγω
And I include you among these
λέγων ἔοικα πολλὰ καὶ μάτην ἐρεῖν
I seem to be speaking much and in vain
οὐκ ἄκαιρα φαίνε-ται λέγειν
He does not seem to speak untimely
λέγειν τὰ καίρια
To speak what is fitting
λέγει μεγίστην προσβολὴν Ἀχαιίδα νυκτηγορήσθαι
He says that a great Achaean assault was made by night
ξυνά δ᾽ ἐλπίζω λέγειν
And I hope to speak in common
κωφῇ λέγω ;
Am I speaking to a deaf person?
λέγοις ἂν ὡς τάχιστα
You would speak as quickly as possible
οὐδ᾽ ἀπ᾿ ( hoc ex ὕδατά τ᾽ corruptum ) Ἰσμηνοῦ λέγω
Nor do I speak from (this is corrupted from 'waters') Ismenus
λέγοιμ᾽ ἂν εἰδὼς εὐ τὰ τῶν ἐναντίων
I would speak knowing well the affairs of the enemy
νύκτα ταύτην ἣν λέγεις ἐπ᾿ ἀσπίδος ἄστροισι μαρμαίρουσαν οὐρανοῦ κυρεῖν
This night which you speak of, gleaming with stars on a shield, belongs to heaven
λέγ᾽ ἄλλον ἄλλαις ἐν πύλαις εἰληχότα
Speak of another assigned to other gates
τὸν ἐντεῦθεν λαχόντα πρὸς πύλαις λέξω
I will tell of the one who drew the lot for the gates
μηδέ μοι φθόνει λέγων
Do not begrudge me by speaking
cit.note: ubi nunc λόγωνof words legitur, ab Valckenario restitutum.
where now λόγων [of words] is read, restored by Valckenaer.

cit.quote: τὸν δὲ πέμπτον αὐ λέγω
And the fifth I say
τῷδ᾽ ὃν λέγεις τὸν Ἀρκάδα
To this one whom you call the Arcadian
ἕκτον λέγοιμ᾽ ἂν ἄνδρα σωφρονέστατον
The sixth I would say is a most prudent man
λέγει δὲ τοῦτ᾽ ἔπος διὰ στόμα
He speaks this word through his mouth
καλόν τ᾽ ἀκοῦσαι καὶ λέγειν μεθυστέροις
A fine thing to hear and to say for those who are drunk
τὸν ἕβδομον δὴ - λέξω
The seventh indeed - I will tell
ὡς τὰ γράμματα λέγει
As the letters say
λέγουσα κέρδος πρότερον ὑστέρου μόρου
Saying that gain comes before later doom
λέγοιτ᾽ ἂν ὧν ἄνη τις
One might speak of what one has accomplished
παλαιγενῆ γὰρ λέγω παρβασίαν ὠκύποινον
For I speak of an ancient transgression swiftly avenged
διανταίαν λέγεις [ πλαγάν ]
You speak of a piercing [blow]
διπλᾶ λέγειν
To speak double
ὀλοὰ λέγειν
To speak destructive things
οὕτω μὲν ἀμφὶ τοῦδ᾽ ἐπέσταλται λέγειν
Thus it has been commanded to speak about this
ἐγὼ δὲ Καδμείων γε προστάταις λέγω
But I speak to the leaders of the Cadmeans
λέξω δέ σοι
And I will tell you
καὶ ταῦτα μὲν δὴ νυκτὸς εἰσιδεῖν λέγω
And these things I say I saw at night
δεινά τοι λέγεις
You speak terrible things
κατθανόντα λέγεις φέρεσθαι
You say that he is carried off dead
τὸ μήτε λέξαι μήτ᾽ ἐρωτῆσαι πάθη
The suffering that one can neither speak nor ask about
λέξον καταστάς
Speak, having taken your stand
ἔλεξε παιδὶ σῷ Ξέρξη τάδε
He said these things to your son Xerxes
τοσαῦτ᾽ ἔλεξε
So much he said
λέξον
Speak
πολλά δ᾽ ἐκλείπω λέγων
I omit many things in speaking
σέβομαι δ᾽ ἀντία λέξαι
I revere to speak against
μή τι μακιστῆρα μῦθον, ἀλλὰ σύντομον λέγων
Not a lengthy speech, but a concise one, speaking
λέξας δύσλεκτα φίλοισιν
Having spoken things hard to say to friends
σαφές τί μοι λέξον
Tell me something clear
λέγουσι δ᾽ ὡς σὺ μὲν μέγαν τέκνοις πλοῦτον ἐκτήσω
They say that you acquired great wealth for your children
πῶς ταῦτ᾽ ἔλεξας ;
How did you say these things?
Πέρσαις ἀγαυοῖς κακὰ πρόκακα λέγεις
You speak of evils before evils for the noble Persians
στυγνὰ πρόκακα λέγων
Speaking hateful things before evils
τί τόδε λέγεις σεσωσμένον ;
What do you say has been saved?
σαφέστατ᾽ ἂν λέξειεν
He would speak most clearly
τούτων λέξαις ( sic Hartung.pro λέξασ ' ) ὅ τι καὶ δυνατόν
Of these things you might speak (thus Hartung for 'speak') whatever is possible
οὐδὲν λέξαι
To say nothing
cit.note: ubi versum explevit Schuetzius οὐδὲν ἂν λέξαιwould say nothing : sed sententia postulať oὐδὲ λέξεται πρὶν ὤνnor will he speak before... , quod restituit H. L. Ahrensius.
where Schuetz filled out the verse with οὐδὲν ἂν λέξαι [would say nothing]: but the sense requires οὐδὲ λέξεται πρὶν ὤν [nor will he speak before being], which H. L. Ahrens restored.

cit.quote: ή τορῶς λέγω ;
Or do I speak clearly?

τῆς νῦν τεκούσης φῶς τόδ᾽ εὐφρόνης
λέγω
I speak of the light of this night that has now given birth
τέκμαρ τοιοῦτο ξύμβολόν τε σοὶ λέγω
Such a proof and token I give you
λόγους δ᾽ ἀκοῦσαι τούσδε – θέλοιμ᾽ ἂν, οὓς λέγεις, πάλιν
And I would like to hear these words again, which you speak
cit.note: ubi οὓςwhom pro ὡςas ex Bothii coniectura, λέγειςyou say pro λέγοιςyou might say ex apographo Veneto restitutum.
where οὓς [whom] for ὡς [as] from Both's conjecture, λέγεις [you say] for λέγοις [you might say] restored from the Venetian copy.

cit.quote: σώφρον᾽ εὐφρόνως λέγεις
You speak prudent things kindly
στένουσι δ᾽ εὐ λέγοντες ἄνδρα
They groan, speaking well of the man
τὸ χαίρειν μᾶλλον ἐκβάξει λέγων
He will utter the word of joy rather than speaking
ποθεῖν ποθοῦντα τήνδε γῆν στρατὸν λέγεις
You say that the army longs for this land, longing for it
τὰ μέν τις ἂν λέξειεν εὐπετώς ἔχειν
One might say that some things are easy to bear
μόχθους γὰρ εἰ λέγοιμι
For if I were to speak of the toils
χειμῶνα δ᾽ εἰ λέγοι τις
And if one were to speak of the storm
τί τοὺς ἀναλωθέντας ἐν ψήφῳ λέγειν – χρή ;
Why should one speak of those who perished in the vote?
τὰ μάσσω μὲν τί δεῖ σ᾽ ἐμοὶ λέγειν ;
Why need you tell me the greater things?
οὐκ ἔσθ᾽ ὅπως λέξαιμι τὰ ψευδή καλά
There is no way I would call false things good
οὐ ψευδή λέγω
I do not speak falsely
πῶς γὰρ λέγεις χειμῶνα ναυτικῷ στρατῷ ἐλθεῖν ;
For how do you say that a storm came upon the naval army?
πρέπει λέγειν παιᾶνα τόνδ ' Ερινύων
It is fitting to sing a paean of the Erinyes
λέγων χειμῶν᾽ Ἀχαιῶν οὐκ ἀμήνιτον θεοῖς
Saying that the storm of the Achaeans was not without the wrath of the gods
λέγουσιν ἡμᾶς ὡς ὀλωλότας
They say that we are destroyed
ἐλθεῖν ἐς Ἰλίου πόλιν λέγοιμ᾽ ἄν
I would say that he went to the city of Ilium
εἰδὼς λέγοιμ᾽ ἄν
I would speak knowing
εἴτ᾿ οὖν θανόντος εἴτε καὶ ζῶντος πέρι λέγω
Whether I speak of him dead or alive
οὐκ αἰσχυνοῦμαι τοὺς φιλάνορας τρόπους λέξαι πρὸς ὑμᾶς
I will not be ashamed to speak to you of my husband-loving ways
ἐμαυτῆς δύσφορον λέξω βίον
I will tell of my own hard-to-bear life
τέτρωται δικτύου πλέον λέγειν
He is wounded more than a net, so to speak
τὴν κάτω γὰρ οὐ λέγω χθονός
For I do not speak of the land below
λέγοιμ᾽ ἂν ἄνδρα τόνδε
I would say this man
σοί τοι λέγουσα παύεται σαφή λόγον
Speaking to you, she ceases her clear speech
ἔσω φρενῶν λέγουσα πείθω νιν λόγῳ
Speaking within her mind, I persuade her with words
cit.note: versu corrupto.
the verse being corrupt.

cit.quote: τὰ λῷστα τῶν παρεστώτων λέγει
He speaks the best of the present circumstances.
ἐγὼ λέγω σοί
I tell you.
δολοφόνου λέβητος τύχαν σοι λέγω
I tell you the fate of the murderous cauldron.
οὐ γὰρ εὖ λέγει
For he does not speak well.
ἀλλόθρουν πόλιν κυρεῖν λέγουσαν
To come upon a city speaking a foreign tongue.
αἰδὼς ἦν ἐμοὶ λέγειν τάδε
I was ashamed to say these things.
οἷα γλῶσσα μισητῆς κυνὸς λέξασα κἀκτείνασα φαιδρόνους -
Such things as the tongue of a hateful dog, having spoken and having killed the bright-minded—
cit.note: ubi recte λείξασαhaving licked Tyrwhittus.
where Tyrwhitt rightly has λείξασα [having licked].

cit.quote: οὐ Σύριον ἀγλάϊσμα δώμασιν λέγεις
You do not speak of a Syrian adornment for the house.
ἐγὼ μὲν ὑμῖν τὴν ἐμὴν γνώμην λέγω
I tell you my opinion.
οὐκ οἶδα βουλῆς ἡστινος τυχὼν λέγω
I do not know what counsel I have obtained in speaking.
πρὸς εἰδότας λέγω
I speak to those who know.
λέγω δέ σοι
And I tell you.
οὔ σε προσήκει τὸ μέλη-μα λέγειν τοῦτο
It is not fitting for you to say this care.
ἐπεὶ δοκεῖς τάδ᾽ ἔρδειν καὶ λέγειν
Since you seem to do and say these things.
δεχομένοις λέγεις θανεῖν σε
You say to those who receive that you will die.
πότερα λέγουσα παρὰ φίλης φίλῳ φέρειν γυναικὸς ἀνδρί ;
Whether speaking to bring from a dear wife to her husband?
λέγοις ἂν, εἴ τι τῶνδ᾽ ἔχοις ὑπέρτερον
You might speak, if you have anything better than these.
λέξω, κελεύεις γὰρ, τὸν ἐκ φρενός λόγον
I will speak, since you bid me, the word from my heart.
λέγοις ἄν
You might speak.
πότερα δικαστὴν ἢ οικηφόρον λέγεις ;
Do you mean a judge or a housekeeper?
λέγω καλοῦσα, πάτερ, ἐποίκτειρόν τ᾽ ἐμὲ φίλον τ᾽ Ορέστην
I speak calling, father, and pity me and dear Orestes.
κείνοις λέγουσα τήνδε τὴν κακὴν ἀράν
Speaking to them this evil curse.
οὐχ ήσσον εὐδάκρυτά μοι λέγεις τάδε
You tell me things no less worthy of tears.
τὸ πᾶν ἀτίμως ἔλεξας
You have spoken everything dishonorably.
λέγεις πατρῷον μόρον
You speak of your father's fate.
ὡς αὐτὴ λέγει
As she herself says.
ὑπέρτολμον ἀνδρὸς φρόνημα τίς λέγοι ;
Who could speak of the over-bold thought of the man?
λέγοιτ᾽ ἂν εἴ τι δεῖ
It might be said, if it is necessary.
εἰ δὲ τυγχάνω τοῖς κυρίοισι καὶ προσήκουσιν λέγων
If I happen to speak to those who have authority and are fitting.
λέγ᾽ αὖθις
Speak again.
ἄσκοπον δ᾽ ἔπος λέγων
Speaking a word without aim.
νέαν φάτιν δὲ πεύθομαι λέγειν τινάς
I hear that some report a new saying.
ἐξ ἀμαυρᾶς κληδόνος λέγει μαθών
He speaks from an obscure report, having learned.
τί λέγω ;
What am I to say?
τὸν ζῶντα καίνειν τοὺς τεθνηκότας λέγω
I mean that the living kill the dead.

cit.note: Ἀἰγίσθου γὰρ οὐ λέγω μόρονfor I do not speak of Aegisthus' death , ubi λέγωI say pro ψέγωI blame restitutum ex schol.
Ἀἰγίσθου γὰρ οὐ λέγω μόρον [For I do not speak of Aegisthus' death], where λέγω [I speak] for ψέγω [I blame] restored from the scholia.

cit.quote: πάντας Ἀργείους λέγω καὶ μαρτυρεῖν μοι
I mean all the Argives, and that they bear witness for me.
δεινὰ λέξαι
Terrible things to say.
οὔτοι γυναῖκας, ἀλλὰ Γοργόνας λέγω
I do not mean women, but Gorgons.
ἔλεξα τῆς ἐμῆς περὶ ψυχῆς
I spoke about my own life.
ἐπίσταμαι – λέγειν ὅπου δίκη
I know how to speak where justice is.
λέξαι τε λάχη τὰ κατ᾿ ἀνθρώπους ὡς ἐπινωμᾷ στάσις ἀμά
And to speak the lots among men, how faction distributes them.
πᾶσι δ᾽ ἐς κοινὸν λέγω
I speak to all in common.
λέγειν δ᾽ ἄμορφον ὄντα τοὺς πέλας κακῶς –
And being shapeless, to speak ill of one's neighbors—
εἰ λέγοι τις ἐμφανή λόγον
If someone should speak a clear word.
λέξας δὲ χώραν καὶ γένος
Having spoken of the land and the race.
τεκμήριον δὲ τῶνδέ σοι λέξω μέγα
I will tell you a great proof of these things.
ξύμμετρον δ᾽ ἔπος λέγω
I speak a measured word.
τί τοῦδε σοὶ μέτεστι πράγματος λέγε
What share do you have in this matter? Speak.
πρότερος ἐξ ἀρχῆς λέγων
Speaking first from the beginning.
λέγω
I say.
λέξομεν δὲ συντόμως
We will speak briefly.
λέξω πρὸς ὑμᾶς
I will speak to you.
cit.note: ubi cum πρόςtowards et accusativo personae constructum est ut loco infra afferendo Suppl.247.
where it is constructed with πρός [to] and the accusative of the person, as in the passage to be cited below, Suppl. 247.

cit.quote: ὡς λέγεις σύ
As you say.

πῶς ταῦτα τούτοις οὐκ
ἐναντίως λέγεις ;
How do you not say these things contrary to them?
καὶ τοῦτο λέξω
I will say this too.
λέγεις
You say.
τί δεῖ λέγειν ;
What need is there to speak?
ἐνοικίου δ᾽ ὄρνιθος οὐ λέγω μάχην
I do not speak of the battle of the house bird.
οὔτοι καμοῦμαί σοι λέγουσα τἀγαθά
I will not tire of telling you the good things.
ἔξεστι γάρ μοι μὴ λέγειν ἃ μὴ τελῶ
For it is possible for me not to say what I do not accomplish.
τὰν ἐμὰν χάριν λέγω
I speak of my own favor.

cit.note: λέγωνsaying corruptum ex d᾽ ἐγώI .
λέγων [saying] corrupted from δ᾽ ἐγώ [but I].

cit.quote: τορῶς λέγουσαι τάσδ᾽ ἀναιμάκτους φυγάς
Speaking clearly these bloodless exiles.
πρὸς σὲ πότερον ὡς ἔτην λέγω ;
Do I speak to you as to a kinsman?
λέγ᾽ εὐθαρσῶς ἐμοί

γένος τ᾽ ἂν ἐξεύχοιο καὶ λέγοις πρόσω
