Hoc πέδουροςhigh in air , quod in versu Aeschyli metrum non fert, annotarunt Hesychius et Photius per μετέωροςhigh in air interpretati.

Thus Stanley for παιδάμαροι [child-?], which is in M, but with the e changed. The scholiast read πεδάμεροι [daily], who explains: ἀκτῖνες τοῦ ἡλίου αἱ καθημεριναί, διορθωτής [the rays of the sun, the daily ones, the corrector], but the corrector wrote in the margin: οἶμαι πέδουροι, ἵν᾿ ἢ τὸ σημαινόμενον μετέωροι [I think πέδουροι, so that the meaning is high in air]. This πέδουρος [high in air], which does not fit the meter in Aeschylus's verse, Hesychius and Photius noted, interpreting it as μετέωρος [high in air].

sense.def: the same as μετάρσιος, high in air

cit.quote: πρὸς πέτραις πεδαρσίοις
against the high rocks
πλεκτάς στέγας πεδάρσιοι ναίουσ᾽ ἐπ᾿ εὐκύκλοις ὄχοις
they dwell in woven shelters high in air on well-wheeled chariots
τοῖς πεδαρσίοις κτύποις πιστός
trusting in the sounds from on high
λόγοι πεδάρσιοι θρώσκουσι
words leap high in air
ἐν δ᾽ ἀτέρμονι κόπτει πεδήσασ᾽ ἄνδρα δαιδάλῳ πέπλῳ
and in the endless robe she strikes, having bound the man with the cunning garment
ἀδαμαντίνων δεσμῶν ἐν ἀρρήκτοις πέδαις
of adamantine bonds in unbreakable fetters
cit.note: ubi Μ ἀδαμαντίνων πέδησιν ἐν ἀρρήκτοις πέτραις (πέραιςwith adamantine fetters in unbreakable rocks (rocks pr.), quod correctum est ex schol. Aristoph. Ran. 827.
where M has ἀδαμαντίνων πέδησιν ἐν ἀρρήκτοις πέτραις (πέραις pr.) [with adamantine fetters in unbreakable rocks (rocks pr.)], which was corrected from the scholia on Aristophanes' Frogs 827.

cit.quote: θεῖνε διατόρους πέδας
strike the piercing fetters
πέδαις σφυρηλάτοις περιβαλών
having cast around hammered fetters
πέδαις δ᾽ ἀχαλκεύτοις ὅθ᾿ ἡρέθης
and with fetters not forged by bronze you were provoked
πέδας τε χειροῖν καὶ ποδοῖν ξυνωρίδα
and fetters for hands and feet, a pair
πέδας μὲν ἂν λύσειεν
he might release the fetters
Θρήκης ἂμ πεδιήρεις δυσχίμους τε κελεύθους
through the Thracian plains and the wintry paths

sense.note: Vocabulum alibi non lectum.
A word not read elsewhere.

cit.quote: πρὸς Γοργόνεια πεδία Κισθήνης
to the Gorgonean plains of Cisthene
πεδία δ᾽ ἀργηστὴς ἀφρὸς χραίνει
and the white foam stains the plains
τῶν μεγάλων πεδίων ἀμοίρους
deprived of the great plains
Σπερχειός ἄρδει πεδίον
Spercheus waters the plain
ἔνθα πεδίον Ἀσωπὸς ῥοαῖς ἄρδει
where Asopus waters the plain with his streams
ὑπερθοροῦσα πεδίον Ἀσωποῦ
leaping over the plain of Asopus
δελφινοφόρον πόντου πεδίον διαμειψάμεναι
having crossed the dolphin-bearing plain of the sea

cit.note: [σπίδιον πεδίονa small plain Eustath. p. 882, 58 Aeschylo tribuit, qui σπίδιον μήκος ὁδοῦa short length of road dixerat.]
[σπίδιον πεδίον [a small plain] Eustath. p. 882, 58 attributes to Aeschylus, who had said σπίδιον μήκος ὁδοῦ [a short length of road].]

cit.quote: ἄειλα πεδία
stormy plains
τοῖς πολισσούχοις θεοῖς, πεδιονόμοις τε κἀγορᾶς ἐπισκόποις
to the city-protecting gods, both those who dwell in the plains and the overseers of the assembly

form.gloss: a monstrous word in M Sept. 83, on which see under ποτιχρίμπτομαι

sense.def: in M Sept. 83, monstrum vocabuli, de quo v.s.v. ποτιχρίμπτομαιto approach .
in M Sept. 83, a monstrous word, on which see under ποτιχρίμπτομαι

sense.note: Dorice pro πεδοβήμωνwalking on the ground
Doric for πεδοβήμων [walking on the ground]

cit.quote: πτανά τε καὶ πεδοβάμονα
winged and ground-creeping creatures
πέδοι δὲ βᾶσαι
but going on the ground
cit.note: ubi πεδοground î scribebatur consentiente Eustathio p. 1839, 57, quod correxi ex Ioanne Alex. τον. παραγγon accents . p. 30, 8 τὰ ἀπὸ βαρυτόνων βαρύνεται, ἔξω ἔξοι, πέδον πέδοι. “πέδοι δὲ βᾶσαι” Αἰσχύλος Προμηθεῖ δεσμώτηwords from barytones are barytone, except ἔξω [outside] ἔξοι, πέδον [ground] πέδοι [on the ground]. "But going on the ground" Aeschylus in Prometheus Bound . Idem praecipit schol. Dionys. Thr. in Bekk. Anecd. p. 945, 2; contra inter περισπώμεναperispomena numeratur in Reg. prosod. 173.

where πεδοî [on the ground] was written with the agreement of Eustathius p. 1839, 57, which I corrected from Ioannes Alex. τον. παραγγ. p. 30, 8: τὰ ἀπὸ βαρυτόνων βαρύνεται, ἔξω ἔξοι, πέδον πέδοι. “πέδοι δὲ βᾶσαι” Αἰσχύλος Προμηθεῖ δεσμώτη [words from barytones are barytone, except ἔξω [outside] ἔξοι, πέδον [ground] πέδοι [on the ground]. "But going on the ground" Aeschylus in Prometheus Bound]. The same is prescribed by the scholiast on Dionysius Thrax in Bekker's Anecdota p. 945, 2; on the other hand it is counted among the perispomena in Reg. prosod. 173.

sense.note: Eadem significatione πέδῳon the ground dictum legitur
In the same meaning πέδῳ [on the ground] is read

cit.quote: πέδῳ σκήψασα
having propped herself on the ground

cit.note: et similia
and similar instances
cit.quote: πεσόντος αἵματος πέδῳ
of the blood that fell to the ground
αἷμα τὸ διερὸν πέδῳ χύμενον οἴχεται
the liquid blood poured on the ground is gone
ἰὺς πέδῳ πεσών
the arrow fell to the ground
αἷμ᾽ ὅμαιμον ἐκχέας πέδῳ
having shed kindred blood on the ground
τοῦ δὲ πίπτοντος πέδω
of him falling to the ground
νῆμά θ᾽ ἵετο πέδῳ
and the thread was sent to the ground
θεὶς ἴχνος πέδῳ
placing his foot on the ground
cit.note: et si qui sunt similes loci, quibus omnibus antiqua restituenda scriptura πέδοιon the ground . Idem adverbium duobus aliis locis Aeschyli recte restitutum est ubi nune πέδονground legitur,

and if there are similar passages, in all of them the ancient spelling πέδοι [on the ground] must be restored. The same adverb has been correctly restored in two other places of Aeschylus where now πέδον [ground] is read,

cit.quote: τῆς μελλοῦς κλέος πέδον πατοῦντες
treading on the ground the fame of the future
τὸ μή θέμις – λὰξ πέδον πατούμενον
what is not lawful—trampled underfoot on the ground
πεδοίκου χελιδόνος
of a cohabiting swallow
cit.note: quod per συνοίκουof a cohabitant exp. Hesychius, per μετοικούσηςof a resident alien Photius p. 403, 24. Vocabulum aliunde non cognitum, nisi quod πεδάξοικοιcohabitants cum digammo est in inscr. Argiva ap. Boeckh. vol. 1 p. 33 n. 14 et p. 37 n. 19.

which Hesychius explains by συνοίκου [of a cohabitant], Photius p. 403, 24 by μετοικούσης [of a resident alien]. The word is not known from elsewhere, except that πεδάξοικοι [cohabitants] with digamma is found in an Argive inscription in Boeckh. vol. 1 p. 33 n. 14 and p. 37 n. 19.

form.gloss: ground, earth, a poetic word used only in the singular

sense.def: solum, terra, vocabulum poeticum numero tantum singulari dictum.
ground, earth, a poetic word used only in the singular

cit.quote: Εὐρώπης πέδον
the ground of Europe
νέους ἕρποντας εὐμενεῖ πέδῳ
young men creeping on the kindly ground
στένει πέδον φίλανδρον
the man-loving ground groans
χαράσσεται πέδον
the ground is furrowed
κρόκου βαφάς δ᾽ ἐς πέδον χέουσα
pouring saffron dyes on the ground
Διός μακέλλη, τῇ κατείργασται πέδον
the mattock of Zeus, with which the ground has been worked
αἷς ἐπέσταλται τέλος, πέδον κελεύθου στορνύναι πετάσμασιν
to whom the task has been assigned, to strew the ground of the path with tapestries
πέδον ῥαντήριον
a vessel for sprinkling the ground
cit.note: vitiose pro πεδορραντήριονa place where the ground is sprinkled , quod v.
erroneously for πεδορραντήριον [a vessel for sprinkling the ground], which see

cit.quote: ἐγὼ δὲ θερμόνους τάχ᾽ ἐν πέδῳ βαλῶ
and I shall soon cast warm-minded men to the ground
πατρῷον αἱμάξαι πέδον
to stain the ancestral ground with blood
φονίας σταγόνας χυμένας ἐς πέδον
murderous drops poured on the ground
λειχὴν ἄφυλλος, ἄτεκνος πέδον ἐπισύμενος
a leafless, childless lichen creeping over the ground
τοῦδ᾽ ἀπόξενος πέδου
a stranger to this ground
ἄνδρας γυναικῶν οὕνεχ᾽ αἱμάξαι πέδον
to stain the ground with blood for the sake of women
μηδ᾽ αἵματος πέμφιγα πρὸς πέδῳ βάλης
and do not cast a drop of blood on the ground
πᾶν Ἐρέχθειον πέδον
the whole land of Erechtheus
μεσόμφαλόν θ᾽ ἵδρυμα, Λοξίου πέδον
and the navel-centered seat, the ground of Loxias
Εὐρώπης πέδον
the land of Europe
Ἀπίας πέδον τόδε
this land of Apia
γῆς Ἀχαιίδος πέδον
the ground of the Achaean land
χθονός μὲν ἐς τηλουρὸν ἥκομεν πέδον
we have come to a far-off land
ποῖον δ᾽ ἀμείψεσθε γαίας πέδον?
what land will you exchange for this?
πτώμασιν αἱματίσαι πέδον γᾶς
to stain the ground of the earth with corpses

sense.note: [πέδῳon the ground et πέδονground locis pluribus male scriptum pro πέδοιon the ground v.s.hoc v.]
[πέδῳ [on the ground] and πέδον [ground] in many places wrongly written for πέδοι [on the ground], see under this word.]

form.gloss: a place where the ground is sprinkled

sense.def: locus ubi solum conspergitur. De loco qui sanguine occisi contaminatur
a place where the ground is sprinkled; of a place that is defiled by the blood of a slain person

cit.note: ubi praecedit στέγην Ἀτρειδῶνthe house of the Atreidae
where στέγην Ἀτρειδῶν [the house of the Atreidae] precedes
cit.quote: ἀνδροσφαγεῖον καὶ πεδορραντήριον
a man-slaughtering place and a ground-sprinkling place
cit.note: ubi Μ ἀνδρὸς σφαγεῖονM: a man's slaughter-place (correctum σφάγιον) καὶ πέδον (νslaughter) and ground (ν ex p facto) ῥαντήριονsprinkling-place , ubi ἀνδροσφαγεῖονman-slaughtering place restituit Dobraeus, ut ἀνδροκτονεῖονman-murdering place dictum est, ego πεδορραντήριονground-sprinkling place .

where M has ἀνδρὸς σφαγεῖον [a man's slaughter-place] (corrected to σφάγιον [slaughter]) and πέδον [ground] (ν made from p) ῥαντήριον [sprinkling-place], where Dobree restored ἀνδροσφαγεῖον [man-slaughtering place], as ἀνδροκτονεῖον [man-murdering place] is said, I [restored] πεδορραντήριον [ground-sprinkling place].

cit.quote: πᾶς γὰρ ἱππηλάτας καὶ πεδοστιβὴς λεώς
for all the horse-driving and land-walking people
κνώδαλα πτεροῦντα καὶ πεδοστιβή
winged creatures and those that walk on the ground

sense.def: to whom land has fallen, terrestrial

cit.quote: ἐλαύνει διχόθεν, πεζονόμοις ἔκ τε θαλάσσας
he drives from both sides, from land-dwellers and from the sea
οἱ μὲν ἐφ᾽ ἵππων, οἱ δ᾽ ἐπὶ ναῶν πεζοί τε βάδην
some on horses, others on ships, and foot soldiers on the march
πεζῷ παραγγείλας ἄφαρ στρατεύματι
having quickly given orders to the infantry army
πεζούς τε καὶ θαλασσίους νᾶες ἄγαγον
they brought foot soldiers and ships of the sea
ναυτικός στρατὸς κακωθεὶς πεζὸν ὤλεσε στρατόν
the naval force, having suffered, destroyed the infantry
πεζός ἢ ναύτης δὲ πεῖραν τήνδ᾽ ἐμώρανεν τάλας?
did a foot soldier or a sailor, wretched man, make this attempt in folly?
πῶς δὲ καὶ στρατὸς τοσόσδε πεζός ἤνυσεν περᾶν?
how did such a large infantry force manage to cross?

sense.def: bearing a border or wearing it, fringed

cit.quote: πεζοφόροις Ζώμασιν: Αἰσχύλος Τοξότισιν (fr. 210), ὥσπερ πέζαν ἐχόντων τῶν χιτώνων, τινὲς δὲ ποδήρεσι
with border-bearing girdles: Aeschylus in Toxotides (fr. 210), as having a border on their tunics, but some say reaching to the feet

sense.note: πεζοφόρα ζώματαborder-bearing girdles ex Aeschylo memorat Pollux 7, 51. Apud Photium p. 405, 15 πεζοφοροῦσινthey wear borders · (corruptum ex πεζοφόροις) ἤτοι πέζαν ἐχόντων τῶν χιτώνων. ἢ τοῖς ποδήρεσινborder-bearing) either having a border on their tunics or those reaching to the feet .

Pollux 7, 51 mentions πεζοφόρα ζώματα [border-bearing girdles] from Aeschylus. In Photius p. 405, 15 πεζοφοροῦσιν [they wear borders] (corrupt from πεζοφόροις [border-bearing]) is explained as either πέζαν ἐχόντων τῶν χιτώνων [having a border on their tunics] or τοῖς ποδήρεσιν [those reaching to the feet].

cit.quote: τὸν δὲ μὴ πειθάνορα ζεύξω βαρείαις οὔ τι μὴ σειραφόρον κριθώντα πῶλον
but the one who is not obedient to a man I will yoke with heavy bonds, not as a trace-horse, a colt feeding on barley
πειθαρχία γάρ ἐστι τῆς εὐπραξίας μήτηρ
for obedience is the mother of success

sense.note: Recta haec est scriptura vocabuli, cuius alia exempla v. in Thes. vol. 6 p. 658, non πιθαρχίαobedience , quod probat grammaticus in cod. Paris. 2630 apud Bekker. ad Apollon. de synt. p. 414.

This is the correct spelling of the word, for other examples see Thes. vol. 6 p. 658, not πιθαρχία [obedience], which a grammarian in cod. Paris. 2630 approves, in Bekker's edition of Apollonius on syntax p. 414.

cit.quote: πειθάρχῳ φρενί
with an obedient mind

form.gloss: to persuade, to bend by speech

sense.def: I persuade, I bend by speech
sense.note: cum imperfecto ἔπειθονI was persuading , perfecto πέποιθαI trust , aoristo primo ἔπεισαI persuaded et ἐπίθησαI obeyed , altero ἔπιθονI obeyed , futuro πείσωI will persuade . Passivi formae πείθομαι ἐπείσθην πεισθήσομαιI am persuaded, I was persuaded, I will be persuaded , medii πείθομαι ἐπιθόμην πείσομαιI obey, I obeyed, I will obey .

with imperfect ἔπειθον [I was persuading], perfect πέποιθα [I trust], first aorist ἔπεισα [I persuaded] and ἐπίθησα [I persuaded], second aorist ἔπιθον [I persuaded], future πείσω [I will persuade]. Passive forms: πείθομαι [I am persuaded], ἐπείσθην [I was persuaded], πεισθήσομαι [I will be persuaded]; middle: πείθομαι [I obey], ἐπιθόμην [I obeyed], πείσομαι [I will obey].

cit.quote: πάντως γὰρ οὐ πείσεις νιν
For in no way will you persuade him.
cit.note: πείθεις [you persuade] M

cit.quote: ἄλλο τιφώνει καὶ παραμυθοῦ μ᾽ ὅ τι καὶ πείσεις
Say something else and comfort me with whatever you can persuade me.
αἰθερία κόνις με πείθει
The heavenly dust persuades me.
πείθω νιν λόγῳ
I persuade him with a word.
cit.note: Versus interpolatus, qui non persanatur Elmsleii coniectura πεῖθέ νινpersuade him . Nam sensus tale quid postulat, εἴσω φρενῶν ξυνεῖσα δέξεται λόγονhaving understood within her mind, she will receive the word , ut colligi potest ex v. 1060.

An interpolated verse, which is not healed by Elmsley's conjecture πεῖθέ νιν [persuade him]. For the sense requires something like this: εἴσω φρενῶν ξυνεῖσα δέξεται λόγον [having understood within her mind she will receive the word], as can be gathered from v. 1060.

cit.quote: ἔπειθον οὐδέν᾽ οὐδέν
I was persuading no one of anything.
καὶ τῶνδ᾽ ὅμοιον εἴ τι μὴ πείθω
And if I do not persuade you of something similar to these things.
καὶ γὰρ κτανεῖν σ᾽ ἔπεισα μητριον δέμας
For indeed I persuaded you to kill your mother's body.
Μοίρας ἔπεισας ἀφθίτους θεῖναι βροτούς
You persuaded the Fates to make mortals immortal.
πείσω τὸ κοινόν
I will persuade the public.
τοιάνδ᾽ ἔπειθε ῥῆσιν ἀμφ᾽ ἡμῶν λέγων
He was persuading with such a speech about us.

sense.note: Aoristi ἐπίθησαI obeyed , cuius participium πιθήσαςhaving obeyed pro πεισθείςhaving been persuaded vel πεποιθώςtrusting dictum frequens in poesi epica est, unum apud Aeschylum exemplum reperitur
Of the aorist ἐπίθησα, whose participle πιθήσας [having obeyed] is used frequently in epic poetry for πεισθείς [having been persuaded] or πεποιθώς [having trusted], one example is found in Aeschylus.

cit.quote: πιθήσασα δώροισι Μίνω
Having been persuaded by gifts to Minos.
cit.note: sic Abreschius pro πειθήσασαhaving obeyed
Thus Abreschius for πειθήσασα [having persuaded].

sense.note: ΠλούραPlouto alterius aoristi ἔπιθονI obeyed exempla sunt.
Πλούρα [more] are examples of the second aorist ἔπιθον [I persuaded].

cit.quote: εἴπερ εὐσεβής πίθοι λόγος
If a pious word could persuade.
πιθεῖν Τιτᾶνας οὐκ ἠδυνήθην
I was not able to persuade the Titans.
ἄγαγες Ἡσιόναν πιθών δάμαρτα κοινόλεκτρον
You led Hesione, having persuaded her to be your wedded wife.
cit.note: πείθωνpersuading pr. Μ
πείθων [persuading] first in M.

sense.def: Passivum πείθομαιI am persuaded persuaderi mihi patior, pareo.
Passive πείθομαι [I am persuaded] I allow myself to be persuaded, I obey

cit.quote: πείθοι᾽ ἂν, εἰ πείθοι · ἀπειθοίης δ᾽ ἴσως
You might persuade, if you persuade; but perhaps you would fail to persuade.

sense.note: Imperativi πείθουobey et πείθεσθεobey male illati pro aoristo πιθοῦobey et πιθέσθαιto obey exempla infra afferentur. Perfecti πέπεισμαιI have been persuaded imperativus πέπεισθιtrust est

Examples of the imperatives πείθου [be persuaded] and πείθεσθε [be persuaded] wrongly introduced for the aorist πιθοῦ [obey] and πιθέσθαι [to obey] will be given below. The imperative of the perfect πέπεισμαι [I have been persuaded] is πέπεισθι [be persuaded].

cit.quote: νεκροῖσί νυν πέπεισθι μητέρα κτανών
Be persuaded by the dead, having killed your mother.
cit.note: ubi in M adscriptum est ζτseek . (i.e. Ζήτειseek ), quia librarium offenderat haec forma, cuius alia exempla nulla reperiuntur. πέπισθιtrust vel πέποισθιtrust scribi voluit Veitchius Greek verbs irregular p. 458. ed. tert. et post Veitchium Gilbertus in Ritschelii Actis Soc. philol. vol. 2 p. 330. Participium est

where in M is written ζτ. (i.e. Ζήτει [seek]), because this form had offended the scribe, of which no other examples are found. πέπισθι or πέποισθι [be persuaded] Veitch wished to be written, Greek verbs irregular p. 458, third edition, and after Veitch Gilbert in Ritschl's Acta Soc. philol. vol. 2 p. 330. The participle is

cit.quote: σοῖς γόοις πεπεισμένος
Persuaded by your laments.
κεναῖσιν ἐλπίσιν πεπεισμένος
Persuaded by empty hopes.
πρὸς τοῦ δ᾽ ἐπείσθης καὶ τίνος βουλεύμασιν?
By whom were you persuaded, and by whose counsels?
ἐὰν μὴ τοῖς ἐμοῖς πεισθῆς λόγοις
unless you are persuaded by my words
τοιοίσδε πεισθεὶς Λοξίου μαντεύμασιν
persuaded by such oracles of Loxias
φρυκτωρῶν δία πεισθεῖσα
persuaded through the beacon-watchers

sense.note: Futurum medium
Future middle

cit.quote: σοῖς ταῦτα πείσομαι λόγοις
I will obey you in these words

sense.def: Usitatissimum est perfectum medium πέποιθαI trust
The perfect middle πέποιθα [I trust] is very common
sense.note: quod pro loci cuiusque ratione Latinis reddi potest vocabulis persuasum habeo, obsequor, credo, confido.
which according to the sense of each passage can be rendered in Latin by the words persuasum habeo [I have persuaded myself], obsequor [I comply], credo [I believe], confido [I trust].

cit.quote: τοῖς φίλοισι μὴ πεποιθέναι
not to trust friends
τούτοις πεποιθώς εἶμι
trusting in these things I will go
ὀχυροῖσι πεποιθὼς στυφελοῖς ἐφέταις
trusting in the strong, harsh commanders
οὐ πεποιθότες τύχη
not trusting in fortune
ἀλκῇ πεποιθώς
trusting in strength
τοιοίσδε χρησμοῖς ἄρα χρή πεποιθέναι? κεἰ μὴ πέποιθα, τοὔργον ἔστ᾽ ἐργαστέον
Must we trust such oracles? And if I do not trust, the deed must still be done.
πεποιθώς τῇ δίκῃ
trusting in justice
κἀγὼ πέποιθα Ζηνί
and I trust in Zeus
ἔπεμψα, τοὺς πέποιθα μὴ ματᾶν ὁδῷ
I sent them, whom I trust not to wander from the path
πέποιθα δ᾽ αὐτῷ ξὺν δίκῃ τὸν πυρφόρον ήξειν κεραυνόν
I trust that with justice he will come, the fire-bearer lightning
πέποιθα δὴ τὸν Διὸς ἀντίτυπον ἔχοντα κεφαλὰν ἰάψεὶν
I trust that he who has the head that opposes Zeus will be struck
αἰχμὴν, ἣν ἔχει, μᾶλλον θεοῦ σέβειν πεποιθώς
trusting to revere the spear he holds more than the god
πεποιθέναι τὸν αὐτὸν ἀεὶ δαίμον᾽ οὐριεῖν τύχης
to trust that the same deity will always guide fortune
πέποιθ᾽, ἀρωγὰς δ᾽ ἐκ τάφου πέμπει πατήρ
I trust, and my father sends aid from the tomb

sense.def: Aoristi forma media ἐπιθόμηνI obeyed est
The middle aorist form is ἐπιθόμην [I obeyed]
sense.note: in codicibus tragicorum non raro per diphthongum scripta ne metri quidem ratione habita, ut in versu anapaestico Sept. 1065 εἶσιν. τίς ἂν οὖν τὰ πίθοιτοhe goes. Who then would obey these things? ?; ubi πείθοιτοhe would obey M, sed apogr. nonnulla πίθοιτο. Εum. 794 ἐμοὶ πίθεσθε μὴ βαρυστόνως φέρεινhe would obey. Eum. 794: obey me, not to bear it grievously , ubi Turnebus correxit quod est in Μ πείθεσθεM obey . Ag. 206 βαρεῖα μὲν κὴρ τὸ μὴ πιθέσθαιheavy is the doom of not obeying . Sic hic quoque Turnebus: in Μ πειθέσθαιM to obey , ipso accentu aoristum πιθέσθαιto obey , non praesens monstrante πείθεσθαιto obey . Recte vero ib. 943 in initio trimetri (in parte fabulae ex M ablata) πιθοῦobey in apographis. In M fortasse hic quoque πείθουobey scriptum fuit, ut in reliquis locis omnibus, quorum metrum πιθοῦobey vel fert vel postulat, nusquam vero πείθουobey postulat, quo indicio usi recentiores editores ubique vocalem simplicem restituerunt.

in the manuscripts of the tragedians not rarely written with a diphthong even without regard to the meter, as in the anapaestic verse Sept. 1065 εἶσιν. τίς ἂν οὖν τὰ πίθοιτο? [he will go. Who then would obey these things?]; where πείθοιτο [would obey] M, but some copies πίθοιτο [would obey]. Eum. 794 ἐμοὶ πίθεσθε μὴ βαρυστόνως φέρειν [obey me, not to bear heavily], where Turnebus corrected what is in M πείθεσθε [obey]. Ag. 206 βαρεῖα μὲν κὴρ τὸ μὴ πιθέσθαι [heavy is the doom of not obeying]. Thus here too Turnebus: in M πειθέσθαι [to obey], the accent itself showing the aorist πιθέσθαι [to obey], not the present πείθεσθαι [to be persuaded]. Correctly indeed ib. 943 at the beginning of the trimeter (in the part of the play lost from M) πιθοῦ [obey] in the copies. In M perhaps here too πείθου [be persuaded] was written, as in all other places, whose meter either allows or demands πιθοῦ [obey], but never demands πείθου [be persuaded], by which indication recent editors have everywhere restored the simple vowel.

cit.note: simplex
simple
cit.quote: πείθου
obey
cit.note: ubi recte apogr. nonnulla πιθοῦobey .
where correctly some copies πιθοῦ [obey].

cit.quote: πιθοῦ γυναιξί
obey the women
πιθοῦ λιποῦσα τόνδ᾽ ἁμαξήρη θρόνον
obey, leaving this wagon-borne throne
cit.note: Sic utrobique Blomfieldus pro πείθουobey .
Thus in both places Blomfield for πείθου [be persuaded].

cit.quote: πιθοῦ τε καὶ γενέσθω
obey and let it be done
cit.note: sic Stanleius pro πείθουobey
thus Stanley for πείθου [be persuaded]

cit.quote: πίθεσθέ μοι πίθεσθε, συμπονήσατε
obey me, obey, and share the toil
cit.note: Blomfieldus pro πείθεσθέ μοι πείθεσθεobey me, obey . Eadem codicis incon-stantia est apud Sophoclem, de quo dixi in Lex. Soph. p. 394. Librorum in hac re auctoritas prorsus nulla est, quum etiam λειπεῖνto leave et λειπώνleaving in codicibus antiquis non raro pro λιπεῖνto leave et λιπώνleaving scriptum reperiatur.

Blomfield for πείθεσθέ μοι πείθεσθε [obey me, obey]. The same inconsistency of the codex is in Sophocles, about which I have spoken in Lex. Soph. p. 394. The authority of the books in this matter is absolutely nothing, since also λειπεῖν [to leave] and λειπών [having left] are found written in ancient manuscripts not rarely for λιπεῖν [to leave] and λιπών [having left].

cit.quote: μελιγλώσσοις πειθοῦς ἐπαοιδαῖσιν
with honey-tongued charms of persuasion
τίνος ἀγγελίας πειθοῖ περίπεμπτα θυοσκεῖς?
by persuasion of what message do you sacrifice, sent around?
cit.note: male pro πευθοῖinquiry , quod Scaliger restituit.
wrongly for πευθοῖ [inquiry], which Scaliger restored.

cit.quote: νῦν γὰρ ἀκμάζει πειθώ δολία
for now deceitful persuasion is at its height
ἔτι γὰρ θεόθεν και ταπνείει πειθώ μολπᾶν ἀλką σύμφυτος αἰών
for still from the gods breathes persuasion of songs, strength innate, life
cit.note: μολπάνsong corr. in M, quod legit scholiasta. sic Bothius pro ἀλκὰν. πειθώ μολπᾶνstrength. persuasion of songs dicit fiduciam cantuum, quia auguria sua rata fore sperat. Recte sensum reddidit scholiasta, etsi accusativum πειθώpersuasion male pro nominativo habuit, πείθει γάρ με ἡ παρὰ θεῶν πίστις μέλπειν καὶ λέγειν ὅτι εὐ πράξουσιν οἱ Ἀτρείδαι ὅσον ἀπὸ τοῦ σημείουthe trust from the gods persuades me to sing and say that the Atreidae will fare well, as far as from the sign .

μολπάν [song] corrected in M, which the scholiast read. Thus Bothius for ἀλκὰν [strength]. πειθώ μολπᾶν [persuasion of songs] he calls confidence in the songs, because he hopes that his auguries will be fulfilled. The scholiast rendered the sense correctly, although he wrongly took the accusative πειθώ [persuasion] as nominative, for πείθει γάρ με ἡ παρὰ θεῶν πίστις μέλπειν καὶ λέγειν ὅτι εὐ πράξουσιν οἱ Ἀτρείδαι ὅσον ἀπὸ τοῦ σημείου [the trust from the gods persuades me to sing and say that the Atreidae will fare well, as far as from the sign].

sense.note: de qua v. quae collecta sunt in Thes. vol. 6 p. 665.
about which see what has been collected in Thes. vol. 6 p. 665.

cit.quote: βιᾶται δ᾽ ἁ τάλαινα Πειθώ
and wretched Peitho forces
εἰ μὲν ἁγνόν ἐστί σοι Πειθοῦς σέβας
if the reverence of Peitho is holy to you
στέργω δ᾽ ὄμματα Πειθούς
I love the eyes of Peitho
Πειθώ δ᾽ ἕποιτο
and may Peitho follow
Πόθος ᾧ τ᾽ οὐδὲν ἄπαρνον τελέθει θέλκτορι Πειθοῖ
Desire, to whom nothing is denied, with enchanting Peitho
μόνου δὲ Πειθώ δαιμόνων ἀποστατεῖ
and Peitho alone of the gods stands apart
cit.note: Θανάτου [of Death]

cit.quote: τοιοῦδε φωτὸς πεῖραν εὐ φυλακτέον
the attempt of such a man must be well guarded against
πεζός ἢ ναύτης δὲ πεῖραν τήνδ᾽ ἐμώρανεν τάλας?
did a footman or sailor, wretched, make this attempt?
μιανθεῖσαι πειραὶ κοπάνων ἀνδροδαΐκτων
defiled points of man-slaying pestles

sense.note: κόπανονpestle , quod proprie pistillum significat, de quo v. Thes. vol. 4 p. 1810, de securi dixit Aeschylus. πειραίthe points , quod schol. exp. πειραὶ αἱ ἀκμαὶ τῶν ξιφῶν, παρὰ τὸ πείρειν · κοπάνων δὲ τῶν κοπτικῶν ξύλωνthe points are the edges of swords, from piercing; and of pestles, the cutting woods , vocabulum est aliunde non cognitum. Nam quod apud Diodorum in Exc. Vat. p. 48 ed. Mai. legitur, ex σπείραιςcoils corruptum esse animadvertit L. Dindorfius in Thes. vol. 6 p. 669. nec quidquam tribuendum Lentzii coniecturae (Herodian. vol. 1 p. 263, 14) qui pro corrupto σχειρά?? apud Theognostum Can. p. 101, 24 πειράtrial restitui voluit. Pauwii coniecturam πεῖραιattempts probavit Blomfieldus, quod pro πεῖραι κοπάνων μιανθέντωνattempts of defiled pestles dictum sit, ut Ag. 148 ἐκπατίοις ἄλγεσι παίδωνwith out-of-the-way griefs of children pro ἐκπατίων ἄλγεσι παίδωνof out-of-the-way griefs of children . Sed πεῖραιattempts debilius est quam quod huic loco conveniat vocabulum et verbis adiectis multo minus aptum quam πειραίthe points ea qua scholiasta accepit significatione.

κόπανον [pestle], which properly means a pestle, on which see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1810, Aeschylus used of an axe. πειραί [the points], which the scholiast explains as πειραὶ αἱ ἀκμαὶ τῶν ξιφῶν, παρὰ τὸ πείρειν · κοπάνων δὲ τῶν κοπτικῶν ξύλων [the points are the edges of swords, from piercing; and of pestles, the cutting woods], is a word not otherwise known. For what is read in Diodorus in Exc. Vat. p. 48 ed. Mai. has been noticed by L. Dindorf in Thes. vol. 6 p. 669 to be corrupted from σπείραις [coils]. Nor should any weight be given to Lentz's conjecture (Herodian. vol. 1 p. 263, 14) who wanted to restore πειρά [trial] for the corrupt σχειρά [??] in Theognostus Can. p. 101, 24. Blomfield approved Pauw's conjecture πεῖραι [attempts], because it is said for πεῖραι κοπάνων μιανθέντων [attempts of defiled pestles], as Ag. 148 ἐκπατίοις ἄλγεσι παίδων [with out-of-the-way griefs of children] for ἐκπατίων ἄλγεσι παίδων [of out-of-the-way griefs of children]. But πεῖραι [attempts] is weaker than a word suitable for this passage and much less apt with the added words than πειραί [the points] in the meaning the scholiast took it.
Cum genitivo, ut apud Homerum aliosque in Thes. indicatos vol. 6 p. 675,
With a genitive, as in Homer and others indicated in Thes. vol. 6 p. 675,

cit.quote: πειρᾶσθέ μου γυναικὸς ὡς ἀφράσμονος

δαίμονος πειρωμένους

δαίμονος πειρώμενος

θεοῖσιν ἔρδειν πολεμίων πειρωμένων
to do for the gods while the enemy are trying
cit.note: i.e. dum hostes urbem obsident,
i.e. while the enemy are besieging the city,

cit.quote: πειράσομαι, ἐὰν δύνωμαι, τῶνδέ σ᾽ ἐκλῦσαι πόνων
I will try, if I am able, to release you from these toils
cit.note: nisi sublato ante et post δύνωμαιI am able commate πειράσομαιI will try cum ἐάνif construendum, ut apud Platonem Leg. 1 p. 638 πειρώμενος ἂν ἄρα δύνωμαι δηλοῦνtrying if I can make clear .

unless, by removing the comma before and after δύνωμαι [I am able], πειράσομαι [I will try] is to be construed with ἐάν [if], as in Plato Leg. 1 p. 638 πειρώμενος ἂν ἄρα δύνωμαι δηλοῦν [trying if I can make clear].

cit.quote: ὑπαντιάζειν παιδί μου πειράσομαι

μόριμον λάχος περαίνων χεροῖν πεισιβρότῳ τε βάκτρῳ

cit.note: Sic Schuetzius pro πισίμβροτόν τε βάκτρονand the staff that persuades mortals .
Thus Schuetz for πισίμβροτόν τε βάκτρον [and the staff that persuades mortals].

cit.quote: πίσυνοι λεπτοδόμοις πείσμασὶ

πνοαὶ νεῶν τε καὶ πεισμάτων ἀφειδεῖς

πεισμάτων σωτηρία

cit.note: Ιη Μπισμάτων σωτηρίου?? . Correctum ex schol. qui annotavit ἀντὶ τοῦ πείς σματα σωτήριαinstead of saving cables . Probabilius est σωτηρίαsafety , quod restituit Turnebus.
Ιη Μπισμάτων σωτηρίου [??]. Corrected from the scholiast who noted ἀντὶ τοῦ πείς σματα σωτήρια [instead of saving cables]. More probable is σωτηρία [safety], which Turnebus restored.

cit.quote: Στρυμονίου πελάγους Αχελωΐδες εἰσὶ πάροικοι

πέλαγος Αἰγαῖον

sense.def: Improprie de eo dicitur quod immensum est, unde Hesychius per μέγεθος, πλήθοςsize, multitude explicat.

cit.quote: δυσχείμερόν γε πέλαγος ἀτηρᾶς δύης

ἄτης δ᾽ ἄβυσσον πέλαγος οὐ μάλ᾽ εὔπορον

οἷς μὴ πελάζειν

τούτοις σὺ μὴ πέλαζε

οὔκουν πελάζει Ζεὺς ἐπ᾿ εὐκραίρῳ βοΐ?
Does not Zeus approach the fair-horned ox?

sense.def: Futuri πελάσωI will approach forma Attica πελῶI will approach (Attic future) , de qua v. Thes. vol. 6 p. 687,
The Attic form of the future πελάσω [I will approach] is πελῶ [I will approach], on which see Thes. vol. 6 p. 687,

cit.quote: χθονὶ τῇδε πελῶ

sense.def: Transitive: I cause to approach, I bring near.

cit.quote: δεσμοῖς ἀλύτοις ἀγρίως πελάσας
having cruelly brought near with unbreakable bonds

sense.def: Forma media πελάζομαιI approach (middle) appropinquo, accedo.
The middle form πελάζομαι [I approach] means I approach, I come near.

cit.quote: λιταῖσί σε θεοκλύτοις ἀπύουσαι πελαζόμεσθα
calling upon you with god-heard prayers, we approach
τί ποτ᾽ οὐ πελάθεις ἐπ᾿ ἀρωγάν?

sense.note: Est poetica praesentis forma, quae bis legitur apud Euripidem (Rhes. 557. El. 1293) et Aristophanem tragicum sermonem imitatum Thesm. 58. Alia poetica forma est πλάθωI approach (poetic) , quod v.
It is a poetic present form, which is read twice in Euripides (Rhes. 557, El. 1293) and in Aristophanes imitating tragic speech Thesm. 58. Another poetic form is πλάθω [I approach], which see.

form.gloss: a cake offered to the gods

cit.quote: ἀποτρόποισι δαίμοσιν θέλουσα θῦσαι πέλανον
wishing to sacrifice a cake to the averting deities
ἥξω λαβούσα πέλανον ἐξ οἴκων ἐμῶν
I will come bringing a cake from my house

sense.note: De libamine
Concerning the offering

cit.quote: χέουσα τόνδε πέλανον ἐν τύμβῳ πατρός
pouring this cake on my father's tomb

sense.def: id quod concretum est (τὸ πεπηγόςthe congealed thing ), liquor spissus.
that which is congealed (τὸ πεπηγός [the congealed thing]), a thick liquid.

cit.note: de sanguine
concerning blood
cit.quote: ἀπὸ ζῶντος ῥοφεῖν ἐρυθρὸν ἐκ μελέων πέλανον
to drink the red cake from living limbs
τόσος γὰρ ἔστα πέλανος αἱματοσταγής
for so great was the blood-dripping cake
φαρμασσομένη χρίματος ἁγνοῦ μαλακαῖς ἀδόλοισι παρηγορίαις, πελάνῳ μυχόθεν βασιλείῳ
being treated with pure ointment with soft guileless consolations, with a royal cake from the inner sanctuary

sense.note: πέλανοςa cake in quorumvis scriptorum codicibus proparoxytonum est, ut videre licet in Thes. vol. 6 p. 689. Rectum, ut videtur, accentum, πελανόςa cake (with acute accent) constanter servavit Μ, πελανόν πελανός πελανῷM, πελανόν [a cake (acc.)] πελανός [a cake (nom.)] πελανῷ [a cake (dat.)] locis supra allatis, nisi quod in duobus, duplex est accentus πέλανόςa cake (with double accent) Pers. 816 et πέλανόνa cake (acc., with double accent) ib. 524. Confirmat Herodianus apud Arcadium p. 64, 13, ubi de nominibus in avos terminatis agit, σεσημείωται τὸ πελανόςthe word πελανός is marked as exceptional . Utrumque accentum memorat Eustathius p. 1601, 4 θυσιῶν ἃς πέλάνους τινές φασιν ἢ καὶ ὀξυτόνως πελανούςsacrifices which some call πέλανοι or, with acute accent, πελανοί .

πέλανος [a cake] in the manuscripts of various writers is proparoxytone, as can be seen in Thes. vol. 6 p. 689. The correct accent, as it seems, πελανός [a cake] is consistently preserved by M, πελανόν [a cake (acc.)] πελανός [a cake (nom.)] πελανῷ [a cake (dat.)] in the places cited above, except that in two, the accent is double: πέλανός [a cake] Pers. 816 and πέλανόν [a cake (acc.)] ib. 524. Herodianus confirms this in Arcadius p. 64, 13, where he deals with nouns ending in -ανος, σεσημείωται τὸ πελανός [the word πελανός is marked as exceptional]. Eustathius p. 1601, 4 mentions both accents: θυσιῶν ἃς πέλάνους τινές φασιν ἢ καὶ ὀξυτόνως πελανούς [sacrifices which some call πέλανοι or, with acute accent, πελανοί].

On both see Thes. vol. 6 p. 691. Aeschylus used only the plural, οἱ πέλας [those near].

Pleiades, the seven daughters of Atlas received among the stars: which constellation is called either in the singular Πλειάς or in the plural Πλειάδες, on which see Thes. vol. 6 p. 1179.
sense.note: Pro eo poetae interdum ΠελειάδεςPleiades dixerunt, quod Athenaeus docet 11 p. 491a, allatis Aeschyli versibus (fr. 298), in quibus ἄπτεροι Πελειάδεςwingless Pleiades appellantur διὰ τὴν πρὸς τοὺς ὄρνεις ὁμωνυμίανbecause of the homonymy with birds , ut addit Athenaeus.

For it poets sometimes said Πελειάδες [Pleiades], as Athenaeus teaches 11 p. 491a, citing verses of Aeschylus (fr. 298), in which they are called ἄπτεροι Πελειάδες [wingless Pleiades] διὰ τὴν πρὸς τοὺς ὄρνεις ὁμωνυμίαν [because of the homonymy with birds], as Athenaeus adds.

sense.note: Vocabulum alibi non lectum annotavit Hesychius.

what Critias calls πόδεια [foot-coverings], whether one should think them felt or wrappings, these Aeschylus calls πέλλυτρα [shoe-straps] in the Phrygians (fr. 255): "they have shoe-straps in well-fitted boots"

sense.note: Memorat idem 2, 196. Codices partim πέλυτραshoe-straps . Graviores huius voc. corruptelae sunt in tribus glossis Hesychii πελλυταί, πελλύτα, πελλύτεμαshoe-straps (corrupt forms) .
The same mentions 2, 196. The codices partly have πέλυτρα [shoe-straps]. More serious corruptions of this word are in three glosses of Hesychius: πελλυταί, πελλύτα, πελλύτεμα.

cit.quote: μόρον δ᾽ ἄφερτον Πελοπίδαις ἐπεύχεται

sense.def: Pelops, Tantali Phrygiae regis filius, avus Agamemnonis.
Pelops, son of Tantalus king of Phrygia, grandfather of Agamemnon.

cit.quote: Πέλοπος ἐν τόποις

sense.def: sum, verbum poeticum, cuius duo tantum tempora, praesens et imperfectum, usitata sunt, ab comicis prosaeque orationis scriptoribus alienum, de quo v. Thes. vol. 6 p. 710.

εἴ τι δὴ λῷον πέλοι

Thus I corrected for ἀνδρὸς πέλει [of a man it is].

cit.note: γυναικὶto a woman Hermannus

Schol. τοὺς Τιτᾶνας καὶ τοὺς νόμους αὐτῶν [the Titans and their laws].

cit.quote: πεμπάζετ᾽ ὀρθῶς ἐκβολάς ψήφων

τὸν σὸν πιστὸν πάντ᾽ ὀφθαλμόν, μύρια μύρια πεμπαστάν

cit.note: ubi cum accusativo constructum est quem regit verbum πεμπάζωto count by fives . Schol. μετρητὴν στρατοπέδου, οἷον μυριάδα ἀριθμοῦντα τὰς ὅλας ἡγεμονίας. ἀριθμῆσαι κατὰ πεντάδα ἀνὰ μυρίους ἔχοντα τοὺς ἀρχομένουςa measurer of the army, as one counting the whole commands by ten-thousands; to count by fives, having the subjects in groups of ten thousand .

where it is constructed with the accusative which the verb πεμπάζω [to count by fives] governs. Schol. μετρητὴν στρατοπέδου, οἷον μυριάδα ἀριθμοῦντα τὰς ὅλας ἡγεμονίας. ἀριθμῆσαι κατὰ πεντάδα ἀνὰ μυρίους ἔχοντα τοὺς ἀρχομένους [a measurer of the army, as one counting the whole commands by ten-thousands; to count by fives, having the subjects in groups of ten thousand].

cit.quote: πέμπτη δ᾽ ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ γέννα

with imperfect ἔπεμπον [I was sending], aorist ἔπεμψα [I sent], future πέμψω [I will send], passive imperfect ἐπεμπόμην [I was being sent], perfect πέπεμπται [he has been sent], aorist ἐπέμφθην [I was sent]

ἐνταῦθα πέμπει τούσδε

πέμπετ᾽ ἀρωγὴν παισίν

χοὰς ἔπεμψε τάσδε

And then she sends these funeral libations

And graciously send our father here
παρθένων χλιδαῖσιν εὐμόρφοις ἔπι πᾶς τις παρελθὼν ὄμματος θελκτήριον τόξευμ᾽ ἔπεμψεν
Everyone who passed by sent a charming arrow from his eyes upon the beautiful adornments of the maidens
Σφίγγα δυσαμεριᾶν πρύτανιν κύνα πέμπει
He sends the Sphinx, the dog that presides over evil days
οὔπω τις Ἀκτέων᾿ ἄθηρος ἡμέρα κενὸν, πόνου πλουτοῦντ᾽, ἔπεμψεν ἐς δόμους
No day yet sent Actaeon home empty of prey, rich in toil
θανόντι δ᾽, οὐ φρονοῦντι, δειλαία χάρις ἐπέμπετο
But to the dead, not to the living, was the wretched favor sent
καὶ δὴ πέπεμπτ᾽ οὐ κόμπον ἐν χεροῖν ἔχων
And indeed he had been sent, holding no boast in his hands
cit.note: in versu interpolatoris cum elisione vitiosa, quam removit qui in apogr. uno adscripsit γρ. πέπεμπταιwritten: he has been sent .
in a verse of an interpolator with faulty elision, which was removed by one who wrote in one copy γρ. πέπεμπται [the reading is πέπεμπται].

sense.note: genitivus πέμφιγοςof a blast syllaba media longa. De hoc vocabulo docte et copiose dixit Galenus vol. 5 p. 454 ed. Basil. (vol. 9 p. 385 ed. Chart.) allatis triplicis significationis exemplis, πνοήbreath flatus, ἀκτίςray radius solaris, pavis gutta,

The genitive πέμφιγος [of πέμφιξ] has the middle syllable long. Galen discussed this word learnedly and copiously in vol. 5 p. 454 of the Basel edition (vol. 9 p. 385 of the Chartier edition), citing examples of its three meanings: πνοή [breath], flatus; ἀκτίς [ray], solar ray; pavis, gutta [drop].

cit.quote: δοκεῖ μὲν γὰρ αὐτὴν (τὴν πέμφιγα) ἐπὶ τῆς πνοῆς Σοφοκλῆς λέγειν Αἰσχύλος δὲ ἐν Προμηθεῖ δεσμώτη (imo λυομένῳ fr. 195) εὐθεῖαν ἕρπε τήνδε · καὶ πρώτιστα μὲν Βορεάδας ἥξεις πρὸς πνοὰς, ἵν᾽ εὐλαβοῦ βρόμον καταιγίζοντα, μή σ᾽ ἀναρπάσῃ δυσχειμέρῳ πέμφιγι συστρέψας ἄφνω. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἀκτίνων αὐτῶν δοκεῖ χρῆσθαι τῷ τῆς πέμφιγος ὀνόματι Σοφοκλῆς οὕτω καὶ Αἰσχύλος ἐν Ξαντρίαις (fr. 169) ἃς οὔτε πέμφιξ ἡλίου προσδέρκεται οὔτ᾽ ἀστερωπὸν ὄμμα Λητῴας κόρης. ἐπὶ δὲ τῆς ῥανίδος ὁ αὐτός φησιν ἐν Προμηθεῖ (fr. 195) ἐξευλαβοῦ δὲ μή σε προσβάλη στόμα πέμφιξ · πικρὰ γὰρ, κοὐ διὰ Ζόης ἀτμοί. καὶ ἐν Πενθεῖ (fr. 182) “μηδ᾽ αἵματος πέμφιγα πρὸς πέδῳ βάλης

For Sophocles seems to use it (τὴν πέμφιγα [the blast]) of breath, but Aeschylus in Prometheus Bound (or rather in Prometheus Unbound, fr. 195): εὐθεῖαν ἕρπε τήνδε [go straight on this way]; and first you will come to the blasts of the North Wind, where beware the roaring storm, lest it suddenly snatch you up, whirling you with its wintry blast. And Sophocles seems to use the word πέμφιξ [blast] of the rays themselves, and so does Aeschylus in the Wool-Carders (fr. 169): ἃς οὔτε πέμφιξ ἡλίου προσδέρκεται οὔτ᾽ ἀστερωπὸν ὄμμα Λητῴας κόρης [whom neither the sun's ray looks upon nor the starry eye of Leto's daughter]. And of a drop the same poet says in Prometheus (fr. 195): ἐξευλαβοῦ δὲ μή σε προσβάλη στόμα πέμφιξ [beware lest a drop strike your mouth]; for it is bitter, and its vapors are not life-giving. And in Pentheus (fr. 182): μηδ᾽ αἵματος πέμφιγα πρὸς πέδῳ βάλης [do not cast a drop of blood upon the ground].

cit.quote: ποτιτρόπαιον αἰδόμενος οὖνπερ | ἱεροδόκα θεῶν λή- | ματ᾽ ἀπ᾽ ἀνδρὸς ἁγνοῦ
revering the suppliant, where she is the receiver of the gods' gifts from a pure man.
cit.note: ubi quum ab schol. annotatum sit οὐ πτωχεύσειςyou will not be poor , Hermannus scripsit verbis, qualia excidisse stropha docet, ex coniectura suppletis οὐ πενεῖ | καλλιπότμου τύχας · | ἱεροδόκα πέλει θεῶν λήματ᾽ ἀπ᾽ ἀνδρὸς ἁγνοῦhe will not be poor in fortune of fair fate; she is the receiver of the gods' gifts from a pure man In qua coniectura si quid veri sit, πένειhe is poor scribendum erit, non πενεῖhe will be poor , quae inaudita est futuri forma. Praesens autem πένειhe is poor , quum pro futuro hic poni potuerit, scholiastae per πτωχεύσειςyou will be poor interpretari licuit, nisi πτωχεύειςyou are poor scripsit. Lacunam recte indicavit Hermannus et λήματ᾽gifts revocavit, ab Turnebo aliisque in λήμματ᾽receipts mutatum, quod non debebam retinere s.v. λήμμαreceipt . Scholiasta annotavit οἱ θεοὶ δέχονται τὰ ἀπὸ ἀνδρὸς ἁγνοῦ ἱεράthe gods receive the sacred offerings from a pure man .

where, since the scholiast has noted οὐ πτωχεύσεις [you will not be poor], Hermann wrote, with the words supplied by conjecture as the strophe shows they have fallen out, οὐ πενεῖ | καλλιπότμου τύχας · | ἱεροδόκα πέλει θεῶν λήματ᾽ ἀπ᾽ ἀνδρὸς ἁγνοῦ [he will not be poor in fortune of fair fate; she is the receiver of the gods' gifts from a pure man]. In which conjecture if there is any truth, πένει [he is poor] should be written, not πενεῖ [he will be poor], which is an unheard-of future form. But the present πένει [he is poor], since it could be used here for the future, could be interpreted by the scholiast as πτωχεύσεις [you will be poor], unless he wrote πτωχεύεις [you are poor]. Hermann correctly indicated the lacuna and restored λήματ᾽ [gifts], which had been changed by Turnebus and others to λήμματ᾽ [receipts], which I should not have retained under the entry λήμμα [receipt]. The scholiast noted: οἱ θεοὶ δέχονται τὰ ἀπὸ ἀνδρὸς ἁγνοῦ ἱερά [the gods receive the sacred offerings from a pure man].

sense.def: particula enclitica quae aliis orationis partibus annectitur, quamvis, tametsi, licet significans, de qua Apollonius de synt. p. 265,9 ἐναντιότητα ὁ πέρ (ἐπαγγέλλεται) μετ᾿ αὐξήσεως ἐμφαντικήνthe particle περ indicates opposition with emphatic intensification . Qui frequens eius usus est apud poetas epicos, rarior apud tragicos: de quo dictum est in Thes. vol. 6 p. 752.

an enclitic particle which is attached to other parts of speech, meaning although, even if, even though, about which Apollonius de synt. p. 265,9 says: ἐναντιότητα ὁ πέρ (ἐπαγγέλλεται) μετ᾿ αὐξήσεως ἐμφαντικήν [the particle περ indicates opposition with emphatic intensification]. Its use is frequent among epic poets, rarer among tragedians: about which it is said in Thes. vol. 6 p. 752.

sense.note: De εἴπερif indeed et καίπερalthough suis locis diximus. περalthough, even cum adiectivis, pronominibus et particulis relativis compositum intendit significationem vocabuli quocum coniunctum est: v. οἷόσπερ, ὅσοσπερ, ὅσπερ, ὥσπερ, ὡσπερείsuch as, as great as, who, as, just as if .

We have spoken about εἴπερ [if indeed] and καίπερ [although] in their own places. περ compounded with adjectives, pronouns, and relative particles intensifies the meaning of the word with which it is joined: see οἷόσπερ [of what sort], ὅσοσπερ [as much as], ὅσπερ [who], ὥσπερ [as], ὡσπερεί [as if].

cit.quote: Ἀπις γὰρ ἐλθὼν ἐκ πέρας Ναυπακτίας
For Apis came from the land of Naupactia
cit.note: Sic Met Eustathius ad Dionys. Per. 414. χώραςland ed. Aldina ex glossemate, quo deceptus Turnebus verba transposuit χώ-ρας γὰρ ἐλθὼν Ἀπις ἐκ Ναυπακτίαςfor Apis came from the land of Naupactia . Valckenario in Schol. in N. T. vol. 1 p. 331 scribendum videbatur ἐξ ἔραςfrom the land ex terra. πέραςend etiam scholiasta legit, qui per πέρατοςof the end explicat, quod non apparet quomodo πέραbeyond dici potuerit. Adverbium πέραν α πέραbeyond from beyond derivat Eustathius p. 306, 23: τὸ πέρην δηλοῖ μὲν τὸ πέραν, ἔστι δὲ ἐπίρρημα μεταληφθὲν ἀπὸ θηλυκῆς αἰτιατικῆς · πέρα γὰρthe word πέρην means πέραν, and it is an adverb taken from a feminine accusative; for πέρα

Thus M and Eustathius on Dionysius Periegetes 414. The Aldine edition has χώρας [land] from a gloss, misled by which Turnebus transposed the words χώρας γὰρ ἐλθὼν Ἀπις ἐκ Ναυπακτίας [for Apis came from the land of Naupactia]. Valckenaer in Scholia on the New Testament vol. 1 p. 331 thought it should be written ἐξ ἔρας [from the land] meaning 'from the earth'. The scholiast also read πέρας [end], which he explains by πέρατος [of the end], though it is not clear how πέρα [beyond] could have been said. Eustathius p. 306, 23 derives the adverb πέραν [beyond] from πέρα [beyond]: τὸ πέρην δηλοῖ μὲν τὸ πέραν, ἔστι δὲ ἐπίρρημα μεταληφθὲν ἀπὸ θηλυκῆς αἰτιατικῆς · πέρα γὰρ [the word πέρην means πέραν, and it is an adverb taken from a feminine accusative; for πέρα]

ἡ γῆ κατὰ γλῶσσαν, ὅθεν ἡ περαία παράγεται, ἧς ἡ αἰτιατικὴ πέραν [the earth in dialect, from which περαία is derived, whose accusative is πέραν]. Compare the same author p. 84, 4 and 1475, 42.

cit.note: Sic correxi pro πιμπλάντωνfilling , orto ex glossemate πιμπλάνωνfilling ad περαίνωνaccomplishing adscripto, de quo dixi in Fleckeiseni Annal. vol. 87 p. 79. Dativνος πεισιβρότῳ τε βάκτρῳwith the staff that persuades mortals restituit Schuetzius. In M πισίμβροτόν τε βάκτρονand the staff that persuades mortals .

Thus I corrected for πιμπλάντων [filling], arising from the gloss πιμπλάνων [filling] written beside περαίνων [accomplishing], about which I spoke in Fleckeisen's Annals vol. 87 p. 79. Schuetz restored the dative νος πεισιβρότῳ τε βάκτρῳ [with the staff that persuades mortals]. In M it is πισίμβροτόν τε βάκτρον [and the staff that persuades mortals].

Cum genitivo de, saepissime cum verbis dicendi, audiendi, quaerendi, cogitandi.

cit.note: Sic M: in apographis πετεινῶνof winged creatures . Epica forma est πετεηνόςwinged , vulgaris πετεινόςwinged : sed Attici veteres πετηνόςwinged dixisse videntur, quam formam agnoscit Herodianus in Etym. M. p. 666, 35 et praebet navis nomen ΠετηνήPetene (ship name) in inser, navali 4b, 66 p. 317. 4c et 36 p. 318 319, comparandum cum ΠετομένηPetomene (ship name) , quod alius navis nomen est ib. p. 319 et 481. De quo dixi in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1013.

Thus M: in the copies πετεινῶν [of winged creatures]. The epic form is πετεηνός [winged], the common form πετεινός [winged]: but the old Attic writers seem to have said πετηνός [winged], which form Herodian recognizes in Etym. M. p. 666, 35 and the ship name Πετηνή [Petene] provides in the naval inscription 4b, 66 p. 317. 4c and 36 p. 318 319, to be compared with Πετομένη [Petomene], which is the name of another ship there p. 319 and 481. About which I have spoken in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1013.

cit.note: Restitui pro ὄρνισιbirds , quia omnes huius carminis trimetri in stropha et antistropha ex puris compositi sunt iambis. Hoc vocabulo pro usitato πετεινόςwinged usum esse Hesiodum annotarunt grammatici, de quo non erat cur dubitaret Lobeckius Paralip. p. 159. Etiam formam monosyllabam πτήνwinged memorant grammatici.

I restored it for ὄρνισι [birds], because all the trimeters of this song in strophe and antistrophe are composed of pure iambs. The grammarians have noted that Hesiod used this word instead of the usual πετεινός [winged], about which Lobeck had no reason to doubt, Paralip. p. 159. The grammarians also mention the monosyllabic form πτήν [winged].

sense.note: Differt a πέτρος τοa stone quod πέτροςa stone maioris molis lapidem significat, qui manibus machinisve moveri potest, et raro pro πέτραa rock dicitur, quod saxum seu rupem significat, quae moveri non potest nisi forte a Cyclope vel Centimanis montium cacumina deiicientibus. Male igitur πετρῶνof stones pro πέτρωνof rocks in M scriptum est Sept. 673.

It differs from πέτρος [a stone] in that πέτρος [a stone] signifies a stone of larger mass, which can be moved by hands or machines, and is rarely used for πέτρα [a rock], which signifies a rock or crag that cannot be moved except perhaps by a Cyclops or the Hundred-Handers hurling down mountain peaks. Therefore πετρῶν [of stones] is wrongly written for πέτρων [of rocks] in M at Sept. 673.

Utrumque explicat Thomas Mag. γράφεται καὶ πτερῶν, καὶ τὸ μὲν πέτρων εἴποις ἂν οὕτως, τὰ προβλήματα τῶν πετρῶν ἤτοι τὴν ἀσπίδα, ἣν προβαλλόμεθα τοῦ σώματος καὶ δι᾿ ἧς τοὺς ἐκ πολεμίων ἡμῶν ἐπιόντας λιθασμούς δεχόμεθα · τὸ δὲ πτερῶν, προβλήματα τοὺς ὀϊστοὺς νόειit is also written 'of wings', and you might say 'of rocks' thus: the defenses of rocks, that is, the shield, which we hold before our body and by which we receive the stones coming at us from our enemies; but if 'of wings', understand 'defenses' as arrows . sic ex apogr. pro αἰχμῆςof a spear ]

[κνημίδας, αἰχμὴν καὶ πέτρων προβλήματα [greaves, spear, and defenses of stones]. Thus I wrote for πετρῶν [of stones], which is in M. In many copies it is πτερών [of wings]. Thomas Mag. explains both: γράφεται καὶ πτερῶν [it is also written of wings], and you might say πέτρων [of stones] thus: the defenses of stones, that is, the shield, which we hold before our body and by which we receive the stones coming at us from our enemies; but πτερῶν [of wings], understand the defenses as arrows. Thus from the copy for αἰχμῆς [of the spear]]

cit.quote: ἐφυμνῆσαι γένοιτό μοι πευκήεντ᾽ ὀλολυγμὸν ἀνδρὸς θεινομένου γυναικός τ᾽ ὀλλυμένας

cit.note: ubi quum metrum syllabam primam brevem postulet, πυκάεντ᾽dense, thick restitui, collato Theognosto Can. p. 23, 12, qui πυκᾶεςdense, thick per ἰσχυρόνstrong explicat, ubi de vocabulis a πυpy incipientibus agit. Miram autem vocabuli terminationem ne quis librarii errori tribuat, alter eiusdem grammatici locus impedit p. 131, 29 τὰ εἰς ἐς οὐδέτερα οἷον τὸ Κυνόσαργες προπαροξύτονον, καὶ τὸ πεύκαες, ῥώπαες, δονάκαεςneuter nouns ending in -ες, such as Κυνόσαργες [Cynosarges] with antepenultimate accent, and πεύκαες [pine-like], ῥώπαες [brush-like], δονάκαες [reed-like] , ubi πεύκαεςpine-like (quod πύκαεςdense, thick scribendum) et δονάκαεςreed-like nihil aliud est quam quod schol. Homeri Il. 18, 576 (ad verba παρὰ ῥοδανὸν δονακῆαalong the waving reed-bed ) memoravit, φησὶ δὲ Διονύσιος γράφεσθαι καὶ δονακῆεν κατὰ τὸ οὐδέτερον, ὡς καὶ τὸν πευκῶνα πευκᾶενDionysius says that it is also written δονακῆεν [reedy] in the neuter, just as the pine-grove is called πευκᾶεν [piney] . Ad significationem quod attinet, quum non constet πύκηdense pro πεύκηpine dictum esse, fortasse a πύκαdensely est derivandum, ut idem sit quod πυκνόνdense : cui Theognosti interpretatio ἰσχυρόνstrong melius convenit quam adiectivo a πεύκηpine derivato, idemque fortasse scholiasta voluit, qui liberius est interpretatus per πανηγυρικόν, λαμπρόνfestive, splendid .

where, since the meter requires the first syllable to be short, I have restored πυκάεντ᾽ [dense, thick], comparing Theognostus Can. p. 23, 12, who explains πυκᾶες [dense, thick] by ἰσχυρόν [strong], where he discusses words beginning with πυ [py]. But lest anyone attribute the strange ending of the word to a scribal error, another passage of the same grammarian prevents it, p. 131, 29: τὰ εἰς ἐς οὐδέτερα οἷον τὸ Κυνόσαργες προπαροξύτονον, καὶ τὸ πεύκαες, ῥώπαες, δονάκαες [neuter nouns ending in -ες, such as Κυνόσαργες [Cynosarges] with antepenultimate accent, and πεύκαες [pine-like], ῥώπαες [brush-like], δονάκαες [reed-like]], where πεύκαες [pine-like] (which should be written πύκαες [dense, thick]) and δονάκαες [reed-like] are nothing other than what the scholiast on Homer Il. 18, 576 (on the words παρὰ ῥοδανὸν δονακῆα [along the waving reed-bed]) mentioned: φησὶ δὲ Διονύσιος γράφεσθαι καὶ δονακῆεν κατὰ τὸ οὐδέτερον, ὡς καὶ τὸν πευκῶνα πευκᾶεν [Dionysius says that it is also written δονακῆεν [reedy] in the neuter, just as the pine-grove is called πευκᾶεν [piney]]. As for the meaning, since it is not established that πύκη [dense] was said for πεύκη [pine], perhaps it should be derived from πύκα [densely], so that it is the same as πυκνόν [dense]: to which Theognostus' interpretation ἰσχυρόν [strong] better suits than an adjective derived from πεύκη [pine], and perhaps the scholiast meant the same, who interpreted it more freely as πανηγυρικόν, λαμπρόν [festive, splendid].

Buttmann conjectured in Lexil. vol. 1 p. 17 that the original meaning was sharp, piercing, as Homer said πικρὰ βέλεμνα [sharp arrows] and πικρὸς ὀϊστός [sharp arrow], and Sophocles πικρᾷ γλωχίνι [with sharp point] and πικροῦ κνώδοντος [of the sharp blade] (of a sword). Codex Aeschylus and Cratinus in the Cretan Women. These notations of the grammarians are perhaps to be understood as meaning that Cratinus said πισσοκωνήτῳ πυρί [with pitch-coned fire], Aeschylus πισσοκωνήτῳ μόρῳ [with pitch-coned doom] for μόρῳ πισσοκωνήτων νεκρῶν [doom of pitch-coned corpses], who are called πισσήρεις [pitched] in the oracle in Athenaeus 12 p. 524a. sense.note: Est poetica verbi πίπτωI fall forma (ut μίμνωI remain pro μένωI remain ), qua tragici saepe sunt usi. Frequens autem in codicibus tragicorum accentus vitium est πιτνεῖνto fall et πίτνῶνfalling pariterque in compositis ἐμπίτνωI fall upon et προσπίτνωI fall before . Rectum accentum plerumque servarunt antiquiores codices, inter eosque Mediceus Sophoclis, et testantur grammatici veteres: de quo dixi in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1128 post Elmsleium ad Eur. Heracl. 77 et Med. 53.

It is a poetic form of the verb pipto (like mimno for meno), which the tragedians often used. Moreover, in the manuscripts of the tragedians there is a frequent accentual error pitnein and pitnon, and likewise in the compounds empitno and prospitno. The correct accent has generally been preserved by the older manuscripts, among them the Medicean of Sophocles, and the ancient grammarians attest it: on which I have spoken in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1128 after Elmsley on Eur. Heracl. 77 and Med. 53.

Adiectivi πολύςmuch gradus comparativus est πλείωνmore et genere neutro πλέονmore . Attici etsi saepissime πλέονmore pro πλεῖονmore dixe-runt nec raro vocalem simplicem in casibus ad-miserunt trisyllabis πλέονος πλέονιof more, to more et ceteris, in nominativo tamen πλείωνmore et formis contractis πλείωmore et πλείουςmore diphthongum praetulerunt: quod recte observanti Reisigio Coni. in Aristoph. p. 43 non debebat repugnare Elmsl. ad Eur. Med. 88. Nam quod tragici interdum πλέων πλέω πλέουςof more, more, more dixisse vulgo creduntur, partim criticorum nititur erroribus, partim vitiosa scriptura librorum. Sic ter peccatum aqud Aeschylum est,

The comparative degree of the adjective πολύς [much] is πλείων [more] and in the neuter πλέον [more]. The Attics, although they very often said πλέον [more] for πλεῖον [more] and not rarely admitted the simple vowel in the trisyllabic cases πλέονος [of more], πλέονι [to more] and the rest, nevertheless in the nominative πλείων [more] and the contracted forms πλείω [more] and πλείους [more] preferred the diphthong: which Reisig, Coni. in Aristoph. p. 43, rightly observing, Elmsley on Eur. Med. 88 ought not to have opposed. For the fact that the tragedians are commonly believed to have sometimes said πλέων [more], πλέω [more], πλέους [more] rests partly on the errors of critics, partly on the faulty writing of the manuscripts. Thus three times the mistake is made in Aeschylus,

cit.note: Δαριου [of Darius]
cit.quote: θεομήστωρ δ᾽ ἔσκεν, ἐπεὶ στρατὸν εὐ ποδούχει
He was a godlike ruler, since he guided the army well with his foot
cit.note: Sic emendavi quod est in Μ στρατὸν ὑποδώκειhe guided the army under (his foot) , a m. secunda in eὐ ἐποδώκειhe guided well muta-tum. Scholiasta, ὑπὸ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ πόδα ἡνιόχειhe drove it under his own foot . Proxime ab vero aberat Tan. Faber Epist. 1, 67 p. 223 εὐ ἐποδόχειhe guided well corrigens, quod εὐ ποδούχειhe guided well with his foot scribendum erat. De verbo ποδουχεῖνto guide with the foot , in libris plerumque ποδοχεῖνto guide with the foot scripto, videndi loci grammaticorum collecti in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1280 et in Philologo vol. 13 p. 486 487.

Thus I emended what is in M στρατὸν ὑποδώκει [he guided the army under (his foot)], changed by a second hand to εὐ ἐποδώκει [he guided well]. The scholiast says, ὑπὸ τὸν ἑαυτοῦ πόδα ἡνιόχει [he drove it under his own foot]. Tan. Faber Epist. 1, 67 p. 223 was closest to the truth in correcting to εὐ ἐποδόχει [he guided well], which should have been written εὐ ποδούχει [he guided well with his foot]. On the verb ποδουχεῖν [to guide with the foot], usually written ποδοχεῖν in the books, see the passages of grammarians collected in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1280 and in Philologus vol. 13 p. 486 487.

In M the gloss is ποίμνιον [flock] and the scholia, τὸ ἀνδρικὸν πλῆθος, σημαῖνον τὸ στράτευμα παρὰ τὸ τοὺς βασιλεῖς λέγεσθαι ποιμένας. ποιμανόριον τὸ ἐκ ποίμνης ἀνδρῶν συνηγμένον βασίλειον [the manly multitude, signifying the army because kings are called shepherds; poimanorion is the royal assembly gathered from a flock of men]. On the form of this and the next word ποιμάνωρ [shepherd of men] see Lobeck. Paral. p. 218. The neuter is not found in other writers.

as Homer says πολιὴν ἅλα [the gray sea] and πολιὴν θάλασσαν [the gray sea], others have said other such things, collected in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1344. Catullus used the verb incanesco at 61, 13 tortaque remigio spumis incanuit unda [and the wave, churned by the oar, grew white with foam]. Schol. exp. άφριζο-μένης τῷ ἀφρῷ τῆς κωπηλασίας [foaming with the foam of the rowing].

Thus Porson for πολισσούχοι [city-guardians], which in some copies was ineptly changed to πολισοῦχοι [city-guardians]. The form πολισσούχος [city-guarding] will be discussed in its place.

Thus I corrected what is in M (with ἰὼ ἰὼ [io io] omitted) θεοὶ πολιάοχοι χθονός [gods who hold the city of the land], from which in the copies was made πολισούχοι [city-guardians] or πολισσούχοι [city-guardians].

Ib. 1006. [Ch. 289.] Rarius in aliis metris. Sept. 165 προφρόνως | ἑπτάπυλον πόλεως ἕδος ἐπιρρύουgraciously | the seven-gated seat of the city . Ib. 418. 761. Suppl. 902. Dicitur non solum de urbe ipsa, sed etiam de civitate, i.e. communione hominum in urbe habitantium.

with genitive πόλεως [of the city] or where the meter demands πόλεος [of the city]. πόλεως [of the city] not rarely with synizesis, as in the trimeters Sept. 2 ἐν πρύμνη πόλεως [in the stern of the city]. [273] 539 572 Ag. 1412 1586. Eum. 617 [701] 704. 868. Suppl. 248 388 619 902 and at the beginning of trimeters, where it is rather an iamb than an anapest, as Sept. 471 πόλεως ἀπείργειν [to keep from the city]. and at the end of trimeters Sept. 57 ἄνδρας ἐκκρίτους πόλεως [chosen men of the city]. Ib. 1006. [Ch. 289.] More rarely in other meters. Sept. 165 προφρόνως | ἑπτάπυλον πόλεως ἕδος ἐπιρρύου [graciously protect the seven-gated seat of the city]. Ib. 418. 761. Suppl. 902. It is said not only of the city itself, but also of the state, i.e. the community of people living in the city.

σικ κορρεχτι προ πόλεως πολύβοτος τ᾽. Βρεβιτερ σχολ. εν Μ ὁ ὑπὸ πολλῶν ἐμβατευόμενος ἀνδρῶν, ἢ ὁ ἐπιπολὺ ἐκτεινόμενος, θυαρωμ ιντερπρετατιονυμ πριορ αδ πολύβατος, αλτερα αδ πολύτατος σπεχταρε βιδετυρ. Σχολιασταε βετερις αννοτατιονεμ συις αλλαδιταμεντις αυξιτ σχολιαστα Βυζαντινυς ἁπλῶς πάντες οἱ ἄνθρωποι · τοῦτο γὰρ δηλοῖ τὸ “πολύ-βοτος αἰὼν βροτῶν, ἤγουν ἡ ζωὴ καὶ ὁ βίος τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὁ πολύβοτος καὶ ὁ πολλοὺς τρέφων, ἢ ὑπὸ τῶν πολλῶν ἐμβατευόμενος ἢ ὁ ἐπὶ πολὺ ἐκτεινόμενος. Θομας Μαγ. ὁ πολύβοτος ἢ ἀντὶ τοῦ πολυκτήμων λογιστέον, ἢ ὁ πολλοὺς βό-σκωνsic correcti pro πόλεως πολύβοτος τ᾽. Breviter schol. in M ὁ ὑπὸ πολλῶν ἐμβατευόμενος ἀνδρῶν, ἢ ὁ ἐπιπολὺ ἐκτεινόμενος, quarum interpretationum prior ad πολύβατος, altera ad πολύτατος spectare videtur. Scholiastae veteris annotationem suis additamentis auxit scholiasta Byzantinus ἁπλῶς πάντες οἱ ἄνθρωποι [simply all men] · τοῦτο γὰρ δηλοῖ τὸ “πολύ-βοτος αἰὼν βροτῶν, ἤγουν ἡ ζωὴ καὶ ὁ βίος τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὁ πολύβοτος καὶ ὁ πολλοὺς τρέφων, ἢ ὑπὸ τῶν πολλῶν ἐμβατευόμενος ἢ ὁ ἐπὶ πολὺ ἐκτεινόμενος [for this is what “much-nourishing lifetime of mortals” means, that is the life and livelihood of men, the much-nourishing and the one feeding many, or the one frequented by many, or the one extending far]. Thomas Mag. ὁ πολύβοτος ἢ ἀντὶ τοῦ πολυκτήμων λογιστέον, ἢ ὁ πολλοὺς βό-σκων [“much-nourishing” is to be understood either as “rich in possessions” or as “feeding many”] .

cit.note: ubi suspectum est prius πολύςmuch, many , non tam propter iteratum πολύςmuch, many in versu proximo πολὺς ὄλβοςgreat wealth , etsi hoc quoque aliquid offensionis habet, quam quod nihil causae erat cur πολὺς πλούτου λιμήνgreat harbor of wealth diceret, quum in promptu esset μέγας πλούτου λιμήνgreat harbor of wealth , quod dixit Euripides Or. 1077 ὦ δῶμα πατρὸς καὶ μέγας πλούτου λιμήνO house of my father and great harbor of wealth . Hoc igitur Aeschylo quoque restituendum videtur Nauckio in Mélanges Gréco-Romains vol. 3. a. 1871 p. 295, idque tanto magis quod πολύςmuch, many pro μέγαςgreat dictum Byzantinae potius quam veteris Graecitatis est. Recte vero dictum

where the first πολύς [much] is suspect, not so much because of the repeated πολύς [much] in the next verse πολὺς ὄλβος [great wealth], although this too has something offensive, but because there was no reason why he should say πολὺς πλούτου λιμήν [a great harbor of wealth], when μέγας πλούτου λιμήν [a great harbor of wealth] was ready, which Euripides said Or. 1077 ὦ δῶμα πατρὸς καὶ μέγας πλούτου λιμήν [O house of my father and great harbor of wealth]. This therefore seems to Nauck in Mélanges Gréco-Romains vol. 3. a. 1871 p. 295 to be restored to Aeschylus too, and that all the more because πολύς [much] for μέγας [great] is characteristic of Byzantine rather than ancient Greek. But rightly said

Σεδ τραγικι φορμαμ Δορικαμ βιδεντυρ πραετυλισσε, υτ πόρ-παμα, νον πόρπημα διξιτ Ευριπιδες: β. Θες. βολ. 6 π. 1501. Δε θυο γενερε εν υνιβερσυμ διξιτ Λοβεχκ. αδ. Πηρυν. π. 205, χυιυς εχασμπλις φορ-τασσε αλλαδενδυμ αὔδασον εν τριμετρο Ευριπιδες ΠηοενThe letter α θυμ προδυχατυρ [the letter alpha with the theta?] makes it clear that the present is not πορπάζω [to fasten with a pin], but πορπάω [to fasten with a pin], whence the aorist πορπῆσαι [to fasten with a pin]. But the tragedians seem to have preferred the Doric form, as Euripides said πόρπαμα [a pin], not πόρπημα [a pin]: b. Thes. vol. 6 p. 1501. Ηαεχ διχι εν Πραεφ. εδ. Λιπς. θυιν-ταε π. ΛΧΧΧΙΙThe rushing bird sends with the spear the avenger of justice to the Teucrian land .

Πέμπει σὺν δορὶ δίκας πράκτορι θούριος ὄρνις Τευκρίδ᾽ ἐπ᾽ αἰαν [The rushing bird sends with the spear the avenger of justice to the Teucrian land], where the gloss δίκας [of justice] explains two words of the poet, which Aristophanes preserved in Frogs 1288: πέμπει σύν δορὶ καὶ χερὶ πράκτορι [sends with spear and avenging hand], although this reading labors under a slight corruption. For since the verse is antispastic dactylic tetrameter catalectic in disyllabum and therefore ends with a spondee, πράκτορι [avenger] cannot have been placed by Aeschylus in the strophe, who had written πράκτωρ [avenger]: if the scribes had left it untouched after the datives σὺν δορὶ καὶ χερί [with spear and hand], it would be much more surprising than that they changed it to πράκτορι [avenger]. But rightly the eagle, by whose portentous authority the Atreidae had been sent against Troy to exact vengeance, is called πράκτωρ [avenger], who πέμπει σὺν δορὶ καὶ χερί [sends with spear and hand], i.e. with arms and men. This I said in the Preface to the Leipzig edition, fifth, p. LXXXII.

form.gloss: to do, act; to exact punishment, avenge; to fare

sense.note: In codicibus tragicorum interdum male πράττεινto do, to fare scriptum, ut Ag. 1331.
In the manuscripts of the tragedians sometimes wrongly written πράττειν [to do], as at Ag. 1331.

cit.note: Sic correxi pro δικαίωςjustly , quod est in M, sed ou in litura, superscripto a m. antiqua w, quod est δικαίωςjustly . Non animadvertit corrector ex adiectivo δίκαιοςjust ad verbum πρᾶξαιto do, to accomplish intelligendum esse δικαίωςjustly .

Thus I corrected for δικαίως [justly], which is in M, but ou in an erasure, with w written above by an old hand, which is δικαίως [justly]. The corrector did not notice that from the adjective δίκαιος [just] δικαίως [justly] must be understood with the verb πρᾶξαι [to do].

ἐμασχαλίσθη δ᾽, ἔθ᾽ ὡς τόδ᾽ εἰδῇς. | ἔπρασσε δ᾽ ἁπέρ νιν, ὧδε θάπτει, | μόρον κτίσαι μωμένα | ἄφερτον αἰῶνι σῷ

cit.note: sic Schuetzius pro ἅπερthe very things which . ubi scholiasts κατεσκεύασε δὲ τὸ τὸ μασχαλισθῆναι αὐτὸν ἡ Κλυταιμνήστρα. ἢ καὶ οὕτως ἀτίμως αὐτὸν θάψασα δυστυχίαν μεγίστην κατασκευάζουσα τῷ σῷ βίῳ, ὦ Ὀρέστα · ὅ ἐστιν, ἵνα δυστυχή βίον Ζήσης, τοῦ Ἀγαμέμνονος μὴ δυναμένου σοι συμμαχῆσαι πρὸς τὴν τιμωρίαν ΚλυταιμνήστραςAnd she prepared the mutilation of him, Clytemnestra. Or also thus dishonorably burying him, preparing the greatest misfortune for your life, Orestes; that is, in order that you may live an unfortunate life, Agamemnon being unable to assist you in the punishment of Clytemnestra. .

thus Schuetz for ἅπερ [which things]. where the scholiast says: κατεσκεύασε δὲ τὸ τὸ μασχαλισθῆναι αὐτὸν ἡ Κλυταιμνήστρα [Clytemnestra contrived his mutilation]. ἢ καὶ οὕτως ἀτίμως αὐτὸν θάψασα δυστυχίαν μεγίστην κατασκευάζουσα τῷ σῷ βίῳ, ὦ Ὀρέστα [or, having buried him so dishonorably, she is preparing the greatest misfortune for your life, Orestes] · ὅ ἐστιν, ἵνα δυστυχή βίον Ζήσης, τοῦ Ἀγαμέμνονος μὴ δυναμένου σοι συμμαχῆσαι πρὸς τὴν τιμωρίαν Κλυταιμνήστρας [that is, so that you may live a miserable life, since Agamemnon is unable to help you in avenging Clytemnestra].

χἀρπαγὰς [and plunderings] Tyrwhitt. ὑπερκόπους [excessive] Heath. which he explained by ἀπητήσαμεν, ἤτοι καθείλομεν [we demanded, that is, we destroyed], Triclinius changed to ἐφραξάμεσθα [we fenced ourselves], which should rather be written ἐφαρξάμεσθα [we fenced ourselves].

sense.def: πράσσεινto do, to fare intransitive se habere de statu rerum dicitur in quibus quis versatur (cuiusmodi exempla multa collecta sunt in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1570-1573), adiuncto plerumque adverbio, velut εὐ, κακῶς. καλῶςwell, badly, nobly .

πράσσειν [to fare] is used intransitively of the state of affairs in which one finds oneself (many examples of this kind are collected in Thes. vol. 6 p. 1570-1573), usually with an adverb, such as εὐ [well], κακῶς [badly], καλῶς [finely].

sense.note: Vocabulum haud dubie ab Aeschylo, si sic scripsit, formatum pro πρόβουλος παῖςa child who is a counselor ut εὐφιλόπαιςdear to children pueris amicissimus infra 723. "Male haec a multis intellecta sunt. Urget, inquit, ut quis in perniciem ruat, audax suada, consultrix filia effrenata culpae. Nam semel admissa culpa suadet opus potentiamque ad tuendum conferre quod iniuria possidetur, subministratque ei rei consilia. Referuntur haec ad ea quae proxime praegressa sunt diciturque suada πρόβουλοςa counselor , quod ἔπαλξιν πλούτουa bulwark of wealth quaerit.” HERMANN. Similiter Klausenus interpretatur "noxa quae mentem lae-sit, progignit persuasionem suppeditantem argu-menta quibus ad exsequenda noxae consilia com-movetur aliquis." Thomae Mag. scholion hoc est ἥτις (ἡ Πειθώ) βιάζει αὐτοὺς πρόνοιαν δῆ-θεν τοῦ πλουτῆσαι (πλουτίσαιwho (Persuasion) forces them, pretending to have forethought for enriching (to enrich Victorius) τοὺς παῖδας ποιουμένηmaking the children , et Triclinii ἡ προβουλευομένη πλουτῆσαι τοὺς παῖδαςshe who plans beforehand to enrich the children . Male Karstenus et Wei-lius scripserunt βιᾶται δ᾽ ἁ τάλαινα πειθὼ πρόβουλος, παῖς ἄφερτος ἄταςand wretched Persuasion, the counselor, the unbridled child of Ruin, forces , (et in versu strophico 368 πάρεστινis present pro πάρεστιis present ) quae prava interpunctio est, in quam nemo in-cidcre potest nisi quem comma post πρόβουλοςa counselor positum admoneat. Melius Hartungus πειθώ, προβούλου παῖς ἄφερτος ἄταςPersuasion, unbridled child of Ruin the counselor . Nam ἄτηRuin con-silia dat, ad quae exsequenda πειθώPersuasion compellit. Recte igitur πειθώPersuasion fiiia esse dicitur ἄτης προ-βούλουof Ruin the counselor . Similiter Todtius Comment. p. 34.

A word undoubtedly formed by Aeschylus, if he wrote it thus, for πρόβουλος παῖς [a child who is a counselor], like εὐφιλόπαις [dear to children] below at 723. "These words have been badly understood by many. He says, 'Persuasion, the audacious counselor, the unbridled daughter of Ruin, urges one to rush into destruction. For once guilt has been admitted, it persuades one to bring to bear the work and power to protect what is unjustly possessed, and supplies plans for that purpose.' These words refer to what immediately precedes, and Persuasion is called πρόβουλος [a counselor] because she seeks an ἔπαλξιν πλούτου [a bulwark of wealth]." HERMANN. Similarly Klausen interprets: "the guilt that has injured the mind begets persuasion that supplies arguments by which one is moved to carry out the plans of guilt." The scholion of Thomas Magister is: ἥτις (ἡ Πειθώ) βιάζει αὐτοὺς πρόνοιαν δῆθεν τοῦ πλουτῆσαι (πλουτίσαι Victorius) τοὺς παῖδας ποιουμένη [who (Persuasion) forces them, pretending to have forethought for enriching (to enrich Victorius) the children], and that of Triclinius: ἡ προβουλευομένη πλουτῆσαι τοὺς παῖδας [she who plans beforehand to enrich the children]. Karsten and Weil wrongly wrote βιᾶται δ᾽ ἁ τάλαινα πειθὼ πρόβουλος, παῖς ἄφερτος ἄτας [and wretched Persuasion, the counselor, the unbridled child of Ruin, forces], (and in the strophic verse 368 πάρεστιν for πάρεστι), which is a faulty punctuation, into which no one can fall unless warned by a comma placed after πρόβουλος. Hartung is better: πειθώ, προβούλου παῖς ἄφερτος ἄτας [Persuasion, unbridled child of Ruin the counselor]. For Ruin gives the plans, to the execution of which Persuasion compels. Rightly, therefore, Persuasion is said to be the daughter of Ruin the counselor. Similarly Todt in his Commentary p. 34.

cit.note: ubi in Μ προμήθειανM forethought , sed supra scri-pto 1, i.e. προμηθίανforethought . Utraque aque forma recte ha-bet, sed tragici προμηθίαforethought videntur praetulisse, quam formam apud Sophoclem et Euripidem me-trum ubique vel fert vel postulat: de quo dixi in Thes, vol. 6 p. 1776.

Both forms are correct, but the tragedians seem to have preferred προμηθία [forethought], which form in Sophocles and Euripides the meter everywhere either allows or demands: on which I have spoken in Thes., vol. 6 p. 1776.

sense.note: Μυθουμ δε Προ-μεθεο, δε θυο βιδενδυς Απολλοδορυς 1, 7, 1, τριβυς φαβυλις τραχταβι Αεσχυλυς, τραγοεδιις δυα-βυς, Προμηθεῖ δεσμώτη, θυα συπερεστ, ετ λυο-μένῳ, φαβυλα σατυριχα υνα, θυα σιμπλιχι Προ-μηθέως νομα ενσχριπτα φυιτ αβ Αεσχυλο, Προ-μηθεὺς πυρφόρος αβ γραμματιχις Αλεξανδρινις. Δε ηις φαβυλις σκριπτορ Βιταε Αεσχυλι εν Σχολ. εδ. Οχον. π. 8, 1 ταύτῃ καὶ ἄριστος εἰς τραγῳ-δίαν Αἰσχύλος κρίνεται, ὅτι εἰσάγει πρόσωπα μεγάλα καὶ ἀξιόχρεα. καὶ τινὲς ἤδη τῶν τραγῳ-διῶν διὰ μόνων οἰκονομοῦνται τῶν θεῶν, καθά-περ οἱ Προμηθεῖς. Δε βανα μυλτορυμ οπινιονε, θυι τετραλογιαμ Προμεθεαμ εχ τριβυς τραγοεδιις Προμηθεῖ πυρφόρῳ, δεσμώτη, λυομένῳ (λιχετ εν δεσμώτη ρεσ Προμεθει ιτα εχποναντυρ υτ νυλλαμ αλιαμ φαβυλαμ πραεχεσσισσε αππαρεατ) ετ φαβυλα σατυριχα ιγνοτα χομποσιταμ φινχερυντ, δρα-μα αυτεμ σατυριχυμ Προμηθέα, θυο ολυμπ. 76, 4 χυμ τριβυς τραγοεδιις (Φινεῖ, Πέρσαις, Γλαύ-κῳ) αχτυμ εσσε νοβιμυς, νον Προμηθέα πυρφό-pov, σεδ Πολλυχιs (9, 156) Προμηθέα πυρκαέα, χυ-ιυς νυλλυς υνθυαμ αλιυς τεστις προδυχετυρ, φυισσε χρεδιδερυντ, διχι εν Βιτα Σοπηοχλις εδ. Οχον. α. 1860. βολ. 8 π. ΛΧΙΙ. υβι ερρορισ α Πολλυχε χομ. μισσι οριγινεμ πατεφεχι. Αλιι Προμηθέα πυρφόρον τερτιαμ φυισσε χρεδιδερυντ τετραλογιαε φαβυλαμ, νομινε νον προπτερ φυρτυμ ιγνις ιμποσιτο, σεδ αδ λαμπαδοδρομίας, Αθενις εν ηονορεμ Προμε-θει θυοταννις χελεβρατας ρεφερεβδο: θυοδ ινστι-τυτυμ μεμοραρι ποτυερατ εν εχστρεμα παρτε Προ-μηθέως λυομένου (εν θυα ετιαμ δε χορονα Προ-μεθει σερμο φυιτ: βιδ. φρ. 204), υτ ηονορες Ευ-μενιδιβυς ηαβενδι εν φινε φαβυλαε χογνομινις, θυαε σολλεμνι πομπα χλαυδιτυρ, εχπονοντυρ, σεδ χυομοδο ιντεγραε τραγοεδιαε χομπονενδαε, ει-θυε ταλι θυαλεσ Αεσχυλυς φαχερε σολεβατ, συφφι-χερε ποτυεριτ νον περσπιχιτυρBut about Prometheus, as we see in Apollodorus 1, 7, 1, three fables were treated by Aeschylus, in two tragedies, Prometheus Bound, which survives, and Prometheus Unbound, and in one satyr play, which was inscribed by Aeschylus with the simple name Prometheus, Prometheus the Fire-Bearer by the Alexandrian grammarians. About these fables the writer of the Life of Aeschylus in the Scholia, ed. Oxon. p. 8, 1 says: ταύτῃ καὶ ἄριστος εἰς τραγῳδίαν Αἰσχύλος κρίνεται, ὅτι εἰσάγει πρόσωπα μεγάλα καὶ ἀξιόχρεα. καὶ τινὲς ἤδη τῶν τραγῳδιῶν διὰ μόνων οἰκονομοῦνται τῶν θεῶν, καθάπερ οἱ Προμηθεῖς [In this way Aeschylus is judged best in tragedy, because he introduces great and worthy characters. And some of the tragedies are managed by the gods alone, as the Prometheus plays]. But about the vain opinion of many, who have imagined that a tetralogy Promethea was composed of three tragedies, Prometheus the Fire-Bearer, Bound, Unbound (although in the Bound the affairs of Prometheus are so set forth that no other fable appears to have preceded), and an unknown satyr play, but that the satyr drama Prometheus, which we know was performed in Olympiad 76, 4 with three tragedies (Phineus, Persians, Glaucus), was not Prometheus the Fire-Bearer, but Pollux (9, 156) Prometheus the Fire-Kindler, of whom no other witness is ever produced, they have believed; I have said in the Life of Sophocles, ed. Oxon. a. 1860, vol. 8 p. LXII, where I have revealed the origin of the error committed by Pollux. Others have believed that Prometheus the Fire-Bearer was the third play of the tetralogy, the name being imposed not on account of the theft of fire, but referring to the torch-races celebrated at Athens every year in honor of Prometheus: which institution could have been mentioned in the final part of Prometheus Unbound (in which also there was a speech about the crown for Prometheus: see fr. 204), as the honors to be given to the Eumenides are set forth at the end of the play of that name, which is closed with a solemn procession, but how it could have sufficed for the composition of a whole tragedy, and such as Aeschylus was accustomed to make, is not clear. .

The myth of Prometheus, as seen in Apollodorus 1, 7, 1, was treated by Aeschylus in three plays, two tragedies, Prometheus Bound, which survives, and Prometheus Unbound, and one satyr play, which was inscribed by Aeschylus with the simple name Prometheus, Prometheus the Fire-Bearer by the Alexandrian grammarians. About these plays the writer of the Life of Aeschylus in the Scholia, ed. Oxon. p. 8, 1 says: ταύτῃ καὶ ἄριστος εἰς τραγῳδίαν Αἰσχύλος κρίνεται, ὅτι εἰσάγει πρόσωπα μεγάλα καὶ ἀξιόχρεα. καὶ τινὲς ἤδη τῶν τραγῳδιῶν διὰ μόνων οἰκονομοῦνται τῶν θεῶν, καθάπερ οἱ Προμηθεῖς [In this way Aeschylus is judged best in tragedy, because he introduces great and worthy characters. And some of his tragedies are managed by the gods alone, as the Prometheus plays]. From the vain opinion of many, who have imagined that the Prometheus tetralogy was composed of three tragedies, Prometheus the Fire-Bearer, Bound, Unbound (although in the Bound the affairs of Prometheus are so set forth that no other play seems to have preceded), and an unknown satyr play, but the satyr drama Prometheus, which we know was performed in Olympiad 76, 4 with three tragedies (Phineus, Persians, Glaucus), was not Prometheus the Fire-Bearer, but Pollux (9, 156) Prometheus the Fire-Kindler, of whom no other witness is ever produced, they have believed; see the Life of Sophocles, ed. Oxon. a. 1860. vol. 8 p. LXII, where I have revealed the origin of the error of Pollux. Others have believed that Prometheus the Fire-Bearer was the third play of the tetralogy, the name imposed not on account of the theft of fire, but referring to the torch-races celebrated at Athens every year in honor of Prometheus: which institution could have been mentioned in the final part of Prometheus Unbound (in which there was also a speech about the crown for Prometheus: see fr. 204), as the honors to be given to the Eumenides are set forth at the end of the play of that name, which is closed with a solemn procession, but how it could have sufficed for the composition of a whole tragedy, and such as Aeschylus was accustomed to make, is not clear.

the seer shrieked out another remedy for the storm, heavier for the leaders

the leaders and chiefs of the Achaeans

cit.quote: κόναβος ἐν πύλαις χαλκοδέτων σακέων
the din of bronze-bound shields in the gates

sense.note: Ad hunc versum nihil aunotatum in scholiis Mediceis; re-centiores interpretes ad κόναβοςdin, clash intelligunt ἐστίis , quod etsi nemo ignorat saepissime omitti, tamen qui praecedentes versus similes comparaverit, quorum unusquisque significantius al aliquod verbum additum habet, vix verisimile esse iudicabit nullum gravius Aeschylo hic in promptu fuisse verbum quam debile illud ἐστίis , idque ne expres-sum quidem, sed cogitatione supplendum. Ve-rum hic quoque Aeschylus non sua, sed libra-riorum culpa sui dissimilis factus est. Hinc conieci κόναβος ἐν πύλαις δεινὰ προμυχθίζει χαλ-κοδέτων σακέωνthe din of bronze-bound shields groans terribly in the gates , trimetro dochmiaco inter di-metros posito, quemadmodum in prima huius carminis parte trimetri et dimetri mixti sunt. Post ἐν πύλαιςin the gates duae exciderunt syllabae, quae etsi facile sic possunt suppleri ut ἐν πύλαισι δὲand in the gates scribatur, tamen probabilius est vocabulum ali-quod disyllabum excidisse, velut quod exempli causa inserui δεινάterribly . Verbum προμυχθίζειgroans forth sup-plevi ex glossa Hesychii sic scripta in codice, προμυχθίζει χαλκοδεσμῶν ὁπλῶν: ἀντὶ τοῦ προσ-χωρίουgroans forth of bronze-bound weapons: instead of advances . Quae sic sunt in ordinem redigenda, προμυχθίζει χαλκοδέτων σακέων: ἀντὶ τοῦ πρό-σω χωρεῖ χαλκοδέσμων ὅπλωνgroans forth of bronze-bound shields: instead of advances of bronze-bound weapons . Brevius Pho-tius p. 455, 25 προμυθίζει: πρόσω χωρεῖadvances , ubi προμυθίζειadvances pro προμυχθίζειgroans forth vel librarii errore scriptum est vel ipsius Photii, quum glossa ante προμυλαίαthe forecourt posita sit, etsi huic argumento non multum tribuendum est, quum ordo saepe ne-glectus ab Photio sit. Alio huius verbi compo-sito ἀναμυχθίζεσθαιto groan back Aeschylus usus est in Pro-metheo v. 743.

On this verse nothing is noted in the Medicean scholia; recent interpreters understand ἐστί [is] with κόναβος [the din], which although everyone knows is very often omitted, nevertheless whoever compares the preceding similar verses, each of which has some more significant verb added, will judge it hardly likely that no weightier verb was at hand for Aeschylus here than that weak ἐστί [is], and that not even expressed, but to be supplied in thought. But here too Aeschylus has been made unlike himself not by his own fault but by that of the scribes. Hence I conjectured κόναβος ἐν πύλαις δεινὰ προμυχθίζει χαλκοδέτων σακέων [the din of bronze-bound shields groans terribly in the gates], with a dochmiac trimeter placed among dimeters, just as in the first part of this song trimeters and dimeters are mixed. After ἐν πύλαις [in the gates] two syllables have fallen out, which although they can easily be supplied so that ἐν πύλαισι δὲ [and in the gates] is written, nevertheless it is more probable that some disyllabic word has fallen out, such as δεινά [terribly], which I inserted by way of example. The verb προμυχθίζει [groans forth] I supplied from a gloss of Hesychius written thus in the codex, προμυχθίζει χαλκοδεσμῶν ὁπλῶν: ἀντὶ τοῦ προσχωρίου [groans forth of bronze-bound weapons: instead of advances]. Which are to be arranged thus, προμυχθίζει χαλκοδέτων σακέων: ἀντὶ τοῦ πρόσω χωρεῖ χαλκοδέσμων ὅπλων [groans forth of bronze-bound shields: instead of advances of bronze-bound weapons]. More briefly Photius p. 455, 25 προμυθίζει: πρόσω χωρεῖ [advances], where προμυθίζει [advances] is written for προμυχθίζει [groans forth] either by a scribal error or by Photius himself, since the gloss is placed before προμυλαία [the forecourt], although not much weight should be given to this argument, since the order is often neglected by Photius. Aeschylus used another compound of this verb, ἀναμυχθίζεσθαι [to groan back], in Prometheus v. 743.
