ὁρκάνα πυργῶτις.
a turreted fence.
ἴστω δ' ὅστις οὐχ ὑπόπτερος φροντίσιν, τὰν δαεῖσ᾽ ἀ παιδολυμὰς τάλαινα Θεστιάς μήσατο πυρδαῆτιν πρόνοιαν, καταίθουσα παιδὸς δαφοινὸν ἥλικα.
Let him know who is not winged in his thoughts, that the child-destroying, wretched daughter of Thestius devised a fire-consuming forethought, burning the bloody age-mate of her son.
cit.note: Sic Hermannus pro φροντίσιν δαεὶς τὰν ἁ πυρδαή τινα πρόνοιανhaving been taught in thoughts the fire-consuming forethought . Schol. οὕτω τὸ ἑξῆς, ἥντινα μήσατο πρόνοιαν τάλαινα Θεστιὰς ἡ παιδολυμὰς καὶ πυρδαήςthus the sequence: what forethought the wretched Thestias, child-destroying and fire-consuming, devised , qui πυρδαήςfire-consuming legit.

Thus Hermann for φροντίσιν δαεὶς τὰν ἁ πυρδαή τινα πρόνοιαν [having been taught in thoughts the fire-consuming forethought]. Schol. οὕτω τὸ ἑξῆς, ἥντινα μήσατο πρόνοιαν τάλαινα Θεστιὰς ἡ παιδολυμὰς καὶ πυρδαής [thus the sequence: what forethought the wretched Thestias, child-destroying and fire-consuming, devised], who reads πυρδαής [fire-consuming].

cit.quote: στόμια πυριβρεμετᾶν χαλινῶν.
the bits of fire-thundering bridles.
cit.note: Legebatur πυριγενετᾶνborn in fire (in igni natorum). Restitui πυριβρεμετᾶνthundering with fire , quod latet in Timachidae Rhodii glossa ab Hesychio excerpta, πυριβρεμέτας: ὁ χαλινός. Τιμαχίδας δέ· ἤτοι ὁ πυρὶ βρέμων, ἢ διὰ πυρὸς βρέμοντος γεγονώςthe bridle. But Timachidas says: either he who roars with fire, or he who was born through roaring fire . ubi nihil causae est cur post χαλινόςbridle aliquot verba interpretandi causa addita excidisse putentur.

It was read πυριγενετᾶν [born in fire]. I restored πυριβρεμετᾶν [thundering with fire], which is hidden in the gloss of Timachidas of Rhodes excerpted by Hesychius, πυριβρεμέτας: ὁ χαλινός. Τιμαχίδας δέ· ἤτοι ὁ πυρὶ βρέμων, ἢ διὰ πυρὸς βρέμοντος γεγονώς [fire-thundering: the bridle. But Timachidas: either he who thunders with fire, or he who was born through thundering fire]. Where there is no reason why after χαλινός [bridle] some words added for the sake of interpretation should be thought to have fallen out.

cit.quote: πυριδάπτῳ λαμπάδι τερπόμεναι.
delighting in the fire-devouring torch
πυρίφατον τάνδε Πελασγέαν
this Pelasgian land slain by fire
cit.note: quod per πυρὶ ἀναλωθεῖσανconsumed by fire exp. scholiasta.
which the scholiast explains by πυρὶ ἀναλωθεῖσαν [consumed by fire]

cit.quote: κάμακες πεύκης οἱ πυρίφλεκτοι.
the pine shafts, the fire-burned ones
πυροφόροιο Γέλας.
of wheat-bearing Gela
cit.note: In elegia.
In an elegy.

cit.quote: μακρὰν ὀσφῦν πυρώσας.
having burned the long loin
πυρωθέν ἐξ Ἰλίου φίλοισι πέμπει βαρύ (βραχύ Schuetzius) ψήγμα.
burned from Ilium, he sends to his friends a heavy (small, according to Schuetz) piece of metal
στέγην πυρώσω.
I will burn the house
φλογὸς παραγγέλμασιν νέοις πυρωθέντα καρδίαν.
with new commands of flame, having burned the heart
θερμοῖς ἀπλάτου βέλεσι πυρπνόου ζάλης.
with hot missiles of unapproachable fire-breathing storm
τινάσσων τ᾽ ἐν χεροῖν πύρπνουν βέλος
brandishing in his hands a fire-breathing missile
cit.note: ubi Porsonus coniecit τινάσσων χερσὶ πυρπνόον βέλοςbrandishing in his hands a fire-breathing missile .
where Porson conjectured τινάσσων χερσὶ πυρπνόον βέλος [brandishing in his hands a fire-breathing missile]

cit.quote: Τυφῶν᾽ ἱέντα πυρπνόον διὰ στόμα λιγνὺν μέλαιναν.
Typhon sending forth through his mouth fire-breathing black smoke
πυρπνόον Τυφώνα.
fire-breathing Typhon

entry.note: Photius p. 477, 11. πυρσοκόρσου λέοντος: Αἰσχύλος ἐν Κήρυξι σατύροιςof a red-maned lion: Aeschylus in the satyr play Kerykes (fr. 111). Hesychius, πυρσοκόρσου λέοντος: πυρροκεφάλου, ξανθοτρίχουof a red-maned lion: red-headed, yellow-haired .
Photius p. 477, 11. πυρσοκόρσου λέοντος [of a red-maned lion]: Aeschylus in the satyr play Kerykes (fr. 111). Hesychius, πυρσοκόρσου λέοντος [of a red-maned lion]: red-headed, yellow-haired.

cit.quote: πυρσὴν Ζαπληθῆ δάσκιον γενειάδα.
a red, very thick, shaggy beard
cit.note: Sic Porsonus. πυρὰνred pr. Μ, πυρρὰνM, red ab correctore, quod contra dialectum tragicorum peccat.
Thus Porson. πυρὰν [red] first hand M, πυρρὰν [red] by a corrector, which sins against the dialect of the tragedians.

cit.quote: φονεύει, τὰ δὲ καὶ πυρφορεῖ.
he kills, and some things he sets on fire
ἄνδρα πυρφόρον.
a fire-bearing man
τὸν πυρφόρον κεραυνόν.
the fire-bearing thunderbolt
πυρφόροισιν ἀετοῖς.
with fire-bearing eagles

entry.note: Προμηθεὺς πυρφόροςPrometheus Fire-bearer inscriptum fuit Aeschyli drama satyricum (fr. 187-199), quod Προμηθεύς πυρκαεύςPrometheus Fire-burner appellatur a Polluce 9, 156, qui Sophoclis fabulam in mente habuit Ναύπλιος πυρκαεύςNauplius Fire-burner inscriptam: de quo dixi ad fr. 187.

Prometheus Fire-bearer was the title of a satyr play of Aeschylus (fr. 187-199), which is called Prometheus Fire-burner by Pollux 9, 156, who had in mind Sophocles' play entitled Nauplius Fire-burner: on which I have spoken at fr. 187.

cit.quote: πυρωπόν (sic ex apographis pro πυρωτόν) κεραυνόν.
fiery (thus from the copies for πυρωτόν) thunderbolt
ἥλιος πυρωπός.
the fiery sun
καὶ τῶνδε πύστις οὐκ ὄκνῳ χρονίζεται
and inquiry about these things is not delayed by hesitation
cit.note: ubi πίστιςtrust ex Stobaei Flor. 7, 11 restitui.
where I restored πίστις [trust] from Stobaeus' Florilegium 7, 11

cit.quote: ὡς μὲν ἀναίτιος εἰ τοῦδε φόνου τίς ὁ μαρτυρήσων ; πῶ πῶ ;
How shall I be innocent of this murder? Who will testify? Where? Where?
cit.note: Hoc pro πόθεν πόθενwhence, whence dictum acceperunt interpretes, Dorica adverbii forma, de qua v. Thes. vol. 6 p. 2293, sed qua non est verisimile Aeschylum usum esse, qui haud dubie πῶς πῶςhow, how scripserat, ut correctum est in marg. Askewii.

The interpreters took this as said for πόθεν πόθεν [whence, whence], a Doric form of the adverb, on which see Thes. vol. 6 p. 2293, but it is not likely that Aeschylus used it, who without doubt wrote πῶς πῶς [how, how], as corrected in the margin of Askew.

sense.def: (encliticum) aliquo modo. Pr. 27 ὁ λωφήσων γὰρ οὐ πέφυκέ πω. 511 οὐ ταῦτα ταύτη Μοῖρά πω τελεσφόρος κρᾶναι πέπρωταιFor the one who will bring relief has not yet been born. 511 Not yet has Fate the fulfiller been destined to accomplish these things in this way. .

(enclitic) in some way. Pr. 27 ὁ λωφήσων γὰρ οὐ πέφυκέ πω [for the one who will relieve has not yet been born]. 511 οὐ ταῦτα ταύτη Μοῖρά πω τελεσφόρος κρᾶναι πέπρωται [not yet has Fate, the fulfiller, been destined to accomplish these things in this way].

entry.note: Cum negationibus οὐnot et μήnot coniunctum in unam vocem coalescit οὔπωnot yet et μήπωnot yet , de quibus suo loco dictum est. Interiecto vocabulo.
Joined with the negatives οὐ and μή it coalesces into one word οὔπω and μήπω, on which see in their proper place. With a word interposed.

cit.quote: οὔτ᾽ ἐν τροφαῖσιν οὔτ᾽ ἐφηβήσαντά πω.
neither in my upbringing nor yet when I reached manhood
ἀλλ᾽ οὐ τί πω τοιόνδ᾽ ἐναργὲς εἰδόμην.
but never yet have I seen such a clear thing
ἀλλ᾽ οὐ τί πω τοιόνδε πῆμ᾽ ἀνεσχόμην.
but never yet have I endured such a calamity
οὐ κειμένῳ πω τόνδε κομπάζεις λόγον.
You boast this word over one not yet laid low.
νῦν δ᾽ οὐ κέκραγά πω τὸ γενναῖον μέλος.
But now I have not yet cried out the noble strain.

sense.def: barba. Improprie de flamma quae sparsim erumpens in conum acuitur.
beard. Improperly of a flame which, bursting forth in scattered fashion, is sharpened into a cone.

cit.quote: φλογὸς μέγαν πώγωνα.
the great beard of flame.

entry.note: Pollux 2, 88 πώγων πυρός ἡ εἰς ὀξὺ ἀναδρομὴ τῆς φλογόςthe beard of fire is the upward rush of the flame to a point . Hesychio et Photio p. 478, 3 ἡ ἀναφορὰ τῆς φλογόςthe rising of the flame ex Phrixo Euripidis.

Pollux 2, 88 πώγων πυρός ἡ εἰς ὀξὺ ἀναδρομὴ τῆς φλογός [the beard of fire is the upward rush of the flame to a point]. In Hesychius and Photius p. 478, 3 ἡ ἀναφορὰ τῆς φλογός [the rising of the flame] from Euripides' Phrixus.

sense.def: of a maiden (as maidens are called πῶλοι [fillies]).

cit.quote: πωλικῶν θ᾽ ἑδωλίων.
and of the seats of maidens.
ὡς νεοζυγὴς πῶλος.
like a newly yoked foal.
κριθῶντα πῶλον.
a barley-fed foal.
πώλοις ἀκμαίοις τόνδ᾽ ἐπιζεύξασ᾽ ὄχον
having yoked this chariot to vigorous foals
cit.note: ubi Wakef. κώλοιςlimbs coniecit, de quo dixit Hermannus Opusc. vol. 6, 2 p. 174. πώλοιςfoals defendit Weckleinius Stud. Aesch. p. 10.
where Wakefield conjectured κώλοις [limbs], about which Hermann spoke in Opuscula vol. 6, 2 p. 174. Wecklein defended πώλοις [foals] in Studien zu Aeschylus p. 10.

cit.quote: ὃς εἶχε πώλους τέσσαρας Ζυγηφόρους.
who had four yoke-bearing foals.
ἐν διρρυμίᾳ πῶλοι.
foals in a two-horse chariot.
ἀνδρὸς φίλου (Agamemnonis) πώλον εὖνιν (Orestem) ζυγέντ᾽ ἐν ἅρμασιν πημάτων.
the foal of a dear man (Agamemnon), bereft (Orestes), yoked in the chariot of woes.
ὕδωρ τε Διρκαῖον εὐτραφέστατον πωμάτων.
and Dircean water, the most nourishing of drinks.
βοσκάν φεροίμαν πώματος δυσπότου.
may I bring food of a drink hard to swallow.
ποταμοὺς δ᾽ οἳ διὰ χώρας θελεμὸν πῶμα χέουσιν.
and rivers which through the land pour a gentle drink.

sense.def: quomodo? Ponitur plerumque in initio sententiae, rarius in media sententia, vel in fine.
how? It is placed mostly at the beginning of a sentence, more rarely in the middle, or at the end.

cit.quote: ἀνηκουστεῖν δὲ τῶν πατρὸς λόγων οϊόν τε πῶς ;
But how is it possible to disobey the words of one's father?
δόξει δὲ πῶς ;
But how will it seem?

entry.note: poniturque vel solum vel aliis adiunctis particulis, ut πῶς ἄν, πῶς δ᾽ ἄν, πῶς ἄρα, πῶς γάρ, πῶς δέ, πῶς δή, πῶς δῆτα, πῶς δ᾽ οὔ, πῶς δ᾽ οὐχίhow then, how indeed, how then, for how, how then, how then, how then, how not, how not , et quod frequentissimum est καὶ πῶςand how , ubi prioris personae verba continuantur. Exempla omnis generis haec sunt:

and it is placed either alone or with other particles added, such as πῶς ἄν [how then], πῶς δ᾽ ἄν [but how then], πῶς ἄρα [how then], πῶς γάρ [for how], πῶς δέ [but how], πῶς δή [how indeed], πῶς δῆτα [how in the world], πῶς δ᾽ οὔ [how not], πῶς δ᾽ οὐχί [how not], and what is most frequent, καὶ πῶς [and how], where the words of the previous person are continued. Examples of every kind are these:

cit.quote: πῶς ἐτόλμησας ;
How did you dare?
πῶς δ᾽ οὐ κλύω τῆς οἰστροδινήτου κόρης ;
But how do I not hear the gadfly-driven maiden?
πῶς δ᾽ οὐκ ἄν ;
But how not?
πῶς εἶπας ;
How did you say?
πῶς δ᾽ οὐχὶ ταρβεῖς ;
But how do you not fear?
πῶς με κελεύεις κακότητ᾽ ἀσκεῖν ;
How do you bid me practice wickedness?
πῶς σοι σύμμαχος γενήσεται ;
How will he become an ally to you?
πῶς τολμήσω ;
How shall I dare?
πῶς ἄρα πράσσει Ξέρξης ;
How then is Xerxes faring?
πῶς ἂν οὖν μένοιεν ;
How then could they remain?
πῶς δὲ καὶ στρατὸς τοσόσδε πεζός ἤνυσεν περᾶν ;
But how did such a large army on foot manage to cross?
πῶς τε δὴ καὶ ποῖ τελευτᾶν ;
And how and to what end?
πῶς τάδ᾽ οὐ νόσος φρενῶν εἶχε παῖδ᾽ ἐμόν ;
How did not madness of mind possess my child in these things?
πῶς ἂν ἐκ τούτων ἔτι πράσσοιμεν ὡς ἄριστα ;
How then might we fare best from these things?
πῶς τοῦτ᾽ ἔλεξας ;
How did you say this?
πῶς δ᾽ οὔ ;
But how not?
πῶς λιπόναυς γένωμαι ;
How shall I become a deserter of the fleet?
πῶς φής ;
How do you say?
πῶς δή ; διδαχθεὶς τοῦδε δεσπόσω λόγου.
How indeed? Having been taught, I will master this word.
καὶ πῶς ; ἀπόντων κοιράνων ἔτρεις τινάς ;
And how? Did you fear any of the absent rulers?
καὶ πῶς ἂν ὅρκου πήγμα γενναίως παγὲν παιώνιον γένοιτο ;
And how could a healing bond of an oath, nobly fixed, come about?
καὶ πῶς ;
And how?
καὶ πῶς ἐκεῖνος δεῦρ᾽ ἐτόλμησεν μολεῖν ;
And how did he dare to come here?
καὶ πῶς βέβηλον ἄλσος ἂν ῥύοιτό με ;
And how could a profane grove protect me?
πῶς δῆτ᾽ ἂν εἰπὼν κεδνὰ τἀληθῆ τύχοις ;
How in the world, then, could you, speaking good things, hit upon the truth?
πῶς δῆτ᾽ ἄνατος ἦσθα ;
How in the world were you unharmed?
πῶς γὰρ λέγεις χειμώνα ναυτικῷ στρατῷ ἐλθεῖν ;
For how do you say that a storm came upon the naval army?
πῶς κεδνὰ τοῖς κακοῖσι συμμίξω ;
How shall I mix good things with the bad?
πῶς σε προσειπω ; πῶς σε σεβίζω ;
How shall I address you? How shall I revere you?
πῶς φράσω τέλος ;
How shall I speak of the end?
πῶς θεηλάτου βοὸς δίκην πρὸς βωμὸν εὐτόλμως πατεῖς ;
How do you boldly tread to the altar like a god-driven cow?
πῶς γάρ τις πημονῆς ἀρκύστατ᾽ ἂν φάρξειεν ;
For how could one fence off the nets of ruin?
ἀλλὰ κοινωσαίμεθ᾽ (sic Porsonus pro κοινωσώμεθ᾽) ἂν πῶς ἀσφαλῆ βουλεύματα ;
But let us share (thus Porson for κοινωσώμεθ᾽) how we might make safe plans?
cit.note: Sic Blomfieldus pro ἄν πωςsomehow .
Thus Blomfield for ἄν πως [somehow].

cit.quote: πῶς σε δακρύσω ;
How shall I weep for you?
πῶς πῶς ;
How? How?
cit.note: ab Askewio restitutum pro πῶ πῶhow? how? ;
restored by Askew for πῶ πῶ [how? how?].

cit.quote: πῶς εὔφρον᾽ εἴπω ; πῶς κατεύξωμαι πατρί ;
How shall I speak auspicious words? How shall I pray to my father?
πῶς δ᾽ οὐ τὸν ἐχθρὸν ἀνταμείβεσθαι κακοῖς ;
How is it not right to repay an enemy with evils?
πῶς οὖν παλαιὰ παρὰ νεωτέρας μάθω ;
How then shall I, an old woman, learn from a younger one?
πῶς γὰρ ἐλπίσω ;
For how shall I hope?
πῶς γὰρ οὔ ;
For how not?
πῶς οὖν κελεύει νιν μολεῖν ἐσταλμένον ;
How then does he bid him come equipped?
cit.note: ubi altera persona respondet ἢ πῶς ; λέγ᾽ αὖθις, ὡς μάθω σαφέστερονor how? Speak again, so that I may understand more clearly. , ubi Valckenarius recte correxit ὅπωςhow :
where the other person answers ἢ πῶς ; λέγ᾽ αὖθις, ὡς μάθω σαφέστερον [or how? speak again, so that I may learn more clearly], where Valckenaer rightly corrected to ὅπως [so that].

cit.quote: πῶς ταῦτ᾽ ἀληθῆ καὶ βλέποντα δοξάσω ;
How shall I deem these things true and alive?
πῶς ἴσον εἰπὼν ἀνύσωμαι ;
How shall I accomplish it by speaking fairly?
πῶς ἔχει ; πῶς κέκρανται δόμοις ;
How is it? How has it been accomplished in the house?
τὰς τοῦ πατρὸς δὲ (ἐγκότους κύνας) πῶς φύγω ;
But how shall I escape my father's (wrathful hounds)?
πῶς δή ;
How then?
πῶς δ᾽ οὐ ;
How not?
πῶς γάρ σ᾽ ἔθρεψεν ;
For how did she nourish you?
πῶς ταῦτα τούτοις οὐκ ἐναντίως λέγεις ;
How do you not say these things contrary to those?
πῶς γὰρ τὸ φεύγειν τοῦδ᾽ ὑπερδικεῖς ;
For how do you defend his escape?
πρὸς ὑμῶν πῶς τιθεῖσ᾽ ἄμομφος ὦ ;
How, being placed by you, may I be blameless?
πῶς ἀγὼν κριθήσεται ;
How will the contest be decided?
ὄρνιθος ὄρνις πῶς ἂν ἁγνεύοι φαγών ;
How could a bird be pure after eating a bird?
πῶς δ᾽ ἂν γαμῶν ἄκουσαν ἄκοντος πάρα ἁγνὸς γένοιτ᾽ ἄν ;
How could one who marries an unwilling woman from an unwilling father be pure?
πῶς οὖν τελευτᾷ βασιλέοιν νείκη τάδε ;
How then do these quarrels of the kings end?
πῶς πατρῷα δώματα λιπεῖν ἔτλητε ;
How did you dare to leave your ancestral home?
πῶς οὖν πρὸς ὑμᾶς εὐσεβὴς ἐγὼ πέλω ;
How then am I pious toward you?
πῶς οὐχὶ τἀνάλωμα γίγνεται πικρόν ;
How does the expense not become bitter?
ἐγὼ δὲ πῶς δρῶ ;
But what am I to do?
πῶς δ᾽ οὐχί ;
How not?
πῶς φῶ ;
How shall I speak?
πάτερ, ἐποίκτειρόν τ᾿ ἐμὲ φίλον τ᾽ Ὀρέστην πῶς ἀνάξομεν δόμοις.
Father, pity me and dear Orestes—how shall we bring them back to the house?
μένω δ᾽ ἀκοῦσαι πῶς ἀγὼν κριθήσεται.
I wait to hear how the contest will be decided.
κρατεῖται πῶς τὸ θεῖον
How is the divine power overcome?
cit.note: ubi Hermannus κρατεῖ ται δ᾽ ἔποςthe word is fulfilled coniecit.
where Hermann conjectured κρατεῖ ται δ᾽ ἔπος [the word prevails].

cit.quote: αἰνιγματῶδες τοὔπος · ἀλλὰ πῶς φράσον
The word is riddling; but tell me how.
cit.note: ubi recte Abreschius ἀλλ᾽ ἁπλῶςbut simply .
where Abresch rightly [conjectured] ἀλλ᾽ ἁπλῶς [but simply].

cit.quote: ἔνεστι γάρ πως τοῦτο τῇ τυραννίδι νόσημα.
For this disease is somehow inherent in tyranny.
θεοῖς μὲν μὲν ἤδη ἤδη πως παρημελήμεθα. θα. Ας.
We have somehow already been neglected by the gods. θα. Ας.
ἀλλὰ μὴ γένοιτό πως.
But may it not happen somehow.

cit.note: male ἄν πωςsomehow pro ἂν πῶςhow then .
wrongly ἄν πως [somehow] for ἂν πῶς [how then].

cit.quote: πεπραμένοι γὰρ νῦν γέ πως ἀλώμεθα.
For now we wander somehow, having been sold.
μνῆμον (sic Hermannus pro ἥμενον) ἄνω φρόνημά πως αὐτόθεν ἐξέπραξεν ἔμπας.
A mindful (thus Hermann for ἥμενον) spirit somehow accomplished it from there, nevertheless.
τέλεα δέ πως πελόμενά μοι.
And somehow perfect things are coming to me.
τό τ᾽ εἰπεῖν εὐπετὲς μύσαγμά πως.
And to say it is easy—somehow a pollution.

entry.note: Littera p vocalem brevem, qua praecedens vocabulum terminatur, producit, ubi metrum postulat, sive cadentem sub ictum sive non cadentem, cuiusmodi exempla plurima collegerunt Dawesius Miscell. crit. p. 282 et seqq., Monkius ad Eur. Hipp. 461, Gaisfordus ad Hephaest. vol. 2 p. 11 aliique. Sic apud Aeschylum Pr. 1073 διαρταμήσει σώματος μέγα ῥάκοςhe will rend the great tatters of the body . Eum. 190 ὑπὸ ῥάχιν παγέντεςpierced under the spine . et aliquoties apud Sophoclem, de quo dixi in Lexico Sophocleo p. 435. Rarissime sine ictu, ut in versu anapaestico Arist. Ran. 1059

The letter p lengthens the short vowel with which the preceding word ends, where the meter demands it, whether falling under the ictus or not, of which kind very many examples have been collected by Dawes Miscell. crit. p. 282 ff., Monk on Eur. Hipp. 461, Gaisford on Hephaest. vol. 2 p. 11 and others. Thus in Aeschylus Pr. 1073 διαρταμήσει σώματος μέγα ῥάκος [he will rend the great tatters of the body]. Eum. 190 ὑπὸ ῥάχιν παγέντες [pierced under the spine]. And several times in Sophocles, about which I have spoken in my Lexicon Sophocleum p. 435. Very rarely without ictus, as in the anapaestic verse of Arist. Ran. 1059

form.gloss: then, so, in that case (enclitic particle from ἄρα)

sense.def: particula enclitica ex ἄραthen, so, therefore facta, quam per δήindeed, truly, now explicant grammatici in Thes. indicati vol. 6 p. 2312, de quo v. Apollon. in Bekk. Anecd. p. 525, 16. Frequentissimus eius usus est apud epicos, nec rarus in poesi lyrica, sed rarissimus apud tragicos.

enclitic particle formed from ἄρα, which the grammarians cited in the Thesaurus vol. 6 p. 2312 explain by δή; on this see Apollonius in Bekker's Anecdota p. 525, 16. Its use is very frequent among the epic poets, not rare in lyric poetry, but very rare among the tragedians.

cit.quote: ἢ ῥ᾽ ἀΐει μου βασιλεύς ?
Does the king hear me?
cit.note: Aeschyli unum est exemplum.
There is one example in Aeschylus.

cit.quote: ἢ ῥά σε ῎Αρτεμις ὥρμασε πανδάμους ἐπὶ βοῦς ἀγελαίας, ἤ πού τινος νίκας ἀκαρπώτου χάριν, ἤ ῥα κλυτῶν ἐνάρων ψευσθεῖσα – ?
Did Artemis urge you against the herds of cattle belonging to the whole people, or for the sake of some victory without fruit, or deceived in glorious spoils?
cit.note: tria Sophoclis.
three in Sophocles.

cit.quote: ἢ ῥα κελαινώπαν θυμὸν ἐφυβρίζει ?
Does he insult my dark-faced heart?

sense.def: virga, baculus. Pro ῥαβδούχοςrod-bearer, staff-bearer , quod μεγάλων γνωμῶν καὶ διανοιῶν ἴσα καὶ τὰ ῥήματα τίκτεινto produce words equal to great thoughts and ideas . Manifestum est autem huiusmodi in locis duo vocabula tanquam unum esse pronuntianda littera p duplicata, velut μεγαρράκος, ὑπορράχιν, ταρρήματαμεγαρράκος, ὑπορράχιν, ταρρήματα et quae sunt reliqua. Ubi vero metrum syllabam brevem vel fert vel postulat, vocalis brevis ante litteram o brevis manet, velut apud Aeschylum Pr. 713 χρίμπτουσα ῥαχίαισιν ἐκπερᾶν χθόνα. 390 ἐπώνυμόν τε ῥεῦμα καὶ πετρηρεφή. 902 πρὸς ταῦτα ῥιπτέσθω μὲν αἰθαλοῦσσα φλόξgrazing the rocky shores to cross the land. 390 and the stream that gives its name and the rocky roof. 902 against these let the smoky flame be hurled . Eum. 232 ἐγὼ δ᾽ ἀρήξω τὸν ἱκέτην τε ῥύσομαιI will help and protect the suppliant , et apud Sophoclem OR. 72 δρῶν ἢ τί φωνῶν τήνδε ῥυσαίμην πόλινby doing or saying what could I save this city . Miro enim errore Dawesius, Gaisfordus aliique vocalem brevem ante litteramp constanter produci crediderunt, ita ut poetae qui corripuerint aut regulam, quae nunquam exstitit, violasse credendi sint aut tradita in codicibus scriptura corrigenda sit, velut OR. 72, ubi Hermannus levi apographi cuiusdam vitio τήνδ᾽ ἐρυσαίμηνI might save her (ut in L librarius primo scripserat τήνδ᾽ ἐρυσάμηνI saved her , ex quo manus recentior τήνδε ῥυσαίμηνI might save her fecit) ad futilem abusus est coniecturam τήνδε γ ' ἐρυσαίμηνI might save her at least , alii nihilo prudentius τήνδε λυσαίμηνI might release her coniecerunt. praeconem vel ministrum templi significare potest, dictum videtur.

rod, staff. For ῥαβδούχος [rod-bearer], which is said to produce words equal to great thoughts and ideas. It is clear that in such places the two words are to be pronounced as one with the letter p doubled, like μεγαρράκος, ὑπορράχιν, ταρρήματα and the rest. But where the meter either allows or requires a short syllable, the short vowel before the letter p remains short, as in Aeschylus Pr. 713 χρίμπτουσα ῥαχίαισιν ἐκπερᾶν χθόνα [grazing the rocky shores to cross the land]. 390 ἐπώνυμόν τε ῥεῦμα καὶ πετρηρεφή [and the stream that gives its name and the rocky roof]. 902 πρὸς ταῦτα ῥιπτέσθω μὲν αἰθαλοῦσσα φλόξ [against these let the smoky flame be hurled]. Eum. 232 ἐγὼ δ᾽ ἀρήξω τὸν ἱκέτην τε ῥύσομαι [I will help and protect the suppliant], and in Sophocles OR. 72 δρῶν ἢ τί φωνῶν τήνδε ῥυσαίμην πόλιν [by doing or saying what could I save this city]. For Dawes, Gaisford and others believed with remarkable error that the short vowel before the letter p is always lengthened, so that poets who shortened it must be thought to have violated a rule that never existed, or the reading transmitted in the manuscripts must be corrected, as at OR. 72, where Hermann, on the basis of a slight error in some copy, τήνδ᾽ ἐρυσαίμην (as in L the scribe had first written τήνδ᾽ ἐρυσάμην, from which a later hand made τήνδε ῥυσαίμην), used the futile conjecture τήνδε γ᾽ ἐρυσαίμην, while others no more wisely conjectured τήνδε λυσαίμην. It can also mean herald or temple servant, as it seems.

cit.quote: πότερα πρὸς ἔτην λέγω, ἢ τηρὸν ἱροῦ (sic correxi pro ήεροῦ, quod est in Μ) ῥάβδον, ἢ πόλεως ἀγόν
Am I speaking to a private citizen, or the keeper of the holy staff (I corrected thus for ήεροῦ, which is in M), or the leader of the city?
cit.note: ubi διορθωτὴςcorrector in M adscripsit οἶμαι ἢ Ἑρμοῦ ῥάβδονI think either the staff of Hermes , quae ipsius est coniectura. ἱερόραβδονholy staff coniecit Schuetzius.
where the corrector in M wrote in the margin οἶμαι ἢ Ἑρμοῦ ῥάβδον [I think either the staff of Hermes], which is his own conjecture. Schuetz conjectured ἱερόραβδον [holy staff].

sense.def: mobilis. Per λεπτός, ἰσχυρὸς, εὐκίνητος, ἁπαλὸς, εὐδιάσειστος, κούφος, ἐλαφρόςthin, strong, easily moved, soft, easily shaken, light, nimble explicant grammatici.
mobile. The grammarians explain it by λεπτός [thin], ἰσχυρός [strong], εὐκίνητος [easily moved], ἁπαλός [soft], εὐδιάσειστος [easily shaken], κούφος [light], ἐλαφρός [light].

cit.quote: δακρυσίστακτον ἀπ᾿ ὄσσων ῥαδινῶν δ᾽ εἰβομένα ῥέος παρειὰν νοτίοις ἔτεγξα παγαῖς.
Shedding a tear-dripping stream from my eyes, and letting fall a slender flow, I wet my cheek with moist springs.
cit.note: De oculis mobilibus vel teneris dictum. In apogr. nonnullis padινόνslender .
Said of mobile or tender eyes. In some copies padινόν.

cit.quote: διώσει ῥᾳδίως Λίγυν στρατόν.
He will easily rout the Ligyan army.

form.gloss: to break, to crush, to destroy

sense.def: to break, to crush, to destroy

cit.quote: μαλακογνώμων ἔσται ποθ᾽ (ὁ Ζεὺς), ὅταν ταύτη ῥαισθῇ.
He will become soft-minded (Zeus), whenever he is broken by this.
ῥαιστῆρι θεῖνε.
Strike with the hammer.
διαρταμήσει σώματος μέγα ῥάκος.
He will tear apart the great rag of the body.
τὴν πεπρωμένην δὲ χρὴ αἶσαν φέρειν ὡς ῥᾶστα.
One must bear the destined fate as easily as possible.
κἀγὼ δίκαιος τοῦδε τοῦ φόνου ῥαφεύς.
And I am justly the stitcher of this murder.
ἁλιστόνοις πόδα χρίμπτουσα ῥαχίαισιν
grazing her foot on the sea-groaning rocky shores
cit.note: ubi in M scriptum est ἀλλ᾽ ἁλιστόνοις γύποδας | χρίμπτουσα ῥαχίαισινbut with sea-groaning vultures' feet | grazing the rocky shores , quod correxit Turnebus restituto πόδαςfeet , recte, nisi quod πόδαfoot scribere debebat, ut s. v. πούςfoot dixi. Ex corrupto γύποδαςvultures' feet scholiastae Byzantini Γυπόδωνthe Gypodes populum finxerunt, etsi diversa memorata scriptura γε πόδας. γύποδαςat least feet. vultures' feet autem librarius scripserat oculis ad γύαςfields , quo terminatur v. 708, aberrantibus: de quo dixi in Praefat. ad Promethei editionem Londinensem (a. 1866) p. VII.

where in M is written ἀλλ᾽ ἁλιστόνοις γύποδας | χρίμπτουσα ῥαχίαισιν [but with sea-groaning vultures' feet | grazing the rocky shores], which Turnebus corrected by restoring πόδας [feet], rightly, except that he should have written πόδα [foot], as I said under πούς [foot]. From the corrupt γύποδας [vultures' feet] the Byzantine scholiasts invented a people called Γυπόδων [the Gypodes], although a different reading γε πόδας [at least feet] is recorded. The scribe had written γύποδας [vultures' feet] with his eyes straying to γύας [fields], which ends line 708: about which I spoke in the Preface to the London edition of Prometheus (1866) p. VII.

cit.quote: θραύμασίν τ᾽ ἐρειπίων ἔπαιον, ἐρράχιζον.
They struck with fragments of ruins, they split.
ὤτρυνε θεσμὸν μὴ ῥαχίζεσθαι πυρός.
He urged that the ordinance of fire not be broken.
cit.note: Sic correxi leve codicis Med. vitium μὴ χαρίζεσθαιnot to be gratified , de quo videnda quae dixi in Fleckeiseni Annalibus a. 1863. vol. 87. p. 83. 84. Verbum ῥαχίζεινto split grammatici explicant per διακόπτεινto cut through , quod ipsum quoque non raro de oratione interrupta dicitur, de quo in Thesauro dixi vol. 2 p. 1188. ubi addi potest διακόπτειν τὸ συνεχὲς τοῦ λόγουto cut through the continuity of speech , quod dixit Clemens Alex. p. 829. Ceterum simili metaphora primus quantum novimus et solus Aeschylus usus infra dixit V. 505. πολλῶν ῥαγεισῶν ἐλπίδωνmany hopes having been shattered .

Thus I corrected a slight error of the Medicean manuscript μὴ χαρίζεσθαι [not to be gratified], about which see what I said in Fleckeisen's Annals 1863 vol. 87 p. 83-84. The grammarians explain the verb ῥαχίζειν [to split] by διακόπτειν [to cut through], which itself is also not rarely said of interrupted speech, about which I spoke in the Thesaurus vol. 2 p. 1188, where can be added διακόπτειν τὸ συνεχὲς τοῦ λόγου [to cut through the continuity of speech], which Clement of Alexandria said p. 829. Moreover, Aeschylus, as far as I know, first and alone used a similar metaphor below, line 505: πολλῶν ῥαγεισῶν ἐλπίδων [many hopes having been shattered].

cit.quote: ὑπὸ ῥάχιν παγέντες.
fixed under the spine

form.gloss: Rhea, daughter of Uranus and Earth

sense.def: Rhea, daughter of Uranus and Earth

cit.quote: πρὸς μέγαν κόλπον Ρέας.
to the great bosom of Rhea
ῥέγκουσι δ᾽ οὐ πλατοῖσι φυσιάμασιν.
They snore with not broad blasts.
cit.note: ῥέγκωI snore dialecto Atticae, ῥέγχωI snore communi tribuunt grammatici: v. Thes. vol. 6 p. 2356.
The grammarians assign ῥέγκω [I snore] to the Attic dialect, ῥέγχω [I snore] to the common: see Thes. vol. 6 p. 2356.

cit.quote: ῥέεθρον ἁγνοῦ Στρυμόνος.
the stream of holy Strymon
ὅταν περάσης ῥεῖθρον ἠπείροιν ὅρον.
when you cross the stream that is the boundary of the two continents
μιαίνων παρθενοσφάγοισι | ῥείθροις πατρώους χέρας.
defiling with maiden-slaying streams his father's hands
cit.note: De sanguine. Sic Triclinius pro ῥεέθροις. ῥοαῖςstreams. streams Schoemannus propter versum strophicum, qui ab iambo incipit: quod nullius momenti est in hoc metri genere.
Of blood. Thus Triclinius for ῥεέθροις [streams]. Schoemann proposed ῥοαῖς [streams] because of the strophic verse, which begins with an iamb: which is of no importance in this kind of meter.

cit.quote: τί ῥέξεις ?
What will you do?
τί ῥέξας τύχοιμ᾽ ἂν καθ᾽ ἓν οὐρίσας ?
What could I do to succeed in one thing, having set a fair wind?
τί ῥέξω ?
What shall I do?
πρὸς εὔποτόν τε Κερχνείας ῥέος.
to the well-drinking stream of Cenchreae
ἵησι σεπτὸν Νεῖλος εὔποτον ῥέος.
the Nile sends forth a holy, well-drinking stream
ὁδοιπόρῳ διψῶντι πηγαῖον ῥέος.
a spring-fed stream for a thirsty traveler.
δακρυσίστακτον ἀπ᾿ ὄσσων ῥαδινῶν δ᾽ εἰβομένα ῥέος παρειὰν νοτίοις ἔτεγξα παγαῖς.
a tear-dripping stream from my eyes, and as it flowed down my tender cheek, I wet it with moist springs.
cit.note: De lacrimis.
Of tears.

cit.quote: τίν᾿ αὐ φὴς τήνδε συμφορὰν στρατῷ ἐλθεῖν κακῶν ῥέπουσαν ἐς τὰ μάσσονα ?
What calamity do you say has come upon the army, inclining toward the greater evils?
βλεμμάτων ῥεπει βολή.
the glance of the eyes inclines.
cit.note: Sic Salmasius pro ῥεπιβουλήa leaning of counsel , quod legitur apud Antig. Car. Hist. Mir. c. 127 p. 174 ed. Beckm.
Thus Salmasius for ῥεπιβουλή [a leaning of counsel], which is read in Antigonus of Carystus, Hist. Mir. c. 127 p. 174 ed. Beckm.

cit.quote: τὸ μητρὸς ἐς σέ μοι ῥέπει στέργηθρον.
my mother's love inclines toward you.
καὶ νῦν μὲν ἐς τόδ᾽ ἦμαρ εὐ ῥέπει θεός.
and now up to this day the god inclines favorably.
τῶνδ᾽ ἐξ ἴσου ῥεπομένων (i. e. his aequaliter inclinantibus) μεταλγεῖς τὸ δίκαιον ἔρξαι
when these things are equally balanced (i.e. these inclining equally), you regret having done justice.
cit.note: Singularis est formae passivae s. mediae usus. quod refertur ad praecedens Ζεὺς ἑτερορρεπήςZeus who inclines the balance .
The use of the passive or middle form is singular. It refers to the preceding Ζεὺς ἑτερορρεπής [Zeus who inclines the balance].

cit.quote: τοῦ περὶ πᾶσάν θ᾽ εἱλισσομένου χθόν᾽ ἀκοιμήτῳ ῥεύματι παῖδες πατρὸς Ὠκεανοῦ.
the children of father Ocean, who wind around the whole earth with sleepless stream.
λιπὼν ἐπώνυμόν τε ῥεῦμα.
leaving the stream that bears his name.

sense.def: Improperly, of a crowd of people.

cit.quote: μεγάλῳ ῥεύματι φωτῶν.
with a great stream of men.
ῥεῦμα Περσικοῦ στρατοῦ.
the stream of the Persian army.
cit.note: Similiter Sophocles et Euripides: v. Thes. vol. 6 p. 2363.
Similarly Sophocles and Euripides: see Thes. vol. 6 p. 2363.

cit.quote: ὅστις Ἑλλήσποντον ἱρὸν – ἤλπισε σχήσειν ῥέοντα Βόσπορον ῥόον θεοῦ.
who hoped to check the sacred Hellespont, the flowing Bosporus, a stream of the god.
ἀφρὸς βορᾶς βροτείας ἐρρύη κατὰ στόμα.
foam of human flesh flowed down from his mouth.
cit.note: Sic Porsonus pro έρρυηκόταhaving flowed .
Thus Porson for έρρυηκότα [having flowed].

cit.quote: ῥεῖ πολὺς ὅδε λεὼς πρόδρομος ἱππότας.
this great host of horsemen flows forth as a vanguard.
ὃς οὐκ ἐάσει γλῶσσαν ἐργμάτων ἄτερ εἴσω πυλῶν ῥέουσαν ἀλδαίνειν κακά.
who will not allow a tongue flowing within the gates without deeds to foster evils.
cit.note: ubi schol. ὃς τούτου τὸν κόμπον ἐφέξει τῶν πράξεων ἀποδέοντα μὴ ἔσω πυλῶν γενέσθαι τὴν Σφίγγαwho will check his boast, since his deeds fall short, so that the Sphinx did not come within the gates .

where the scholiast says: ὃς τούτου τὸν κόμπον ἐφέξει τῶν πράξεων ἀποδέοντα μὴ ἔσω πυλῶν γενέσθαι τὴν Σφίγγα [who will check his boast, since his deeds fall short, so that the Sphinx did not come within the gates].
εὐ ῥέονταflowing well vitiose M pro εὑρεθένταhaving been found .
εὐ ῥέοντα [flowing well] is corrupt in M for εὑρεθέντα [having been found].

sense.def: Rhegium, urbs in finibus Italiae prope Siciliam sita.
Rhegium, a city situated on the borders of Italy near Sicily.

cit.quote: ἀφ᾽ οὗ δὴ ῾Ρήγιον κικλήσκεται.
from which indeed it is called Rhegium.
πέπλους ῥήγνυσιν ἀμφὶ σώματι.
she tears her robes around her body.
ῥήξας δὲ πέπλους.
and tearing her robes.

sense.def: ἐρρώγέναι [to have burst] to have broken in, to have rushed in.

cit.quote: κακῶν δὴ πέλαγος ἔρρωγεν μέγα Πέρσαις.
a great sea of evils has burst upon the Persians.
μάλιστα νῦν σοί που τάδ᾽ ἔρρωγεν κακά.
these evils have burst upon you especially now.
cit.note: Similiter.
Similarly.

sense.def: ῥήγνυμαι [I am broken] I am broken.

cit.quote: πολλῶν ῥαγεισῶν ἐλπίδων.
many hopes having been shattered.
ἅπαξ ἔτ᾽ εἰπεῖν ῥῆσιν ἢ (οὐ Hermannus) θρήνον θέλω.
I wish to speak once more a speech or (Hermann: not) a lament.
μακράν γε μὲν δὴ ῥῆσιν οὐ στέργει πόλις.
the city does not love a long speech.
τοιάνδ᾽ ἔπειθε ῥῆσιν ἀμφ᾽ ἡμῶν λέγων.
he was persuading with such a speech about us.
εἰ ῥητὸν, φράσον.
if it is utterable, tell me.
οὐ γὰρ ῥητὸν (θεμιτὸν Brunckius) αὐδᾶσθαι τάδε.
for it is not lawful (Brunck: not right) to speak these things.
ἰπούμενος ῥίζαισιν (ῥίζησιν Μ) Αἰτναίαις ὕπο.
pressed down beneath the roots of Etna.
χθόνα δ᾽ ἐκ πυθμένων αὐταῖς ῥίζαις πνεῦμα κραδαίνοι.
and may the blast shake the earth from its foundations with its very roots.
ῥίζης γὰρ οὔσης φυλλὰς ἵκετ᾽ ἐς δόμους.
for when the root exists, the leaves came to the house.
cit.note: Figurate.
Figuratively.

cit.quote: ὅστε ματρὸς ἁγνὰν σπείρας ἄρουραν, ἵν᾽ ἐτράφη, ῥίζαν αἱματόεσσαν, ἔτλα.
who dared to sow the holy field of his mother, where he was nourished, a bloody root.
σπαρτῶν δ᾽ ἀπ᾿ ἀνδρῶν ῥίζωμ᾽ ἀνεῖται.
the root of the sown men is raised up.
βέβακεν ῥίμφα διὰ πυλᾶν.
he has gone swiftly through the gates.

sense.def: naribus (i. e. narium olfactu) persequor. Improprie persequor indagando, indago.
to track by scent (i.e. by the sense of smell). Improperly, to pursue by tracking, to track down.

cit.quote: μαρτυρεῖτε συνδρόμως ἴχνος κακῶν ῥίνηλατούσῃ τῶν πάλαι πεπραγμένων.
bear witness together with me as I track the scent of evils of things done long ago.

sense.def: montes Rhipaei, montes fabulosi ap. Strabon. 7 p. 297 οἱ τὰ ῾Ριπαῖα ὄρη καὶ τοὺς Ὑπερβορέους μυθοποιοῦντεςthose who make myths about the Rhipaean mountains and the Hyperboreans . Steph. Byz. ' Ριπαῖα: ὄρος ὙπερβορέωνRhipaia: a mountain of the Hyperboreans , quod ὄmountain pn potius scribendum, ut schol. Soph. OC. 1248. dixit, ἀπὸ τῶν ὀρῶν τῶν προσαγορευομένων ῾Ριπῶν· τινὲς δὲ οὕτω καλοῦσι, ‘ Ριπαῖα ὄρηfrom the mountains called Rhipai; but some call them thus, Rhipaean mountains . Eorum de situ dissenserunt veteres: v. Thes. vol. 6 p. 2397.

Rhipaean mountains, fabulous mountains in Strabo 7 p. 297: those who make myths about the Rhipaean mountains and the Hyperboreans. Stephanus of Byzantium: Rhipaia: a mountain of the Hyperboreans, which should rather be written ὄpn, as the scholiast on Sophocles OC 1248 says, from the mountains called Rhipai; but some call them thus, Rhipaean mountains. The ancients disagreed about their location: see Thesaurus vol. 6 p. 2397.

cit.quote: ap. schol. Soph. 1. c. Ρίπαι μὲν δὴ πατρός.
in the scholiast on Sophocles, cited passage: Rhipai indeed of my father.
cit.note: Aeschylus.
Aeschylus.

cit.quote: ἐλαφραῖς πτερύγων ῥιπαῖς.
with light beats of wings
λεπταῖς ὑπαὶ κώνωπος ἐξηγειρόμην ῥιπαῖσι θωύσσοντος.
I was being roused by the thin beats of a gnat buzzing
cit.note: de culice cum susurro advolante.
of a gnat flying with a buzzing sound

cit.quote: τοιάδ᾽ ἐπ᾿ ἐμοὶ ῥιπὴ Διόθεν τεύχουσα φόβον στείχει.
such a rush from Zeus comes upon me, causing fear
ἔρριψ᾿ ἐμαυτὴν τῆσδ᾽ ἀπὸ στύφλου πέτρας.
I threw myself from this rugged rock
ἔς τε κελαῖνὸν Τάρταρον ἄρδην ῥίψειε δέμας τοὐμόν.
and may he hurl my body headlong into dark Tartarus
τεκοῦσα γάρ μ᾽ ἔρριψας ἐς τὸ δυστυχές.
for having borne me, you cast me into misfortune
ὅς ποτ᾽ ἀμφ᾿ ἐμοὶ βέλος γελωτοποιόν, τὴν κάκοσμον οὐράνην, ἔρριψεν.
who once at me a laughter-provoking missile, the ill-smelling chamber pot, threw
εἰ δ᾽ ὧδε τραχεῖς καὶ τεθηγμένους λόγους ῥίψεις.
but if you will hurl such harsh and sharpened words
cit.note: De sermone.
of speech

cit.quote: οὐ μὴν πλέω (πλέον ?) ρίψασ᾽ ἀτιμωθήσομαι.
I will not be dishonored by throwing away more (or: by having thrown away more?)
πρὸς ταῦτα ῥιπτέσθω μὲν αἰθαλοῦσσα φλόξ.
in response to this, let the blazing flame be hurled
ἐπ᾿ ἐμοὶ ῥιπτέσθω μὲν πυρὸς ἀμφήκης βόστρυχος.
upon me let the two-edged lock of fire be hurled
ὡς ὅδ᾽ οὐ πεπλασμένος ὁ κόμπος, ἀλλὰ καὶ λίαν εἰρημένος.
since this boast is not fabricated, but indeed all too true
cit.note: Sic in apographis correctum est quod in M primo scriptum fuit εἰριμμένος, ειhaving been thrown, ει ex alia littera facto: quod ἐρριμμένοςhaving been thrown esse potest.
Thus it has been corrected in the copies from what was first written in M as εἰριμμένος [having been thrown], ει having been made from another letter: which can be ἐρριμμένος [having been thrown].

cit.quote: πύργων ἀνδρολέτειραν νοσο νόσον, ῥίψοπλον ἄταν.
a man-destroying plague of towers, a shield-throwing ruin
ὀξυγλύκειάν τἄρα κοκκιεῖς ῥόαν.
you will crack a bitter-sweet pomegranate

sense.def: Rhodes, an island of the Carpathian sea

cit.quote: καὶ ' Ρόδον ἠδὲ Κνίδον.
and Rhodes and Cnidus
ἔνθα πεδίον Ασωπός ῥοαῖς ἄρδει.
where the Asopus waters the plain with its streams
ἐπ᾿ Εὐρίπου ῥοάς.
to the streams of the Euripus
ἐν ῥοθοῦντι κριβάνῳ.
in a boiling oven
cit.note: Sic correxi pro νοθοῦντιbeing sluggish , quod est ap. Athen. 9 р. 375 с.
Thus I have corrected for νοθοῦντι [being sluggish], which is in Athenaeus 9 p. 375 c.

cit.quote: κώπης ῥοθιάδος Συνεμβολῇ.
with the joint stroke of the dashing oar
κύμα δὲ πόντου τραχεῖ ῥοθίῳ συγχώσειεν.
and may the wave of the sea with rough surge overwhelm
γᾶς δόσις οὐτιδανοῖς ἐν ῥοθίοις φορεῖται.
the gift of earth is borne on worthless surges
Περσίδος γλώσσης ῥόθος.
the noise of the Persian tongue
ἐξ ἑνὸς ῥόθου παίουσι.

entry.note: Hesychius ῥύσια: ἐνεχυράσματα, σωτήρια, λύτρα, λεηλασίαιthings seized as surety, means of deliverance, ransoms, plunderings . Similiter alii grammatici: v. Etym. M. p. 706, 40, Photium, Suidam, Zonaram p. 1622, scholiastam Homeri Il. 11, 673, Eustathium p. 877, 35 et ad Dionys. Per. 527. quorum de notationibus Hermannus in annot. ad Ag. 513 (535) vol. 2 p. 410. "Non satis explicate haec a grammaticis sunt tradita. ῥύσιονa thing seized as surety , ab ῥύεσθαιto protect, deliver factum, proprie significat rem ademptam, quae vi vindicanda est atque ita salva praestanda. Ita Aeschylus Suppl. 412 (de Danaidibus quas Aegypti filii sibi vindicant) καὶ μήτε δῆρις ῥυσίων ἐφάψεται —. 728 ἄγειν θέλοντες ῥυσίων ἐφάπτορεςand let no strife lay hold of the sureties —. 728 wishing to lead them away, laying hold of the sureties . (ubi schol. ἐνεχύρων. ἐνεχυράζοντες ἡμᾶς διά τινος ἁρπαγῆςof pledges. taking us as pledges through some seizure .) Sic apud Sophoclem Oed. Col. 858. Creon Oedipum una cum filiabus abstrahens dicit, καὶ μεῖΖον ἀρα ῥύσιον πόλει τάχα θήσεις ? ἐφάψομαι γὰρ οὐ ταύταιν μόναινwill you then soon make a greater seizure for the city? For I will lay hold not of these two alone . Eo modo etiam in Ag. 535 Helena a Paride rapta, a Graecis vindicata, ῥύστονa thing seized as surety vocatur, τοῦ ῥυσίου θ᾽ ἥμαρτεand he missed the surety . Secunda significatio est pignoris, quod pro ea re, quae adempta est, capitur. Ita in Il. 11, 673 ῥύσι᾿ ἐλαυνόμενοςdriving off cattle as surety . Hinc tertius nascitur significatus, qui est satis dationis sive vindictae, quum pignus, si res ipsa retitui non potest, ad satis faciendum laeso adhibetur. Ita Sophocles in Phil. 959 φόνον φόνου δὲ ῥύσιον τίσω τάλαςI, wretched, will pay murder as a surety for murder . Alia est quarta potestas, ex primo deducta significatu, quo liberatio rei ex aliena potestate atque in integrum restitutio indicatur. Sic Io, quum Iovis contactu Epapho gravida facta formam humanam recuperasset, eam formae restitutionem ῥύσιαmeans of deliverance dixit Aeschylus in Suppl. 314. Ἔπαφος ἀληθῶς ῥυσίων ἐπώνυμοςEpaphus truly named from the deliverance . Hinc denique quiutus prodit usus, quo quidquid pro salute fit intelligitur, eoque modo accipiendum hoc vocabulum apud Dionysium Perieg. 527 ῥύσια δ᾽ Ἀπόλλωνι χοροὺς ἀνάγουσιν ἅπασαιand all the women lead up choirs as thank-offerings to Apollo .”

Hesychius ῥύσια [things seized as surety, means of deliverance, ransoms, plunderings]: ἐνεχυράσματα [pledges], σωτήρια [means of safety], λύτρα [ransoms], λεηλασίαι [plunderings]. Similarly other grammarians: see Etym. M. p. 706, 40, Photius, Suidas, Zonaras p. 1622, the scholiast on Homer Il. 11, 673, Eustathius p. 877, 35 and on Dionysius Periegetes 527. On their explanations Hermann in his note on Ag. 513 (535) vol. 2 p. 410: "These matters have not been explained sufficiently clearly by the grammarians. ῥύσιον [a thing seized as surety], formed from ῥύεσθαι [to protect, deliver], properly means a thing taken away, which must be claimed by force and thus kept safe. So Aeschylus Suppl. 412 (about the Danaids whom the sons of Aegyptus claim for themselves) καὶ μήτε δῆρις ῥυσίων ἐφάψεται — [and let no strife lay hold of the sureties] —. 728 ἄγειν θέλοντες ῥυσίων ἐφάπτορες [wishing to lead them away, laying hold of the sureties]. (where the scholium has ἐνεχύρων [of pledges]. ἐνεχυράζοντες ἡμᾶς διά τινος ἁρπαγῆς [taking us as pledges through some seizure].) So in Sophocles Oed. Col. 858. Creon, dragging Oedipus away together with his daughters, says, καὶ μεῖΖον ἀρα ῥύσιον πόλει τάχα θήσεις ? ἐφάψομαι γὰρ οὐ ταύταιν μόναιν [will you then soon make a greater seizure for the city? For I will lay hold not of these two alone]. In this way also in Ag. 535 Helen, having been seized by Paris and claimed by the Greeks, is called ῥύστον [a thing seized as surety], τοῦ ῥυσίου θ᾽ ἥμαρτε [and he missed the surety]. The second meaning is that of a pledge, which is taken in place of the thing that has been taken away. So in Il. 11, 673 ῥύσι᾿ ἐλαυνόμενος [driving off cattle as surety]. From this arises a third meaning, which is that of satisfaction or vengeance, when a pledge, if the thing itself cannot be restored, is used to give satisfaction to the injured party. So Sophocles in Phil. 959 φόνον φόνου δὲ ῥύσιον τίσω τάλας [I, wretched, will pay murder as a surety for murder]. There is a fourth meaning, derived from the first, by which the liberation of a thing from another's power and its restoration to its original state is indicated. So Io, when she had become pregnant with Epaphus by the touch of Zeus and had recovered her human form, Aeschylus called that restoration of form ῥύσια [means of deliverance] in Suppl. 314. Ἔπαφος ἀληθῶς ῥυσίων ἐπώνυμος [Epaphus truly named from the deliverance]. From this finally comes a fifth use, by which whatever is done for safety is understood, and in this way the word is to be taken in Dionysius Periegetes 527 ῥύσια δ᾽ Ἀπόλλωνι χοροὺς ἀνάγουσιν ἅπασαι [and all the women lead up choirs as thank-offerings to Apollo]."

entry.note: De accentu dissenserunt grammatici. Arcadius p. 104, 25 τὸ μέντοι σαγή τὸ πλῆθος τινὲς μὲν ὀξύνουσι, τινὲς δὲ βαρύνουσινthe word σαγή in the plural some accent on the last syllable, others on the first . Apud Eur. Rhes. 207 cod. Vat. in textu σάγηarmor , sed in scholio ἡ σαγήthe armor (codex σφαγή) ὀξυτόνως Ηρωδιανόςslaughter) with acute accent, according to Herodian . In M Sept. 391 σαγαῖςwith armors et Pers. 240 σαγαίarmors , sed σάγηνarmor Ch. 560 et σάγῃwith armor 675.

The grammarians disagreed about the accent. Arcadius p. 104, 25: "τὸ μέντοι σαγή τὸ πλῆθος τινὲς μὲν ὀξύνουσι, τινὲς δὲ βαρύνουσιν [the word σαγή in the plural some accent on the last syllable, others on the first]." In Eur. Rhes. 207 the Vatican codex has σάγη [armor] in the text, but in the scholium ἡ σαγή [the armor] (codex σφαγή [slaughter]) with acute accent, according to Herodian. In M Sept. 391 σαγαῖς [with armors] and Pers. 240 σαγαί [armors], but σάγην [armor] Ch. 560 and σάγῃ [with armor] 675.

cit.note: Incertum exemplum est. ubi metrum ποτισαίνουσαfawning upon postulat, quae est Hermanni coniectura, probabilior quam Seidleri, qui deletis verbis τὸ πρῶτον παράγειfirst leads astray coniecerat φιλόφρων γὰρ παρασαίνει βροτὸν εἰς ἄρκυας ῎Αταfor friendly Ate fawns upon mortals into her nets : de quo dixi s. v. προσσαίνωto fawn upon . Pro ἄρκυας Ἄταthe nets of Ate autem in M scriptum est ἀρκύσταταnet-like , quod correxit Hermannus collata de ῎ΑτηAte annotatione scholiastae, recte, nisi quod ἄρκυας Ἄταςthe nets of Ate scribere debebat, ut postea fecit Hartungus: nam subiectum verbi παράγειleads astray non est "ΑταAte , sed δολόμητις ἀπάτα θεοῦthe wily deceit of a god , quod intellexit scholiasta, qui ad φιλόφρωνfriendly annotavit ἡ θεῶν ἀπάτηthe deceit of the gods et haud dubie genitivum legit ῎Αταςof Ate .

The example is uncertain. where the meter requires ποτισαίνουσα [fawning upon], which is Hermann's conjecture, more probable than Seidler's, who, deleting the words τὸ πρῶτον παράγει [first leads astray], conjectured φιλόφρων γὰρ παρασαίνει βροτὸν εἰς ἄρκυας ῎Ατα [for friendly Ate fawns upon mortals into her nets]: about which I have spoken under προσσαίνω [to fawn upon]. But for ἄρκυας Ἄτα [the nets of Ate] in M is written ἀρκύστατα [net-like], which Hermann corrected by comparing the scholiast's note on ῎Ατη [Ate], rightly, except that he should have written ἄρκυας Ἄτας [the nets of Ate], as Hartung later did: for the subject of the verb παράγει [leads astray] is not "Ατα [Ate], but δολόμητις ἀπάτα θεοῦ [the wily deceit of a god], which the scholiast understood, who on φιλόφρων [friendly] noted ἡ θεῶν ἀπάτη [the deceit of the gods] and undoubtedly read the genitive ῎Ατας [of Ate].

Αἰσχύλος “ άσαλὴς μανίαcarefree: the one without care, the one who thinks about nothing. For σάλη is care. Carefree is the one without anxiety. Aeschylus: "carefree madness" .” Anecd. Bekk. p. 450, 28. ἀσαλὴς μανία: ἡ μηδενός φροντίζουσα· σάλη γὰρ ἡ φροντίς. οὕτως Αἰσχύλοςcarefree madness: the one who thinks about nothing; for σάλη is care. Thus Aeschylus . Hinc Nauckius repetitum putat quod Photius habet p. 497, 14. σάλα: φροντίς. οὕτως Αἰσχύλοςσάλα: care. Thus Aeschylus : quod omisso Aeschyli nomine Suidas per φροντίςcare , Hesychius per φροντίςcare et βλάβηharm explicat. Similis formae vox est μάναmana , de qua Photius p. 246, 4.

Etym. M. p. 151, 49. ἀσαλής [carefree]: ἡ ἄφροντις [the one without care], ἡ μηδενός φροντίζουσα [the one who thinks about nothing]. σάλη γὰρ ἡ φροντίς [for σάλη is care]. ἀσαλὴς ὁ ἀμέριμνος [ἀσαλής is the one without anxiety]. Aeschylus: "άσαλὴς μανία [carefree madness]." Anecd. Bekk. p. 450, 28. ἀσαλὴς μανία [carefree madness]: ἡ μηδενός φροντίζουσα [the one who thinks about nothing]; σάλη γὰρ ἡ φροντίς [for σάλη is care]. Thus Aeschylus. Hence Nauck thinks that what Photius has at p. 497, 14 is repeated: σάλα: φροντίς [σάλα: care]. Thus Aeschylus: which, with the name of Aeschylus omitted, Suidas explains by φροντίς [care], Hesychius by φροντίς [care] and βλάβη [harm]. Of similar form is the word μάνα [mana], about which Photius p. 246, 4.
