ἐν μήκει χρόνου.
in the length of time.
ἐς τὸν πολὺν φίλοισι καρποῦσθαι χρόνον.
to enjoy for a long time for friends.
ὑστέρῳ χρόνῳ.
at a later time.
ἀμφὶ σοὶ πάθη ὁρῶσα πλείω τοῦ ξυνεύδοντος χρόνου.
seeing your sufferings more than the time of sleeping.
χρόνος δ᾽, ἐπεὶ παρήβησεν.
but time, when it has passed its prime.
οὐκ ἔστ᾽ ἄλυ-Εις, οὔ, ξένοι, χρόνῳ πλέω,
there is no release, no, strangers, in time,
cit.note: ubi vitiosum est χρόνῳ πλέωI sail in time , pro quo Hermannus χρόνον πλέωI sail for a time coniecit, quod πλείω χρόνονfor a longer time dicendum fuisset. Valckenarius χρονουλκίᾳby wasting time coniecit.

where χρόνῳ πλέω [I sail in time] is corrupt, for which Hermann conjectured χρόνον πλέω [I sail for a time], which should have been πλείω χρόνον [for a longer time]. Valckenaer conjectured χρονουλκίᾳ [by prolongation of time].

cit.quote: ó δ᾽ ὕστατός γε τοῦ χρόνου πρεσβεύεται.
but the last of time is honored.
σὺν χρόνῳ.
with time.
πολὺν ἄγαν χρόνον χαμαιπετεῖς ἔκεισθ. ἀεί.
for a very long time they lie on the ground always.
τάχα δὲ παντελὴς χρόνος ἀμείψεται πρόθυρα δωμάτων.
soon all-fulfilling time will change the doors of the house.
φόνου δὲ κηκὶς ξὺν χρόνῳ ξυμβάλλεται.
The stain of murder is compounded with time.
1563 ἐν χρόνῳ.
1563 in time.
cit.note: Sed ib. 1563 μένει δὲ μίμνοντος ἐν χρόνῳ Διὸς παθεῖν τὸν ἔρξανταIt remains, while Zeus remains, in time for the doer to suffer. , Schuetzius correxit ἐν θρόνῳon the throne .
But at line 1563 μένει δὲ μίμνοντος ἐν χρόνῳ Διὸς παθεῖν τὸν ἔρξαντα [it remains for the doer to suffer from Zeus in time while he remains], Schuetz corrected to ἐν θρόνῳ [on the throne].

cit.quote: τὸν πρὸ τοῦ φεύγων χρόνον.
fleeing the time before.
θεσμὸν τὸν εἰς ἅπαντ᾽ ἐγὼ θήσω χρόνον.
I will establish this ordinance for all time.
εἰς τὸν αἰανῆ χρόνον,
for everlasting time,
εἰς τὸ πᾶν χρόνου.
for the whole of time.
εἰς ἅπαντα πλειστηρη χρόνον.
for all the longest time.
οὑπιρρέων γὰρ τιμιώτερος χρόνος ἔσται πολίταις τοῖσδε.
For time flowing on will be more precious to these citizens.
καί μοι πρόπαντος ἐγγύην θήσει χρόνου;
And will he give me a pledge for all time?
χρόνῳ τεταγμένῳ.
at the appointed time.
παντὶ χρόνῳ δ᾽ ἐπιβριθεῖς.
and heavy upon you for all time.
ἀλλ᾽ οὔτι δαρὸν χρόνον ἐρημώσει πατήρ,
But not for long will my father leave me desolate,
cit.note: ubi Hermannus δαρόν σ' ἐξερημώσει πατήρyour father will leave you desolate for long .
where Hermann has δαρόν σ' ἐξερημώσει πατήρ [your father will long leave you desolate].

cit.quote: εἰσόπιν χρόνου.
for the time to come.
μῆκος δ᾽ οὐδὲν ἐν μέσῳ χρόνου.
And there is no length of time in between.
ἀγνῶθ᾽ ὅμιλον ὡς ἐλέγχεσθαι χρόνῳ.
an unknown crowd, to be tested by time.
ταὐτοῦ χρόνου.
of the same time.
κἀκ τῶνδ᾽ ἔπινε βρῦτον ἰσχναίνων χρόνῳ.
And after that he drank beer, wasting away with time.
πόνου γὰρ ἄκρον οὐκ ἔχει χρόνος.
For time has no limit to toil.

sense.def: χρόνῳ: at some time, at length

cit.quote: χρόνῳ μὲν ἀγρεῖ Πριάμου πόλιν ἅδε κέλευθος.
In time this expedition captures the city of Priam.
Ἐρινύες χρόνῳ τυχηρὸν ὄντα τιθεῖσ᾽ ἀμαυρόν.
The Erinyes, in time, make dim the fortunate man.
γνώσει δὲ χρόνῳ διαπευθόμενος.
You will learn by inquiring in time.
τέκνον δ᾽ ἐπεισφέρει δόμοις | αἱμάτων παλαιτέρων | τίνειν μύσος χρόνῳ κλυτὰ βυσσόφρων Ερινύς.
And the renowned deep-thinking Erinys brings a child into the house to pay for the pollution of older bloodshed in time.
ἔμολε μὲν δίκα Πριαμίδαις χρόνῳ.
Justice came to the sons of Priam in time.
μὴ κάμνειν χρόνῳ.
not to weary with time.
χρόνῳ τοι κυρίῳ τ᾽ ἐν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ δώσει δίκην.
In time, indeed, and on the appointed day, he will pay the penalty.
ὁ χρυσαμοιβός δ᾽ ῎Αρης σωμάτων φίλοισι πέμπει βραχύ ψήγμα,
But Ares, the gold-exchanger, sends to the loved ones of the bodies a small dust,
cit.note: Improprie Mars, qui occisorum corpora cineribus permutat, i.e. qui pro corporibus cineres reddit, ut interpretatur Wellauerus. Vocabulum apud alios non lectum, sed annotatum ab Hesychio, qui per ἀργυρογνώμωνone who knows silver explicat.

Improperly, Mars, who exchanges the bodies of the slain for ashes, i.e. who gives ashes in return for bodies, as Wellauer interprets it. The word is not found in other authors, but is noted by Hesychius, who explains it by ἀργυρογνώμων [one who knows silver].

sense.def: et forma contracta χρυσοῦςgolden , de qua dixi in Thes. vol. 8 p. 1719, aureus.
and the contracted form χρυσοῦς, about which I have spoken in Thes. vol. 8 p. 1719, golden.

cit.quote: χρυσοῖς δὲ φωνεῖ γράμμασιν.
And he speaks with golden letters.
ἀργυρηλάτοις κέρασι χρυσᾶ στόμια προσβεβλημένοις.
with silver-wrought horns and golden mouthpieces attached.
χρυσεοστόλμους δόμους,
gold-adorned houses,
cit.note: ubi apographorum vitia sunt χρυσεοστόλους χρυσεοστόλβους χρυσεοστίλβουςgold-robed, gold-gleaming, gold-glittering . Substantivo στολμόςequipment, array bis usus est Aeschylus Ch. 29 et Suppl. 715. Euripides vero Herc.f. 414 πέπλων χρυσεόστολον φάροςa gold-adorned robe of cloth dixit.

where the errors of the copies are χρυσεοστόλους χρυσεοστόλβους χρυσεοστίλβους [gold-robed, gold-gleaming, gold-glittering]. Aeschylus used the noun στολμός [equipment, array] twice, Ch. 29 and Suppl. 715. Euripides, however, in Herc.f. 414 said πέπλων χρυσεόστολον φάρος [a gold-adorned robe of cloth].

sense.def: Chrysensis, adiectivum gentile ab ΧρύσηChryse , quae Troadis urbs fuit, vel alia eiusdem nominis: nam plures fuerunt, de quibus v. Thes. vol. 8 p. 1724.
Chrysean, a gentile adjective from Χρύση, which was a city of the Troad, or another of the same name: for there were several, about which see Thes. vol. 8 p. 1724.

cit.quote: Χρυσεὺς Μάταλλος μυριόνταρχος,
Chryseus Matalus, commander of ten thousand,
cit.note: dux Persarum. Male Thomas Μ. ΧρυσεύςM. Chryseus pro nomine proprio, ΜάταλλοςMatalus pro epitheto habuit. Cum nomine ΜάταλλοςMatalus Weilius comparavit ΜατίλλαςMatillas in nummo Ephesio apud Mionnet. 3 p. 87.
a leader of the Persians. Wrongly Thomas Magister took Χρυσεύς as a proper name and Μάταλλος as an epithet. With the name Μάταλλος Weilius compared Ματίλλας on an Ephesian coin in Mionnet. 3 p. 87.

sense.def: Chryseis, Chrysae filia, nota ex Homero, cui nomen proprium fuisse ἈστυνόμηAstynome annotavit schol. Homeri 11. 1, 392.
Chryseis, daughter of Chryses, known from Homer, whose proper name was Ἀστυνόμη, as the Homeric scholiast notes on Il. 1, 392.

cit.quote: Χρυσηΐδων μείλιγμα τῶν ὑπ᾽ Ἰλίῳ.
a delight of Chryseis-like girls from those under Ilium.
cit.note: Numero plurali, ut puellae significentur qualis Chryseis fuit.
In the plural number, to signify girls such as Chryseis was.

cit.quote: χρυσήλατον γὰρ ἄνδρα τευχηστὴν ἰδεῖν ἄγει γυνή τις.
For a woman leads a man in golden armor, a warrior, to see.
ἀργηστὴν ὄφιν χρυσηλάτου θώμιγγος ἐξορμώμενον.
a bright serpent rushing forth from a golden-wrought cord.
χρυσογόνου γενεᾶς ἰσόθεος φῶς.
a godlike man of the race born of gold.
cit.note: Sic ex apogr. pro χρυσονόμουof golden pasture , quod est in M. Utramque scripturam memorat scholiasta, qui ad χρυσονόμουof golden pasture annotavit νῦν τῆς πλουσίας · τινὲς γὰρ ἀνέγνωσαν χρυσογόνου διὰ τὸ τὸν Περσέα ἀπὸ χρυσοῦ γεγενῆσθαι · ὁ καὶ βέλτιονnow of the rich one; for some read χρυσογόνου because Perseus was born from gold; which is also better . et in alio scholio, τῆς Περσέως γενεᾶς ἀπόγονος · ἢ τῆς τῶν χρυσῶν ἀνθρώπων · ἢ πολυχρύσουdescendant of the race of Perseus; or of the golden race of men; or rich in gold . Similiter Soph. Ant. 950 Ζεὺς ταμιεύεσκεZeus dispensed (Danaae) γονὰς χρυσορύτουςgold-flowing offspring , i.e. Persei.

Thus from the apograph, instead of χρυσονόμου [of golden pasture], which is in M. The scholiast records both readings, who on χρυσονόμου [of golden pasture] noted: νῦν τῆς πλουσίας · τινὲς γὰρ ἀνέγνωσαν χρυσογόνου διὰ τὸ τὸν Περσέα ἀπὸ χρυσοῦ γεγενῆσθαι · ὁ καὶ βέλτιον [now of the rich one; for some read χρυσογόνου because Perseus was born from gold; which is also better]. And in another scholium: τῆς Περσέως γενεᾶς ἀπόγονος · ἢ τῆς τῶν χρυσῶν ἀνθρώπων · ἢ πολυχρύσου [descendant of the race of Perseus; or of the golden race of men; or rich in gold]. Similarly Soph. Ant. 950 Ζεὺς ταμιεύεσκε (Danaae) γονὰς χρυσορύτους [Zeus dispensed (to Danae) gold-flowing offspring], i.e. Perseus.

cit.quote: χρυσοκμήτοισιν ὅρμοις.
with necklaces wrought of gold.
cit.note: Sic Hermannus pro χρυσεοδμήτοισινbuilt of gold .
Thus Hermann, instead of χρυσεοδμήτοισιν [built of gold].

cit.quote: τὰ χρυσόπαστα δ᾽ ἔδεθλα λιπούσα.
leaving the gold-sprinkled dwellings.
cit.note: Sic Auratus pro δ᾽ ἐσθλάbut good things .
Thus Auratus, instead of δ᾽ ἐσθλά [but good things].

cit.quote: ὦ χρυσοπήληξ δαίμον (Mars).
O golden-helmeted god (Mars).
cit.note: Alterum huius vocabuli exemplum est apud Eurip. Phoen. 946, qui χρυσοπήληκα στάχυν σπαρτῶνthe golden-helmeted crop of the Sown Men dixit.
Another example of this word is in Eurip. Phoen. 946, who said χρυσοπήληκα στάχυν σπαρτῶν [the golden-helmeted crop of the Sown Men].

cit.quote: χρυσόρρυτον οἰκοῦσιν ἀμφὶ νᾶμα Πλούτωνος πόρου.
they dwell around the gold-flowing stream of Pluto's passage.
cit.note: χρυσορύτουςgold-flowing est apud Soph. Ant. 950. Post Aeschylum et Sophoclem infimae tantum aetatis scriptores nonnulli usi sunt in Thes. indicati vol. 8 p. 1745.
χρυσορύτους [gold-flowing] is in Soph. Ant. 950. After Aeschylus and Sophocles only some writers of the lowest age used it, as indicated in the Thesaurus vol. 8 p. 1745.

cit.quote: χαλκόν, σίδηρον, ἄργυρον χρυσόν τε.
bronze, iron, silver, and gold.
ταῦτα μὲν, ὦ παῖ, κρείσσονα χρυσοῦ — φωνεῖς.
These things, my child, you say are better than gold.
χρυσότευκτα γράμματα.
letters wrought of gold.
χρυσότευκτα κἀργυρᾶ σκυφώματα.
gold-wrought and silver cups.
τὸ χρυσοφεγγὲς, ὥς τις ἥλιος, σέλας παρηγγάρευσε Μακίστου σκοπαῖς.
the gold-shining light, like a sun, sent word to the watch-posts of Macistus.

sense.def: [De accentu et declinatione v. Thes. vol. 8 p. 1761 et 1764. Casus obliqui sunt χρωτός χρωτί χρῶταof the skin, to the skin, the skin (accusative) et ubi metrum postulat χροός χροΐof the skin, to the skin (s. χρῷ) χρόαto the skin) the skin (accusative) .] cutis, corporis superficies.
[On accent and declension see Thes. vol. 8 p. 1761 and 1764. The oblique cases are χρωτός χρωτί χρῶτα and, where the meter requires, χροός χροΐ (or χρῷ) χρόα.] skin, surface of the body.

cit.quote: ἀμείβων χρῶτα πορφυρέᾳ βαφή,
changing his skin with purple dye,
cit.note: ubi de colore cutis sanguine conspersi mutato dictum est: de quo v. Thes. vol. 8 p. 1763.
where it is said of the changed color of skin sprinkled with blood: on which see Thes. vol. 8 p. 1763.

cit.quote: ἵν᾽ ὁ παντόπτης Ἥλιος ἀεὶ χρῶτ᾽ ἀθάνατον κάματόν θ᾽ ἵππων ἀναπαύει.
where the all-seeing Sun always rests his immortal skin and the toil of his horses.
πρὶν ἄνδρ᾽ ἀπευκτὸν ὧδε χριμφθῆν χροϊ.
before a man hateful to me should come near my skin.
cit.note: Dativus χροῒto the skin Sic correxi quod in Mest πρὶν ἄνδρ᾽ ἀπευκτὸν τῷδ᾽ ἐχριμφθῆν χροῖνbefore a man hateful to me should come near my skin , ex quo in apogr. Scorialensi factum τῷδ᾽ ἐγχριμφθῆναι χροΐto come near this skin , in aliis τῷδ᾽ ἐγχριμφθῆναι χεροῖνto come near these hands , ex coniectura librarii. Ad hunc locum haud dubie referendae glossae Hesychii, χρημφθῆναιto come near (sic codex, idque postulante litterarum ordine, ut χρήμπτειhe/she/it brings near in glossa praecedente): προσελάσαι, ἐγγίσαι, ἐνορμῆσαιto drive to, to approach, to rush upon . et infra χριμφθῆναι: ἐμπελασθῆναι, ἐκριφῆναι (?), ἀνορμῆσαιto come near: to approach, to be cast out (?), to rush upon . Et χροΐ: σώματι, ἐπιφανείᾳto the skin: to the body, to the surface .

Dative χροΐ [to the skin]. Thus I corrected what is in M: πρὶν ἄνδρ᾽ ἀπευκτὸν τῷδ᾽ ἐχριμφθῆν χροῖν [before a hateful man should touch this skin], from which in the Scorialensian apograph was made τῷδ᾽ ἐγχριμφθῆναι χροΐ [to touch this skin], in others τῷδ᾽ ἐγχριμφθῆναι χεροῖν [to touch with hands], by conjecture of a copyist. To this passage undoubtedly refer the glosses of Hesychius: χρημφθῆναι (thus the codex, and that is required by the order of letters, as χρήμπτει in the preceding gloss): προσελάσαι, ἐγγίσαι, ἐνορμῆσαι [to drive near, to approach, to rush upon]. And below χριμφθῆναι: ἐμπελασθῆναι, ἐκριφῆναι (?), ἀνορμῆσαι [to approach, to be cast out (?), to rush up]. And χροΐ: σώματι, ἐπιφανείᾳ [to the body, to the surface].

cit.quote: τάδ᾽ ἐκχέασα γάποτον χύσιν.
pouring out these earth-drunk libations.
cit.note: De libatione.
Of a libation.

cit.quote: πρώτας δίκας κρίνοντες αἵματος χυτοῦ.
judging the first cases of shed blood.

ἐγχυτριεῖς: ἀπὸ τῶν ἐκτιθεμένων παιδίων ἐν χύτραις. διὸ καὶ Σοφοκλῆς ἀποκτεῖναι χυτρίζειν ἔλεγεν ἐν Πριάμῳ καὶ Αἰσχύλος Λαΐῳ (fr. 120) καὶ Φερεκράτης. "Putandus est autem Aeschylus istud verbum de Oedipo dixisse, quem recens natum exponi iusserit Laius”

you will pot: from the children exposed in pots. Therefore Sophocles said 'to pot' for 'to kill' in Priam, and Aeschylus in Laius (fr. 120), and Pherecrates. "But Aeschylus must be thought to have said this word about Oedipus, whom Laius ordered to be exposed as a newborn."
cit.note: HERMANN. Opusc. 7 p 103.
HERMANN. Opusc. 7 p 103.

cit.quote: πότνι᾽ ἀκτὴ χώματος.
O lady shore of the mound.
κατά Σαρπηδόνιον χῶμα πολύψαμμον ἀλαθείς,
wandering along the sandy Sarpedonian mound,
cit.note: quod per Σαρπηδονίαν ἄκρανthe Sarpedonian headland explicat scholiasta,
which the scholiast explains by Σαρπηδονίαν ἄκραν [the Sarpedonian headland],

form.gloss: land, region, especially of a certain people or city.

sense.def: terra, regio, inprimis certi populi certaevitatis.
land, region, especially of a certain people or city.

cit.quote: πρόπασα δ᾽ ἤδη στονόεν λέλακε χώρα.
and now the whole land resounds with groaning.
χώρας τοῖς πολισσούχοις θεοῖς.
to the gods who hold the land.
τὰν ἁρπαξάνδραν κῆρ᾽ ἀφελόντα χώρας.
taking away the man-stealing doom from the land.
πρίν γε χώραν τήνδε κινδύνῳ βαλεῖν.
before casting this land into danger.
οὓς αὐτὸς ἄναξ εἵλετο χώρας ἐφορεύειν.
whom the lord himself chose to oversee the land.
εἰς ἀντίπορον γείτονα χώραν
to the neighboring land across the strait
ἦλθ᾽ ἐπ᾿ αἷαν δάαν Ἑλλάδα χώραν.
he came to the land, the Greek land.
ἔς τε Μακεδόνων χώραν ἀφικόμεσθα.
and we arrived at the land of the Macedonians.
Δαρείος ἄρχε χώρας.
Darius ruled the land.
πολλοὶ φῶτες, χώρας ἄνθος.
many men, the flower of the land.
στόλον Ἀργείων χιλιοναύτην τῆσδ᾽ ἀπὸ χώρας ἦραν.
they raised the thousand-ship expedition of the Argives from this land.
ὕπατός τε χώρας Ζεύς.
and Zeus, highest of the land.
γυνή, χώρας μίασμα.
a woman, a pollution of the land.
εἰ τῆσδε χώρας μήποτε ψαύσει ποδί.
if he ever touches this land with his foot.
πιστὰ γένοιτο γένοιτο χώρα. χώρᾳ.
may it be trustworthy, may it be trustworthy for the land. to the land.
ἴδεσθε χώρας τὴν διπλῆν τυραννίδα.
see the double tyranny of the land.
χώρας τῆσδε πρυμνήτης ἄναξ.
the lord of this land, the helmsman.
χώρας ἄνασσαν τῆσδ᾽ Ἀθηναίαν.
the queen of this land, Athena.
χώρας ἐν τόποις Λιβυστικῆς.
in the regions of the Libyan land.
cit.note: Sic Auratus pro ΛιβυστικοῖςLibyan .
Thus Auratus for Λιβυστικοῖς [Libyan].

cit.quote: λέξας δὲ χώραν καὶ γένος καὶ ξυμφορὰς τὰς σας.
and telling your land and race and misfortunes.
χώρᾳ μεταῦθις ἰὸς ἐκ φρονημάτων πέδοι πεσὼν ἄφερτος αἰανὴς νόσος.
afterwards in the land a poison from the mind falls to the ground, an unbearable, grievous disease.
ἔρυμά τε χώ- ρας καὶ πόλεως σωτήριον.
a defense of the land and a savior of the city.
βαρεῖα χώρα τῇδ᾽ ὁμιλήσω πάλιν.
I will again consort with this land, heavy as it is.
χώρᾳ τῇδε καὶ τῷ σῷ | στρατῷ όρκωμοτήσας.
having sworn an oath to this land and to your army.
817 βροτοφθόρους κηλίδας ἐν χώρα βαλεῖ.
817 he will cast mortal-defiling stains upon the land.
πολλῆς δὲ χώρας τῆσδ᾽ ἔτ᾽ ἀκροθίνια ἔχουσα.
and still holding the first-fruits of this great land.
χώρας μετασχεῖν τῆσδε θεοφιλεστάτης.
to share in this land most beloved of the gods.
τάδε τοι χώρᾳ τήμῇ προφρόνως ἐπικραινομένων γάνυμαι
I rejoice that these things are being fulfilled favorably for my land.
τὸ μὲν ἀτηρὸν χώρας κατέχειν.
to hold the ruinous part of the land.
τίν᾽ ἂν οὖν χώραν εὔφρονα μᾶλλον τῆσδ᾽ ἀφικοίμεθα;
to what kinder land than this could we come?
δέξαιθ᾽ ἱκέτην τὸν θηλυγενῆ στόλον αἰδοίῳ πνεύματι χώρας.
may it receive the suppliant band of women with the land's reverent breath.
ὅπως δὲ χώραν μολεῖν | ἔτλητ᾽ ἀτρέστως.
how did you dare to come to the land without fear?
αὐτῆς δὲ χώρας Ἀπίας πέδον τόδε πάλαι κέκληται.
and this ground of the Apian land itself has long been called.
χώρᾳ δ᾽ ἄχθος ἀείζων πέλοι.
and may an everlasting burden be upon the land.
ποταμοὺς δ᾽, οἳ διὰ χώρας θελεμὸν πῶμα χέουσιν.
and the rivers that pour a gentle stream through the land.
Κίλιξ δὲ χώρα καὶ Σύρων ἐπιστροφαί.
The land is Cilician, and there are gatherings of Syrians.
8 τε γὰρ νεαρός μυελός στέρνων ἐντὸς ἀνάσσων | ἰσόπρεσβυς, ῎Αρης δ᾽ οὐκ ἔνι χώρᾳ,
For the young marrow ruling within the breast is equal in age, and Ares is not in his place.
cit.note: Mire dictum ubi scholiasta explicat τῷ τόπῳ ἐκείνῳin that place , i.e. corpori senili. Male in apographo uno ἐνὶ χώρᾳin one place , quod ἐν χώρᾳin place dicendum fuisset. Recte legi ἔif vi docet locus similis Suppl. 749 γυνὴ μονωθεῖσ᾽ οὐδέν· οὐκ ἔνεστ᾽ ῎Αρηςa woman left alone is nothing; Ares is not present .

Strangely said where the scholiast explains τῷ τόπῳ ἐκείνῳ [that place], i.e. the aged body. Wrongly in one copy ἐνὶ χώρᾳ [in one place], which should have been said as ἐν χώρᾳ [in a place]. That ἔvi [in one] is correctly read is shown by a similar passage Suppl. 749 γυνὴ μονωθεῖσ᾽ οὐδέν· οὐκ ἔνεστ᾽ ῎Αρης [a woman left alone is nothing; there is no Ares in her].

cit.quote: χωρεῖ κάτω, σκέλη δὲ κίρκωσον βίᾳ,
Go down, and force his legs into rings.
cit.note: ubi Vulcanus postquam superiores Promethei corporis partes rupi affixit, ad inferiores progredi iubetur, ubi schol. διὰ τοῦ “χωρεῖ κάτω” τὸ μέγεθος ἐνέφηνε τοῦ δεσμευομένου θεοῦby means of “go down” he indicated the size of the bound god .

where Vulcan, after he has fastened the upper parts of Prometheus' body to the rock, is ordered to proceed to the lower parts, where the scholiast says: διὰ τοῦ “χωρεῖ κάτω” [by means of “go down”] he indicated the size of the bound god.

cit.quote: ἐγγὺς γὰρ ἤδη πάνοπλος Ἀργείων στρατός χωρεῖ.
For already the fully armed army of the Argives is coming near.

sense.def: of those departing or going out, I advance

cit.quote: τόπων μετά που χωρεῖτ᾽ ἐκ τῶνδε θοῶς.
Go quickly from these places.
πᾶς ἀνὴρ κώπης ἄναξ ἐς ναῦν ἐχώρει.
Every man, lord of the oar, went to the ship.
ἔξω, κελεύω, τῶνδε δωμάτων τάχος χωρεῖτε.
Go out, I command you, from this house quickly.
χωρεῖτ᾽ ἄνευ βοτῆρος αἰπολούμεναι.
Go, wandering without a shepherd.

sense.def: Futuri forma media, qua sola utuntur Attici,
the middle form of the future, which alone the Attics use

cit.quote: ὃς οὔτι μάργων ἱππικῶν φρυαγμάτων βρόμον φοβηθεὶς ἐκ πυλῶν χωρήσεται.
Who, not fearing the din of raging equine snortings, will go out from the gates.
καὶ νὺξ ἐχώρει.
And night advanced.
χωρίς τε γένους οὐκ ἔστιν ὅτῳ μείζονα μοῖραν νείμαιμ ' ἢ σοί.
And apart from your race, there is no one to whom I would assign a greater portion than to you.
δεκὰς δ᾽ ἦν τῶνδε χωρίς ἔκκριτος.
And a chosen ten were apart from these.
χωρὶς ποδοψήστρων τε καὶ τῶν ποικίλων κληδὼν ἀϋτεῖ.
Apart from the foot-scrapers and the embroidered robes, a voice cries out.
χωρίς μυρηρῶν τευχέων πνέουσ᾽ ἐμοί (οὐράνη).
Breathing apart from the perfumed vessels for me (heaven).
χωρὶς ἡ τιμὴ θεῶν.
The honor of the gods is separate.
εὐφαμεῖτε δὲ, χωρῖται.
Keep holy silence, inhabitants of the land.
ὁδοιπόρων δήλημα χωρίτης δράκων.
A native snake, a destroyer of travelers.
cit.note: Sic χωρίτην ὄφινa native snake dixit Sophocles fr. 219.
Thus Sophocles fr. 219 said χωρίτην ὄφιν [a native snake].

cit.quote: τὸν αὐτὸν χῶρον ἐκλιπὼν ἐμοί.
Leaving the same place for me.
Βρόμιος ἔχει τὸν χώρον.
Bromius holds the place.
ἀηδόνος, ἅτ᾽ ἀπὸ χώρων ποταμῶν τ᾽ ἐργομένα.
Of the nightingale, as if driven from places and rivers.
cit.note: Scriptura incerta. Conieci ἀπὸ χώρων ποθ᾽ ἑῶν εἰργομέναdriven from her own places , Hermannus ἀπὸ χλωρῶν πετάλων ἐγρομέναawakened from green leaves .
The reading is uncertain. I conjectured ἀπὸ χώρων ποθ᾽ ἑῶν εἰργομένα [driven from her own places], Hermann ἀπὸ χλωρῶν πετάλων ἐγρομένα [awakened from green leaves].

cit.quote: Βερέκυντα χῶρον.
The Berecyntian place.
πᾶς χῶρός ἐστι μαλθακός.
Every place is soft.
λευρὸν γὰρ οἶμον αἰθέρος ψαίρει πτεροῖς τετρασκελὴς οἰωνός.
For the four-legged bird grazes the smooth path of the air with its wings.
cit.note: de leni alarum motu. Quod in apographis nonnullis in ψαύειtouches mutatum. Utramque scripturam interpretatur scholiasta recentior.
of the gentle motion of wings. In some copies it has been changed to ψαύει [touches]. The later scholiast interprets both readings.

cit.quote: βάλλει μ᾿ ἐρεμνῇ ψακάδι φοινίας δρόσου.
He strikes me with a dark drop of bloody dew.
ψακὰς δὲ λήγει.
And the drop ceases.
cit.note: Sic Blomfieldus pro ψεκάςdrop . Antiquior forma est ψακάςdrop et ψακάζωI drip , cui librarii saepe ψεκάςdrop et ψεκάζεινto drip substituerunt, de quo dixi in Thes. vol. 8 p. 1828. 1829.

Thus Blomfield for ψεκάς [drop]. The older form is ψακάς [drop] and ψακάζω [I drip], for which scribes often substituted ψεκάς [drop] and ψεκάζειν [to drip], as I have discussed in Thes. vol. 8 p. 1828. 1829.

cit.quote: καὶ δὴ πρόχειρα ψάλια δέρκεσθαι πάρα˙
And indeed the bridles are ready to be seen.
cit.note: de vinculis Prometheo iniiciendis ubi scholiasta ψάλιά ἐστι κυρίως τὰ περιστόμια τῶν ἵππωνψάλια are properly the muzzles of horses . Quocum comparari potest ν. 562 τόνδε χαλινοῖς ἐν πετρίνοισιν χειμαζόμενονv. 562 this one storm-tossed in rocky bridles . In apogr. Guelf. ψέλιαarmlets , quod restitui, quum de armillis dictum esse proxima ostendant verba βαλών νιν ἀμφὶ χερσὶν ἐγκρατεῖ σθένει ῥαιστῆρι θεῖνε, πασσάλευε πρὸς πέτραιςhaving cast them around his arms with mighty strength, strike with the hammer, nail him to the rocks .

of the bonds to be placed on Prometheus, where the scholiast says: ψάλιά ἐστι κυρίως τὰ περιστόμια τῶν ἵππων [ψάλια are properly the muzzles of horses]. With this can be compared v. 562 τόνδε χαλινοῖς ἐν πετρίνοισιν χειμαζόμενον [this one storm-tossed in rocky bridles]. In the Guelferbytanus copy ψέλια [armlets], which I restored, since the following words show that it is said of armlets: βαλών νιν ἀμφὶ χερσὶν ἐγκρατεῖ σθένει ῥαιστῆρι θεῖνε, πασσάλευε πρὸς πέτραις [having cast them around his arms with mighty strength, strike with the hammer, nail him to the rocks].

cit.quote: μέγα τ᾽ ἀφηρέθην ψάλιον κετῶν (sic Franzius pro οἴκων),
and I have been robbed of the great bridle of the sea-monsters (thus Franzius for 'of the houses'),
cit.note: de vinculo domui indito. Per χαλινόνbridle exp. scholiasta.
of a bond placed on a house. The scholiast explains it by χαλινόν [bridle].

cit.quote: καὶ ψάλλ᾽ ἔθειραν καὶ κατοίκτισαι στρατόν.
And pluck your hair and lament for the army.
cit.note: ubi scholiasta, ψάλλε ἀντὶ τοῦ τίλλε · καὶ χοιροψάλας Διόνυσος ὁ τίλλων τὰ μόρια τῶν γυναικῶνψάλλε instead of τίλλε; and χοιροψάλας Dionysus is the one who plucks the private parts of women . Pariter Hesychius et Suidas per τίλλεινto pluck explicant: v. Thes. vol. 8 p. 1835.

where the scholiast says: ψάλλε ἀντὶ τοῦ τίλλε · καὶ χοιροψάλας Διόνυσος ὁ τίλλων τὰ μόρια τῶν γυναικῶν [ψάλλε instead of τίλλε; and χοιροψάλας Dionysus is the one who plucks the private parts of women]. Likewise Hesychius and Suidas explain it by τίλλειν [to pluck]: see Thes. vol. 8 p. 1835.

form.gloss: song or striking of the lyre

sense.def: song or striking of the lyre
sense.note: Schol. Arist. Αν. 218 ψαλμός κυρίως ὁ τῆς κιθάρας ἦχοςAv. 218 ψαλμός is properly the sound of the lyre .
Schol. Arist. Av. 218 ψαλμός κυρίως ὁ τῆς κιθάρας ἦχος [ψαλμός is properly the sound of the lyre].

cit.quote: ψαλμὸς δ᾽ ἀλαλάζει.
And the lyre's strain resounds.

form.gloss: sand, same as ψάμμος. A form, as it seems, peculiar to the Doric dialect: hence in Arist. Lys. 1260 ἦν γὰρ τὤνδρες οὐκ ἐλάσσως τᾶς ψάμ μας [for the men were no fewer than the sand].

sense.def: arena, i.q. ψάμμοςsand . Forma, ut videtur, Doricae dialecti propria: unde apud Arist. Lys. 1260 ἦν γὰρ τὤνδρες οὐκ ἐλάσσως τᾶς ψάμ μαςfor the men were no fewer than the sand .
sand, same as ψάμμος. A form, as it seems, peculiar to the Doric dialect: hence in Arist. Lys. 1260 ἦν γὰρ τὤνδρες οὐκ ἐλάσσως τᾶς ψάμ μας [for the men were no fewer than the sand].

cit.quote: πλανᾷ τε νῆστιν ἀνὰ τὰν παραλίαν ψάμμαν,
and she wanders fasting along the sandy shore,
cit.note: ubi longam in fine versus syllabam brevi praetulit poeta. In M super scriptum ονον , i.e. ψάμμονsand , quod transiit in apographa.
where the poet preferred a long syllable at the end of the verse to a short one. In M is written above ον, i.e. ψάμμον [sand], which passed into the copies.

cit.quote: ψαμμίας ἀκάτα,
sandy shore,
cit.note: scriptura corrupta. ψαμμὶς ἀκτάsandy shore Ahrensius, ψαμμίας ἀκτάςsandy shores Tyrwhittus.
corrupt reading. Ahrens proposes ψαμμὶς ἀκτά [sandy shore], Tyrwhitt ψαμμίας ἀκτάς [sandy shores].

cit.quote: χεροῖν καλλιρόου ἔψαυσα πηγῆς.
with my hands I touched the fair-flowing spring.
εἰ τῆσδε χώρας μήποτε ψαύσει ποδί.
if he ever sets foot on this land.
κλάοις ἂν, εἰ ψαύσειας.
you would weep, if you touched it.

sense.def: Hoc vocabulum variis modis interpretantur grammatici, de quo v. Thes. vol. 8 p. 1848. Per ξηρόν, αὐχμηρόν, ἀσθενὲς, ἐλαφρὸνdry, parched, weak, light explicat Hesychius, quorum postremum ἐλαφρόνlight , leve, aptum est epitheton cineribus urbis incendio vastatae

This word is interpreted in various ways by the grammarians, on which see Thes. vol. 8 p. 1848. Hesychius explains it by ξηρόν [dry], αὐχμηρόν [parched], ἀσθενὲς [weak], ἐλαφρὸν [light], of which the last, ἐλαφρόν [light], is a fitting epithet for the ashes of a city devastated by fire

cit.quote: οἰκτρὸν γὰρ πόλιν ὧδ᾽ ὠγυγίαν Ἀΐδᾳ προϊάψαι, δορὸς ἄγραν, δουλίαν ψαφαρᾷ σποδῷ ὑπ᾽ ἀνδρὸς Ἀχαιοῦ θεόθεν περθομέναν ἀτίμως,
For it is pitiful that the ancient city should be hurled to Hades, a spear's prey, a slave, destroyed dishonorably by an Achaean man, by divine will, into dry ash.
cit.note: ubi scholiasta per ἀσθενεῖ, ἐλαφρᾷweak, light explicuit.
where the scholiast explained it by ἀσθενεῖ [weak], ἐλαφρᾷ [light].

cit.quote: μάντιν οὔτινα ψέγων.
blaming no prophet
σὺ δ᾽ αἰνεῖν εἴτε με ψέγειν θέλεις ὅμοιον.
But you may praise or blame me alike.
δέδοται δ᾽ ῾Αρμονίᾳ μοῖρ᾽ Ἀφροδίτας ψεδυραὶ τρίβοι τ᾽ ἐρώτων.
And to Harmonia is given the portion of Aphrodite, the whispering paths of love.
cit.note: ubi in Μ ψεδυρα/ψεθυραM ψεδυρα/ψεθυρα [whispering] sine accentu. Recte Stanleius ψεδυραίψεδυραί [whispering] , quum μοῖρ᾽ Αφροδίταςμοῖρ᾽ Αφροδίτας [the portion of Aphrodite] epitheto facilius carere possit quam τρίβοι ἐρώτωντρίβοι ἐρώτων [the paths of love] , etsi ψεδυράψεδυρά [whispering] legit scholiasta, ἡ Αρμονία μετέχει τῆς Ἀφροδίτης · ψευδὴς δὲ, ὅτι πολλὰ ψεύδονται οἱ ἐρῶντεςἡ Αρμονία μετέχει τῆς Ἀφροδίτης · ψευδὴς δὲ, ὅτι πολλὰ ψεύδονται οἱ ἐρῶντες [Harmonia partakes of Aphrodite; and she is false because lovers tell many lies] , pariterque apud Hesychium ψέδυραψέδυρα [whispering] (in ψέδυροςψέδυρος [whispering] mutatum ab Musuro): ψίθυροςψίθυρος [whispering] . Superscriptum in Me alludit ad ψίθυραψίθυρα [whispering] , quod verba susurra et maledica significat: v. Thes. vol. 8 p. 1903. Ἀφροδίτην ψίθυρονἈφροδίτην ψίθυρον [whispering Aphrodite] et Ἔρωτα ψίθυρονἜρωτα ψίθυρον [whispering Eros] Athenis cultos memorant grammatici in Thes. indicati ib. p. 1905.

where in M ψεδυρα/ψεθυρα [whispering] without accent. Stanley rightly reads ψεδυραί [whispering], since μοῖρ᾽ Αφροδίτας [the portion of Aphrodite] can more easily do without an epithet than τρίβοι ἐρώτων [the paths of love], although the scholiast reads ψεδυρά [whispering], 'Harmonia partakes of Aphrodite; and she is false because lovers tell many lies,' and similarly in Hesychius ψέδυρα [whispering] (changed to ψέδυρος [whispering] by Musurus): ψίθυρος [whispering]. The superscript in Me alludes to ψίθυρα [whispering], which means whispering and slanderous words: see Thes. vol. 8 p. 1903. Ἀφροδίτην ψίθυρον [whispering Aphrodite] and Ἔρωτα ψίθυρον [whispering Eros] were worshipped at Athens, as the grammarians cited in Thes. record, ibid. p. 1905.

sense.def: balbus, balbutiens. Improprie ψελλόνψελλόν [stammering] dicitur id quod non intelligimus, non magis sc. quam balbutientis verba, ut explicat Stephanus in Thes. vol. 8 p. 1856.
stammering, lisping. Improperly ψελλόν [stammering] is said of what we do not understand, no more, that is, than the words of a stammerer, as Stephanus explains in Thes. vol. 8 p. 1856.

cit.quote: τῶν δ᾽ εἴ τί σοι ψελλόν τε καὶ δυσεύρετον, ἐπανδίπλαζε καὶ σαφῶς ἐκμάνθανε,
And if any of these things is stammering and hard to find, repeat it and learn it clearly.
cit.note: Sic ubi per ἄσημον, ἄναρθρονἄσημον, ἄναρθρον [unclear, inarticulate] explicat scholiasta et annotavit Antiatticista in Bekk. Anecd. p. 116, 18 ψελλός: Αἰσχύλος Προμηθεῖ. τέθεικε δὲ τὴν λέξιν ἐπὶ τοῦ μὴ σαφῶς εἰρημένουψελλός [stammering]: Aeschylus in Prometheus. He has used the word of what is not clearly spoken. .

Thus where the scholiast explains it by ἄσημον, ἄναρθρον [unclear, inarticulate], and the Antiatticist noted in Bekker's Anecdota p. 116, 18: ψελλός [stammering]: Aeschylus in Prometheus. He has used the word of what is not clearly spoken.

cit.quote: ψευδηγορεῖν γὰρ οὐκ ἐπίσταται στόμα τὸ Δίον.
For the mouth of Zeus does not know how to speak falsely.
μηδέ μ᾽ οἰκτίσας Σύνθαλπε μύθοις ψευδέσιν.
Do not pity me and warm me with false words.
cit.note: De rebus ementitis vel quocunque consilio fictis.
Of things invented falsely or fabricated for any purpose.

cit.quote: οὐκ ἔσθ᾽ ὅπως λέξαιμι τὰ ψευδή καλά.
There is no way I could call false things noble.
οὐ ψευδή λέγω.
I do not speak falsehoods.
ψευδῶν δὲ καιρὸν ἔσθ᾽ ὅπου τιμᾷ θεός.
There is a time when god honors falsehood.
καὶ ψευδόδειπνα πολλὰ μαργώσης γνάθου έρρυσίαζον στόματος ἐν πρώτη χαρᾷ.
And many false feasts of the raging jaw they snatched from the mouth in first joy.
ἢ ψευδόμαντίς εἰμι θυροκόπος φλέδων;
Am I a false prophet, a door-knocking babbler?
ὡς ἄρ᾽ ἔψευσας φρενών Πέρσας.
How you deceived the Persians in your mind.
ξυναινέσασα Λοξίαν ἐψευσάμην.
Consenting, I deceived Loxias.
μάντις ὢν δ᾽ οὐ ψεύσομαι.
Being a prophet, I will not lie.
πολλὰ δ᾽, οἴομαι, ψευσθεῖσα παιδὸς σπαργάνων φαιδρύντρια.
And many, I think, were deceived, the woman who cleansed the swaddling clothes of the child.
ἥξεις δ᾽ ὑβριστὴν ποταμὸν οὐ ψευδώνυμον.
You will come to a violent river, not falsely named.
ἢ δῆτ᾽ ἂν εἴη πανδίκως ψευδώνυμος Δίκη.
Or indeed Justice would be justly called falsely named.
ψευδωνύμως σε δαίμονες Προμηθέα καλοῦσιν.
The gods call you Prometheus under a false name.
πυρωθὲν ἐξ Ἰλίου φίλοισι πέμπει βραχύ ψήγμα δυσδάκρυτον.
Burned from Ilium, he sends to his friends a small, tearful scraping.
cit.note: De cinere.
Of ash.

cit.quote: ψηφίζομαί τι δρᾶν.
I vote to do something.
δήμου δέδοκται παντελή ψηφίσματα.
The people have decreed full decrees.

form.gloss: pebble used in counting; vote; to count

cit.quote: τί τοὺς ἀναλωθέντας ἐν ψήφῳ λέγειν χρή;
Why must one speak of those who were killed in the vote?
cit.note: i.e. enumerare.
i.e. to count

cit.quote: ψῆφος κατ᾿ αὐτῶν ὀλεθρία βουλεύσεται.
A destructive vote will be decided against them.
εἰς αἱματηρὸν τεύχος οὐ διχορρόπως ψήφους ἔθεντο.
They cast their votes into the bloody urn without dissent.
ἀλλ᾽ εἴ σε μάρψει ψῆφος ἀλλ᾽ ἐρεῖς τάχα.
But if the vote seizes you, you will soon speak.
οἵ τ᾽ ἐφήμενοι ψήφῳ διαιρεῖν τοῦδε πράγματος πέρι.
And those who are appointed to decide by vote about this matter.
ἤδη κελεύω τούσδ᾽ ἀπὸ γνώμης φέρειν ψῆφον δικαίαν.
Now I bid these men to cast a just vote according to their judgment.
ἐν δὲ καρδίᾳ ψῆφον φέροντες ὅρκον αἰδεῖσθε.
And in your hearts, as you cast your vote, respect your oath.
ὀρθοῦσθαι δὲ χρὴ καὶ ψῆφον αἴρειν.
And you must stand up and raise your vote.
ψήφον δ᾽ Ορέστη τήνδ᾽ ἐγὼ προσθήσομαι.
And I will cast this vote for Orestes.
πεμπάζετ᾽ ὀρθῶς ἐκβολὰς ψήφων.
Count the cast votes correctly.
βαλοῦσά τ᾽ οἶκον ψῆφος ὤρθωσεν μία.
And a single vote, cast, set the house upright.
οὔτιν᾿ ἐφ᾽ αἵματι δημηλασίαν ψήφῳ πόλεως γνωσθεῖσαι.
No banishment for bloodshed was decided by the city's vote.
ψῆφον δ᾽ εὔφρον᾽ ἔθεντο.
And they cast a kindly vote.
οὐδὲ μετ᾿ ἀρσένων ψήφον ἔθεντο.
Nor did they cast a vote with the men.
ἐπεὶ τελεία ψῆφος Ἀργείων.
Since the vote of the Argives is complete.
τοιάδε δημόπρακτος ἐκ πόλεως μία ψῆφος κέκρανται.
Such a public vote from the city has been decided.
ὧνπερ ἥδε κραίνεται ψῆφος.
Of which this vote is being decided.
περὶ δὲ τοῦ ψιλῆτος παρ᾿ Αἰσχύλῳ (fr. 344) καὶ τοῦ “Κουρῆτές τ᾽ ἐμάχοντο” καὶ τοῦ κριτής ἐν τοῖς περὶ ὀνομάτων ἀποδώσομεν.

But concerning the word ψιλής [light-armed soldier] in Aeschylus (fr. 344) and the phrase “Κουρῆτές τ᾽ ἐμάχοντο” [and the Curetes fought] and the word κριτής [judge], we will give an account in the work on nouns.
cit.note: Est notatio Herodiani excerpta ab Choerobosco in Theodos. p. 55, 4 et Eustathio p. 515, 11.
This is the explanation of Herodian, excerpted by Choeroboscus in Theodos. p. 55, 4 and Eustathius p. 515, 11.

cit.quote: τὸν ἀνθρώπειον αἰδεσθεὶς ψόγον.
Respecting human blame.
ἔπειτα τόνδ᾽ ἀμυναθοῦ ψόγον.
Then ward off this blame.
πᾶς τις ἐπειπεῖν ψόγον ἀλλοθρόοις εὔτυκος.
Everyone is ready to utter blame against those of other tongues.

Ψό: ἐπὶ τοῦ σαπροῦ καὶ μὴ συναρέσκοντος: ἔστι δὲ ἀποκομματικοῦ λεξειδίου (ἀπόκομμα Αττικοῦ λεξειδίου Bernhardyus, ἀποκομματικὸν λεξείδιον Dobraeus) · ψόθον γὰρ καλοῦσιν. Ἀριστοφάνης (fr. 706) “πλέω γράσου καὶ ψοθοίου καὶ ῥύπου γε καὶ ψόθου.”

Ψό [the syllable 'pso']: used of what is rotten and not pleasing; it is a clipped expression (Bernhardy: a clipping of an Attic expression; Dobraeus: a clipped expression). For they call it ψόθον [filth]. Aristophanes (fr. 706): “πλέω γράσου καὶ ψοθοίου καὶ ῥύπου γε καὶ ψόθου” [full of stench and filth and dirt and filth].
cit.note: Ἀἰσχύλος ΘεωροῖςAeschylus in The Theori (fr. 76) "Lege πλέω γράσου τε καὶ ψόθου · οἷον, καὶ ῥύπου. Αἰσχύλος Θεωροῖςfull of stench and filth; that is, also of dirt. Aeschylus in The Theori . et intellige quasi statim post ψόthe syllable 'pso' sequeretur ΑἰσχύλοςAeschylus .” DOBRAEUS in indice p. 735. Theognostus in Crameri Anecd. Oxon. vol. 2 p. 53, 28. ubi de nominibus in otos agit, ῾ψοθοιὸς ὁ ἀκάθαρτος.᾿psothoios, the unclean one

Aeschylus in The Theori (fr. 76): "Read πλέω γράσου τε καὶ ψόθου · οἷον, καὶ ῥύπου [full of stench and filth; that is, also of dirt]. Aeschylus in The Theori. And understand as if immediately after ψό [the syllable 'pso'] came Αἰσχύλος [Aeschylus]." DOBRAEUS in the index p. 735. Theognostus in Cramer's Anecd. Oxon. vol. 2 p. 53, 28, where he deals with nouns in -otos, says: ψοθοιὸς ὁ ἀκάθαρτος [psothoios, the unclean one].

sense.note: Per καπνός, φλόξ, αἰθάλη, ἀσβόληsmoke, flame, soot, soot exp. Hesychius.
Hesychius explains it by καπνός [smoke], φλόξ [flame], αἰθάλη [soot], ἀσβόλη [soot].

cit.quote: κάρφει παλαιῷ κἀπιβωμίῳ ψόλῳ.
With old twig and altar soot.
εἴ τι θεῖόν ἐστι μὴ ψύθος.
If there is anything divine and not a lie.
εὔχομαι δ᾽ ἐξ ἐμᾶς ἐλπίδος ψύθη (sic H. Stephanus pro ψύδη) πεσεῖν ἐς τὸ μὴ τελεσφόρον.
And I pray that from my hope the lie (thus H. Stephanus for ψύδη) may fall to no fulfillment.
καὶ τάδ᾽ οὐκ ἐρεῖς ψύθη.
And you will not say these things are lies.
Νίκανδρος ὁ Θυατειρηνός καλεῖσθαί φησι ψυκτήρας καὶ τοὺς ἀλσώδεις καὶ συσκίους τόπους τοὺς τοῖς θεοῖς ἀνειμένους, ἐν οἷς ἔστιν ἀναψύξαι.
Nicander of Thyateira says that ψυκτήρες [cooling places] are also called the grove-like and shady places dedicated to the gods, in which one can cool off.
cit.note: Ἀἰσχύλος ΝεανίσκοιςAeschylus in The Youths (fr. 145) σαύρας (αὔραςlizards (breezes Valcken.) ὑποσκίοισιν ἐν ψυκτηρίοιςin shady cooling places .
Aeschylus in The Youths (fr. 145): σαύρας (αὔρας Valcken.) ὑποσκίοισιν ἐν ψυκτηρίοις [lizards (breezes Valcken.) in shady cooling places].

cit.quote: ψυχαγωγοῖς ὀρθιάζοντες γόοις.
raising shrill laments with soul-conjuring wails.

sense.def: Phrynichus Bekkeri p. 73, 10. Ψυχαγωγός: οἱ ἀρχαῖοι τοὺς τὰς ψυχὰς τῶν τεθνηκότων γοητείαις τισὶν ἄγοντας (ἀνάγοντας Νauckius). τῆς αὐτῆς ἐννοίας καὶ τοῦ Αἰσχύλου τὸ δρᾶμαΨυχαγωγός [conjurer of souls]: the ancients called those who lead the souls of the dead by certain enchantments (or bring up, Nauck). Of the same meaning is also the play of Aeschylus (fr. 269-275).

Phrynichus in Bekker p. 73, 10. Ψυχαγωγός [conjurer of souls]: the ancients called those who lead (or bring up, Nauck) the souls of the dead by certain enchantments. Of the same meaning is also the play of Aeschylus (fr. 269-275).

cit.quote: οὔποτ᾽ ηὔχουν ὧδε δυσθέατα καὶ δύσοιστα πήματα ἐμὰν ψήξειν ψυχάν.
Never did I think that such hard-to-see and hard-to-bear sufferings would rub my soul.
cit.note: λύματα, δείματ᾽ ἐμὰν ἀμφάκει κέντρῳdefilements, fears, it pierces my soul with its goad ubi Meinekius ψήχεινto rub correxit, quod ψήξεινto rub (future) potius scribendum erat. ψήχωI rub autem significat rado, frico.

λύματα, δείματ᾽ ἐμὰν ἀμφάκει κέντρῳ [defilements, fears, it pierces my soul with its goad], where Meineke corrected to ψήχειν [to rub], which should rather be written ψήξειν [to rub (future)]. ψήχω [I rub] means I scrape, I rub.

cit.quote: τοιγὰρ θέλουσ᾽ ἄκοντι κοινώνει κακῶν, ψυχή.
Therefore, willing, she shares in evils with an unwilling partner, my soul.
δεινοὶ δὲ μάχην ψυχῆς εὐτλήμονι δόξῃ.
Terrible are they in battle, with steadfast resolve of soul.
ψυχήν τ᾽ ἄριστοι κεὐγένειαν ἐκπρεπεῖς.
And they are best in soul and conspicuous in noble birth.
ψυχὴν διδόντες ἡδονῆ (sic Pauwius pro ψυχῇ ἡδονήν) καθ᾿ ἡμέραν.
giving up their lives to pleasure (thus Pauw for ψυχῇ ἡδονήν [soul to pleasure]) day by day.
τί δὴ τὸν ἄνδρα τόνδ᾽ ἀπὸ ψυχῆς κακῆς οὐκ αὐτὸς ἠνάριζες;
Why did you not yourself slay this man, from your cowardly soul?
φίλον δ᾽ Ορέστην, τῆς ἐμῆς ψυχῆς τριβήν.
And dear Orestes, the delight of my life.
ἢ σὺ τόδ᾽ ἔρξαι τλήσει, κτείνασ᾽ ἄνδρα τὸν αὐτῆς ἀποκωκῦσαι ψυχήν;
Or will you dare to do this, after killing her husband, to bewail her own life?
πέμψατ᾽ ἔνερθεν ψυχὴν ἐς φῶς.
Send up from below the soul to the light.
ψυχῆς κόμιστρα τῆσδε μηχανωμένη.
devising a ransom for this life.
τὰς πάνυ πολλὰς ψυχὰς ὀλέσαο᾽ ὑπὸ Τροίᾳ.
having destroyed very many lives under Troy.
πολλῶν ἀνδρῶν ψυχὰς Δαναῶν ὀλέσασα.
having destroyed the lives of many Danaan men.
ὡς ἔλεξα τῆς ἐμῆς περὶ ψυχῆς.
as I said, about my own life.
ὅταν δὲ τεύχη Ζεὺς ἀπ᾿ ὄμφακος πικρᾶς οἶνον, τότ᾽ ἤδη ψύχος ἐν δόμοις πέλει.
But when Zeus makes wine from the bitter unripe grape, then at once there is cold in the house.
cit.note: Improprie.
Improperly.

sense.def: was the title of a tragedy of Aeschylus (fr. 276-279).

cit.quote: οὔποτ᾽ ηὔχουν — ὧδε δυσθέατα καὶ δύσοιστα πήματα, λύματα, δείματ᾽ ἐμὰν ἀμφάκει κέντρῳ ψύχειν ψυχάν.
Never did I think — such hard-to-see and hard-to-bear sufferings, defilements, fears, it pierces my soul with its goad, to chill my soul.
cit.note: ubi Meinekius ψήχεινto rub correxit, quod ψήξεινto rub (future) potius scribendum erat. ψήχωI rub autem significat rado, frico.
where Meineke corrected to ψήχειν [to rub], which should rather be written ψήξειν [to rub (future)]. ψήχω [I rub] means I scrape, I rub.

entry.note: Vocativum articuli ὁthe (masculine nominative singular article) esse multorum grammaticorum opinio fuit, memorata ab Apollonio de synt. p. 29, 25. 51, 28. 53, 21. 54, 27. Ipse eam improbat p. 69, 26, quia etiam ὦ οὗτοςO you there! dicatur, cui pronomini non praeponatur articulus. Improbavit etiam Herodianus, ex quo Arcadius p. 100, 17 τὸ ὦ ψιλοῦται · οὐ γὰρ ἄρθρον, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπίρρημα κλητικόνThe word ὦ [O] is written with a smooth breathing; for it is not the article, but a vocative adverb. . Copiosius illos refutant schol. Dionysii Thr. in Bekk. Anecd. p. 903 et Helladius apud Photium Bibl. p. 530, 14-31 recte ὦO appellantes ἐπίρρημα κλητικόνvocative adverb . Alteram opinionem sequitur Hesychius, ὦ, ἄρθρον κλητικῆς πτώσεως, οἷον ὦ ἄνθρωπεὦ [O], article of the vocative case, as in ὦ ἄνθρωπε [O man] . Coniungitur autem plerumque cum vocativo, saepe tamen etiam cum nominativo nominum, adiectivorum, participiorum, et ita quidem ut vel exclamamantis sit vel alloquentis, locis tamen non paucis ita comparatis ut nihil intersit utrum ὦO exclamantis, nulla habita personae ratione, aut certam quandam personam vel praesentem vel absentem alloquentis esse putetur.

That the vocative is the article ὁ was the opinion of many grammarians, recorded by Apollonius in On Syntax p. 29, 25; 51, 28; 53, 21; 54, 27. He himself rejects it at p. 69, 26, because even ὦ οὗτος [O you there] is said, to which pronoun the article is not prefixed. Herodian also rejected it, from whom Arcadius p. 100, 17: τὸ ὦ ψιλοῦται · οὐ γὰρ ἄρθρον, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπίρρημα κλητικόν [the word ὦ has a smooth breathing; for it is not an article, but a vocative adverb]. Those grammarians are refuted at greater length by the scholia on Dionysius Thrax in Bekker's Anecdota p. 903 and by Helladius in Photius' Bibliotheca p. 530, 14-31, rightly calling ὦ a vocative adverb. Hesychius follows the other opinion: ὦ, ἄρθρον κλητικῆς πτώσεως, οἷον ὦ ἄνθρωπε [O, article of the vocative case, as in O man]. It is generally joined with the vocative, but often also with the nominative of nouns, adjectives, participles, and in such a way that it is either of one exclaiming or of one addressing, yet in not a few places the situation is such that it makes no difference whether ὦ is thought to be of one exclaiming, with no regard to a person, or of one addressing a certain person, whether present or absent.

entry.note: Vocativi sine w positi in exclamandi vel alloquendi formulis etsi apud poetas scenicos exempla multo sunt pauciora quam additi w, non raro tamen vocativus etiam sine w ponitur, ut exempla docent sub vocabulis singulis allata: v. ἄναξ, γυνή, δεσπότης, θυγάτηρ, μήτηρι ξένος, παῖς, πατήρ, τέκνονlord, woman, master, daughter, mother, stranger, child, father, child . Haec autem ceterorumque poetarum scenicorum exempla qui inspicere volet, facile animadvertet in plerisque w propter solam metri necessitatem esse omissum, praesertim in sedibus paribus senariorum. Non improbabile tamen est poetas interdum alias praeter metrum ὦO vel addendi vel omittendi rationes habuisse, de quo dixi in Lexico Sophocleo p. 525 allato Euripidis ex Andromeda exemplo ὦ θεοὶ, τίν᾽ ἐς γῆν βαρβάρων ἀφίγμεθαO gods, to what land of barbarians have we come? ; ubi bene sensit Euripides ὦ θεοίO gods cum synizesi pronuntiandum in initio orationis aptius et ponderosius esse quam levem iambum θεοίgods sine ὦO .

Vocatives placed without ὦ in exclamatory or address formulas, although among the scenic poets examples are much fewer than those with added ὦ, yet not rarely the vocative is placed even without ὦ, as the examples cited under the individual words show: see ἄναξ, γυνή, δεσπότης, θυγάτηρ, μήτηρ, ξένος, παῖς, πατήρ, τέκνον. But whoever wishes to inspect these examples and those of the other scenic poets will easily notice that in most cases ὦ has been omitted solely on account of metrical necessity, especially in the even positions of senarii. Yet it is not improbable that the poets sometimes had other reasons besides meter for adding or omitting ὦ, about which I have spoken in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 525, citing the example from Euripides' Andromeda ὦ θεοὶ, τίν᾽ ἐς γῆν βαρβάρων ἀφίγμεθα; [O gods, to what land of barbarians have we come?] where Euripides well perceived that ὦ θεοί [O gods], to be pronounced with synizesis at the beginning of the speech, is more fitting and weightier than the light iambus θεοί [gods] without ὦ.

Ab w perispomeno oxytonum w distinguunt grammatici in Thes. indicati vol. 8 p. 1981, velut Etym. M. p. 79, 13 τὸ ὦ ἡνίκα θαυμαστικὸν λαμβάνεται, ὀξύνεται καὶ χωρεῖ εἰς ἐπιρρηματικὴν σύνταξιν, οἷον ὦ Ἡράκλειςτὸ ὦ [the word O] when it is taken as expressing wonder is accented acute and goes into adverbial construction, as ὦ Ἡράκλεις [O Heracles] . Etym. Gud. p. 576, 40 ὦ κλητικὸν ἐπίρρημα, ὤ ὀξυνόμενον σχετλιαστικὸν, ὦ τοῦ ἰδίου, ὦ ἐγώὦ [O] vocative adverb, ὤ [O] accented acute expressing indignation, as ὦ τοῦ ἰδίου [O the wretch], ὦ ἐγώ [O me] . Explicatius Thomas M. p. 930 (408 Ritschl.) τὸ ὦ μετὰ τῆς κλητικῆς οὐδέποτε ὀξύνεται, εἰ καὶ ἔκπληξιν ὁ λόγος ἔχει καὶ θαῦμα, οἷον ὦ Ἡράκλεις, ὦ θαῦμα θαυμάτων · οὐ γὰρ τὸ ὦ ἐν τούτοις ἐμφαίνει τὴν ἔκπληξιν καὶ τὸ θαῦμα, ἀλλὰ μετὰ τῶν κλητικῶν, ὅτε δὲ ἐπάγεται γενική, ἐξ ἀνάγκης ὀξύνεται · τότε γὰρ πάντως ἢ σχετλιαστικόν ἐστιν, οἷον ὦ τῆς ἐμῆς ἀθλιότητος, ἢ θαυμαστικόν, οἷον ὦ τοῦ ξένου μετάλλου. διὸ καὶ τὴν γενικὴν ἔχει ἐπαγομένην λαμβανομένου ἔξωθεν τοῦ ἕνεκαThe word ὦ [O] with the vocative is never accented on the ultima, even if the speech contains astonishment and wonder, e.g. ὦ Ἡράκλεις [O Heracles], ὦ θαῦμα θαυμάτων [O wonder of wonders]; for the ὦ [O] in these does not indicate the astonishment and wonder, but together with the vocatives; but when a genitive is added, it is necessarily accented on the ultima; for then it is always either exclamatory, e.g. ὦ τῆς ἐμῆς ἀθλιότητος [O my wretchedness], or expressing wonder, e.g. ὦ τοῦ ξένου μετάλλου [O the stranger's mine]. Therefore it also has the genitive added, with ἕνεκα [for the sake of] understood from outside. . Oxytonum w passim servatum est in libris: de quo dixi in Lexico Sophocleo p. 525.

The grammarians cited in the Thesaurus vol. 8 p. 1981 distinguish the oxytone ὤ [O] from the perispomenon ὦ [O], as Etym. M. p. 79, 13: "τὸ ὦ [the word O] when it is taken as expressing wonder is accented acute and goes into adverbial construction, as ὦ Ἡράκλεις [O Heracles]." Etym. Gud. p. 576, 40: "ὦ [O] vocative adverb, ὤ [O] accented acute expressing indignation, as ὦ τοῦ ἰδίου [O the wretch], ὦ ἐγώ [O me]." More explicitly Thomas M. p. 930 (408 Ritschl.): "τὸ ὦ [the word O] with the vocative is never accented acute, even if the speech has astonishment and wonder, as ὦ Ἡράκλεις [O Heracles], ὦ θαῦμα θαυμάτων [O wonder of wonders]; for the ὦ [O] in these does not indicate the astonishment and wonder, but with the vocatives, when a genitive is added, it is necessarily accented acute; for then it is either expressing indignation, as ὦ τῆς ἐμῆς ἀθλιότητος [O my wretchedness], or expressing wonder, as ὦ τοῦ ξένου μετάλλου [O the stranger's metal]. Therefore it has the genitive added, with ἕνεκα [for the sake of] understood from outside." The oxytone ὤ [O] is preserved here and there in the manuscripts: about which I have spoken in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 525.

cit.quote: ἰοὺ ἰοὺ, ὦ ὦ κακά,

ΟΙ. δύσμορος. ΧΟ. ὠώCHORUS: Alas, alas! OEDIPUS: Ill-fated! CHORUS: Alas! , ubi in codice est ἰὼ ὣ ὣ ὥAlas! O! O! O! .

It is doubled, but in the copies (for in M this part of the play is lost) as perispomenon, which according to the analogy of other interjections I wrote as one word ὠὠ [O O], as I restored to Sophocles OC. 224: ΧΟ. ὠὼ ὠώ [O O]. ΟΙ. δύσμορος [ill-fated]. ΧΟ. ὠώ [O], where in the codex is ἰὼ ὣ ὣ ὥ [io o o o].

I restored it tripled where in M is ὦ ὦ δάων [O O of torches]: with which can be compared the four-syllable oοοώ [O O O O], which I restored to Sophocles OC. 219 for ὣ ὣ ἰού [O O io], as required by the meter of the antistrophic verse (221).

φιλεῖ ὠδῖνα τίκτειν νὺξ κυβερνήτη σοφῷ.
